content: Genesis “Believe me, it is no idle curiosity. I have a motive of which, be sure, she would have approved. I have them all here. I took them before we knew that all was yours, so that no strange hand might touch them—no strange eye look through words into her soul. I shall keep them, if I may; even you may not see them yet, but I shall keep them safe. No word shall be lost; and in the good time I shall give them to you. It is a hard thing I ask, but you will do it, will you not, for Lucy’s sake?” [154]. Bram Stoker’s Notes for “Dracula” transcribes and annotates a sheaf of hand- and typewritten notes that, after long decades of passing from hand to hand, found a home in the collections of Philadelphia’s Rosenbach Museum and Library. In part 1, “Handwritten Notes on the Plot,” a single-page doc- ument, labeled Rosenbach #38c, records the following: The dinner party at the Mad doctor’s Thirteen—each has a number Each asked to tell something strange—order of numbers makes the story complete—at the end the Count comes in— The divisional surgeon being sick the doctor is asked to see man in cofﬁn restores him to life [22]. Footnote 50 asserts that what is to be heard in this outline is an echo of the “celebrated literary gathering at the Villa Diodati,” apparently predicated on ﬁguring Dr. Polidori as “the mad doctor” and Percy Shelley as “the man in the cofﬁn.” Eschewing Polidori’s contemporaneous journal, the authors elab- orate their thought by quoting the 1818 “preface” to Frankenstein—a dubious account written by Percy posing as Mary—which describes the stormy 16 17

June 1816 Cologny soirée that led to Mary’s celebrated novel, Polidori’s Ernestus Brechtold and The Vampyre, Byron’s Fragment and, ultimately, Manfred. Rosen- bach #38’s Note 52, claims that Dracula’s “early drafts include a parody of the Last Supper, with the Count fulﬁlling the role of the anti–Christ.” The editors further remark that “Bram Stoker’s Original Foundation Notes & Dates for His ‘Dracula’ list many of his research documents but, surprisingly, they do not mention any of his literary inspirations” (309). Stoker spent nearly a decade on his version of the Vampire Tale. The Notes likely reﬂect but a small portion of his research, their preservation seem- ing largely due to sheer good fortune. But they, and the editors’ comment on literary inspiration, raise the interesting question of whether anyone would recognize a reference to Stoker’s literary guiding lights should they come upon them. Could Stoker’s inﬂuences go undetected even where he largely points them out because—like the golden treasure of Transylvania—they stem from sources secreted in unfamiliar terrain? The Vampire Tale in all its concatenated manifestations springs from a vine-like structure—with grasping tendrils and racing underground roots— whose ostentatiously colored fruits break through the sheltering soil to appear and reappear here and there, less a mottled whole than a multiplicity of coher- ent fragments. Like Russian dolls, each further iteration contains and subsumes all earlier instantiations. The problem for researchers stems from what Miller and Eighteen-Bisang term “the myth of Dracula” (291), something regularly posited by writers ranging from Maud Ellman (viii) to William Patrick Day (143–49) to James B. Twitchell (124). It would be more reasonable to assume, based on all evidence, that Stoker inherited ancient myths reworked to accom- modate modernity to an unchanging subject—the mysteries of life that embrace those of death—and was led by them. Building upon foundations laid long ago, and working within the Vampire Tale ethos, Stoker furthered ancient myth and belief, forging a robust syncretic amalgam of startling depth and relevance. In many respects Stoker’s notes are but what they seem. Stoker,—trying to keep track of focused research on narrow detail necessary to lend his nar- ration verisimilitude, and to keep up with the undoubtedly shifting calendrical plotting that furnishes his project its hinge,—felt no need to record the grand lines and themes that motivated him, nor to list those that preceded and inﬂuenced him; these he knew intimately. Still, between the lines, the notes— Rosenbach #38c in particular—reveal more than has so far been discerned. Much of what forms the body of Dracula, a novel frankly purporting to be a cento, are earlier vampire texts recycled, both in the surface incidents of plot and the rigidity of a skeletal structure in whose marrow is implanted the Vampire Tale’s Logos. It is this Logos that has gone unseen even when laid 18 The Theology of Dracula

bare. As Heraclitus observes: “Although this account holds forever men fail to comprehend it, both before they hear it and when they ﬁrst hear. Even though all happenings are in accordance with this account, people behave like the unlearned when they experience works and words” (Fr. 1). The way forward is lengthy, but it is very possible to elucidate a literary reference being made in the excerpt from Rosenbach #38c which will help illuminate the sacred nature of Dracula and its meaning. It requires sifting through three generations of the Vampire Tale, particularly as it developed in France. Con- sidering that the ritual-encoding initiatic plots to most of these now ancient works are obscure, interpretative summaries of the principal markers are needed. Plot summary, held in contempt by literary critics, constitutes, for the analyst, the descriptive act, a primordial, critical and interpretative step upon which meanings depend. By the end of the next chapter, after a forced march through these forgotten ﬁrst drafts of Stoker’s magnum opus, the sense of Rosenbach #38c should be clearer and certain literary inﬂuences revealed. The Corinthian Bride The unlikely region of Lac Léman, near Geneva, is the birthplace of the prose vampire, and Germaine de Staël’s French-language recounting of the conceit of Goethe’s 1797 “Die Braut von Korinth” was instrumental to its establishment. Her account converts the récit of Goethe’s ballad, itself an embellishment of “Philinnion’s story” in Phlegon of Tralles’ Book of Wonders, into prose. Goethe’s reworking of the classical-era supernatural tale, blazing the path for the Vampire Tale to come, superposes a theological gloss that pits Christian against pagan, as Staël’s French résumé makes clear. Betrothed as children by their fathers, two young people matured as in their hearts grew a love which, sewn in the knowledge that they were promised one to the other, possessed them though they had never met. Over this period of maturation, the Gospel of Christ was carried to Corinth and the bride’s family converted to the new religion, while the young man’s Athenian family remained faithful to the ancient gods. Stricken by a serious illness, the mother of the bride prayed to Jesus to spare her life, pledging her eldest daughter to a religious life in exchange for her recovery. When her prayers were answered, it was determined that a younger sister would replace her elder in fulﬁlling the marriage contract, the elder being given instead to Jesus. Late one evening, the groom, now a ﬁne young man, arrives in Corinth unannounced to claim his bride. Welcomed by the mother, he is placed in the best room of the house. Servants appear with wine and food with which he can refresh himself and he is provided a bed on which to retire. He has Genesis 19

just settled in when a veiled maiden clad in white, a black and gold ribbon banding her forehead, enters. Seemingly taken aback by the stranger, she begins to withdraw as if in perplexed embarrassment. The young man, dis- covering she is his promised one, begs her to stay and share with him the gifts of Ceres and Bacchus, honoring the gods by indulging in their pleasures. She replies that she no longer belongs to joy, that the only gods left to the house were an invisible being in the heavens and a dying god on the cross; no longer were bulls or lambs offered in sacriﬁce but in their stead her own youth and humanity. She warns the young man off, but he persists in his courtship. The midnight hour arrives to comfort and set her at ease; she avidly drinks the bloodred wine—similar, says Staël, to that The Odyssey’s shades take to retrace their memories—but she obstinately refuses to partake of a crumb of bread. She gives a gold chain to her would-be husband, asking for a lock of his hair. The exchange made, the young man, enchanted by the beauteous maiden, takes her in his arms, but feels neither the beating of her heart nor the warmth of her limbs. It doesn’t matter, he exclaims, I’ll know how to revive you with the heat of my love even when it is the tomb itself that sends you to me. So begins, enthuses Staël, the most extraordinary scene delirium or imagination could devise, blending love and fright, a redoubtable union of death and life. The sound of their lovemaking breaks the night’s solemn silence. The mother, thinking a brash, lusting slave has penetrated the stranger’s room, enters, ready to give vent to her just wrath; but the maiden rises off the couch and swells like a shadow till she reaches the ceiling’s vault, and reproaches her mother for having caused her death by making her take the veil. She asks: Why do you trouble me on this wedding night? Isn’t it enough that in my youth you had me covered in a shroud and carried to the tomb? A wretched curse has forced me from my cold dwelling place; the chants of your priests have not relieved my heart; the salt and the water have not appeased my youth: Ah! Earth herself cannot cool love. This young man was promised me when Venus’s serene temple was still not overthrown. My mother, should you fail to keep your word in order to honour your mad vows? No god received your oath when you refused the marriage of your daughter. And you, handsome youth, can no longer live; you will linger within this place where you have taken my chain and I a lock of your hair: Tomorrow your hair will whiten and you will only ﬁnd your youth in the Empire of Shades. Listen at least, my mother, to the last prayer I would make to you. Order a pyre lit; open the narrow shroud that encloses me; send us lovers to rest through the ﬂames; and when the sparks ﬂare and ashes are aglow, we will hurry off together to join our ancient gods. The bride, revenant and devotee of the ancient gods, is a romanticized version of the Assyrian vampire and Levantine ghoul: a female daemon emer- gent from remotely ancient traditions. Ceres and Bacchus, Roman gods of 20 The Theology of Dracula

bread and wine, authentically Demeter and Dionysus, are central to Goethe’s composition. On one hand, these are gods of pleasure, terrestrial life, and sexual reproduction; on the other, chthonic masters of death and resurrection. They rule and are ruled by cyclic forces of dark and light. The only gods left to the house of Corinth, in contrast, are depicted as effete and ineffective: an invisible being in the heavens, and a dying god on a cross. In the new dying god that has displaced Dionysus, the mystery of resur- rection mingles bread with wine as ﬂesh and blood, combining the masculine and feminine, but it is the ancient gods that triumph in returning the bride to earth. For the bride, Jesus is a god of renunciation, far paler and less potent than orgiastic Dionysus. The bride accepts the bloodred wine but rejects the ﬂesh that the gift of Ceres represents. Her rejection of Demeter’s bread reﬂects her own bitter anger with her Christian mother. She resides buried in the sheltering earth so nearby the Bay of Eleusis, insensitive to the salted waters of its nourishing sacred spring. In the salt and water, the Christian rites of Extreme Unction are confounded with the initiative, purifying rites of the Eleusinian Mysteries, just as matrimony and holy orders are conﬂated through the symbol of the veil, and the rites of marriage and of the dead are entwined in the bride’s black and gold headband. The forehead wreathed with black and gold ﬁgures the maiden as bride, corpse, Hekate: Persephone. Staël’s French-language recounting of Goethe’s ballad’s récit was trans- lated into English in 1813, six years prior to the translation of Goethe’s poem into English. The French-English give-and-take establishes a cross-Channel intellectual commerce critical to the Vampire Tale’s development. Staël’s is but the ﬁrst of many French-to-English exchanges concerning the sacred wed- ding of the living and the dead. Byron and Polidori Across the lake from Staël’s Chateau de Coppet, in spring 1816, Lord Byron began a “ghost-tale” in which he invested but a single evening. He later had his story fragment published to distance himself from The Vampyre by John William Polidori, Byron’s one-time personal physician. Polidori’s novella initially appeared in an unauthorized publication with the ironic sub- title “A Tale by the Honourable Lord Byron,” which goes far to explain Byron’s insistence on publishing his own incomplete draft. Byron’s prose fragment recounts the incidents of a voyage whose itinerary noticeably mirrors the com- ing of age tour he undertook in the company of John Cam Hobhouse. Poli- dori’s father, Gaetano, in an 1818 letter to his brother Luigi, contends that, despite his best efforts to discourage John William from accepting Byron’s Genesis 21

offer of employment, Hobhouse’s published record of their tour, A Journey Through Albania and Provinces of Turkey, convinced John William to put aside his paternal counsel and accompany Byron to the Continent.* Over the summer months of 1816, Polidori, goaded by a lady encountered at Madame de Staël’s Coppet into illustrating how Byron’s tale might have con- cluded, scribbled out The Vampyre over the few love-drenched mornings he passed at her side. By the time it was completed, Hobhouse had rejoined Byron, and Polidori was dismissed from service. Polidori went his own way, and though his path crisscrossed with Byron’s on several occasions in Italy over the autumn and winter months of 1816, his story remained in Geneva with his shrewd inamorata. Three years later it reached the hands of Byron tormentor publisher Henry Colburn, apparently supplied by the lady or a confederate, and Colburn published it along with appended extraneous material as Byron’s in the 1 April 1819 edition of New Monthly Magazine, causing Byron to order his own publisher, John Murray, to publish his only prose work in its unﬁnished state. Murray tacked it on to the end of Mazeppa, much to Byron’s conster- nation. One hundred and ﬁfty years later, E. F. Bleiler had the good sense to publish both texts together as part of his inﬂuential Three Gothic Novels. Byron’s reﬂexive tale breaks off with its dying protagonist, Darvell, charging his companion, the tale’s narrator, to complete a mission in his stead, and to bear a ring on his behalf. The journey begun was one whose destination was enlightenment. The ring, symbol of continuity, suggests that such a voyage shall have no end. Yet by the morning after Byron began work on it, the journey was deﬁnitely ruptured, Byron retiring his pen and ceasing work on his “ghost- story.” Curiously, however, the ﬁctional incident neatly describes what occurred in the world when Polidori is charged with driving Byron’s spirit to its destined conclusion. While the Byron-Polidori relationship has been much discussed through The Vampyre, what remains obscure is that through their ﬁction(s) they collectively retrace the ancient Sacred Way of classical-era Athens, Iera Odos. Byron’s tale opens with its anonymous narrator reaching into cobwebbed memories to a day whose sublime events remained crystalline. The narrator, who boasts, “I was yet young in life, which I had begun early” (287), carries half the ﬁction; Augustus Darvell, “man of considerable fortune and ancient family,” having “a power of giving to one passion the appearance of another” (287), sus- tains the other. They form a dichotomy, the narrator confessing that Darvell “had been deeply initiated into what is called the world ... I was yet in my novi- tiate” (287). Contrast between knowledge and ignorance, mystagogue and myste threads their paths on the labyrinthine Way. The narrator consciously ingratiates himself with Darvell in order to undertake this journey: “It was my secret wish 22 The Theology of Dracula *See McDonald, Poor Polidori, pp. 55–56.

that he might be prevailed upon to accompany me; it was also a probable hope, founded upon the shadowy restlessness which I observed in him ... and his appar- ent indifference to all by which he was more immediately surrounded” (288). Dispatched upon an “intended journey” become journey-of-intent, the narrator soon remarks that, having wound their way through southern Europe, their “attention was turned towards the East” (288). The phrase’s passive con- struction reads as if their turning were involuntary, but we are soon reassured their “intent” had always been thus. In Western Christendom, to turn towards the East is to embrace the sacred: The faithful ranged in Gothic churches prayed towards altars situated at the eastern extreme of cruciform structures, the architecture serving to point assembled worshippers as a uniﬁed body, corpus mysticus, towards Jerusalem, resurrecting God, rising sun: the Levant. Yet given Byron’s tale’s geography, being “turned toward the East” is, more narrowly, to turn against both Roman “Mother” and her Protestant churches, for ﬁnding themselves on the schismatic fault dividing East from West, our protagonists irrevocably turn East. Tradition tells us that cardinal points East and West symbolize birth and death, sunrise and sunset, Jerusalem and the Western Isle; aberrantly, Darvell suffers from an afﬂiction whose debilitating effects become increasingly acute relative to his eastward position. Despite Darvell’s condition, our protagonists determine to undertake “an excursion to the ruins of Ephesus” (289). From Smyrna, they push through “that wild and tenantless tract through the marshes and deﬁles which lead to the few huts yet lingering over the broken columns of Diana—the rooﬂess walls of expelled Christianity, and the still more recent but complete desolation of abandoned mosques” (289). Intentionality leads to a disputed, then abandoned crossroad of civilizations, sites of the huntress’s temples and haunted realm, a land from which Christianity has been exorcised and in which the more recent enveloping faith of the Turk has failed to take root. Geography and pathology working in tandem, Darvell’s incapacitation forces a stop at a “Turkish cemetery, the turbaned tombstones of which were the only indication that human life had ever been a sojourner in this vastness” (289). Reclining upon a grave, Darvell sends for water, describing to his janis- sary a hidden desert fountain from which it might be procured. Observing his companion’s stupefaction at this prescience, Darvell reveals that he had passed that way before. Having drunk from the occult source, Darvell declares his life over, exhorting his companion to indulge his ﬁnal request and swear to not reveal his death to anyone. The oath taken, Darvell removes a ring from his ﬁnger, presents it to his companion with instructions: “‘On the ninth day of the month at noon, ﬂing the ring into the salt springs which run into the Bay of Eleusis, the day after, the tenth day ... repair to the ruins of the temple of Ceres and wait one hour’” (290). Genesis 23

When, just then, a stork “perched upon a tombstone near” (291), a snake clamped in its beak, the narrator compulsively tries to chase the bird off. After circling overhead, the stork, with its writhing cargo, returns to the same spot. Darvell instructs his companion to bury him where the bird has lighted. Our narrator wonders at this unnatural spectacle. Grinning “in a ghastly manner,” Darvell explains the stork has not swallowed the snake because “‘it is not yet time’” (291). At Darvell’s conclusive observation on temporality, the stork takes ﬂight, drawing the narrator’s gaze aloft. Within that nearly imperceptible interval of distraction, Darvell’s mass surrendered itself to Earth. Instantly, Darvell’s ﬁgure became “nearly black” (291). The story cuts off with the tale- bearer recalling how a grave was rapidly prepared, the soil having previously been broken to accommodate “some Mahometan tenant” (291). With the exclamation, “‘Between astonishment and grief, I was tearless’” (291), the mystery travelogue ceases to meander. Darvell has connected the Eleusinian Temple of Demeter (Ceres) to the Ephesian Temple of Artemis (Diana). The latter divinity, both chaste goddess of the hunt and potent fertility deity, embodies one aspect of the Olympian virgin triune, ruling over the moon and subconscious; in her inverted form of black Hekate, she is goddess of shadows, the damned, haunter of crossroads, wearer of serpents. Before having Darvell turn black, Byron insistently empha- sizes stork and serpent, symbols expressing the paradox of the goddess, the stork representing purity, chastity; the serpent, evil. Darvell seems to also ref- erence Jeremiah 8:9: “Yea, the stork in the heaven knoweth her appointed times ... but my people know not the judgment of the Lord.” The stork and serpent are concerned individually with the spring, birth, and resurrection, collectively with the hieroglyph for light; confounding stork and ibis, the iconography is Isiac. R. E. Witt reconciles the goddess’s paradox: Artemis is ... a puzzling ﬁgure ... young virgin of the chase ... vowed to perpetual chastity and ﬁlled with loathing for sex even when it is exercised within the marriage bond.... No less indubitably, however, there stands ... an Artemis ripe for motherhood, a fertility goddess from Asia Minor with her main cult centre at ... Ephesus. The ardent votaries of this Artemis are the Amazons. The Amazons ... indulge, once yearly, in sexual intercourse, but then simply for one reason, to produce girl descendants.... Divine blending of Virgin and Mother contradicts human experience, for bringing forth a child means, for a woman, the loss of maidenhood. How are the two views of Artemis to be reconciled? —The secret seems to lie in the religious thinking of the Mediterranean world as early as the Mycenaean age. The Great Goddess was revered both as virgin and as mother. [Persephone] the daughter and Demeter the mother were one person looked at under two aspects [141]. 24 The Theology of Dracula

Between his July reading of the Henry Colburn–published, Byron-damn- ing Glenarvon by Caroline Lamb and his late September Genevan departure, Polidori gallantly dashed off his novella for the lady who had challenged him. Releasing Darvell from his service and appropriating the name “Ruthven” from Lady Lamb’s roman à clef, Polidori concocted The Vampyre. To complete Darvell’s voyage, Ruthven begins anew. Ruthven too envelops contradiction, binding a being “material” to one “astral.” Titled “a nobleman” (265), he is “more remarkable for his singularities than his rank” (265). Disdain separates him from life’s hubbub; a “dead grey eye” (265) unable to perceive the material, pierces “through to the inward workings of the heart” (265). The more contemptuously Ruthven regards society, the more enthusiastically society regales in his regard. Painted as immune to seduction by the debauched, seemingly without vice, Ruthven’s interest is seized by the virginal or virtuous. “In spite of the deadly hue of his face” (265), his magnetic appeal captivates society during London’s winter “season.” Aubrey, wealthy orphan, arrives in London having “cultivated more his imagination than his judgement” (266). Disappointed by the world, by moder- nity, keen on exploring vestiges of earlier ages, the youth, steeped in ruinously romantic notions of “honour and candour” (266), “believed all to sympathise with virtue, and thought that vice was thrown in by Providence merely for the picturesque effect of the scene, as we see in romances” (266). “Handsome, frank, and rich” (266), pursued by mothers and daughters alike, his romance will be more picaresque than picturesque. A cleavage between the real and imagined furnishes Aubrey with his internal contradiction. As he was set to reconcile his mind to the real, fate introduced him to the reality of an image materialized. Noticing at a “draw- ing-room” Ruthven, “a man entirely absorbed in himself, who gave few other signs of his observation of external objects, that the tacit assent to their exis- tence, implied by the avoidance of their contact” (267), Aubrey transfers his nearly-discarded notions of the hero onto him. Discovering that Ruthven, lacking in funds, is preparing to voyage abroad, Aubrey contrives to “perform the tour, which for many generations has been thought necessary” (267). The verb “perform” invests a ritualistic sense in “the tour” as initiatory ordeal. The pair traverses Flanders on, on Ruthven’s part, a rampage of corrup- tion. Wherever he passes, Ruthven spreads an infectious degeneracy, contact with his corrosive loadstone effecting a moral polar shift. When Ruthven sets to deﬂower a Roman matron’s daughter, Aubrey denounces his hero. Alone, Aubrey reaches Greece. Taking up lodgings with a nameless Athenian family, he passes time “tracing the faded records of ancient glory upon monuments that apparently, ashamed of chronicling the deeds of freemen only before Genesis 25

slaves, had hidden themselves beneath the sheltering soil” (270)—“sheltering soil” sounding a phrase that resounds across centuries. His hosts’ daughter, Ianthe, replaces Ruthven as Aubrey’s guide. This beautiful “conductress” (273) an apparition from Delacroix as rendered by Ingres, is Romanticism itself, a pure spirit steeped in the superstitions of her native soil: Her earnestness and apparent belief of what she narrated excited the inter- est even of Aubrey: and often as she told him the tale of the living vampyre ... forced every year, by feeding upon the life of a lovely female to prolong his existence for the ensuing months, his blood would run cold [271]. Unlike Artemis’s Amazons, engaging once yearly in procreative sex, the Vampyre annually feeds on life to animate death on a speciﬁc matrimonial day. “Matrimonium,” describing the rite of transformation that changes The Maiden into The Mother, becomes, as will be seen, thoroughly perverted by the Vampire. While dismissing Ianthe’s stories as ridiculous, Aubrey “wondered at the many coincidences which had all tended to excite a belief in the supernatural power of Lord Ruthven” (271). Ianthe’s presence banished from his mind all thoughts of classical relics, the simple play of light in her hair inﬂicting for- getfulness on a tour-performing youth become Pausanias–led “antiquary”: He fell in love. Polidori’s phrase—“her tresses falling, as she ﬂitted around, exhibit in the sun’s ray such delicately brilliant and swiftly fading hues” (270)—invests sense in his sole name. Ianthe is portrayed ﬂitting about in the light of Aubrey’s regard. In “Aubrey,” the notion of aube, referencing the rising sun’s light, is apposed to “ray,” a beam of light, or rey, “king,” invoking a Dawn King, Eastern Light: the Levant. One evening, as Aubrey announces his intent to visit a “particular des- tination” (272) the following day, Ianthe’s family, “when they heard the name of the place” (272), insists he reconsider—woods that must be traversed en route are the ‘resort of vampires’ (272). Should he go, he must return by sun- set, ‘ere night allowed the power of these beings to be put in action’ (272). Humouring his hosts, Aubrey dismissively, condescendingly agrees. Next morning Aubrey set off ... unattended; he was surprised to observe the melancholy face of his host ... Ianthe came to the side of his horse, and earnestly begged of him to return, ere night.... He was, however, so occu- pied in his research, that he did not perceive that day-light would soon end, and that in the horizon there was one of those specks which, in the warmer climates, so rapidly gather into a tremendous mass, and pour all their rage upon the devoted country.—He ... mounted his horse, deter- mined to make up by speed for his delay.... Twilight, in these southern cli- mates, is almost unknown; immediately the sun sets, night begins [272–73]. 26 The Theology of Dracula

A polarizing land knowing but day and night having tricked him into overstaying his allotted time, Aubrey set off homeward at a gallop. Thunder caused his horse to bolt, charge through an “entangled forest” (273), and stop before a “hovel” (273). Dismounting, Aubrey started as a ﬂash of blue light radiated “at his very feet” (273). Alarmed by a woman’s scream that, inter- mingled with salacious laughter, resonated between thunderclaps, he rushed into the hut to ﬁnd himself locked in battle against “one whose strength seemed superhuman” (273). Aubrey was “lifted from his feet and hurled with enormous force against the ground:—his enemy threw himself upon him, and kneeling upon his breast, had placed his hands upon his throat—when the glare of many torches penetrating through the hole that gave light in the day, disturbed him” (273). Aubrey’s assailant ran crashing into the woods. The storm was now still ... Aubrey, incapable of moving, was soon heard by those without. They entered; the light of their torches fell upon nothing but the mud walls, and the thatch loaded on every individual straw with heavy ﬂakes of soot, though at this moment it was apparently untenanted. There was one spot slippery with blood but it was hardly visible [273]. Aubrey, dispatching the party to locate the vanished woman, “was again left in darkness; but what was his horror, when the light of the torches once more burst upon him, to perceive the airy form of his fair conductress brought in a lifeless corpse” (273). He “shut his eyes, hoping that it was but a vision” (273): ...no colour upon her cheek, not even upon her lip: yet there was a stillness about her face that seemed almost as attaching as the life that once dwelt there:—upon her neck and breast was blood, and upon her throat were the marks of teeth having opened the vein: to this the men pointed, crying, simultaneously struck with horror, “A Vampyre!” [274]. Aubrey was stretched upon a litter, Ianthe, “who had lately been to him the object of so many bright and fairy visions, now fallen with the ﬂower of life that had died within her,” by his side; his hand “held almost unconsciously ... a naked dagger ... found in the hut” (274). They were “met by different parties who had been engaged in the search of her whom a mother had missed. Their lamentable cries, as they approached the city, forewarned the parents of some dreadful catastrophe” (274). Beholding Ianthe’s corpse, her horriﬁed parents expired. Aubrey, fevered, succumbed to tortured visions of himself imploring Ruthven to spare Ianthe’s life. Returning to his senses, Aubrey is bewildered to ﬁnd at his side he whom delirium had confounded with the Un-Dead. Swayed by Ruthven’s tender min- istries, Aubrey forgives all. Resuming Aubrey’s interrupted activities as before, the pair revisits scenes of previous excavation; yet wherever within the “Athenian Genesis 27

neighborhood” (275) they roam, Aubrey is haunted by Ianthe, pale-faced, stigmatized, “wandering amidst the underwood, in quest of the humble violet” (275). One day, beyond Athens, while passing through a “narrow deﬁle” between two hills, the pair falls into an ambuscade, as if set upon by the god of war himself. During the altercation, Ruthven is mortally wounded. To save his companion, Aubrey contracts a ransom if only their assailants convey Ruthven to a nearby hut. There, Ruthven obtains Aubrey’s promise to keep secret his demise for a year-and-a-day. On Aubrey’s utterance of the oath, Ruthven expires. Aubrey withdraws to rest, but, haunted by his pledge, can- not. At dawn, he starts for “the hovel in which he had left the corpse, when a robber met him, and informed him that it was no longer there, having been conveyed ... to the pinnacle of a neighbouring mount, according to a promise they had given his lordship, that it should be exposed to the ﬁrst cold ray of the moon that rose after his death” (277). Alarmed, Aubrey hastens to bury the cadaver, but Ruthven’s remains have vanished. Robbers, having stripped the corpse, buried it to obscure their crime, Aubrey rationalizes. As if returning from Ephesus, Aubrey arrives “at Smyrna” (277) with Ruthven’s effects. “There were several daggers and ataghans ... examining their curious forms, what was his surprise at ﬁnding a sheath apparently ornamented in the same style as the dagger discovered in the fatal hut ... his horror may be imagined, when he discovered that it ﬁtted” (277). Ruthven had plucked his “ﬂower of life” (274). Aubrey returns westward. From Calais, “a breeze, which seemed obedient to his will, soon wafted him to the English shores” (278) where his virgin sister awaited. Neither worldly nor urbane, this “melan- choly” (278) maiden lived for fraternal approbation. In his absence, she hadn’t debuted in society. Thus “it was ... resolved that the next drawing-room ... should be the epoch of her entry into the ‘busy scene’” (278), whose perform- ance constituted a feminine equivalent to “the tour.” Eons had passed since that fateful “drawing-room” where he ﬁrst beheld Ruthven, but Aubrey was back at another elegant London occasion, now as his sister’s protector. Society’s hubbub being unchanged, Aubrey retires to a shadowed corner. He is soon startled by a hand upon his back, words mur- mured into his ear by a voice uncannily familiar: “remember your oath” (279). Afar, he can perceive if not the voice’s source, its master. The Vampyre plied the crowd. Clutching the arm of an acquaintance, Aubrey struggles towards transport home. Collecting himself, he returns to recover his sister and verify his senses. Indeed, it was Ruthven. Aubrey “sprang forward, seized his sister’s arm, and ... forced her towards the street; at the door he found himself impeded by the crowd ... he again heard that voice close to him—‘Remember your oath!’—He dared not turn” (279–80). 28 The Theology of Dracula

Aubrey, much altered by this encounter, is presumed mad. Informed of his sister’s betrothal to the earl of Marsden, he quickly surrenders his blessing, relieved to see her pledged to anyone but Ruthven. Yet perceiving a miniature of the earl in a locket dangling over his sister’s heart, his torment is transported beyond limits. Realization of Ruthven’s impending triumph speeds Aubrey towards a relapse of delirium, though he is sufﬁciently lucid to calculate that 365 days have passed since he pledged silence. The nuptials are set for the morrow. Ruthven, citing an obligation to leave for the continent by dawn, strives to hasten a wedding Aubrey struggles to delay. In extremis, Aubrey violates his soul-damning oath. Dismissed as insane, Aubrey bursts an artery and dies. Midnight brings realization that Aubrey’s sister has disappeared. Polidori concludes, taunting, she “had glutted the thirst of a Vampyre” (283). Polidori’s uniquely unsatisfying ﬁnal line hardly justiﬁes a tragedy’s heap of cadavers; nothing cathartic is left to retain, but grim spectacle climaxed by surprise. Rather than cleansing and renewing, the ending pollutes. Ianthe dead, Sun–king departed, the Vampire—intoxicated on Miss Aubrey’s blood—free to wreak another leap year’s havoc on a disbelieving world, The Vampyre yields but grotesque comedy with as many deformities as strokes of genius competing for attention. While with Polidori causality does not spur the rationalizing contortions of Ann Radcliffe, the obvious lack of it inevitably leads to the appearance of maladroitness: the crowd that happens by with torches in “a wood, where no Greek would ever remain, after the day had closed” (272); the malleable, amenable robbers always ready to lend a hand whenever the plot is bogged down; Aubrey’s weak-willed readiness to forget Ruthven’s transgressions. Ruthven’s attack on Aubrey’s unnamed sister seems aimed at Aubrey, rather that the victim herself. Could not Ruthven have found some other maiden? Somewhere “between astonishment and grief” the reader, like Byron’s narrator, is left “tearless.” The limits of Polidori’s craftsmanship inevitably cause his tale to fall shy of its mark should that be Coleridgian suspension of disbelief; yet his irreverent pomposity enlivens, his frequent self–conscious touches so amuse that one is tempted to believe he is in command of the aesthetic he deﬁnes: Is it not in Gothic fun that the hero awaits a ship to Otranto? In ridicule that, en route for England, he abandons Athens for Smyrna? As diversion that a vampire is offered to a lady? It nevertheless appears that Polidori’s genius was accidental, residing in the starkness of fortuitous detail recycled until congealed into canon: the throat punctured by vampiric dentition; the moonlight circum- stance and empowerment of evil; the being capable of hurling men about as if babes; the menacing forces of nature which announce the coming of the Vampire (the speck in the air which presages things more ominous, the sudden anaemic dusk, the will-driven winds and tides, the troubled dreams); the Genesis 29

empirical, orphaned hero driven to madness; the ascendant villain, that seduc- tive and sophisticated aristocrat run amok in a modern world; the incestuous ties that bind them. Perchance, Polidori has tersely summarized, catalogued, bequeathed to posterity now familiar attributes, images seemingly torn from delirium and nightmare projected onto a ﬁctional realm representing contemporary bour- geois quotidian experience. Yet in remarking these surface, now familiar ele- ments of a profaning being, we are blinded to the interior sacred contents with which Polidori has invested his story. It is this cleverness that earned The Vampyre Goethe’s highest praise.* Yes, the facile landscape of huts, roving mobs, and bandits, tormenting secrets and guilty suspicions have been pur- loined from the likes of Godwin, yet remarkable differences, concordant with the foundation Byron laid in that sketch he could not bring to completion, exist, separating Polidori’s Vampyre from anything written since Lucius Apuleius. Why has Polidori transposed the setting from Ephesus to Athens? For what is Aubrey searching so unrelentingly? What dangerous road leads him out of Athens on his expedition? Why is he so absorbed by Pausanias? Who are the torch-bearing souls wandering woods in the dead of night? Why can’t Ruthven leave Aubrey and those he loves alone? What mother has lost her daughter? What is the signiﬁcance of Ianthe? Ianthe, who conducts Aubrey to the Sacred Way he must descend alone, bears a name signifying “Flower of Violet”; this explains much. The Homeric “To Demeter” lists Ianthe as one of the maidens who accompanied Persephone as she went ﬂower-gathering on the day she was abducted and became against her will queen of the underworld. Inspired by Lamb’s Glenarvon, Polidori’s is a novel roman à clef. In recalling Darvell’s dying imperative to have his ring tossed into “the salt springs which run into the bay at Eleusis,” we fathom the depths to which Polidori plunged to retrieve Byron’s discarded bauble. The salt springs bubble at the mouth of the Rheitoi, near which “is Erineos, the place where Plouton descended, they say, when he carried off” Persephone and “Eumolpos and the daughters of the Keleus performed the holy rites of the two goddesses” (Pausanias 1971: 107). We can conﬁdently assert Polidori’s familiarity with Neo- platonist Thomas Taylor’s 1796 translation of Pausanias, an edition Byron used when trekking Eleusis and Ephesus with Hobhouse in 1809 to 1810: In a letter written just after the Darvell ﬁction was begun, Byron invites Hobhouse to Geneva, requesting that he bring “some of Waite’s red tooth powder and tooth- brushes, Taylor’s Pausanias, and I forget the other things” (23 June 1816). Pausanias and a Neolithic myth, relating the story of mothers and daugh- ters, fathers and sons, gods who represent our complex natures and Nature’s 30 The Theology of Dracula *See Butler, Goethe and Byron, p. 55.

complexities, who become lost in and emergent from one another, provide a template for enlightenment. At the myth’s darkest depths, two ﬁgures appear, one recognizably feminine, another generally, if intermittently, masculine: a “gentle” man, effeminate in his courtly nature, who reveals himself to be a savage hunter who periodically becomes the hunted, and whose double nature expresses ancient dualities. Its canonical rendition concerns Demeter, her brothers Zeus and Plouton, and daughter. Aware that Zeus had promised their daughter Persephone to brother Plouton, Demeter hid her before leaving to worship her mother Rhea. Discovering Persephone’s whereabouts, Zeus sped Aphrodite, Athena, and Artemis to lure the maiden to a place where she might be ambushed and abducted. The goddesses, ﬁnding the girl embroi- dering a scarf for her mother that incorporated the sacred symbol of the initial chaos, the primordial void, into its fabric, entreated her to come ﬂower-gath- ering with the daughters of Okeanus. Persephone consented. In a meadow lying by the briny sea, the divine Maiden spied a magniﬁ- cent Narcissus and went to pluck it. As she pulled on its stem, the earth “gaped” as if the plant’s roots burrowed into Hades. When the many-named lord of the underworld burst through, Persephone let out a piercing cry. None but “Hekate of the shining headband ... from her cave” (“To Demeter” ¶25) and distant Demeter admitted to hearing it. According to Taylor’s translation of Discourse on the Mysteries, Persephone, “in the new spring, was ravished ... and being carried from thence through thick woods, and over a length of sea, was brought by Plouton into a cavern, the residence of departed spirits, over whom she afterward ruled” (87). “The place where this happened was pointed out by the river Kephisos near Eleusis” (Kerényi 35). Alerted by the scream, Demeter descended, tearfully wandering for nine days, not bathing, taking neither food nor drink, combing the world “with bright torches in her hand” (“To Demeter” ¶48). The “nine days” reference suggests that Demeter bears torches by night and day in order to apperceive one who has become darkness, earning her “the name of Pheraia, the torch- bearing goddess seated on a running horse” (Jung, Kerényi 198). On Demeter’s passion’s tenth day, the dark goddess “Hekate carrying a light in her hands, met her”—her light reﬂecting the renewed moon. Demeter’s question, who had seized Persephone?, Hekate could not answer, for she had heard cries without seeing. At Hekate’s instigation Demeter asks Helios-Who-Sees-All: “No other immortal is to be blamed save cloud-gathering Zeus who gave her to Hades, his own brother, to become his buxom bride” (“To Demeter” ¶78– 80). Imperceptible at night, the lord of darkness, appearing from below as masked Dionysus, is detected in the sun’s presence, for, as Heraclitus reveals, Hades and Dionysus are one and the same. Darvell’s request that his ring be immersed in Eleusinian waters on a Genesis 31

lunar ninth day in anticipation of his emissary’s temple visit on the tenth, recalls Demeter’s passion, for on the tenth day she arrived at Eleusis to even- tually become reunited with Persephone. Polidori, indebted to Caroline Lamb for attributing “Ruthven” Dionysian characteristics and Byronian associations, understanding the implications of Darvell’s ring, harnessed Taylor’s Pausanius to their development. With Aubrey about to leave Athens, his host appeared with “melancholy face” (272) to see him off; “Ianthe came to the side of his horse” (272), her mother was ostensibly absent. This dawn-lit tableau presages and mirrors the nocturnal incident in which the horse led Aubrey to a mystery destination from which it refused to advance. When we recall that Ianthe was within the nearby hovel, it seems as if the horse was determined to stand by Ianthe’s side as Ianthe had stood by the horse as Aubrey set off. To review: Triggered by a Zeusian thunderbolt, Aubrey’s mare, Demeter embodied, charged through an entangled forest, pulling up at the place of “orgies” that Ianthe’s father, Okeanus, had warned of—the Telesterion. “[T]he animal, at last, through fatigue, stopped” (273), leaving the spiritual to carry on. Blue light falling before Aubrey “to radiate at his very feet” (273) conﬁrms Mystery Night’s arrival. At a “hovel which hardly lifted itself up from the masses of dead leaves” (273), Aubrey hoped “to ﬁnd some one to guide him” (273). When a woman’s scream, Persephone’s, compelled him to enter the structure, he “found himself in utter darkness: the sound, however, guided him” (273). Demeter has led Aubrey to her daughter. Aubrey struggled with a shadowy assailant who, unseen, disappears in a burst of light. Clearly, during Aubrey’s “unaccompanied” initiation into life’s mysteries, Ianthe-Persephone, through her scream, “guided him” and remained his “con- ductress.” The torchlight of those following the Sacred Way sent the Nocturnal One crashing into woods to disappear into darkness. Taylor teaches that Perse- phone was carried “through thick woods, and over a length of sea ... into a cavern, the residence of the dead: where by woods a material nature is plainly implied” (100). In examining the desolate dwelling they found only Aubrey, soot-laden thatch and earthen ﬂoor with a bloody spot. Polidori’s story unfolds within a sustained Neoplatonic projection. The hovels scattered across a landscape of material entanglements must be viewed as temporal abodes: Bodies that contained the spirit, once abandoned, are marked by soot, the residue of material man, a substance originating in Iakchos’s Titan-fragmented, Zeus-incinerated body. An insistence on straw, an element associated with Dionysus in death, afﬁrms this. Ianthe’s spirit has quit a “hovel” to live a “Kashmere butterﬂy” upon a spiritual plane. With “a stillness about her face that seemed almost as attaching as the life that once dwelt there” (274), Ianthe, imbued with new beauty, personiﬁes Persephone. Even in death, Aubrey 32 The Theology of Dracula

sees her wandering “in quest of the modest violet” (275); “amidst the ruins he had formerly frequented, Ianthe’s form stood by his side” (275). Ruthven’s death, too, was occasioned as the twin explorers processed along the Sacred Way: In consequence of thus neglecting the advice of the inhabitants they trav- elled on one occasion with only a few guards.... Upon entering, however, a narrow deﬁle, at the bottom of which was the bed of a torrent, with large masses of rock brought down from the neighbouring precipices, they had reason to regret their negligence; for scarcely were the whole of the party engaged in the narrow pass, when they were startled by the echoed report of several guns, and by the whistling of bullets [275]. As Heinrich Schliemann points out, “at the foot of the conical hill of Poikilus, at the entrance to the deﬁle, the Sacred Road appears to have to the right, whilst the modern way turns to the left. The deﬁle is bordered on the right by Mount Icarus, on the left by Mount Corydallus” (122). The sanctuary of Aphrodite, situated between the temple of Daphnia Apollo at the Sacred Way’s highest point and the Ploutonium at its lowest, stands just above the deﬁle one must pass through to negotiate the Sacred Way. Repeatedly, the goddess of love, aided by the god of war, divides her two heroes, Day and Night. When Hobhouse and Byron passed though in January 1810, they searched for the place where Scirus was said to have fallen; the deﬁle was later named after him. In examining Ruthven’s effects, Aubrey revisits Mystery Night’s hovel, Genesis 33 The Sanctuary of Aphrodite along the Sacred Way. © Rarignac

transporting the reader into a detective story, a mystery. Although he seems to discover the murder weapon, it is written that Ianthe only bore teeth marks on her neck. While a vampire needs no knife, ceremonially spilling sacriﬁcial blood upon the earth as a chthonian libation requires a consecrated blade “adapted to ensure the death of the victim” (277)—a Dionysian high priest’s, a hierophant’s—Ruthven’s. The bloodied ﬂoor also marks the locus classicus where the earth gaped, the symbolic afﬁrmation of Persephone’s rape. As if Perse- phone, Ianthe, “Flower of Violet,” was deﬂowered at Erineos. While Hekate’s lunar Ruthven, Dionysian “Nocturnal One,” accomplished the deed, it is Helios’ solar Aubrey, Apollonian diurnal ﬁgure, who ﬁnds himself clutching the blade. This article’s transmission manifests the protagonists’ doppelganger bond. At Eleusis, the ineffable goddess was summoned, a Visio Beatiﬁca, from darkness; upon the Hierophant’s command “a great light burst forth” (Kerényi 92), Persephone appearing. Polidori describes the occurrence: Aubrey “was again left in darkness; but what was his horror, when the light of the torches once more burst upon him, to perceive the airy form of his fair conductress brought in a lifeless corpse. He shut his eyes, hoping that it was but a vision arising from his disturbed imagination; but he again saw the same form” (273–74). Polidori writes that “lamentable cries, as they approached the city, forewarned the parents of some dreadful catastrophe” (274). As on Mystery Night of yore, calls of “Iakchos!” rang out. The clearest indication of the sym- bolic order employed is caught in the tangle of a gnarled sentence: “They were soon met by different parties who had been engaged in the search of her whom a mother had missed” (274). This mother, Demeter, searches this night for her Kore. Dispatched conjointly by Hekate and Helios, Demeter will soon arrive at Eleusis. Dr. Polidori drew his image brilliantly, contrasting Aubrey’s sketching with Ianthe’s told tale: “In tracing the scenes of her native place; she would then describe to him the circling dance upon the open plain, would paint to him in all the glowing colours of youthful memory, the marriage pomp she remembered viewing in her infancy” (271). The marriage was Persephone’s; the circling dance, that performed in great antiquity around the temple complex’s Kalli- choron. Although Ianthe had quit her temporal abode, Aubrey remained upon the material plane to mix with Ruthven in a vacillating relationship—like Apollo and Dionysus, bound at the omphalos, dividing supremacy over the Delphic temple. Mystery Night occurred 40 days before Dionysus’s rebirth, perhaps explaining why Ruthven did not extract his oath, initiatory apporheton,* and die with Ianthe, beginning his haematological new year then. 34 The Theology of Dracula *Arrheton refers to the ineffable secret; apporheton to that which is kept “secret under a law of silence.” See Kerényi, Eleusis, p. 26.

Aubrey’s solar westward return, Ruthven in pursuit, balances Aubrey’s eastward accompaniment of Ruthven. Solar-informed polarity has Death give rise to Life as East meets West. Although crepuscular Aubrey, red-faced, dies haemorrhaging from Ruthven-inspired lunacy, he will be as likely to reappear to share another eastward journey with Ruthven as the sun is to rise tomorrow. Ruthven and Aubrey, darkness and light, divide the year, returning us to Byron’s Darvell, for Apollo’s sister, Aubrey’s in this roman à clef, is Artemis Hekate, virgin mother goddess venerated at Ephesus. Indeed, it is there, in the East, that Darvell awaits by an occult source for his wedding band to be returned from Dionysian depths on an Eleusinian tenth day, which effects his return from beneath the sheltering soil, Aubrey having completed the mission Darvell set for his narrator. Nodier’s Vampires Polidori’s insightful novella, developing the theological aspect of the Un- Dead that Goethe ﬁrst implanted in The Bride of Corinth, set the thematic direction for the Vampire Tale for the century to come while ﬁxing as a ritual sequence of transformation numerous aspects of plot. This enduring inﬂuence however was not due to any great success of the tale in England or in English- speaking countries, but to its repeated and resounding triumphs in France. Genesis 35 The Kallichoron. © Rarignac

On the heels of Ruthven’s New Monthly Magazine apparition, Henri Faber translated The Vampyre into French, publishing it again, despite Poli- dori’s protestations, as Byron’s intellectual fruit, the Byronian attribution being accentuated to assure sales. Charles Nodier reviewed Faber’s work in the 1 July 1819 Journal des Débats, heaping praise on The Vampyre’s author and scorn on its translator—an irony, considering a tendency to ascribe The Vampyre’s continental success to translator-engineered stylistic improvements. Nodier had to “admit the reader must make quite an effort to judge the merit of this work through the veil of lead with which the translator has covered it. The reader will not be able to enjoy its worth unless an author worthy of the pen of Lord Byron—and I am told that such an author is at present busy with this work of translation—repairs the unﬂattering homage that the French press has just paid him” (tr. qtd. Oliver 126), predicting that the anonymous translator “then will offer all these trappings of melodrama to one of the boulevard theatres; and what success will be in store for him!” (126). In com- plimenting Byron, Nodier praises himself, for he is himself the worthy trans- lator that his reported rumour hails. Nodier’s prognostication was proven just; as a Lord Byron whose attitude towards The Vampyre evolved over the years came to admit to Thomas Medwin, The Vampyre was only truly granted life once it “was got up as a melo-drame at Paris” (120): It was Nodier whose fatherly touch sparked that improbable life in the given-up-for-dead Vam- pire. As early as 1813 Charles Nodier was writing on vampire lore he encoun- tered while serving in Ljubljana as editor of Télégraphe Ofﬁciel, a Napoleonic propaganda organ. During this period Nodier ﬂeshed out his major literary theme: transformative love, love forged from the chivalrous ardor of the medieval romance, tempered with a transcendental spiritual passion, ultimately Christian yet deeply mystic, seen as essential to man’s resuscitation and renewal. A. Richard Oliver deﬁnes Nodier’s conception of love as something which manifests itself through “eternal union, which could be achieved ... only beyond the grave” (124). While the Vampire expresses themes of renewal and resuscitation of a certain kind, the use of superstition to communicate Nodier’s spiritually-charged love as a Christian force may appear problematic, but here is where a certain syncretism is brought to bear, or, rather, becomes a critical aspect of the Vampire Tale. Like Polidori, Nodier was a Catholic and a Mason and many of his novels feature initiatory plots, André Lebois going so far as to argue that Nodier’s La Fée aux Miettes rivals Schikandere and Giesecke’s Die Zauberﬂöte for discoursing on the rites of Freemasonry (27). Like fellow Romantic Johann Goethe, Nodier perceived Polidori’s novella as an initiatic “fable,” which undoubtedly furnishes one explanation for why he was drawn to the subject; but it is also true that Nodier, intime of the great 36 The Theology of Dracula

melodramatist Pixérécourt, envisioned a new kind of Romantic drama even before The Vampyre’s publication. Polidori’s subject offered a uniquely prom- ising vehicle for founding a renewed melodrama that was not just moralistic, but supernatural, mystic, and cosmic, exactly what Nodier wanted. Polidori had also established a symbolic language that gracefully permitted the occult- ing of his tale’s most profound essence, exactly what Nodier needed. Complementing his several reviews and articles on the theme that appeared in the Débats and the Drapeau Blanc, two creative works published in 1820 link Nodier, ambiguously, to the vampire: the roman Lord Ruthwen [sic], ou les Vampires and the melodrama Le Vampire, ou Lord Rutwen [sic]. If these titles read as anagrammatic, suggesting the melodrama is the novel inverted and vice versa, the novel bears little similarity to either Polidori’s story or the melodrama, recalling only tales yet to be written. Perhaps to emphasize their divergent natures, Nodier modiﬁes the spelling of the prin- cipals’ names in the two works: “Aubrey” and “Ruthwen” in the ﬁction becom- ing “Aubray” and “Rutwen” in the play. As the theatrical work was the more enduringly inﬂuential, comments on the roman (to call it a novel would be misleading) and its innovations can be limited to a few remarks on notable aspects that may have been inﬂuential on Stoker’s project. In Lord Ruthwen, a shambling Varney before Varney, Dracula before Drac- ula, the Vampire’s iconography is ﬁxed for a century. More than a singular “dead grey eye,” Ruthwen becomes a tall, thin, distinguished ﬁgure, draped in a long black cape; a smooth-talking, courtly gentleman when circumstances demand, seductive lady-killer when discretion permits. While Nodier signed the work’s introductory “observations préliminaires,” which, like the New Monthly Magazine’s “Vampyre” and the compendium Fantasmagoriana, includes distracting notes on the vampire phenomenon with references to Dom Augustin Calmet, Voltaire, etc., the novel’s only authorial attribution took the form of the initials “C. B.” along with the note “publié par l’auteur de Jean Sbogar et de Thérèse Aubert,” referencing Nodier’s better known con- temporary works. For his entire life Nodier attempted to attribute the roman to his friend and non–author, theatre manager Cyprien Bérard, apparently fearful that his having written the piece might interfere with his eventually realized ambition to join “the immortals” of the Académie Française, with its guaranteed lifetime revenues. The speed at which it appeared following The Vampyre’s publication suggests that portions of the text existed when Polidori’s story reached print. The roman unfolds as a sequence of told tales, interweaving narratives from multiple sources ﬂeshing out a meagre outline. The plot, easily summa- rized, is as familiar as Dracula: The Vampire attacks, is pursued for 400 pages by an expanding crew of raconteurs, and, when all their narratives have been Genesis 37

related, is trapped in its grave. Lord Ruthwen himself tells two vampire tales to listeners who are thoroughly sceptical as to the existence of vampires. Antic- ipating Stoker, Nodier has his hero, Aubrey, joined by confederates: the Vene- tian Léonti and Arab Nadour-Héli—three protagonists whose names index the solar: Aubrey, dawn; Nadour-Héli, midday; Léonti, mid–summer. Each of them having been deprived of a loved one by Ruthven, they form a posse and pursue the vampire across the woods and gardens of the Italian Renais- sance, ﬁnally tracking it down and destroying it as the cadaver is rising from its tomb, burning its eyes out and staking its heart with a white-hot iron— a treatment akin to that Pitton de Tournefort actually witnessed performed on what he hoped was a corpse (though he suspected otherwise) on the Ionian isle of St George on the ﬁrst day of the 18th century. The 13 anecdotes and curious stories recounted by the roman’s various actors place it in the tradition of Boccaccio’s Decamerone or the Arabian Nights, Nodier speciﬁcally attaching the vampire to the Tale’s Ghoul. Unfortunately, little represented action interrupts the told tales, resulting in an indirect quality that renders the work anaemic and antique. While it is tempting to make short shrift of its nearly 500 pages, several incidents and thematic departures merit mention. Sequentially, these are: the ﬁguration of the demiurge return- ing on a boat at a hybrid of the Dionysian festival of Anthesteria, Festa della Sensa, and Carnival; a Tyrolean fortune-teller’s construction of a mysteries nexus; Ruthwen’s initial attack; the forming of the posse; a vampire–infected female called to return from death; the triumph of Christianity that allows her to aid her betrothed defeat the vampire; Demeter’s incest reﬁgured through the love of Thelemy [the Will] and brother Oscar; Artemis–Diana personiﬁed, preserved yet desecrated. Most importantly, across the entire work Nodier depicts the hunter becoming the hunted, the enduring motif that motivates Dracula. Once Lord Ruthwen is disposed of, the dead are released to rest in peace and the novel ends. The roman’s introduction of the Vampire again returns the story to Byron’s Fragment, ﬁnally published in June 1819, and Darvell’s instructing his comrade to throw a mystical ring into the waters of the Bay of Eleusis (290). The Doge’s marriage to the Adriatic, accomplished by throwing a sacred ring into the waters of the lagoon, brings a ﬁgure ﬂoating ashore as if the ancient Dionysus was approaching his awaiting faithful aboard his carrus navalis at Anthesteria. Should the lord of Venice take the sea as his bride, Ruthwen, underworldly Dionysian lord, will take his own Basilinna from among Venice’s maidens, choosing the Lido’s pale beauty Bettina, ﬁancée of Léonti. At the evening festivities, the Tyrolean seer sings and dances for the revellers, sound- ing a theme worthy of Thomas Taylor as she proclaims that the “‘stars con- sulted in the ﬁelds of Chaldea, the mysteries honoured on the banks of Egypt’s 38 The Theology of Dracula

shores, and the famous oracle of Greece have revealed to us their formidable secrets’” (18–19). With that as an introduction and a rattling of her tam- bourine, the Tyrolean peers into Bettina’s palm and is horriﬁed to ﬁnd reﬂected there Bettina’s sacriﬁce to the Vampire. Ruthwen drives away the gypsy before she can say more. Later that evening, in the early pre–dawn hours, Ruthwen, having granted Léonti a commission in the Scottish army, will have him arrested for treason to Venice. Ruthwen then tricks Bettina into accompanying him to a secluded woods where he claims Léonti awaits her, but where he will drain her life away. When the body of Bettina revives after her mortal encounter with Ruth- wen, an angel appears to her in an annunciation-like scene: Because of her exquisite purity and chastity, she will be spared from an eternity of vampirism. The angel commands her to go to the Adriatic where an oarsman awaits to take her to the East, her soul undergoing a return to the eternal on a barque from the sea of death. As Bettina’s soul is saved, grieved ﬁancé Léonti wanders Venice, searching out the murderous Scottish nobleman Ruthwen to exact vengeance. He is at last gratiﬁed to ﬁnd the unholy criminal by a canal. Léonti is preparing his attack when, sensing a melancholy air of sadness about the man, he realizes the person he is about to kill is not Ruthwen. It is thus that Léonti comes to meet Aubrey, who has arrived at Venice from Scotland in search of his sister’s killer. Through their shared resemblance, Nodier renders the Ruthwen-Aubrey doppelganger status clear. In his tales of the material enwrapping the spiritual, Nodier makes fre- quent use of the image of woods and forests that enclose magical sources and clearings, places where the normally unknowable is revealed by the supernat- ural. As in Polidori’s story, and following Taylor, through the representation of woods ‘material nature is clearly implied” (100). Bettina now becomes the supernatural emissary who appears to guide endangered mortals to defeat the vampire and thus gain her own salvation. For instance, Ruthwen’s ﬁancée, the princess of Modena, separated from her party during a prenuptial hunt, is approached by Bettina in the heart of the wood with a message of warning about her betrothed’s unnatural nature. Bettina also appears in an urban noc- turnal pleasure garden, when she is afraid that Léonti will be seduced by a corrupt Roman. In tribute to James MacPherson—the writer from the village of Ruthven, Perthshire, who claimed to resurrect Ossian, ancient bard and Celtic Homer— Nodier places a ﬁgure named Oscar (Ossian’s son) in his roman. Oscar, a princely only son, falls in love with a girl given the Rabelais-inspired name Thelemy, daughter of her mother’s trusted servant and conﬁdante. Borrowing from the Persephone myth, Thelemy is pictured in a delightful garden weaving a scarf for her lover, knotting his name into its fabric. Oscar is torn with Genesis 39

jealousy until he realizes that his is the name of the one Thelemy loves. They delight in each other among the garden’s fruit trees, and consummate their love, ignorant of their consanguinity—for Thelemy is Oscar’s illegitimate half-sister. When they belatedly learn the terrible news from the mouth of their nearly mad mother, their torment is augmented by the punishment of the king, who, visiting the garden, overheard their story and learned of his wife’s inﬁdelity. The wood and garden, constant elements in the novel’s many tales of love and wonderment, doubly frame Oscar and Thelemy’s story, taking the ill-fated lovers from an enchanted garden where love blooms to a savage wilderness where guilt-wracked, despairing Thelemy is lost. Thelemy’s story ends with the discovery of her veil, partially entangled in a wild willow’s branches, ﬂoating on the waters of a torrent. In his introduction to the collected works of Bryon, Nodier warned of the epistemological difﬁculties emergent from the “contemporary social rev- olution,” saying, Thought has become a torture to man; as the old stand-bys fell away and he became more individualistic, a wave of doubt concerning his ability to know and understand swept over him, and in the succeeding chaos man experienced a kind of voluptuousness in plunging into nihilism. Romanti- cists, wanting to pierce to the reality of things, ripped away the veils of Isis in the horrible expectation of ﬁnding a corpse [qtd. Oliver 137–38]. The announcing of various incidents or their denouement through the “rustling of a garment” or the shedding of a veil is frequent and may be attached to Nodier’s image of the goddess being unveiled. Nodier, tellingly, ﬁnally inserts the story of a Diana-like ﬁgure, Cymadore, who, having been sheltered by a priest of the old beliefs, survived into the modern era, hiding in the ruins of a classical-era Greek temple by a blessed bay near Athens. She is pictured with her bow and arrows, one breast exposed, virginal, and a huntress. Nadour-Héli, as he traveled through Athens, glimpsed her and fell painfully in love. Armed with a lyre rather than a bow, he managed to win her conﬁdence through his music, enchanting Cymadore with his voluptuous Lydian mode and the story of Timothy’s lyre’s seventh string. The octave-deﬁning seven strings associate musician Timothy of Miletus with Saint Timothy, ﬁrst bishop of Ephesus (said by Paul to play his congre- gation like a lyre), who was martyred for attempting to stop Diana-Artemis’s licentious annual festival. Love-struck Nadour-Héli was so worshipful of the virginal beauty that the normally solitary misandrist Cymodore agreed to grant him a further audience to continue his effort at love-making. This was her downfall. When Nadour-Héli arrived at the appointed hour he was greeted only by Cymodore’s distant cries for help. While she awaited the musical Arab youth, Ruthwen had seized her. Cymodore is represented in chains leaving 40 The Theology of Dracula

on a galley with Ruthwen as her captor, Nadour-Héli watching helplessly from shore. Later, Cymodore is discovered deﬁled, Ruthwen having sold the pure virgin and huntress into a potentate’s harem. While the old goddesses are defeated, the Christian virgin and her agent Bettina will help assure Ruth- wen’s defeat. Nodier’s Melo-drame Soon after his novel’s publication, Nodier’s melodrama Le Vampire, ou Lord Rutwen opened at the Porte Saint-Martin Theatre on the Boulevards, listing stage manager Carmouche and backer Jouffroy d’Abbans as co–authors. This time Nodier dared add his own name to the play. Nodier’s reworking of the Polidori novella as melodrama was immediately inﬂuential, spawning a veritable craze. Though frequently mentioned, this genre–transforming play is little considered by researchers. Like Fantasmagoriana, that French anthology of German Gothic tales being read at Villa Diodati when Byron threw down his “ghost story” challenge, which (when considered) is always approached through Mrs. Utterson’s related-though-materially-different Tales of the Dead, English-speaking commentators on Vampire literature content themselves with James Robinson Planché’s adaptation of Nodier’s play as if it were Nodier’s own, with nothing made of the differences between them. Even then, discussion of Planché’s Bride of the Isles is usually limited to repeating E. F. Bleiler’s story that the play was set in Scotland because of a stock of kilts in wardrobe (xxxviii), a blatant distortion of Planché’s statement: The Vampire, or the Bride of the Isles, was produced at the Lyceum, or English Opera House, as it was then called, on August 9, 1820. Mr. Samuel James Arnold, the proprietor and manager, had placed in my hands, for adaptation, a French melodrama, entitled Le Vampire, the scene of which was laid, with the usual recklessness of French dramatists, in Scotland, where the superstition never existed. I vainly endeavoured to induce Mr. Arnold to let me change it to some place in the east of Europe. He had set his heart on Scotch music and dresses—the latter, by the way, were in stock—laughed at my scruples, assured me that the public would neither know nor care [Planché 39–40]. The Scottish connection was hardly due to Gallic recklessness. Remaking the Ossianic connection Lady Caroline Lamb’s novel Glenarvon established with her character Clarence de Ruthven, Lord Glenarvon, Nodier infuses Rutwen with a Celtic dimension anchoring the vampire in the turbulent cross- currents of the classic and the Romantic, ultimately attracting the Anglo- Irish. As Montague Summers aptly observes, Le Vampire costumed the Genesis 41

Athenian revenant “in the true transpontine tradition of Ossianic attire” (307). Nodier, having set his revolutionary melodrama on the arch–Romantic Isle of Staffa, left Planché no choice but to follow suit. Pierced by Fingal’s Cave, the island of Staffa, which was “discovered” in 1772, attracted to its cathe- dral-like, sea-washed cavern such Romantic luminaries as Turner, Keats, Wordsworth, Scott, Tennyson, Mendelssohn, and Nodier. Developing the Ossianic element, Nodier introduces the entire MacPher- son-embroidered Ossian genealogy: Fingal, Malvina, Cromal and Oscar and their druidic transmigrating soul take up roles in the Vampire drama and eventually inform Stoker’s plural Quinceys. Moreover, Nodier’s insistence on Scottish rites seems hardly accidental, and may be due to something beyond Romantic love of highland mists. Nodier, son of Besançon’s Masonic lodge’s orator, was also a lodge member; recent years have seen repeated claims he was head of the Templar-like Magdalenian Gnostic cult Dan Brown features in The DaVinci Code, the Priory of Sion (431). Polidori penned an initiatory drama that nonetheless reads as a grotesque comedy. In it the principal, the Ruthven-Aubrey duality, traces a comic circuit that, after the course of a year, pirouettes towards the tragic on the 366th day’s ﬁnal reversal, when, in a race against midnight (one o’clock), Darkness extinguishes Light. English critics decried this departure as “odious”; a Parisian theatrical public would hardly have reacted more kindly. As melodrama insists on light’s triumph as its perfect plagal cadence, plot changes were unavoidable. Even with changes, one French critic, particularly complaining of an offstage attack on a young woman whose pursuit spills across the proscenium, force- fully questioned the play’s moral foundation, demanding to know how gov- ernment could allow such a “hideous and immoral play” (Collin de Maury back notices “de Quelques Nouveautés” 271) to be performed. To liquidate Rutwen, Nodier prolongs Polidori’s plot by minutes; too late for the Vampire to renew his lease on life through his annual marriage-feast, he, soulless, is condemned to the “void,” primordial chaos. Nodier’s three-act composition begins nearly where Polidori’s circuit reaches completion, with Aubray returned home from his voyage east. The scene, transported to the Western Sea’s isle, is given an emphatic Gothic quality. An interlude of light in darkness constitutes a prologue that ﬂows from Byron, Manfred’s Faust-inspired ﬁrst scene. The curtain rises to darkness, nothingness, “the void.” As gaslights ﬂare, a basaltic cavern, grottes de Staffa, is progressively revealed, the grottes reﬂecting the subject’s grotesque nature. Roughly carved geometrical tombs, pyramidal, cubic, columnar, ﬁll its depths. A sleeping beauty sprawled across the ground in this place where “all breathes of trepidation and terror” (330) brings forth protective spirits: Ituriel, angel of the moon, issues from above the proscenium; Oscar, genie of marriage, from within the cavern’s 42 The Theology of Dracula

depths. Ituriel evokes the angel of Paradise Lost whose spear unmasks the dia- bolic, no matter its disguise; Oscar incarnates Ossian’s son. Night’s ﬁrst moon- beams transform the Caledonian cavern into a Celtic Telesterion. A Shakespearean tempest drove the ingénue, who is due to marry on the morrow, into the malignant basaltic womb. The innocent ﬁancée hardly sus- pects that instead of falling into Love’s embrace, she risks falling into Death’s clutches, the sage Oscar observes. Ituriel demands an explanation, could it be “true that horrible phantoms sometimes appear, and under the pretence of exerting seigniorial rights of the hymen, cut the throat of a timid virgin to drink her blood?” (331) “Such monsters are called Vampires” (331), speciﬁes Oscar, remarking that one such, having desolated 20 countries, must add one more soul to his infamous roster within the coming hours. “He can take any form, make use of any language, ply any seduction” and though he appears alive, “his eyes expose his veritable status” (331). As a distant clock strikes one, the tombs yield their dead. A specter in his death shroud leaves his down- stage grave; approaching Miss Aubray he cries out “Malvina!” In a line Stoker would adapt, he claims: “She belongs to me!” (334) “She belongs to God,” retorts Oscar, “and you’ll soon belong to the void” (334). The pure, antique spirits watch over the maiden and spout Christian dogma as the clock’s somber tone fades and the darkening stage depletes vision. The tolling clock announces a French classic “unity” of time; the Vam- pire’s tragic day, like the Dionysian Anthesteria, runs from night to night, provoking a question as to whether a Dionysian imperative underlies Aristotle’s maxim on conﬁning a tragedy to a single circuit of the sun, or not much exceeding. Act one opens in Castle Staffa with servants discussing Malvina Aubray’s return, after their having searched her out all night. Hearing that she was lost near the grottoes, Scrop, a servant, remarks, “By St. George; that’s the only bit of forest that we neglected to search,” thereby connecting St. George to the literary vampire for the ﬁrst time. The domestics huddle to listen to for- bidden lore of the House of Staffa’s last heiress, who, on the day of her nuptial to a Scottish lord, disappeared near the caves, to be found soon thereafter covered in blood, her throat slashed. Her betrothed was never seen again. With the lord of Staffa having disappeared, Castle Staffa passed into the family of Sir Aubray. Periodicity, stressed from the beginning, is endowed with added resonance, as the murderous marriage occurred precisely 100 years prior. In possible incestuous reference, Scrop claims his grandfather’s great-uncle had heard from his grandmother’s grandfather that the lovers were victims of vam- pires. When Malvina’s domestic Brigitte thanks the gods that she had till then avoided the caves, Scrop derides her fears, saying that vampires only crave maidens’ blood. Genesis 43
