Malvina’s ﬁancé, Count Marsden, though endowed with vast holdings on the mainland facing the western isle, is unknown to all. Scrop chides fellow servant Edgar that the new lord should arrive just in time to witness his wed- ding. Enter Malvina, claiming to feel ﬁne despite her ordeal, though her soul is agitated—the fruit, she’s certain, of ill-dreamt dreams. She recalls phantoms leaving their graves, most particularly, the face of a young man who emerged from the pyramidal tomb of Fingal. His handsome features, uncanny paleness, and suffering appearance seemed to plead for her aid. As her heart melted in sympathy, his face decomposed, eyes becoming as hollow as the cavern. She dreamt she was destined to serve as victim to a devouring monster, but an unseen force wrenched her away and she found herself, suddenly awake, wan- dering the forest. An old man set her on a path towards the avenue where she almost at once encountered her brother Aubray who was out searching for her. At her mention of his name, enter Aubray to discuss wedding plans. Although he has never met Marsden, he declares Marsden’s brother Rutwen the “most seductive” (350) friend a man ever had. Having met in Athens, each an enthusiast “of Nature’s beauties and monuments to the Arts” (351), they became boon companions in travel and “in pleasure” (351). Sensing some- thing superhuman in Rutwen, Aubray was intent on their knotting a closer relationship. Rutwen sufﬁciently admired Aubrey’s miniature portrait of Malv- ina for him to suggest an alliance through marriage, an idea which Aubray eagerly adopted as his own. With Polidori, a miniature of Marsden had revealed Marsden as Ruthven to Aubrey; Nodier, in substituting a feminine subject while maintaining the motif of the miniature, alters the image’s function, it now serving to replace the drawing-room as a vehicle of introduction. Similar inversions are evi- denced in the exposition that Aubrey provides in recounting to Malvina Rutwen’s fatal day in Athens. One day Rutwen headed into the Athenian countryside to attend the wedding of a maiden whose dowry he had the generous urge to underwrite. Later that afternoon, Aubray set off to rendezvous with his friend as arranged some miles from Athens. Before he could reach their appointed meeting place however he unexpectedly crossed Rutwen’s path, the latter charging by, racing the setting sun towards the city. Rutwen had just enough time to warn Aubray to ﬂee before brigands fell upon them and forced Aubray to the ground. Rutwen had the gallantry and foresight to cover Aubray with his own body, but his heroic act cruelly rewarded him, for he absorbed a mortal blow, surely in Aubray’s place. Despite their absolute advantage, the assailants then van- ished into the dusk. Rutwen proclaimed himself honored to have preserved Aubray’s life, regretting only to die without becoming his brother-in-law. Genesis 45

Urging Aubray to escape lest the murderers return, he asked only to be turned so he might look upon the moon, “astre de la nuit” (352) to comfort him. Aubray complied, before leaving in search of his cowardly servants, all of whom had abandoned him to the brigands. Within the hour he returned to the place he had left Rutwen to discover him gone. Nodier thus amalgamates Polidori’s twin Grecian death scenes, Ianthe’s and Rutwen’s. Rutwen’s banditti have no interest in robbery or in Aubray; they were either hunting dark Death, whom they managed to kill, or seeking vengeance and the expiation of a crime—imperatives now satisﬁed. Aubray concludes by noting that when he forwarded Rutwen’s effects to Venice where Rutwen’s brother Marsden had established residence, he included Malvina’s portrait among the affairs in tribute to a heroic friend and his ill- fated betrothal. He was both delighted and surprised when Marsden wrote back to offer to accomplish what Rutwen no longer could and to unite their families through Malvina’s hand and his own. As Aubray completes his story, Marsden is announced. Malvina, too overwhelmed by her ordeal to welcome her ﬁancé, retires. Marsden, whose resemblance to Rutwen dumbfounds Aubray, admits that he is in fact Rutwen, miraculously saved from death. In a further twist of fate, brother Marsden died in Venice, leaving Rutwen heir to the mainland estates. A second recognition scene soon follows, for upon being presented to her ﬁancé, Malvina faints; his is the spectral face that invaded her cavern dream. Barely recovered, she ﬁnds herself under a spell when Ruthwen takes her hand. She breaks away, begging leave to consider anew his proposal. Rutwen urges Aubray to expedite the wedding; though he is not at liberty to explain his reason, he must reach London within 36 hours on a life or death matter. Aubray takes his leave of Rutwen to speak to his sister about advancing the wedding. A servant, Edgar, takes advantage of the interlude to step forward and request Lord Rutwen’s presence that afternoon at his own marriage to Miss Lovette, servant of Castle Marsden. Rutwen readily accepts, and orders his launch to be readied. Returning with the happy news that Malvina has consented to wed that evening, Aubray insists on accompanying Rutwen to the mainland to witness their servants’ nuptials. At Marsden, Lovette and her father Petterson, the estate manager, eagerly await both Edgar and their new master. Edgar appears ﬁrst to inform Petterson that Lord Rutwen, the new master, was arriving. Petterson, believing Rutwen dead for several years, suspects a fortune-hunting impostor, but when Rutwen appears, despite a seven-year absence, he instantly recognizes his unchanged features. When Petterson presents daughter Lovette to the lord, Rutwen ogles her. When Petterson orders the lovers to dance for the nobles, thunder growls. 46 The Theology of Dracula

When Rutwen declares his desire “to crown the maiden’s head” (371) by con- tributing to her dowry, it rolls to a crescendo. A bard, Oscar, emerges from out of the highland fog. To Lovette’s offer of drink, the old man promises that in exchange he’ll chant an epithalamium to her happiness and pray that the “Great Being” watch over her sleep. “Young virgin of Staffa,” his song begins, “burning with the ﬁrst ﬂame to set your heart a-trembling.... At the moment of uniting with the lover of your dreams, Be on guard of the kiss that brings Death.” With each successive strophe, Rutwen’s agitation increases. “When the desert sun no longer gilds the peaks, then the angels of hell come to caress their victim. If their sweet voices lull you to sleep, Pull back” (374). Oscar teaches that the Vampire is of night, winter, and approaches his victims through their dreams. Discerning Ruthwen’s perturbed state, Petterson interrupts Oscar and sends him away. To Lovette’s request that he visit her the next time he crosses the valley, Oscar replies that the morrow may be too late. Although Oscar’s “Great Being” is speciﬁcally Platonic, his bardic role emphasizes the Celtic, Ossianic frame. Not only does Oscar, son of Ossian, wander the stage as a bard, but Rutwen emerges from the tomb of Fingal, Ossian’s father, usurping heir to a godless reign. In giving Aubray’s previously anonymous sister the name “Malvina” to wear, Nodier attributes to her the name of Ossian’s granddaughter, blind Oscar’s daughter, conductress, muse, and survivor: “Then come thou, O Malvina—with all thy music, come; lay Ossian in the plain of Lutha: let his tomb rise in the lovely ﬁeld” (from MacPherson “Berrathon: A Poem” 193). As Petterson toasts his “virtuous master,” Aubray excuses himself to go to inform outlying lords of the count’s return so their presence might “ajoute à l’éclat de ton hymen” (376), ambiguously referencing either the “splendour of thy marriage” or “bursting of thine hymen.” As the cast ﬁles off, Edgar offers Lovette his arm to join them. Before they can leave, however, Rutwen interrupts. “Lovely Lovette,” he begins, “honour me by hearing me out” (376). Lovette answers that she is no longer her own mistress. “I hope that your betrothed” (376), continues Ruthven, bowing towards Edgar. Edgar, in recog- nition of his subservience, implores Lovette to indulge his lordship’s wishes, and exits. Rutwen orders the girl to come to him, but she hesitates. He urges her to fear not: “If you only knew what seeing you does to me” (377), he sighs, claiming she rekindles love’s once extinguished ﬂames—again he burns! “But sire,” starts Lovette, no doubt thinking of Malvina, “the one you love....” “Is dead!” he interrupts (376). He begs Lovette to indulge him and revive the presence of his departed “celestial” (376) lover. Word by silvered word, he gathers control over the lassie. Oscar’s reappearance with a renewal of his Genesis 47

refrain allows Lovette to break away. Released, she begins to cry. Rutwen, claiming her tears as his, insists she be his totally. She refuses a purse he places in her hand; an addition to her dowry, he says in encouragement. Just then, they are surrounded by people; compromising circumstances force Lovette to accept Rutwen’s binding gift, equivalent to the golden chain of the Corinthian bride. As her wedding feast begins, Lovette senses something has possessed her; her soul, like Malvina’s, is strangely altered. Feeling ill, she leaves the gath- ering; Rutwen follows in pursuit, Edgar pursuing the pursuer. A scream stops the revel. Lovette, clothes torn, rushes on to the stage, crying to her father to save her. Rutwen appears, Edgar at his heels. Edgar curses Rutwen and ﬁres a pistol. “Ah, I am dying!” (382) moans Rutwen as he collapses. The chorus encircles him; Lovette swoons. Action freezes. Aubray, coming to console his friend, restores the clockwork’s movement. He sends away the crowd. In the intimacy of life’s ﬁnal moments, Rutwen exacts from Aubray twin promises: to keep his death secret for 12 hours, and to carry him to a rock where he might pray while gazing upon the “astre de la nuit.” The act ends with Rutwen’s corpse, reunited with his celestial lover at last, bathed in moonlight. In a brightly lit Gothic hall, Brigitte reasons that if Oscar can tell the future, he can read her heart. Oscar replies that she wishes his reassurance about her mistress’s fate, but to save Malvina she must get her away from the castle before the new day’s ﬁrst hour strikes. As Oscar withdraws, Malvina enters, sparkling with pre–nuptial joy. Rutwen has just told her they must be off to London as soon as the ceremony has ended so he can present her to the king, undoubtedly referencing himself. Enter Aubray. Malvina asks her brother if he has seen Rutwen. Aubray sighs, burdened terribly by his sad news. “Milord ... alas!” (389) he struggles to begin. Malvina effervesces about wedding preparations, the voyage to Lon- don, how pleasant it would be should her dear brother accompany them. Heartbroken Aubray impatiently tells her to forget the wedding. When Malv- ina continues, claiming that Rutwen pledged love eternal but moments earlier, Aubray thinks her deluded. As he begins to reveal Rutwen’s death, Rutwen appears to remind him of his pledge. Aubray, revolting against a “phantom,” continues. As if Jesus with Thomas, Ruthven challenges Aubray to touch him. Malvina, with Rutwen’s encouragement, concludes that it is her brother who is mad for believing Rutwen dead. Aubray commands her not to wed, exposing the circumstances that led to Ruthven’s death. “Remember your pledge!” orders Rutwen “in a terrible voice” (393). Rutwen has Aubray seized as a madman. As he is carried off, Aubray tries to exact a promise from Malvina not to wed before the clock strikes one. 48 The Theology of Dracula

Strengthening the incest motif, Malvina confesses that her brother is a father to her, she can hardly act against his wishes. Rutwen tenderly laments his friend’s insanity and woos Malvina with phrases rehearsed on Lovette: She has rekindled a love once dead. He exacts from her a pledge to marry as planned. On Brigitte’s return, Rutwen exits. Malvina voices bright hope for the future; Brigitte, through asides, scep- ticism. Addressing Malvina, Brigitte insists that with Sir Aubray possessed the day will end badly for all. Devastated, Malvina moans that it is her wed- ding day. On those words, the strains of a severe march initiate the ceremony. Enter Rutwen. A door to a chapel opens; within, several servants attend. Rutwen orders Malvina to come. To hurry her along, he grabs her by the wrist and begins to drag her towards the chapel. From the wings, Aubray calls “Sister, my sister!” (399) Struggling against his servants, he enters. She is being led to the tomb, he warns—the priest is a minister of Death; there are torches, funeral ﬂames. Aubray incites the household against Rutwen. Deaf to their cries, Rutwen insists, “This woman is mine” (400), still pulling Malv- ina along by the wrist. With his free hand Rutwen pulls out a dagger and is about to stab brother and sister both when a bell tolls once and thunder rolls. “Le Néant! Le néant!” (401) cries the assembly: The Void! Nothingness! The dagger falls from the hand that clutched it. Featureless shades climb out of the earth to drag Rutwen into the underworld. Above the stage, an extermi- nating angel appears on a cloud; lightning ﬂashes; the curtain falls on a hail of ﬁre as Light triumphs over darkness. The names Rutwen and Aubray unambiguously reference Polidori’s Vampyre. In adapting Polidori’s novella, great efforts were made to maintain Nicolas Boileau’s “classical unities” of action, time, and place. Only in terms of “place” is Corneillean convention violated, permitting the day-night polar- ity’s materialization in Aubray’s Isle of Staffa and Rutwen’s Estate of Marsden. Western Aubrays and Eastern Rutwens, inhabiting contiguous estates and destined to be joined through marriage, have been each other’s heirs for a century, though they must visit a spot near Athens to make one another’s acquaintance. From Marsden, solar Aubray disappears to visit other districts. When Rutwen grabs Malvina by the wrist to drag her towards her marriage, the scene is literally mimetic, imitating the mythic act of Plouton who, appear- ing from the gaping earth, grabs Persephone by the wrist. It even might be imagined that Persephone is the dead true love Rutwen describes to Lovette and Malvina. This time, however, the gaping earth and enveloping shadows swallow Rutwen alone. Nodier has introduced a new grotesque to the stage, personiﬁed an antique god, and placed it in a new form of melodrama inﬂuenced by Byron’s “classical” Manfred. Rutwen has been contained by a melodramatic form, a Genesis 49

comic form, and has thus been rendered non–threatening; no Byronic hero, he becomes in the public’s mind a pure villain, leaving Aubray to share the hero’s role with Oscar. In having his modern grotesque dispatched to noth- ingness, Nodier has also constructed a cautionary tale attached to his concerns for the epistemological difﬁculties of agnosticism, the direction of the “new” Romanticists, warning anew against “a kind of voluptuousness in plunging into nihilism” (qtd. Oliver 138). In representing “the idea upon which is founded those romantic ﬁctions which belong to an order of seething passions unknown to the ancients, but too real and exalted not to be poetic” (qtd. Oliver 138), Nodier represents the Byronic. When Rutwen succumbs, he depicts the Byronic undone, falling to modernity’s inescapable nihilism. The Bride of the Isles Samuel Arnold, proprietor of London’s English Opera House, remarked Le Vampire’s wild Parisian success, and, to cash in on the vogue, commissioned James Robinson Planché to adapt and translate Nodier’s melodrama. Planché’s play, scored by Joseph Binns Hart, premiered in August 1820, barely two months after Rutwen’s Parisian debut. The success that greeted Arnold’s proj- ect was such that the play was exported to France, running before sold-out houses in Paris concurrent to those for Nodier’s at the Porte Saint-Martin. Critics raged now at a fashion, not an aberration. Planché’s trimmed two-act “Romantic Melodrama” resembles Nodier’s, but its discrepancies are noteworthy. The play opens in the familiar cavern on Staffa, Planché labeling his prologue “Introductory Vision,” a terminology suggesting an afﬁnity with “vision scenes” of later melodramas. Miltonian Ithuriel becomes a Shakespearean Ariel; Oscar is replaced by Unda; Malvina is rechristened Lady Margaret, likely in homage to Goethe. Outdoing Nodier, the set inverses the function of the proscenium, positioning the audience as if it were looking out from within the cavern at sea and sky. Unda rises from the depths and works an incantation; reinforced by a new presence, an unseen chorus, she summons Ariel: “By the sun that hath set, In the Waves I love; On the eve that renews: The fair moon’s birth.” The chorus chants, “Appear! appear!” (14) Winged Ariel, draped in a star-spangled white muslin gown and covered by a skyblue robe, descends on a silvery cloud from above the proscenium, head crowned by a tiara, silver wand in hand. The spirits of Heaven and Earth set to work on the behalf of the sleeping virgin, a pearl enclosed in a grotesque shell. Unda, “Spirit of the Flood,” explains that wicked souls exist who, through evil, “enter the dead forms of other men, Assume their speech, their 50 The Theology of Dracula

habits and their knowledge, And thus roam o’er the Earth; but subject still, At stated periods, to a dreadful tribute” (15). The reanimation of cadavers by “wicked souls” separates this vampire from Polidori’s, in the words of the Monthly Review of 1819, “bustling inhab- itant of the world” and Nodier’s soulless body, to place it in a context of demonic possession. The spirits review a vampire’s annual obligation of drain- ing a maiden’s blood to avoid being reduced to “nothingness, total annihila- tion” (15), inexplicably Heaven’s worst punishment for a “wicked soul.” Unda explains that the relics of “Cromal the Bloody,” lie within and that it is he, in the form of the earl of Marsden, who terrorizes the earth. Cromal intends to wed Margaret and thereby renew his terrestrial term. Cromal brings the Vampire once again into direct contact with Ossian. Pagan Cromal, usurper of the theocratic order of the druids in order to assure his position as ﬁrst hereditary chief, Vergobretus, has returned, replacing Nodier’s Fingal in the tomb. It is he, blood-crazed temporal ruler, who must renew himself by activating Marsden’s body. In “Fingal’s rocky sepulchre,” the spirits of air and sea conjure the chthonic vampire before sleeping Margaret: “Let thy vampire–corpse appear To this sleeping maiden’s eyes.... That the form she may know ... And shun thee, till the setting ray... Phantom, from thy tomb so drear, At our bidding rise!—Appear!” (16) To a peal of thunder, Cro- mal’s tomb opens; the vampire lunges at the maiden, claiming her as mine. “Down, down!” (16) Unda commands, driving the vampire back to his grave. In a variation on the Arabian Nights’ “Tale of the Ghoul and the Prince” and certain incidents of Nodier’s roman, Margaret was in pursuit of red-deer (15) when a storm separated her from her hunting party and forced her to shelter in the cavern. The image of virginal Margaret as huntress brings Diana and Darvell’s Ephesian pilgrimage to the fore as embedded associations. Hunter shall become hunted, ﬁrst with Margaret, then with Ruthven. Planché, casually violating another convention of the Vampire Tale, sub- stitutes Lady Margaret’s father, Sir Ronald, for Aubray. Perhaps this was intended to mirror the vampire’s Cromal-Fingal generational shift. James MacPherson claimed Cromal, Fingal’s father, died in battle at the precise moment of Fingal’s birth, son renewing father, father being given new life, his son’s, through blood, his own. A somewhat similar type of metempsychosis is already at work in Planché’s Vampire. Ronald, traveling with his son Aubray, encountered the endearing Ruthven in Greece. A clash with bandits cost Aubray his life, but Ruthven, who saved Sir Ronald, ﬁlled the void in his father’s heart, Ruthven effectively becoming Aubray. The father-brother inver- sion thus serves to intensify dangerous relations, a father vehemently wishing his daughter to marry a man he has come to view as his son, rather than one brother working to mate his sister with another. This innovation displaces a Genesis 51

relationship fundamental to the Vampire Tale—sibling incest—without offer- ing ritual justiﬁcation. It also deprives Margaret of orphan status. Changes of names and idiom little modify the play’s ﬁrst scenes, but when Marsden and Ruthven are discovered to be one and the same a second fundamental departure from canon occurs. When Margaret faints, her father escorts her offstage, leaving an agitated Ruthven alone. Planché has isolated his vampire to set up a soliloquy in which he expresses remorse, recalls a with- ered conscience, and portrays himself as an unwilling agent of murder: Demon as I am, that walk the earth to slaughter and devour! The little that remains of heart within this wizard frame, sustained alone by human blood, shrinks from the appalling act of planting misery in the bosom of this veteran chieftain. Still must the fearful sacriﬁce be made, and suddenly, for the approaching night will ﬁnd my wretched frame exhausted—and darkness—worse than death—annihilation is my lot! Margaret! Unhappy maid! Thou art my destined prey: thy blood must feed a Vampire’s life, and prove the food of his disgusting banquet [26–7]. Planché then labors to lend Nodier’s double wedding what seems to him greater rationality. Hearing of servant Robert’s marriage gives Ruthven the idea to satisfy his need for a ripe maiden’s blood in time for his renewal while relieving him of the need to drain Margaret. This seemingly arbitrary coin- cidence explains his delight at learning of the impending marriage. Substi- tuting himself for Robert, he can glut his thirst by exercising his droits de seigneur over the servile girl he has renamed Efﬁe. When Ruthven declares his love, Efﬁe is confused, ﬂattered, repelled. Ruthven seizes her, carrying her off bodily, stage right. Robert enters stage left; looking afar, he cries out, “Villain!” (31) Drawing a pistol, he chases after them as the stage goes dark. When the lights rise anew Andrew, the mainland bride’s father, and Ronald, the island bride’s father, enter, wondering what could have happened to Ruthven. The sounds of shots ﬁred and Efﬁe screaming “Save me!” send Andrew running off. Ruthven staggers on stage to say: “I die!” Stage directions indicate that the moon can now be seen rising. Ruthven begs Ronald to prom- ise him the fulﬁlment of a last request. Ronald quickly promises, but Ruthven, unsatisﬁed, insists he make solemn oath. With the oath pledged Ruthven orders Ronald to “[c]onceal my death from every human being till yonder moon ... shall be set this night” (31). Resurrecting Byron, he explains that Ronald must take a ring “and, ere an hour shall elapse after I have expired, throw this ring into the waves that wash the tomb of Fingal” (31). As Ronald fervently repeats “I will, I will!” Ruthven dies, a reminder on his lips: “Remem- ber your oath. The lamp of night is descending the blue heavens; when I am dead, let its sweet light shine on me. Farewell!” (31) In an apparent continuity error, Cromal’s tomb has become Fingal’s. 52 The Theology of Dracula

To music, Andrew, Robert and Efﬁe approach Fingal’s Cave in a boat to leave Robert with provisions for his survival until Ronald’s anger has abated. After a farewell duet, Efﬁe is rowed off by her father. Soon thereafter a boat carrying Ronald approaches the island. In the cave, Ronald proclaims that his soul has been altered and wonders what the ceremony he is performing could mean. Why would Ruthven wish his death kept secret till the moon set? He tosses the ring into the waters. Over rolling thunder Ruthven is heard intoning “Remember thy oath!” Ronald calls out, “his spirit speaks! Ruthven, my friend, my preserver!” (34) Robert steals forth from the shadows to claim his inno- cence and explain his role as defender of Efﬁe’s honor. Ronald grabs him, casting him into the sea. Boarding his launch Ronald declaims: “Ruthven, thou art revenged!” (34) As the boat pushes off, Robert is revealed clinging to a rock. At the castle, the wedding is about to begin so that Ruthven can be off “ere daybreak” (34). When Ronald arrives, Margaret tells him to get ready, Ruthven will soon be there. Before he can explain that the wedding cannot go forward, Ruthven is among them. “Fiend!” hisses Sir Ronald. Kept in con- stant reminder of the oath, Ronald rages. Ruthven declares him mad, and has the servants restrain him. Ronald pleads with his daughter not to marry before the moon has set. Margaret can only manage to exclaim “Oh, my poor father!” before fainting into Ruthven’s arms, a transference having been made. As he is taken away, Ronald declaims: “A mist seems clearing from my sight; and I behold thee now—oh, horror! Horror!—a monster of the grave— a—a Vam—” (36). Although he collapses before he can utter the difﬁcult word, Margaret suddenly snaps to her senses. Ronald has suffered a relapse of a con- dition developed when her brother’s death inﬂicted a shock upon his reason, explains Ruthven. Margaret hadn’t known of her father’s fragility of mind, but ﬁnds his wish to delay the wedding until the moon sets reasonable. To Ruthven questioning if she loves him not, Margaret asks how could he doubt her? Ruthven then asks her to accept the ring so recently thrown into the sea as his sacred pledge. In a sublimated wedding ceremony, he kisses it and places it on her ﬁnger, proclaiming in an aside, “her fate is sealed—she cannot now retract” (37). Margaret, her conﬂicted heart ready to burst, is sent off to ready herself. Outside the castle, Andrew and Efﬁe aid sea-battered Robert. Having noticed Ronald’s boat, they returned to the cave and rescued Robert. Robert insists on going to see Ronald: “I know his noble nature too well to fear a continuance of his anger” (38), he says of the man who minutes earlier attempted to murder him. Efﬁe breaks into song. Another voice takes it up. Robert recognizes the singer as Ronald’s “henchman.” The servant staggers in, bemoaning his master’s folly. Accosted by Robert, he explains Ronald’s Genesis 53

condition. Hearing that Marsden lives and the wedding is underway, they charge off to “foil the villain” (39). In a chapel through whose “Gothic Window” “the moon is seen going down” (40), all await as music plays. Ruthven paraphrases Ariel and Unda: “Ere yon orb shall kiss the wave, the tributary victim shall be paid” (40). Thunder peals. Ruthven grabs Margaret’s wrist to drag her to the altar. Mar- garet begs him to wait. “Nay ... Father commence the rites” (41), snarls Ruthven. Before he can, Robert, Ronald, Andrew, Efﬁe, and attendants invade the chapel. Ronald forbids the marriage; Margaret now throws herself into her father’s arms. A blast of wind blows open the casement. Ronald calls out that the moon is disappearing beneath the waves. Ruthven again grabs Mar- garet by the wrist and draws his dagger, taking aim for Ronald, but the servant Robert wrests the arm away. Margaret seeing the moon set, declares herself Ruthven’s, to which he responds, “I am lost” (42). A great thunderclap announces Unda and Ariel; a thunderbolt strikes Ruthven, who disappears into the earth through the famous “vampire trap.” In his Recollections, Planché expresses satisfaction with his Vampire, noting that the play was continually in revival a half-century after its premiere. 54 The Theology of Dracula

Revelation “He had evidently forgotten all about the dark stranger, as in his illness he had forgotten all that this episode had reminded him of. I don’t like this lapsing into forgetfulness; it may make or continue some injury to the brain. I must not ask him, for fear I shall do more harm than good; but I must somehow learn the facts of his journey abroad. The time is come, I fear, when I must open that parcel and know what is written” [156]. While the Vampire Tale retains to this day the Byron-implied Mysteries discourse Polidori so brilliantly embroidered, Polidori’s Vampyre, characterized in the British press as “a ﬁlthy tale” “devoid of all merit” (Edinburgh Monthly Review 1819, 618–20), was doomed to oblivion until, as Byron phrased it, “it was got up as a melo-drame at Paris.” The being that became canonical in Stoker’s hands washed up on English shores not from Transylvania but from across la Manche. Planché’s role in this transaction was both slight and pivotal, he hardly understood the thing he was hired to translate and badly wanted to re-costume, but in earning his daily bread he brought the Vampire an enduring success with English-speaking theatrical audiences. It was Nodier who made the Vampire a stock character in a new and enduring Commedia dell’Arte where it has ﬂourished ever since, a star of stage and screen, but he did so at a remove. In reforming Polidori’s “triﬂe” Nodier bequeathed its occulted theme to later generations of French Romantics, most notably Théophile Gauthier, and Alexadre Dumas, père, and, through him, the Irish, and most particularly Abraham Stoker. Nodier’s Vampire, necessarily not Polidori’s, was in fact scarcely his own. His roman, while defeating the pagan and positing a love beyond the grave, is most concerned with denigrating the amoral, agnostic turn of modernity, even staging a seduction scene in the Sistine Chapel, a Roman matron attempting to corrupt a Moslem Arab youth. His melodrama posits a pagan element, Celtic and Ossianic, existing without gods—the druids having been overthrown 55

and banished by Cromal. In sending the Vampire back to its nihilistic origins Nodier simply defeats godlessness. Although Nodier claimed to be dedicated to making his work subservient to a Christian ideal, passing reference to St. George and the idea of annihilation as divine punishment for the soulless seem far too vague and grossly insufﬁcient. The drama, manifesting little tran- scendent-yet-chivalrously romantic love, reads as a misshaped morality play, conceding the attractiveness of the frénétique while railing against its inherent nihilism. Having interjected the Vampire into the theatrical world Stoker inhab- ited, Nodier abandoned it to pursue his further ambitions. It would wait a generation to be reclaimed until Alexandre Dumas, with silent partner Auguste Maquet, came along to apply a post–Restoration veneer to Le Vampire and to tint it with a dogma so faithfully Catholic that it would make Abraham van Helsing possible. To mitigate Ruthven’s frenzied nature, Dumas injects him into a féerique, a traditional, trouvère–ﬂavored secular theatrical form returned from the middle-ages and related to Adam de la Halle’s Jeu de la Feuillée with Renaissance reverberations in Shakespeare’s A Midsummer’s Night Dream’s Green George and Celtic allusions. This contributory strand of French mélo-drame’s fashion ascended with Napoleon III at mid–century. Surpris- ingly, through the intervention of faeries and pixies, Dumas’ homage, pro- jecting a more clearly articulated statement of love and highly evolved appeal to Christian symbols, better serves Nodier’s thematic priorities than Nodier managed himself. Dumas’ particularly ludic play plays on the polysemous nature of Christian symbols, making his Vampire, as will be shown, narrowly and decisively relevant to Stoker’s. As much as any human agent, Nostalgia wrote this particular Le Vampire. Setting out at mid–century to draft Mes Mémoires, Dumas recalled arriving at the capital the proverbial callow provincial. Fortuitous circumstances on a glorious day of a sudden and unexpected Dionysian initiation conspired to have him see the opening performance of 1823’s revival of Le Vampire, ou Lord Rutwen, in which Nodier adapts certain of Planché’s innovations. It marked both the ﬁrst truly Romantic confection Dumas had ever experienced and his illuminating discovery of melodrama. Through his recollection of that introduction to the Boulevard theatres and the vampire superstition, of his chance meeting with the bafﬂing, erudite Nodier, his subsequent atten- dance at Nodier’s weekly soirées at the Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal at which authors like Hugo and himself gained entry into the burgeoning Romantic literary scene, Dumas went back and consulted Lord Rutwen’s text. Seeing it all re–enacted in his mind, he was inspired, a long, successful quarter-century later, to rewrite the play. Nodier, dead for the better part of a decade at mid– century, had provided Dumas with exceptional insight into his thinking on 56 The Theology of Dracula

the play, nearly in the way that Byron had privileged Polidori with his concept for the Vampire. This thus made the subject a perfect vehicle for Dumas to pay homage to a mentor. Le Vampire, Drame Fantastique en cinq actes, en dix tableaux, en société avec M. Auguste Maquet premiered at the Ambigu-Comique at 1851’s winter solstice. The play, only recently translated into English, formed the basis for Dion Boucicault’s The Phantom. In that the translation, which remains obscure, fails to discern fully the symbolic system engaged, it will be useful to review the play as written. Le Vampire, Drame Fantastique Its curtain rises on a Spanish inn’s courtyard. In an out-of-place nod to classicism, a dialogue between chorus and a gypsy sets the scene. Alternating, they sing about the ruins of Tormenar Castle. Who lives there? their song asks. A double answer returns: terror by day, death by night. Enter innkeeper Juan Rozo, his daughter Petra, her ﬁancé Botaro, and a servant ostentatiously named Lazarus. Rozo chases off the gypsies, saying he needs every inch of space. Lazarus muses he doesn’t see how Senor Rozo will be able to lodge everyone. Botaro, too, ﬁnds it difﬁcult to believe Rozo’s inn will accommodate the entire wedding party. Boasting that his inn has already lodged “50 Chris- tians,” Rozo dismisses their concerns. Lazarus reminds his master the 50 Christians were swearing like 100 pagans by morning, and Botaro rejoins that the wedding party consists of 77, not 50.... But what does it matter, he adds, as long as the bride is well bedded! Lazarus accuses the groom of selﬁshness. Botaro asks his soon-to-be father-in-law what he will do if travelers arrive. “I’ll tell them there’s no room!” comes the ﬁrm reply. Botaro wonders if his attitude is compatible with an innkeeper’s vocation, to which Rozo declares that for his daughter’s wedding, his house is simply his home, not an inn, though guests in residence will not be evicted. As in Nodier’s play, the audience is invited to a simple wedding. Rather than an estate keeper, an innkeeper is giving away his daughter. The sole and singular guest is a Moor who “only eats a few grains of rice ... with a pair of ivory chop-sticks” (402). Lazarus is convinced she gets up in the middle of the night “to eat olla podrida and garbachos” (402) since no human being could survive on her diet. On Botaro’s suggestion, it is decided that to make room at the inn Lazarus should ﬁnd himself some other place for the night. As he is being escorted to the establishment’s gates, visitors arrive. A husband, wife and children join the assembly. Lazarus greets them by advising that the boss says there’s no room at the inn. Rozo calls over to Lazarus to ﬁnd out what they want, and Revelation 57

Lazarus claims that they’ve journeyed since dawn and will accept any uncom- fortable corner. The new arrivals said nothing of the kind—Lazarus is pleading in their stead. Botaro suggests they take the attic where Lazarus slept, an idea that Rozo greedily pounces on, instructing Lazarus to conduct the family to his room. This sparks a series of protests by Lazarus, all dismissed. When Lazarus asks why he is being driven away from his resting place, Rozo reveals he is suspected of ﬂirting with his daughter by her ﬁancé. Lazarus maintains he was only helping her with something in her eye. One might imagine that the something was desire. He is ordered off again. Protesting hunger, he is told to take a crust of bread and cheese. Here it is, the day of a wedding feast, and all I get is bread and cheese, he grumbles. A compromise is negotiated: He can eat at the inn, but must sleep elsewhere. Petra, who has observed the entire exchange, sighs, “Poor Lazarus!” (407) Alone, Lazarus complains bitterly, “put out of doors, into the night, into a mountainous wilderness where evil spirits skulk along the pathways and at midnight the black château of Tormenar expels bats, vultures, owls, serpents ... all because I blew into a young lady’s eye” (407). From a safe distance, he contemplates the Moor, troubled by what he calls her “evil eye.” An odd pair of eyes, one desirous, the other envious, seems to be deliberately formed from the features of Petra and the Moor. While Lazarus ruminates, he is called for, but, since no longer attached to the household, rather than respond, he turns on his heel and wishes them to the devil. In the distance, he claims to spy mules, soon qualiﬁed as a single mule, with a lone voyageur, a woman. Once arrived, the woman asks Lazarus to whom she might speak; he proposes himself. She asks if she hasn’t arrived at a hotel. An inn, corrects Lazarus, that takes no guests. The woman is in need of a servant and will pay generously. Lazarus remarks she has come to the right place; he happens to be looking for work, proposing his service as mule driver, valet, cook. The lady, Juana, seeks a guide only. Lazarus, claiming to know every rock and crevice in the neighborhood, is hired on the spot and pressed to set out. “Now?” asks Lazarus; “Now!” answers his new employer. To Lazarus’s next logical question, “Where are we going?” comes the only possible answer in this pared-down universe: “Tormenar.” Comedy follows, Lazarus listing rea- sons to avoid Tormenar, but Juana is adamant, she must go there that night. She offers him ten times a guide’s normal pay. He swears “not for one hundred, nay a thousand times the pay” (409) will he go. Juana says she’ll ﬁnd someone braver. “You’ll see, senora!” Lazarus cries out, “Hey! Christians! Hey! pagans! Hey! everyone! The senora is ready to pay 10 piastres for a guide” (409). Vol- unteers come rushing. Lazarus continues, “to lead her to Tormenar!” The population of guides as quickly vanishes. In an aside, Juana says, “My God! But he will await me; he’ll believe that I failed to keep my word” (410). 58 The Theology of Dracula

Innkeeper and betrothed enter into the fray, Lazarus identifying the boss to Juana. She sets out her mission, venturing that the innkeeper surely doesn’t share in the pleasants’ superstition. Hearing her destination, he exclaims: “Tormenar! Holy Virgin!” Botaro echoes his prayer, “Tormenar! Lord Jesus!” (410) Juana deﬁantly declares she’ll go alone. From the far side of the courtyard gate a voice calls. The innkeeper orders Lazarus to see who’s there, but Lazarus, no longer employed, refuses. The voice, grown louder, demands the gates opened, a group of eight horsemen and four ladies awaits. To the innkeeper’s claim the house is full, the voice assures the ladies the gates will open. The innkeeper contradicts him. The voice, belonging to a Count Gilbert, says in such a case he should take down the sign advertising his inn, and offers to save him the trouble. Pistol shots explicate the sense of his proposition. Gilbert orders his companions to batter the gate. A storm threatens, he says, and the ladies have no desire to spend the night exposed to the elements. To Rozo’s repeated refusal, the door is bro- ken down. With the company inside, Rozo continues pleading how full his house is, with aunts, uncles, cousins, brothers, and sisters. Gilbert, pointing out the Moor, snaps, there’s a strange one, part of your family, too? Rozo explains her status as a lodger since the previous day. In asides, Gilbert declares the Moor “sombre featured”; she, looking him over, pronounces him “handsome” (414). Gilbert asks if there is no other place nearby, a house, an inn, a castle? Botaro volunteers there is a castle nearby, but... “But what?” (414) challenges Gilbert. The castle’s malignant presence is recounted. Disparaging supersti- tion, Gilbert urges his companions to follow him there. Before they leave, however, stories of what happens to the castle’s visitors are related. Gilbert, suspecting bandits, is assured that corpses are found at the castle with their jewellery and gold intact. Gilbert reminds his party they wield eight swords, declaring himself unafraid. On Lazarus’s suggestion, Juana asks to accompany Gilbert. She introduces herself as the Marquis of Torillas’s only daughter, in ﬂight from a convent where she was conﬁned to prevent her marrying Louis de Figuerroa, to whom she is betrothed before God. She has come to this remote region because of a letter from Luis, Catalonia’s most handsome noble- man, assigning a meeting that night at Tormenar. Gilbert, too, reveals his origins. He hails from Brittany and has a ten- derly-loved sister. Offering his arm, he promises to treat Juana as he would wish his sister treated should she ﬁnd herself in a comparable situation. Lazarus, who has taken a liking to Gilbert, offers his services to this newly arrived hero, an arrangement that is never quite concluded. Gilbert asks the innkeeper for food if he has no room. The groom agrees to hand over part of the wedding feast to be rid of the intruders. Claps of thunder peal as the travelers Revelation 59

take leave of the inn with cries of “adieu”: “to God.” The innkeeper’s family sets off to dine, leaving only the Moor. “It will take you two hours to ﬁnd your ﬁancé,” she remarks. “I’ll have caught up to him in three minutes!” (420) Act two opens in a vast, column-lined salon. The opened frame of a large ruined window reveals a storm gathering over mountains. Old portraits in worm-eaten frames, Gothic furnishings, and an immense ﬁreplace complete the décor. Immediately, the Moor skulks out of a doorway as a distant clock strikes 11. “He was young! handsome! ... and now here am I, young and beau- tiful once again!” (420) Approaching voices tell of Gilbert’s arrival, he is heard helping a laughing woman. Promising, “till next year, Gilbert!” (420) the Moor ﬂies off through the window. Enter the travelers, admiring the room’s magniﬁcence. As some light candles and others gather scraps of wood, provisions from the wedding feast are laid out on a great table. Juana notes that though it is after 11 o’clock Luis hasn’t arrived. Gilbert tries to comfort her, reminding her of the road’s con- dition, the storm’s force, and the trouble their party of 12 had climbing to the château. That is precisely what troubles her. Gilbert offers that don Luis is undoubtedly a brave cavalier, strong enough to face any adversary. Juana reminds Gilbert that some dangers cannot be combated by the sword. Gilbert refuses to believe her intimidated by “chimerical terrors.” Juana is haunted by a sense of foreboding, distraught at not ﬁnding Luis at Tormenar. The Breton recalls how she had so recently been clutching his arm and laughing when the mule carrying their victuals, swept off its feet by the currents, was almost lost, joking that it had threatened to reverse the miracle at Cana by changing their wine into water. Her humor changed, she says, on entering Tormenar, whose cold chilled her soul; she daren’t even look around. She describes a difﬁculty in breathing, and, as if recalling an incident of Nodier’s novel, a sensation, in entering Tormenar, of being a bird who seeking a seed is trapped in a cage set to ensnare her. Cursing Tormenar’s blackened walls for afﬂicting her so, Gilbert, rein- forcing the parallelism established between Juana’s mood and Tormenar, pro- poses ﬁre, food, wine, and conversation to banish gloom from the castle walls and her spirit. The candles on the table, says Gilbert, will serve as beacons to any lost traveler. Another of the company offers that should any ghosts be present they’ll at least be able to see them. Gilbert says that, though a child of the Château de Tiffauges and practically godchild to the fairy Mélusine, he little believes in ghosts, but strongly in bandits of the Spanish Sierras. But, comes the question, why would anyone murder without stealing? In order to terrify and secure Tormenar as a base, reasons Gilbert, proposing to post sen- tries at strategic points throughout the night. He sounds a horn to summon the travelers to the table. Gilbert insists they are 12 to have come to Tormenar, 60 The Theology of Dracula

though at the inn, before Juana joined them, he claimed they were already eight cavaliers and four ladies—a continuity error serving to stress the impor- tance the authors attached to constituting a party of 12. Gilbert, offering Juana “two drops of wine” and some rabbit pâté, says, “We are in the country of Sancho, the kingdom of proverbs” (424). We are also with Nodier at the Porte Saint-Martin in 1823, for after a series of exchanges on Tormenar, superstitions, Bretons, Gilbert (alluding to an entr’acte conversation between Nodier and Dumas at Nodier’s Vampire) asserts that he had never said he didn’t believe in ghosts—only that he wasn’t afraid of them and hadn’t seen any recently. Intrigued companions ask when he had last seen a supernatural being. Gilbert answers, not since coming of age, admitting, however, a belief in the supernatural, asking why should man con- stitute the highest level of creation? Another voyager remarks he has faith in the glass of wine in his hand because he can see it, drink it, but cannot believe in things imperceptible. Gilbert,—further referencing Nodier, asserts the Marquis is mistaken; micro- scopic beings, though invisible, are every bit as real as themselves. He had seen them, with the aid of a microscope, only last year, which doesn’t mean they hadn’t existed for the last six thousand, adding, not a peasant in Brittany goes without an elf to help with his horses, or a sprite to assist with other chores. He himself has a fairy residing in a tapestry, explaining that the lords of Tiffauges see the light of day in a chamber known as the tapestry room, indeed his own case. He spent his infancy there watching the fairy dance quadrilles to a silent melody, and can’t say if it happened in any reality other than his imagination. Every night he would watch Mélusine sweep across the ﬂoor, while a hunter, also a tapestry resident, chased a stag around the room, and birds ﬂuttered forth to fan him in his cradle. The fairy, pale and smiling, would sing him a song “whose melody and lyrics have since been lost in the noise and agitation of this world made up of materialism and the real” (427). Another voyager, saying each country cultivates its native superstitions, tells of visiting Epire, where the population fears a terrible ghoul who appears immensely beautiful to attract handsome youths whose blood she then drinks with abandon. Gilbert, hearing Juana express her horror, adds that if she had been French she would have known of such creatures through Antoine Galland (ﬁrst European translator and, no doubt, partial author of The Thousand and One Nights), and how such a one, who would eat but a few grains of rice with ivory chopsticks at her familial repast, was discovered feasting on a bloody meal by her husband, who followed her during her nocturnal wanderings. Juana asks if any had seen such a creature. The Marquis had seen a woman Revelation 61

reputed to be a ghoul. When he is asked what she was like, he says she was like every other woman but a little paler, thinner, with staring, owl-like eyes. To Gilbert asking if she were beautiful, the Marquis judiciously states, “more beautiful than not” (428). Juana doubts such a monster could be beautiful. The Marquis terms such women “coquettish,” as they carefully select their prey, choosing only men that are handsome or loved by another. “They hide in some desolate place, following in their victim’s wake, to put him to sleep with the whisper of their great wings, and, once asleep, they suck his life’s blood in a deadly embrace; then, invisible, they witness the pain of the ﬁancé whose tears they drink with the same voluptuousness as they had consumed the blood” (428). Juana protests the subject’s grotesque nature, Gilbert conceding the con- versation’s somber turn. She asks Gilbert if he won’t go seek out Luis. Morning brings answers, he replies, outside “branches break, nocturnal birds, fright- ened, collide in the air; we, here, savour the innkeeper’s wedding feast, drink to the health of those dear to us, and ourselves, holding hands, defy fairies, thieves, ghouls and vampires” (429). Unsatisﬁed, Juana repeats her plea. Gilbert suggests they go to the balcony with torches and call out; if Luis replies, they can set out after him. With his proposition accepted, he escorts Juana out to the balcony with a torch, calling out for Luis as they go. Meanwhile, the raconteurs continue, a second voyager telling that though he had never seen one, he once visited a family of Pern, Jews, who had a beau- tiful daughter whose portrait he had seen, and .... Juana’s scream, her torch having been extinguished by the wind, interrupts the story’s thread. Juana and Gilbert re-enter. The storyteller is urged on. The clock begins striking the midnight hour. The traveler says that a noise of the wind, much like that which they were then listening to, continued to howl at the moon as the clock began to strike the ultimate hour, now years ago, when suddenly, at the last chime of the midnight, the door slowly opened to reveal a vampire. At that point in the traveler’s tale, midnight’s 12th tone was, as in the narration, striking. When, in a mise-en-abîme, the door to the chamber of Tormenar squeaks open, the startled members of the party all want to know “Who’s there?” “Oh, excuse me, Mesdames, messieurs, I am so sorry to disturb you,” replies a stranger. “I’m but a simple voyager” (431). His name is Ruthven, Lord Ruthven. Having seen the signals from below, he came seeking shelter for the night. Gilbert demands pardon for their lack of cordiality, but his arrival was so unexpected. Looking at Juana, Ruthven apologizes for any shock he has occasioned. Juana says, in fact, it was merely that his arrival coincided so strangely with their conversation. Ruthven asks what they were discussing. A voyager discloses that they were speaking of vampires. The raconteur insists 62 The Theology of Dracula

that in Hungary it’s not rare to hear of such devils. Ruthven readily agrees, but remarks that what is truly rare is to see one of those monsters. He had been in Hungary and heard the stories, but never actually saw a vampire; he begs they change the subject to something gayer. The assorted nobles present themselves. Gilbert receives an afﬁrmative reply when he ask Ruthven if he is armed. And your provisions? They follow with a servant, a servant undoubtedly aware of Tormenar’s legend which might considerably slow his progress. But, protests Gilbert, they may be lost. Ruthven does not think so. He has hired a local lad encountered in the vicinity of the nearby inn. Taking Luis’ place, Ruthven joins the party, the 13th at table. Enter Lazarus, declaring he hadn’t believed that any man could have lived through the torments of fear he’d just experienced. Having already missed two chances to visit Tormenar, a third opportunity decided him on coming. Juana and Gilbert greet him warmly. A traveler remarks that Ruthven neither drinks nor eats. The cold has stolen my appetite, replies Ruthven. Lazarus ﬁnds the cold’s effects curious, declaring he hadn’t his master’s nature: He is famished. The travelers ask about the legend of Tormenar. Lazarus, too afraid to tell the castle’s story in the castle itself, refuses to recount Tormenar’s history. Offered a glass of wine, he drinks it, but still won’t talk. More wine is forth- coming. When the comic interlude ends after three large glasses are downed, Lazarus is interrogated not on the castle but on the count of Tormenar, and initially denies that any such prior exists. He soon qualiﬁes his absolute. Fifty years earlier, or some say one thousand, while others insist that none of it ever happened, there were three counts of Tormenar, brothers. Today, if Tormenar has a master, it would be a great-great-cousin who didn’t bear the Tormenar family name. Each count of Tormenar had a Catalonian castle. The youngest and most villainous invited his brothers to dine at the table where they now gathered; he brilliantly lit the castle as if he awaited his brothers. To Gilbert asking about the “as if,” Lazarus explains they never arrived, being assassinated along with their children en route. The youngest brother inherited his elders’ properties. But each time he came to dine, he found one of his brothers awaiting him, the same thing happened when he went to bed. Enchanted by the story, Ruthven promises to double Lazarus’s wages. The remaining count had three sons; one studied at Salamanca, the sec- ond at Valladolid, the third at Coïmbre. The father decided to visit his castles in their company. At the ﬁrst castle, the eldest died; at the second, the second died. Reluctant to venture farther, he left his third son to visit the last alone. When this son died, he dared not return to any of his estates, going instead to a convent to confess his crimes. He repented and led a holy life to die with Revelation 63

the odor of a saintly man. Since then, the three castles had been deserted but for fresh corpses regularly found within. Ruthven concludes that he is unlucky then, since misfortune always befalls the last to arrive, which was he. Lazarus, having taken Ruthven’s place at table, corrects him he was the last to arrive. Everyone compliments Lazarus on his narration but Gilbert asks what happened to the heir, the great-great- cousin—why doesn’t he visit? Lazarus reasons that he surely wishes to avoid a broken neck. He struggles to recall the heir’s name, ﬁnally coming up with Figuerroa, Luis de Figuerroa. Juana begins gasping, begging God’s help. Gilbert vainly struggles to console her. She repeats that every heir to cross Tormenar’s threshold dies. Ruthven interrupts, suggesting it’s time to locate a safe place for the ladies to pass the night. Gilbert orders Lazarus to distribute blankets. The Marquis declares that no one need take care of him or the ladies, his wife and daughters; they have heated up a small salon for the night. Juana maintains that she will stay where she is. Gilbert objects that the room is exposed to the wind; opening a door to an antechamber, he tells her to rest there until dawn. Juana replies that the room is as dark as an abyss, or, more literally, a gaping pit or sinkhole: “on dirait un gouffre!” (440). Gilbert proposes to stay by her, but she won’t hear of it. Ruthven salutes Juana, saying “Senora.” She trembles. Gilbert alerts her to the fact that Ruthven is bidding her farewell. She timidly says “Milord,” her eyes downcast. In an effort to cheer, Gilbert observes that an hour has already passed since the clock struck 12, the catastrophic fatal hour ending only by their welcoming a new companion, no ghouls or vampires. To Gilbert asking where he will lodge, Ruthven replies that he shall seek, and he shall ﬁnd, bidding the dames “Adieu!” and the gentilshommes “Bonne Nuit.” Gilbert cautions his comrades to sleep with two pillows but watch with both eyes, which Lazarus ﬁnds amusing. Gilbert asks if Lazarus weren’t going to follow his master, but before Lazarus can respond Ruthven calls back to forbid it. Gilbert reassures his little sister once more, promising that her least sigh will bring him running. In wishing her goodnight, he asks her to pray for him as his sister Hélène is undoubtedly doing at Tiffauges, noting how privileged he is to dwell in the thoughts of two angels. Juana, approaching the open window, says he deserves prayerful consideration. To Gilbert asking where she is going, she declares the moon is soon to rise, illuminating the way for lost travelers. Gilbert persuades her to sleep. She asks Gilbert, should he see Luis before her, to tell him how much she loved him. When Gilbert utters “Oh!” she corrects herself: “How I love him” (443). Exit Juana. Gilbert expresses his pity for her, conceding Luis’ that absence is worrisome, and, he notes, causing her to shed tears. Lazarus agrees she is crying a little, offering his opinion that it might help her ... like him, if he 64 The Theology of Dracula

could only.... Gilbert interrupts to say “cry?” “No, laugh!” (443) replies Lazarus. Gilbert encourages him to indulge himself but Lazarus says it’s as impossible for him to laugh as it will be for him to sleep. Gilbert invites Lazarus to stay with him, should he wish: an offer immediately accepted as Lazarus claims to always feel better in Gilbert’s company. Although he’s not sure why, his master frightens him. Gilbert proposes they retire to an adjoining room, warning Lazarus not to awaken him. As Lazarus enters, he shrieks. Imbecile! scolds Gilbert. Lazarus apologizes, but someone is already in the room. A comic routine about a person’s presence or absence ensues while Gilbert’s torch penetrates the darkness. Stage direc- tions have Gilbert enter the chamber, Lazarus holding his torch at the thresh- old. They report ﬁnding a cadaver bearing a letter from Juana and a wound on its throat, leaving no doubt as to the corpse’s identity. A scream and Juana crying out, “I’m dying!” propel Gilbert towards her, drawing his sword as he advances. “My sister!” he calls. Rushing towards the room sword ﬁrst, he is arrested by Ruthven stepping out. “Lord Ruthven, in Juana’s room!” (446) observes Gilbert, stating the obvious. Ruthven, raising his hand, stops Gilbert’s thoughts from advancing further. Ruthven heard Juana’s call, and ran to her aid. Seeing her try to extricate herself from her room, Ruthven entered to rescue or to avenge her. “You have cut me, Count Gilbert.... I am dying” groans Ruthven. As travelers gather around Juana, Gilbert asks, but the assassin? Escaped by that window, no doubt, Ruthven ventures. “Oh Juana! Oh Lord Ruthven...!” (447) sobs a bewildered Gilbert. Ruthven replies, “Gilbert!” Gilbert, stunned, blurts out, “I’ve killed you!” (447) Ruthven insists Gilbert send everyone away. Once alone, Ruthven says, “Count, in the religion I profess, it is customary for the dead to be exposed freely on the earth, and not enclosed in tombs.... Promise that after my death, you will carry me to the incline of a mountain, exposed to the rays of the rising moon; promise me this, Count, and I forgive you my death, and you will have given me justice” (447). Gilbert promises and starts to rise to seek help, but Ruthven declares it useless, asking only that Gilbert renew his vow. Lazarus, complaining about losing another employ, brings the scene to its end. The act’s concluding tableau shows Gilbert carrying Ruthven’s body on his shoulders. He places the body face up, stage directions specifying that he face west, at the mountain summit. Gilbert prays an instant over the body and climbs back down. Once he is gone, parting clouds reveal the moon. Moonbeams inch up the cadaver; reaching the head, Ruthven’s eyes pop open, a smile twisting across his face, he half rises, then becomes totally erect, and, like the Moor, spreads his now apparent wings and ﬂies off, thanking Gilbert. Revelation 65

Act three unfolds in the cour d’honneur of the Château de Tiffauges in la Vendée. The circular sequence of hours continues: It is morning, but six months have elapsed. A new cast of characters is introduced. Hélène, delighted Gilbert is returning, plans his welcome with Jarwick. Gilbert is arriving sooner than expected, and should be there by noon. They must let everyone know quickly. A servant, Lahennée, remarks that for six months she had received no word from her brother and now on the eve of her wedding he appears out of nowhere. Hélène muses her happiness will now be complete. Some com- motion signals that Gilbert is on his way. Lahennée asks if Lady Hélène isn’t going to inform le Baron de Marsden. Hélène claims Lahennée has read her mind, instructing him to send word of Gilbert’s arrival. Enter a group of peasants. Greeting them, Hélène sees they have heard the news, since their arms are ﬁlled with ﬂowers. A peasant woman answers, yes, wild ﬂowers—we know they’re your favorites. Hélène notices the cornﬂowers and says she will make herself a crown. A peasant says he daren’t offer her the daisies and buttercups he’s gathered, since she has such beautiful ﬂowers in her garden. Give them to me, Yves, says Hélène; a garden’s ﬂowers are those of man; wildﬂowers are God’s. They inundate her with wildﬂowers. She asks they keep some for Gilbert “our hearts’ true lord” (451). They promise to strew ﬂowers every- where. Hélène, calling for the village musicians, sends everyone to dress in their ﬁnest to celebrate Gilbert’s return with a dance. When one demoiselle sighs Hélène interrupts to tell her a new dress awaits her at home. The girl replies, “May Our Lady of Clisson watch over you” (451). Hélène gives a golden cross to another, instructing that her ﬁancé should fasten it around her neck, and to a boy, she presents new ribbons for his pipes, a medallion for his cap. They all shout “Vive la comtesse!” Once alone, Hélène describes her happiness. Every morning, in the sun’s rays and the meadow’s fragrance, she senses God smiling upon her. She is giving thanks for her brother’s return when Lahennée interrupts. He has been to the baron of Marsden’s château to ﬁnd him absent. A messenger arrived the previous evening insisting the Baron be awakened, and no sooner had spoken with him than Marsden saddled his black steed and rode into the night, leaving instruction Héline be told to expect him at noon. Hélène, hear- ing a commotion, asks Lahennée to run on high to see if it’s her brother. Lahennée says there is no need as he has dispatched trumpeters to the château’s towers to sound a fanfare as soon as Gilbert comes within view. Enter Jarwick, urgently calling out “Mademoiselle!” A messenger has come from Spain with word from Count Gilbert” (453). This is surprising as everyone thought Gilbert had left Spain long ago. Jarwick is confused because 66 The Theology of Dracula

at ﬁrst the messenger had said Spain, but changed name of countries so often he can’t remember them all. Soon the messenger appears, followed by peasants. It is Lazarus: “Yes my friends, from Spain, from Egypt, Greece, Dalmatia, we have gone ‘round the world” (454). He’s seen the Red Sea and entered Jerusalem, he continues, then pauses to ask if everyone is Catholic. Hearing that they are, Lazarus starts to fetch a bottle of River Jordan water from his affairs when he sees Hélène. Stopping, he declares her so beautiful that she could only be Hélène. She conﬁrms her identity and asks about Gilbert. Her brother has encountered a small accident. My brother has had an accident! she repeats. No, his horse, answers Lazarus, describing how in Beirut they rode camels, but in Nantes, near Clisson, all four horseshoes fell off Gilbert’s horse at once. So he was sent on to announce Gilbert’s imminent arrival. Hélène notices that Lazarus is pale and trembling. Lazarus, glancing down, notices that indeed he is. When asked why, he says it is because he is Spanish and sensitive to disagreeable things. When pressed on which things exactly, he says that many disagreeable things happen when travelling; in Constantinople, there was a lion; at the Nile, he threw some stones at a trunk of a tree which turned out to be a crocodile; in Circassia there were ban- dits—all kinds of disagreeable emotions. When asked to be more speciﬁc, he says one league from the castle, he noticed he had to pass between two broom- covered hills. Afraid of becoming lost, he paused. Further questioned, he begins by recalling his old master, Ruthven, when Hélène stops him to say he is mixing up two stories and will never get to the end that way. He replies that if there were but two he’d have no problem. He was carrying a lot of money (de l’argent et je veux dire de l’or) jangling in his saddlebags, and worried what would happen if robbers heard that telltale sound. Slowing down, he noticed the branches of a bush quivering on the hill to his right, “in the middle of the leaves, a face covered with a mask, a horrible mask” (457). Told to pass quickly or die, his horse shot off, carrying him to Tiffauges. Hélène thinks it strange, as there are no bandits in the region. On second thought, she wonders if the masked ﬁgure might not be an enemy of Gilbert’s. She instructs everyone to mount up to hunt down the masked man. Lazarus asks if he can’t ﬁrst store away the money he has, that of his deceased English master. Hélène scolds him for contemplating such a thing when Gilbert might be in danger. But here he comes now, exclaims Lazarus as a fanfare blasts. Enter Gilbert, hailing his dear sister, who thanks God. Gilbert remarks she looks as though she’d been crying. She confesses she had, ﬁrst for worry for his danger, now for joy. He wonders how she knew he had faced danger. Lazarus told me, she answers. But how could he know? She asks if he hadn’t Revelation 67

encountered a masked man. Indeed he had, exactly where Lazarus described. As Gilbert approached the twin hills, he noticed a beggar woman, a poor, curbed Breton. As he approached to give her a few coins, she grabbed his coat, pulling him towards her, and, God help him, she gave him a kiss! That is strange, observes Hélène. Yes, agrees Gilbert, but stranger still is that at the instant she so brusquely yanked me to her, a shot rang out, the bullet whistling by my ear. If not for her, I’d be dead. My God! exclaims Hélène. That’s what awaited me, shudders Lazarus. Gilbert says his ﬁrst thought was to make for the woods, but the woman whispered to him “ﬂee” and whipped the horse with a briar branch. A second shot was ﬁred, but, according to Gilbert, he was streaking like lightning. When Gilbert looked back, the woman had dis- appeared. Hélène suggests they ﬁnd and reward her. Studying Gilbert, how- ever, she declares him terribly pale. Gilbert explains that much happens during a year’s journey. To Hélène inquiring if Lazarus is in his service, Gilbert says yes and no. He is attached to him by honest affection, but his money comes from a deceased master. Neither Lazarus or Gilbert are forthcoming as to how this master died, however, Lazarus only noting that he expired in Gilbert’s arms. Gilbert refuses to provide more detail, but Lazarus volunteers that Gilbert promised if no one reclaimed his master’s goods in six months, they would be his by default, adding that the term ends that night. To be rid of him, Gilbert tells Lazarus to take possession of the goods now and be gone. Lazarus says he is right to love Gilbert. Lahennée reminds Gilbert that his sister had wished his arrival to be festive, but if he is sad.... Gilbert declares himself happy and commands the dancing begin! The peasants lead Gilbert towards Hélène. In an aside she again mentions his paleness, expressing relief “Georges” is not there. She will break the news before introducing her ﬁancé. Gilbert, approaching his sister, calls her Tiffauge’s guardian angel and, reinforcing the wildﬂower-bearing peasant’s statements, claims that her prayers cause the meadows to ﬂower and the ﬁelds to yield grain. Hélène replies she loves him as would an only sister. This comment brings to Gilbert’s mind Juana, who was, for an evening, his second sister. Remarking tears in Gilbert’s eyes, Hélène asks the cause. Gilbert evasively asserts that tears can be joyous, swearing himself the happiest of men. Can’t she see the reﬂection of her felicity shining in his heart? Hélène seizes on the word felicity, to thank God again for his return so that her felicity can now be as inﬁnite as God’s goodness. Gilbert imagines she is not only speaking of him, but also of her feelings towards their childhood friend Philippe, but when he intimates as much, Hélène corrects him. Three months earlier she told Philippe she could not love him and he left Brittany. 68 The Theology of Dracula

Gilbert defends Philippe as the best of men; Hélène cannot know love’s meaning. She corrects him again: She is in love, a love that dissolves everything in a “devouring passion” (464). After lonely months peering down the road in search of her returning brother, she has Georges. That’s why she asked him to hurry home. She’d set tomorrow as a limit; had he not come, he would have returned to ﬁnd her a married woman, without the honor of having a brother’s escort to the altar. Stunned, Gilbert asks if she is loved. She believes so. Inquiring into the man, he is told the groom is rich, honored, and living nearby for the past ﬁve months: the Baron Georges de Marsden, believed to be of Scottish origin. His age is difﬁcult to determine, perhaps 30 to 35 years. She begs Gilbert to be neither harsh in his judgments, nor stubbornly loyal to Philippe. Her love is a sweet belief in sympathetic resonance, in souls seeking out their mates. She warns Gilbert if he should ﬁnd Georges’ face a bit too pale, his brow a bit too sombre, pity him, for he suffers from excessive love for her. In accepting his sister’s choice, Gilbert asks reciprocation, her loving generously one she must soon call “sister.” Traveling from Almira to Spalatro, he was attacked by bandits; suffering wounds, he was sheltered in a nearby villa where a blonde Dalmatian, Antonia, lived with her mother. Antonia’s incredible beauty was hidden under a long black veil whose mystery he has penetrated. Indeed, Gilbert would be married were Antonia not still mourning her father. Looking at his sister Gilbert says, in Dalmatia, I inhabited “a par- adise that lacked only you, Hélène” (467). He promised to return for Antonia in six months, when her mourning period would be over. Hélène proposes they go to Spalatro together to trade Antonia’s black veil for a white gown; Marsden, she adds, is a great traveler. Gilbert, asking when can he meet her charming baron, learns he is arriving at noon, but Hélène excitedly suggests she could fetch him now. Gilbert claims to know every step of the sun’s journey and noon will soon arrive. He calls his sister’s attention to the gaily dressed peasants arriving with great pomp as if a living, moving bouquet. Enter Lazarus to ask Gilbert to lend him a scribe to inventory his heritage, so he can acquire property and marry. Gilbert says he can have Lahannée’s help, for the favor of neither mentioning Spain nor his heritage again. Exit Lazarus as the baron is announced. Seeing Marsden, Gilbert exclaims “My God!” Ruthven coolly greets “Monsieur le Comte,” recalling their last encounter. Gilbert asks Hélène to send everyone off while he treats with her ﬁancé. Ruthven explains that his wound, ﬁnally, wasn’t mortal. He had lost con- sciousness and was as good as dead. Coming to, he called for help, but every- one had gone. Once recuperated, he came to Brittany to thank Gilbert for Revelation 69

saving his life in not burying him. He asks for Gilbert’s hand in fraternity. Gilbert, suspicious, wonders about his change of name. Ruthven explains his elder brother died, bequeathing him the title. All very natural, observes Gilbert, but why had he hid their acquaintance from Hélène? Ah, begins Ruthven, he hadn’t wanted to reveal that her brother had—or had thought to have—killed him. Gilbert deems everything “strange.” When Hélène reap- pears, Gilbert admits his fatigue. He’s told his room has been prepared. A peasant woman approaches Gilbert and, whispering, instructs him to sleep in the tapestry room. He recognizes her as the life-saving beggar; the audience, as the Moor. Advising in an aside that he’ll retire to the tapestry room, Gilbert exits. The Moor suddenly disappears. Ruthven, staring at the spot where the Moor had stood, murmurs, “Van- ished!” Enter Lazarus, talking to himself: “Thirty-six thousand pounds! What I wouldn’t give to see the dead man’s shade to say ‘Thank you, Lord Ruthven!’” (472) Ruthven speaks up: “Ah, there you are, Lazarus! Tonight we’ll sleep at Tiffauges, my friend. Bring my things and my treasure” (472). Lazarus curses his ill fortune, declaring himself “ruined” (472). Tableau 6 shows a vast room with a tapestry representing the fairy Mélu- sine, a musette player, a hunter, bird of prey on his arm, sylphs, water sprites, etc., arrayed in a riotous landscape. On the wall at the stage’s depth, a large frame contains the portrait of an ancient baron of Tiffauges, leaning on two knights. Gilbert sleeps in a chair as Mélusine detaches herself from the tapestry to slowly approach him. She observes in verse that, like half the world, Gilbert sleeps; the world is divided into day and night—close your tired eyes, while, with mystery, the other half soundlessly revives. For on two powerful rulers the world depends: one named Light; the other, Darkness. Fecund Night is the mother of Dreams; sterile Day, tyrant of the real. Turning, she addresses the tapestry’s occupants. The day is dethroned, her verse continues, we for 12 hours reign. The night world is ours! Mortals sleep and we deliver them from their residences. Wake up brothers! Shepherd, the day, under the bower, hid from your silenced pipes their joyous sound; but, in darkness, your rustic quadrille rises to be danced in silent steps. Hunter, who, on your gloved hand, thrones the white gyrfalcon, proud suckling of the North, that in the woods the screech owl, bloodied, exhales her last cry under the lethal beak. Sylphs imprisoned in embalmed, perfumed rose; ondines, water sprites, enveloped in watery vapors; salamanders, rolling in smoky wafts; reed-sliding mysterious sprites: Hurry, descend, the fog moans, the rushes groan, but the poorest hearths retain, under their ash, some of yes- terday’s ill-extinguished ﬂame. She launches into a song of greeting, containing the line “You’ll rekindle 70 The Theology of Dracula

a ﬁre in the desolated homestead, as God revived a soul in an inanimate corpse” (474). She summons fairies embodying Earth, Water, Fire, assuming herself the role of “Air” in elemental magic. She asks slumbering Gilbert to recall the song she would serenade him with in gone-by years. She summons the ﬁgures locked into the family portrait, who warn they are forbidden from informing men of the frightening world they abide, though able to talk amongst themselves. Mélusine calls them forward to share with the hope of their race their wisdom about Hélène, endangered by the misery the stranger brings. Their voices will penetrate like a dream that passes, the Night Angel, silently watching, allowing their thoughts to reach Gilbert’s spirit. The old man and his lieutenants step down from their canvas. Mélusine asks who the dark stranger is: a cursed child of shadow, they deem, whose night is too dark even for their eyes, an immortal assassin whose trail is marked by his victims’ graves. Gilbert turns uncomfortably in his sleep. No virgin can escape the determined bloodlust of this hideous oppressor who braves the elements and commands space, they proclaim. When Gilbert calls for his sister, Mélusine reminds him of Juana, Ruthven’s victim. Gilbert calls out again, “Oh my sis- ter!” Yesterday, declares Mélusine, this ﬁend tried to kill you to deprive Hélène of a defender. She leads a prayer for Gilbert against a vampire whose love is death. With the dawn imminent, she hurries everyone back to his represen- tational frame. Act four ﬁnds a deserted terrace. Enter Lazarus. Given a 3 A.M. ren- dezvous there, he complains about a master who doesn’t sleep, eat, laugh, and when dead returns to life, depriving a poor man of his riches. He sent Lazarus searching for news of a nameless old woman. Lazarus misses his master Rozo, and Petra, blaming everything wrong with the world on Tormenar. His solil- oquy ends with Ruthven calling his name. More comedy is indulged before Ruthven asks about “the woman.” Lazarus reports the village holds 80 houses and 97 women, 39 of them elderly. He questioned all but ﬁve, three idiots and two paralytics: None had spoken to Gilbert. Ruthven understands Lazarus had counted on inheriting his fortune, and, as he’d hate his return to life to penalize his servant, he has a proposition, indeed, part of an entertainment. If Lazarus afﬁrms everything he might assert about the past, he’ll give him a guinea; if it’s about an important subject, he’ll give him ten. Lazarus enthuses positively about the project, immediately gain- ing ten guineas. But, Ruthven cautions, if Lazarus doesn’t support his con- tentions, he will be penalized by similar sums. The approach of Hélène interrupts the conference, Lazarus being hurried off. Momentarily alone, Ruthven concludes that if the woman who spoke to Gilbert were human, he would have uncovered her identity. Ruthven greets Hélène as an unexpected pleasure. To her question of Revelation 71

how long he has been there, he calculates about 15 minutes, which she ﬁnds uncanny: Love has planted something marvellous in her. Fifteen minutes ear- lier, in her sleep, she’d felt herself called to the terrace. What can I, who awake each day with the dawn, say? Ruthven wonders. He could not sleep himself. Why not? asks Hélène. He cannot tell—perhaps fever—at any rate he didn’t want to return home, so he spent the night listening to the winds murmur her name. Gilbert is before Ruthven and an open tomb. “For the last time,” he says, “adore God!” Ruthven refuses. “Then, despair and die!” (535) orders Gilbert, thrusting the sword into Ruthven. The vampire falls into the pit with a terrible cry. As a stone falls to cover the tomb, angels ﬁll the sky. Hélène says to Gilbert, “Brother, be happy”; Juana, addressing Antonia, chants: “Sister, be happy!” The curtain falls, leaving the sexual and spiritual union of “brother” and “sis- ter” and their felicitous union with the divine to be imagined. Dumas transports Nodier’s prologue, Planché’s introductory vision, to his ﬁnale. Cluttered with crypts and tombs, it features the descent of twin spirits from above the proscenium—Juana assuming the role of the spirit Unda, Hélène replacing celestial Ariel. Sister spirits, one dark, one light, from the celestial realm greet Ziska, who, with arms outstretched, is assumed into heaven. They join to form a joyous triune, welcoming sister Antonia into their spiritual family and blessing her union with Gilbert. All that is known about Juana, beyond her convent upbringing and love- motivated revolt against paternal authority, is that she sees “a gaping pit” in the room where she goes to rest that fatal night, thus evoking the Homeric poet’s language in describing the aperture from which Plouton, lord of the dead, emerged. She appears as the day exhausts itself and counts on moonlight to reveal her lover. Fair Hélène’s particulars are more ample: Gilbert’s biological sister is said to make grain grow and to love the meadow’s wildﬂowers, proposing to coronate herself with a wreath made from the deep blue cornﬂower blossoms the peasants had gathered in the ﬁelds where they work.
