Even the name Hélène, believed to derive from a vegetation goddess, designates her as an earthy avatar of Kore–Persophone, and of course the name of the beauty over whose love the Trojan war was fought. Ziska, endowed with a more complex and contradictory character, will be considered more fully later, but she is introduced as the drama’s only guide that leads, Lazarus being ﬁgured as the guide that follows. The Christian- pagan tensions that Goethe introduced with “The Bride of Corinth” are quickly dismissed in the ﬁrst scene when both Christian and pagan guides are called by Lazarus but collectively refuse to lead towards the superstition- inhabited domain of Tormenar. Ziska arrives before the others to deprive Luis of his life and to set a rendezvous with Gilbert for the following year, date of the climactic scene. In the brother-lover ﬁgure joining Juana, Hélène, Ziska, and Antonia, a solitary Apollonian entity is readily discernible. Wherever he goes, Gilbert Revelation 79

brings light, often being ﬁgured as carrying a torch, urging a ﬁre be built, even ﬁring a pistol. The extinguishing of light on the other hand brings forth Ruthven. A doppelganger pairing of Gilbert and Ruthven replaces the traveling companions Byron introduced and Polidori and Nodier furthered. Gilbert and Ruthven, both great travelers, move independently, even as they are seen to advance in pursuit of one another. In Dumas’ rendition, Gilbert is more man of the world than neophyte, his only ostensible binding connection to Ruthven comes from inadvertently running him through shortly after their initial meeting. Ruthven nonetheless poses mortal danger to all the women that bask in Gilbert’s love. Ruthven, massively connected to the material through his mountaintop afﬁnity, is regenerated through the feminine, moonlight and the lifeblood of Gilbert’s sisters combining to effect his resurrection. Ruthven’s Tormenar death is ﬁnally a mere skirmish in a biannual battle for predominance, Gilbert and Ruthven each struggling to obliterate the other. Underscoring their interlocking destinies, they are alternately served by the Sancho Panza of Lazarus, who works for each, opportunistically shifting alle- giance between the living and the dead, diurnal and nocturnal, good and evil. When one is in the East, the other remains in the West, their paths crossing only every sixth month. The ﬁnal contest falls near the spring equinox, snows still covering the ground. At Tormenar they met at midnight, at Tiffauges the encounter occurred at noon, 182 and a half days later. Dumas has understood the mythological underpinnings of Romanticism’s vampire and happily reworks the symbol system he claims as heir. It is a drama pitting the sun, Sol, assisted by Mélusine, against the black force of death and darkness for the love of a multi–faceted feminine Luna. It simultaneously sets an explicitly spiritual Christian force against a diabolic nemesis rooted in the material and the corporal. Dumas, at ﬁrst glance, seems to use the Vampire to articulate a radically new discourse, wedding frénétique horror to féerique fantasy. The comic light- ening of the subject does not change its essential symbolic content. Embel- lishing Nodier’s melodrama by importing the Ghoul—a female blood ﬁend on whom Romanticism’s vampire was constructed—from Galland’s Tales of The Arabian Nights, and the Mélusine deus ex machina from folklore, Dumas complicates plot. Perhaps he was recalling the Arsenal Library of the 1820s, for under Nodier’s direction the new library acquired many works on super- natural folklore and the occult. Montague Summers, while failing to under- stand why Dumas would have introduced the Ghoul, celebrates Mélusine’s heavy-handed apparition: Lazare is a capital character, but the intrusion from Oriental legend of the ghoul cannot be considered happy. On the other hand the appearance of Mélusine, whose legend was collected about the end of the fourteenth 80 The Theology of Dracula

century by Jean d’Arras, is certainly effective and entirely in keeping with the history, since according to Paracelsus she was an occult power, and in folk lore she is often represented as protecting ancient houses [311]. It is said Mélusine migrated into French Medieval folklore from Celtic mythology, where she was perhaps a banshee queen. In the 13th century, William de Portenache composed a no longer extant Chronique de Mélusine which is understood to have provided the basis for Jean d’Arras’s La Noble histoire de Mélusine that Summers references. Mélusine was sufﬁciently revered in pre–Renaissance France for several prominent feudal clans to actually claim descent from her, the Lusignan family of Poitou in particular, but the Parthenays, Rochefoucaulds, Sassennages, Saint-Gelais, the ruling family of the Duchy of Luxembourg and ancient royal lines of Cyprus, Bohemia, and Armenia all traced their lineage back to her as well, and, indeed, as with all such ambivalent, bipolar ﬁgures, it is possible Mélusine was occasionally understood as the protector of these noble households. Mélusine is depicted as a beautiful maiden from the waist up, but, like the mermaid, from the naval down, she is a slithering scaled being of blue and white coloration, though she is finless. Instead of being half-ﬁsh, she is half-serpent, a veritable phallic woman, making her more likely a castrating hag than guardian. To add to her incongruent mix of features belonging to species apart, she is at times represented with articulated wings like those of a bat, marking her as closely related to the Welch leather-winged night-hag Gwrach-y-Rhybyn. Henri Donteville connects Mélusine to Luc or Lug from which derives Luncine, Lucinius, Licinius and transmits the idea of light and the root mer, confounding in it the notions of water and maternity, eventually leading him to suggest Mère Lucine. More pointedly, why not Mère Éleusine: Demeter? In the fairy Donteville sees, all at once, the serpent and the bird, or at least the appearance of the bird, since he perceives her as chthonian. The serpent and the bird recall Darvell’s death in Byron’s Fragment as does Mélusine’s association, as part of a feminine triune, with hidden fountains and sacred oaths. Pierre Martin-Civat associates Mélusine with water sources and mega- liths. According to d’Arras, she was ﬁrst perceived at the Fond de Çé or Foun- tain of Thirst; numerous legends make much of her bathing. Her role as a builder of towers and architectural wonders supports the second contention. She is speciﬁcally attributed with having given rise to three castles in a single night: Talmont, Partenay, and Tiffauges, explaining Dumas’ insistence on Tiffauges in the play. A further connection to Tiffauges also seems consequen- tial; it was to Tiffauge’s that the young Maréchal Gilles de Rais retired after his role in the Hundred Years War. Revelation 81

At Tiffauges, as he matured, Baron de Rais pursued vulgar alchemy, spending fortunes to produce gold, maintained a ruinously lavish court, and gave unrestrained vent to a pronounced bloodthirstiness. His sadistic orgies drained the Vendée region of male children, consumed as so many containers of blood for a monstrous appetite, his servants hunting victims far and wide to sate their master’s pleasure. Gilles liked to coddle the youths, stroking their hair, caressing their cheeks, talking sweetly, earning their conﬁdence before slitting their jugulars and watching their lives drain away, as the look of intel- ligence and humanity vacated their disbelieving eyes. He would often sexually violate his victims’ lifeless remains. Rais’ confessional statement concludes by his begging to be forgiven for his sins and spared from excommunication. No stranger to the romantic tale, Gilles, it is said, inspired Charles Pér- rault’s Barbe-Bleue. The tale recounts how, despite a troubling blue beard, ladies ﬁnd Barbe-Bleue irresistible. Marrying a young beauty, he gives her the run of his castle but for a single forbidden chamber. Handing her the keys to his domain, he explains the function of each, repeating his injunction before setting off to tend to business in outlying districts. During her master’s absence, the bride’s curiosity overcomes her will to keep her matrimonial oath. Opening the forbidden door, she discovers her predecessors’ bloody remains. Retreating in horror she locks the door anew, but the key has some- how become indelibly marked with the crimson color of blood. The ogre returns home and sees what has happened. He pursues his young wife from room to room, but before he can add her corpse to his pile of decomposing wives, the woman’s brothers appear and succeed in killing him instead. Dumas, it seems, quite clearly suggests that Gilbert is Gilles’ descendant and heir. When Dion Boucicault liberally adapted the play into English as The Phantom, transporting it all to Raby Castle in Wales, his only reference to the Tiffauges scene survives through a mention of Bluebeard and the inser- tion of an alchemist. When Mélusine encourages the residents of the play’s family portrait to come counsel young Gilbert, Dumas undoubtedly represents Gilles and his execrable lieutenants. The common phoneme of the given names of Gilles and Gilbert signiﬁes “oath,” “pledge,” or “promise”—Gilbert denot- ing “Bright pledge.” While Tiffauges offers a bloodied key to uncovering the darker aspect of Gilbert’s identity, Mélusine’s utility remains more obscure, though her mytho- logical and genealogical background too turns on the oath betrayed. Obviously there is the Celtic connection, maintained since Nodier; the relationship between the Eastern vampire, Oriental ghoul, and ﬁgures like the banshee; the bond between Greek, Celt, and perhaps even Indian mythologies; but whatever his reason, Dumas manifests Mélusine’s importance by placing her at his drama’s center as its omphalus with her magical companions of the 82 The Theology of Dracula

tapestry arrayed around her. She is the point from which the recognizably human changes into the monstrous and fabulous. Introduced by Gilbert through expository dialogue in act two, she only manifests herself in the third of ﬁve acts to prepare the denouement. Mélusine, who spends her time launching a quadrille, explains Dumas’ compositional structure. The term “quadrille” refers to a rustic dance of the 18th century (long after the epoch of Gilles de Rais or the weaving of narrative tapestries) and its accompanying music. American square-dancing retains much of the quadrille’s élan—both in its choreographic and musical dimen- sions; calls such as “dosey-doe” are recognizable as the corruption of the French quadrille’s “dos-à-dos.” Dumas’ quadrille, like all others, is composed of ﬁve movements; its dance requires four couples who, criss-crossing, trace geo- metric patterns upon the ﬂoor that permute from the basis of the square, a quadrille, and whose complexities come from the changing of partners, one ﬁgure substituting for another. The basic quaternary form insists upon the inviolate cross intersected by dancers moving diagonally from quadrant to quadrant in a saltire “X” pattern, relating these movements to Scotland’s St. Andrew’s cross. This and the elemental agents seem intended to exploit the alchemical motif associated with the historical Gilles de Rais. The alchemists’ quaternity device seeks to join opposing base elements and energies into one synthetic, transformative molecule of divine matter. The population of the tapestry, largely related to Mélusine’s complicated her- itage in myth and to Vendéan folklore, is insufﬁcient to perform any quadrille. But the salamanders, ondines, sprites and other mythical beings black, white, red, and yellow, align air, earth, ﬁre, and water in cruciform order along axes north, east, south, west, as they attempt to rekindle the ﬁres that have gone out—even as a solar ﬁgure appears from the east to struggle with a deathly dark hero who has inhabited the neighbourhood since their last meeting— by having others respond to their symbolic order. In her incantation, Mélusine makes it clear that they are effecting in the material world that which Jesus accomplished within the human body, making explicit the analogy between the house and the body previously introduced at Tormenar. The added element of the hunter and the stag seems intended to embody the Celtic hunter, the “White son of Night” the Welsh call Gwyn au Nacht, and his game, the mythic wild stag best recalled as Cernunnos. Their hunt is the Wild Hunt of ancient myth, the hunt of the God of the Underworld. There is an analogous hunt pitting solar Gilbert against the palely luminous Ruthven or vice versa. As the hunt races to its inconclusive conclusion, hunter becoming the hunted, the inhabitants of the tapestry attempt to set the ﬁctive world to dancing. In so doing, they play both upon the notion of the alchemists’ Chymical Wedding and the ultimate Christian symbol, the cross. Revelation 83

The ﬁve movements Dumas provides take the form of his ﬁve acts; the four couples he proposes are Penta and Rebozo, Juana and Louis, Hélène and Ruthven, Gilbert and Antonia. Left unformed are the dreamed-of couples of Lazarus and Ziska and Ziska and Gilbert, though the latter’s spiritual love was at the ﬁnal moment realized through exchange and reciprocation. More- over, it ignited an all-consuming ﬁre which released Ziska from her mortal form and endowed her with a soul. In each act but the third, a couple is either formed or sundered, and it must be argued that a couple is also forged in the third, consisting of Gilbert and Ruthven, who cease to operate independently but become ﬁrmly linked, each vying to dominate their shared identity. In the given theatrical context, one seeing the other as a masked ﬁgure references vegetation-god Dionysus as the embodiment of all doppelgangers, the fact that one arrived in Circassia from the mountains and the other from the depths of the sea, reinforces the Dionysian nature of the doppelganger. Lazarus ﬁrmly states he saw a masked ﬁgure in the leaves: “Suddenly, I notice the branches of a shrub that waved on the hill on the right hand side, and, in the middle of the leaves, I see ... a face covered by a mask...!” (457) thereby marking Ruthven as related to Green Georges, Feuillu: Saint George. The motif of ruins, preoccupation of Byron and Polidori abandoned by Nodier, is restored by Dumas. In châteaux and simple rooms, we ﬁnd the ﬁguration of a material realm, a body, contrasted to the astral, the spirit. One structure, the inn, is ﬁgured as too full of life; a deserted mountain castle is established as its polar opposite. Juana senses Tormenar as a place of the dead on entering its “blackened” walls, the walls functioning like those of Polidori’s soot-encrusted “hovel.” For Luis, Tormenar is his inheritance and destiny; in entering its conﬁnes, through the curse of an original sin, he attains the realm of his mortality. The structure is but the husk he has invited his ﬁancée to wed. Their marriage will be purely spiritual, for they are joined that night as spirits liberated, he at the hands of the Ghoul, she at Ruthven’s. The pattern of the quadrille is displayed in a particularly artful maneuvre: The wedding feast of Penta and Botaro is transported between settings from the ﬁrst act to the second (Rozo’s Inn to Tormenar), to be served in a cele- bration transposed. We were taken from the marriage of Petra and Botaro to the holy union of Juana and Luis; from the physical plane of the wedding bed to the spiritual plane of the grave, a wedding feast marked by the bride and groom through abstention, present absence, and absent presence. In Torme- nar’s geography, a small chamber, offered to Juana for her repose, is her place of death; Luis’ lifeless body occupies a similar space. The blackened chambers yield pale white bodies. Tributary to Tormenar’s large hall, these ﬁgure as chapels in a cathedral of darkness and lend greater sense to the title of baron of Marsden—Mars’ den. Peering into her room from its threshold, Juana 84 The Theology of Dracula

describes it as “gaping.” The blackened walls project constructs—bodies— abandoned by the spirit, as Mélusine’s rhyme declares. Ruthven, like Blue- beard, conﬁnes his deadly missions to closed rooms that are afterwards left dark and deserted. Luis, Juana, and Hélène emptied, are each conﬁned to a deserted room of a noble mansion. In act two, when the Ghoul pledges to see Gilbert in a year, she suggests he will then provide her nourishment, for the Ghoul, who must annually feed to maintain existence, only preys upon men who are loved by a woman or who foolishly fall in love with the Ghoul. This contrasts to the Vampire who, it is later revealed, requires a biannual transfusion of life, at the ends of winter and summer. The insistence on the wedding and sacriﬁce of the maiden, featured in vampire plots since Polidori, is retained by Dumas. It remains a story of a priest, Ruthven, leading a maiden by the wrists to the altar where she will be sacriﬁced and dragged into the underworld. Yet it is not merely the draining away of a victim’s blood that effects the Vampire’s renewal, as in each instance represented it occasions the vampire’s death immediately after the maiden’s sacriﬁce. It seems the Vampire ﬁrst joins his bride in death before resurrecting to life. Polidori inserted an interval between Ianthe’s death and Ruthven’s. Not so Dumas. The play ends with a failed attempt at exorcism, as Ruthven, unrepentant yet cowering before God’s name, falls to a consecrated sword, strengthening Christian overtones ﬁrst heard in Nodier’s pseudonymous novel. Unlike in previous works, Ruthven, rather than being killed twice, experiences a triple death, each killing strengthening Gilbert’s role. Previously, Aubray was a pas- sive victim who aided his friend when another hand delivered the mortal blow, but Gilbert repeatedly, and with increasing deliberateness, kills Ruthven. Gilbert’s ultimate victory over evil is also novel. The solar ﬁgure actively defeats his nemesis in the name of Jesus. Act one introduced three characters who are present throughout the play: Lazarus, Ziska, and Gilbert. That Ziska would provide the sacred key to defeating Ruthven becomes improbable if she were indeed Moorish. The Spanish set was apparently designed to cast this character as Moorish, an Arab-speaking invader of the European heartland. She is presumably staying at the Rozo’s inn because she is stalking the well-loved Luis de Figuerra. Her quality of “Moorish” would indicate her to be Arab and Moslem, yet legend’s ghoul is not Moorish, but a pre–Islamic Mesopotamian ﬁend. What Dumas wishes to signify by assigning her the task of informing Gilbert of Ruthven’s Achilles’ heel at the cost of her own existence, beyond illustrating Nodier’s Christian love, is not immediately clear. No doubt Ziska’s beauty, somber features, and Christian character, yet closeness to the Mesopotamian, were to Revelation 85

be resolved in ultimately assigning her Circassian origins. Circassian women were celebrated in mid–19th-century France as harem beauties of the Ottoman sultan. Ziska’s appearance in Brittany is particularly curious and perhaps clari- fying. She intervenes and, in cooperation with Mélusine, saves Gilbert and initiates him into spiritual knowledge. The ambush between two hills of Poli- dori’s novella is reﬁgured with greater clarity and directness: The masked Dionysian component of the doppelganger attempts to assassinate the Apol- lonian, the attempt thwarted due to Ziska’s intervention. On several occasions, feminine characters—Hélène, and a peasant girl—thank “Our Lady of Clis- son,” likely referring to the miraculous Notre Dame du Roncier, meaning “Our Lady of the Brambles,” venerated by Olivier de Clisson, (it is also the name of a 15th-century basilica he built and a still-extant structure in which he chose to be buried). Notre Dame du Roncier is introduced when Gilbert is miraculously saved by Ziska, who spurs his horse on with a crop made of bramble branches. The confusion of Notre Dame and Ziska is furthered by the prayer scene with Hélène, who asks the intercession of her holy mother which neatly conforms to the advice of Ziska to await a revelation. Indeed, Lazarus appears with a revelation and to renounce the purse he ﬁnally received from his master. The parallel between Ziska and Mélusine is further developed through their entourages. Ziska’s slaves in Circassia are introduced dancing around the couch of Antonia and fanning her. This is precisely the treatment Gilbert describes receiving in his infancy from Mélusine and her companions. There seems to be an intersecting and indeed thorny supernatural feminine presence that joins several avatars, maleﬁc and beneﬁcent, into a single identity—Ziska is last shown being assumed into heaven and welcomed by Hélène and Juana, whose Luis she murdered. This regranting of eternal life to a sanctiﬁed Ziska apparently justiﬁes the demand that Ruthven repent. Repentance will open the gates of the heavenly inn, even to those intrinsically without souls of their own. Ambiguously, Mélusine seems to celebrate the Romantic quality of dark- ness in contrast to the rigid world of light, though she wants nonetheless to rekindle the extinguished ﬂame. The old baron qualiﬁes that some beings and acts are too dark even for him, and Ziska declares the real that men love is but a shadow of the love of the immortal. Dumas compensates for this lack of coherence with enthusiasm. By beginning the play on the theme of “no room at the inn,” Dumas raises a question as to what type of nativity to expect thereafter. By positing two localities, the dramatic universe is polarized. Yet the shifting settings between acts are both transformational and curiously static. There are court- yards: that of the inn and Tiffauges; large, formal chambers: Tormenar’s dining 86 The Theology of Dracula

room, Tiffauge’s Tapestry Room, its large salon where the marriage feast is celebrated, and the Circassian palace’s hall. Visible from their windows and balconies are pits, abysses, and cliffs, no longer caves as with Nodier, but Tar- tarus, or more properly, the issueless pit of Christian damnation and neigh- boring region to Circassia. Dumas has taken the Vampire from celebrating pagan mysteries to subsuming them in a restored Christian order, Christian iconography and credo being immediately stressed through Lazarus. The New Testament makes two references to one of that name. First, there is the Lazarus of Luke 16.19: There was a certain rich man who used to clothe himself in purple and ﬁne linen, and who feasted every day in splendid fashion. And there was a cer- tain poor man, named Lazarus, who lay at his gate, covered with sores, and longing to be ﬁlled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table; even the dogs would come and lick his sores. This is very much the man, being turned away, sent off into the wilderness, encountered in the opening scene. Luke tells that when both the rich man and poor die, their fortunes are reversed. Lazarus is regaled “in the bosom of Abraham” (16:22) while the rich man suffers in hell. When the rich man asks Abraham to have pity and send Lazarus to soothe his suffering by carrying him some water, Abraham refuses. The rich man then asks Abraham to restore Lazarus to life and send him to his family “that he may testify to them, lest they too come into this place of torments” (16:28). Abraham coldly maintains that were Moses’s commandments and the Prophets’ words insufﬁcient to keep his kin mindful of God, then Lazarus’s return from the dead would be of no avail. Dumas represents Ruthwen as the Rich Man, always offering but never yielding Lazarus his fortune. In John 11, Jesus does what Abraham would not, working a miracle to keep mankind mindful of God, “for the glory of God, that through it the Son of God may be gloriﬁed” (11:4). Jesus returns Lazarus to life after four days in the tomb. Considering the role Dumas attributes to light and ﬁre, much of what Jesus says during the incident is noteworthy. “Are there not twelve hours in the day?” He asks. “If a man walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if he walks in the night, he stum- bles, because the light is not in him” (11:10). These things he spoke, and after this he said to them, “Lazarus, our friend, sleeps. But I go that I may wake him from sleep.” His disciples therefore said, “Lord, if he sleeps, he will be safe.” Now Jesus had spoken of his death, but they thought he was speaking of the repose of sleep. So then Jesus said to them plainly, “Lazarus is dead; and I rejoice on your account that I was not there, that you may believe. But let us go to him.” Thomas, who is called the Twin, said therefore to his fellow disciples, “Let us also go, that we may die with him” [11:11–16]. Revelation 87

With the spreading word of Lazarus’s revival, great crowds begin to follow Jesus. He habitually addresses them in parables evocative of the discourse of a Mystery religion: “Unless the grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone. But if it dies, it brings forth much fruit. He who loves his life, loses it; and he who hates his life in this world, keeps it unto life ever lasting” (12:24–25). Returning to his comments on the 12 hours of day and night, Jesus teaches, “Yet a little while the Light is among you. Walk while you have the Light, that darkness may not overtake you. He who walks in the darkness does not know where he goes. While you have the Light, believe in the Light, that you may become sons of Light” (12:35–36). This gloss on darkness and light articulates the operating principle of Le Vampire’s theme, as Mélusine makes clear in her appearance. What will be born in Le Vampire is Light in darkness. It also marks Ziska, only recognizable through her staring and envious eye. Luke 11:33: “The light of the body is the eye: therefore when thine eye is single, thy whole body also is full of light; but when thine eye is evil, thy body also is full of darkness.” When Ziska out of love puts aside envy and protects Gilbert and Antonia, she becomes part of light. A reference to the wedding feast of Cana in which Jesus reportedly turned water into wine, is transformed again: The wedding scene becomes a kind of memorial feast. Dumas has reconstituted, on his post–revolutionary, Restora- tion stage, a Renaissance tableau quite like DaVinci’s Last Supper, Ruthven portraying Judas Iscariot and Juana the Paschal lamb in a cruel ceremony of salvation in which wine becomes blood. Juana is ﬁrst offered a few drops of wine, but then, through substitution for the traitor, it is Lazarus who tosses down glass after glass. Three glasses of wine bring forward the story of three brothers and three sons. After the biblical Lazarus was restored, a banquet, rehearsal for the Passover Last Supper, was given at which “Lazarus was one of those reclining at table” (John 12:2). In the case of Juana’s last supper at Tormenar, Lazarus is eventually pictured receiving a pouch of coin for betraying Gilbert, but in abandoning the purse he betrays Ruthven. Dumas retains another interesting twist on the New Testament that Nodier inserted; it is the resurrected Ruthven who challenges Gilbert and Lazarus to touch him, to verify his true existence, as Jesus had challenged Thomas. The representation of the supper of twelve plus one required a determined construction. The Last Supper reference demands seating 12 plus the indi- vidual to be sacriﬁced and transformed. Dialogue repeatedly insists on the party’s 12 members, even when the arithmetic doesn’t make sense. Ruthven takes the place reserved for Luis, but he does not eat. Lazarus in turn takes his place, but consumes the wine and bread of the sacriﬁcial lamb Juana. The dinner-table conversation makes clear Dumas’ intent to mark Le Vampire as 88 The Theology of Dracula

a tribute to Nodier, for it largely follows the lengthy conversations Mes Mémoires recalls as occurring during the entr’actes of 1823’s Vampire when he, by chance, found himself seated next to Nodier, the play’s author. Gilbert is always heralded before he appears, heard before he is seen. He is awaited by trumpeters, or announced by Lazarus, or called by his lover. Ruthven’s appearances, on the contrary, are unexpected, surprising. While Ruthven was in the West in la Vendée, Gilbert was in the East, Lazarus making much of the Red Sea, the River Jordan, Jerusalem, and his having seen the misperceived wonders of the ancient world. The Jordan is of course associated with the rebirth of baptism; the Red Sea is also a sacred symbol of rebirth and death, a point where God grants his faithful new life and crushes his ene- mies, turning the water into blood with the lives of the damned. Jerusalem marks the particular point of spiritual renaissance for humanity that came on 3 April 33 with the Cruciﬁxion, an event followed by earthquakes and the conjunction of solar and lunar eclipses. Gilbert’s ﬁancée, bears the name of the fortress Rome built to protect Temple Mount—“Antonia.” Most impor- tantly, it is only when solar Gilbert becomes sanctiﬁed in Christ that he ﬁnally is able to defeat darkness, even beneath moonlight. When we meet Ruthven in 1851, he has consumed the lives of Ianthe, Miss Aubray, Malvina, Margaret, Juana and Hélène. With each passing year, Ruthven drains two more lives. Dumas has ﬁxed both spatial and temporal poles. Amplifying the relationship between the inn and Tormenar, he marks a town by the Western Sea as the western extremity of action, and the Black Sea coast as the eastern. Dumas is careful to limit each of his episodes to one portion of the Earth’s rotation, accumulating a period of 24 hours or slightly exceeding from fragments of days, but he has bound his dramatic action by the actual revolution of the earth around the sun, covering the events of exactly one year, each act being separated by precisely six months. Three months before Gilbert arrives at Tiffauges, Philippe left for parts unknown; three months after the arrival at Tiffauges, Lazarus visited Circassia, befriending ﬁshermen who promised to ﬁnd him a servant. We are even told in act 5:3 that the scenes visited are at moments approaching equinox (the ides of March), suggesting a deliberate strategy involved in opening the play at winter solstice. During the season of darkness, from autumnal to vernal equinoxes, Ruthven was present and courting Hélène at Tiffauges. From that point on until the return of the season of dark, when Ruthven is pulled from the Black Sea, he was believed by Gilbert to be dead. He was present at Tiffauges in the season of light, invisible in the season of shadow. Conversely, solar Gilbert knows every moment of the sun’s journey, proclaiming “Je suis le soleil,” ambiguously stating either “I am the Sun” or “I follow the sun.” That the forces of day and night, light and darkness, summer and winter are doomed Revelation 89

to eternal battle and ephemeral victory should come as no surprise. The antique god has died, the New God triumphed. Claims that Stoker’s count is as indebted to Gilles de Rais as he is to Vlad Tepes can only be speculative—the extent to which Dracula was inﬂuenced by either is completely unknown. It can be conﬁdently stated how- ever that the six-month interval Dumas imposed on his Vampire informs Stoker’s novel. More deﬁnitely, in commenting on the 13 visitors who recount stories until the entrance of the Count at the stroke of midnight, Stoker indexes Dumas’ Le Vampire, act 2:2. Dumas’ act 2:3’s “last supper” pays hom- age to the 13 told tales of Nodier’s novel as well as the Sunday evening soirées at Nodier’s Bibliothèque de l’Arsenal at which Dumas was a regular attendee. At these soirées the thirteenth arrival, excluded from conversation, was rele- gated to a separate table (Zimmerman 164). Daniel Farson’s oblique suggestion that Stoker’s knowledge of French was limited to vin, pain, and bain (464) is dispelled when Stoker lists a work by “Maury” in his references (Rosenbach #43a Notes 173). This would be Collin de Plancy’s (a.k.a. Collin de Maury’s) never translated Histoire des Vampires et des Spectres Malfaisans of 1820. Should French inﬂuence on Stoker’s opus remain obscure to Anglo-American researchers, Dracula makes them wholly apparent. 90 The Theology of Dracula

Revolution “It was as though my memories of all Jonathan’s horrid expe- rience were befooling me; for the snowﬂakes and the mist began to wheel and circle round.” [317]. As if to mask his vampire, Bram Stoker covered his best-known work with a preface: How these papers have been placed in sequence will be made manifest in the reading of them. All needless matters have been eliminated, so that a history almost at variance with the possibilities of later day belief may stand forth as simple fact. There is throughout no statement of past things wherein memory may err for all the records chosen are exactly contempo- rary, given from the stand-points and within the range of knowledge of those who made them [5]. Masquerading as bundled narrative fragments, the conceit of Dracula has every character save the eponymous anti–hero contribute some textual artefact to a chronologically determined documentary jigsaw puzzle. The proj- ect is opposed by Count Dracula who, masquerading as his green solicitor guest, attempts to corrupt chronology by sending extorted post–dated dis- patches from “Bistritz, the post town” (10) and by burning all the documentary evidence he encounters. The tale begins with a sole coach-bound chronicler, Jonathan Harker, hurtling down a road “not yet ... put in order after the winter snows” (14), past “a bewildering mass of fruit blossom” (14) into spring’s last “ﬁne, powdery snow” (19) and towards a schismatic fault-line where Roman and Eastern churches fracture as they impale themselves on Islam’s crescent, and institu- tional religion dissolves into the ethers of unforgotten paganism. The forested terrain Harker crosses, Transylvania, is alive with sub-continental and gypsy superstitions that reach beyond forest and mountain to an earlier time-space in which the Celts appeared in Nysian lands that stretch from the Black Sea’s 91

shores to far off Erin, and Dionysus descended from his mountain fasts to liberate the pre–Hellenic lands of Greece. Stoker’s empiricist hero, unable to isolate himself from the theological, the mythic, the superstitious, conﬁdes to his journal a dialogue that consigns the spiritual, the realm of Good and Evil, to a divided temporal frame, as he recalls an old woman pleading with him not to undertake his professional maiden voyage due to a question of time: “Do you know what day it is?” I answered that it was the fourth of May. She shook her head.... “Oh yes! I know that, I know that! but do you know what day it is?” On my saying that I did not understand, she went on: “It is the eve of St. George’s Day. Do you not know that to-night, when the clock strikes midnight, all the evil things in the world will have full sway?” [12]. Here, Christopher Frayling steps in to complain that Stoker has purloined his text, writing: “references to the swallow as the fowl of the Lord, the crow as unlucky and the dates of St. George’s Day are all taken verbatim from Emily Gerard’s Transylvanian Superstitions” (345). Gerard reports that Transylvania welcomes St. George with “occult meet- ings” held “at night in lonely caverns or within ruined walls, and where all the ceremonies usual to the celebration of a witches’ Sabbath are put into practice” (333). “In the night of St. George’s Day ... treasures begin to burn, or, to speak in mystic language, to ‘bloom’ in the bosom of the earth, and the light they give forth, described as a bluish ﬂame resembling the colour of lighted spirits of wine, serves to guide favoured mortals to their place of con- cealment” (333). Gerard’s “mystic language” concerning a “bloom” in the “bosom of the earth,” “bluish ﬂames” comparable to “spirits of wine,” and occulted “treasures” revealed to “favoured mortals” expose at the core of the St. George beliefs a mysteries discourse with Dionysian overtones. The occult gatherings, necessarily concerning the upcoming growing season, identify St. George as a vegetation god of resurrection, a solar Other of a Dionysian dying- god. On St. George’s, Transylvanian peasants deploy the same amulets, buck- thorn, and pitch that Athenians of yore used to ward off revenants during the Lesser Mysteries at Anthesteria, the Dionysian festival of the Dead. Given this, it is unsurprising that the Ionian isle of Saint George is denoted as the place of predilection for the cremation of vampires in Tourne- fort’s 18th-century Voyage du Levant, or that James George Frazer ritually links Saint George, or “Green George ... in Carinthian, Transylvanian, and Roman- ian customs” (93), to Slavic sacriﬁcial rites of spring in his Golden Bough. William Anderson maintains that British St. George legends derive from “the Celtic sun god Belinus,” further remarking that, 1,000 years ago, Arab scholars 92 The Theology of Dracula

“compared St. George with the Mesopotamian vegetation god Tammuz” (28– 9). As Tammuz conforms to the ideal of a dying-god of fertility, St. George embodies his Christianization. Sabine Baring-Gould, whom Stoker cites as a principal source for information on the vampire superstition, takes the rela- tionship between St. George, Tammuz, and other solar gods as his major theme in his lengthy essay on Saint George in Curious Myths of the Middle Ages, correlating St. George’s Day and Beltine. While it is not impossible that Stoker lists the festival’s date and infor- mation concerning totemic beasts and protective amulets merely to pad his text, it seems far more likely that the occult import of the superstitions is in keeping with his authorial intent. If Stoker has plagiarized, it in no way dimin- ishes St. George’s signiﬁcance as the point of departure for a spiritual epic; quite the opposite. Isaac Newton calculated that the likely date of the cru- ciﬁxion fell on St. George’s of A.D. 34 In Roman Catholic traditions, St. George, a martyr who suffered seven deaths but experienced six restorations, was honored by the recitation of the Little Ofﬁce of the Virgin. While these elements may be signiﬁcant, Stoker’s veritable investment in St. George, who is known as “The Quick to Hear,” only becomes manifest when Dracula’s plot concludes at Castle Dracula, precisely six diegetic months after Jonathan’s arrival there and at the instant of his return. The exchange Jonathan so diligently transcribes, beyond exposing St. George’s narrow import, underscores the signifying, sense-bearing role of the novel’s chronological dimension. Mina Harker afﬁrms “‘In this matter dates are everything, ... if we get all our material ready, and have every item put in chronological order, we shall have done much’” (198). A notion that Stoker has Dr Seward second: “‘What a good thing Mrs Harker put my cylinders into type!’” he dictates. “‘We never could have found the dates otherwise’” (199). Indeed, Dracula’s every constituent voice recording, journal entry, news- paper column, memorandum, telegram, and shipping bill is datelined or post- marked; the narrative not only knits “together in chronological order every scrap of evidence” (199) regarding the Vampire, it comments on discrepancies between Julian and Gregorian calendars. Stoker’s intrigue charges the Harkers, Jonathan and Mina, with “an exact ordering” (254) of the papers that the novel purports to be; but everybody inhabiting its pages concurs: narrative is about time. As Seward excitedly reports: “Harker has gone back, and is again collating his material. He says that by dinner-time they will be able to show a whole connected narrative” (199). So it is; as St. George’s Eve bleeds into St. George’s Day and Castle Drac- ula’s gates swallow Jonathan whole, a mad adventure begins. His mysterious coachman, master of wolves: vanished; the fortress ruins: apparently deserted; Harker stands before a massive door wondering what to think when he Revolution 93

perceives “through the chinks the gleam of a coming light” (21). As the door opens, Count Dracula hierophantically appears, “clad in black from head to foot” (21), “an antique silver lamp, in which the ﬂame burned without chimney or globe” (21) in his hand. He demands the ritual engagement of his visitor’s volition, insisting he cross the threshold proprio motu. And so Harker does, to ﬁnd himself conﬁned, isolated from all but the mysterious, priestly count. For nine days, Jonathan will remain sequestered, before being initiated into vampirism by a lamia triune. Harker’s prison consists of a bedroom, a library, and an octagonal room, antechamber to each. This latter room’s form is manifestly important, for Stoker insists upon it in both the novel and its stage adaptation. Still, no functional reason for introducing this space, or theatrical means for its rep- resentation is discernible. A passageway, “seemingly without a window of any sort” (22), containing but a single lamp, linking a space given to dreams to another dedicated to the written word and representation, reads as a symbolic and formal device of the author. The single lamp ambiguously suggests both sun and moon; the eight-sided shape more deﬁnitively projects the octave, eight-step cycle of return, as intrinsic to a way of passage. At cock’s crow, Harker is left alone at the chamber’s threshold, “all in a sea of wonders” (24). He who had so recently detected Dracula’s approach as a “coming light” observes that he could not “help experiencing that chill which comes over one at the coming of the dawn, which is like, in its way, the turn of the tide.” He muses “that people who are near death die generally at the change to the dawn or at the turn of the tide.” (30). His sense of uncanniness serves to situate the novel’s foregrounded principle-though-dual motif, liminality set against the temporal tides that pull Light from darkness. The journal entries that form Dracula’s body are often dated around noon or midnight; several, begun at dawn, are continued at midday, as if to emphazise the importance of these liminal temporal markers. An infected Mina experiences “sunrise and sunset” as “times of peculiar freedom; when her old self can be manifest without any controlling force” (286), since Drac- ula‘s “‘power ceases, as does that of all evil things, at the coming of the day’”(211). Dracula, conﬁned by moon and sun, is a transformational being only able to “‘pass running water at the slack or the ﬂood of the tide’” (212), only empowered to “‘change himself at noon or at exact sunrise or sun- set’”(211). Yet, as Helsing remarks, he “‘can see in the dark, no small power this, in a world which is one half shut from the light’” (211). Not only in the quotidian cycle of day and night is the world half shut from the light, but, as already seen, in the annual solar revolution as well. Within Castle Dracula’s library, Jonathan happens upon a worn map of England, and notices “certain places little rings marked” (29), each indicated 94 The Theology of Dracula

site—Whitby, Exeter, London—foreshadowing some future scene of Drac- ula’s invasion of England—what Jonathan rightly terms Dracula’s diabolical scheme. Within the geography plotted out in his novel, Stoker, circling dates on a calendar, executes his own diabolical scheme, placing in conﬂict two notions of time: It can be the fourth of May and something more ephemeral, something beyond an empiricist’s knowledge. Certain of Dracula’s plot events occur programmatically at lunar/monthly intervals. For example, Jonathan meets the Vampire on May 5; Renﬁeld’s “zoophagy” is diagnosed on June 5; Dracula sails for England 31 days later, arrives at Whitby 31 days after that; Arthur transfuses Lucy the following month; Mina insists on serving as tele- pathic spy on the Vampire the next; and the vampire chronicle breaks off 30 days later. The calendric monthly interval, functioning mechanically like the watch that Jonathan had become “rigorously accustomed to wind ... the last thing before going to bed” (44) each evening, lends Stoker a periodic metric for blocking out plot. Beyond modernity’s linear time, however, a cyclical, antique, pre–Copernican time pervades the novel to delineate a Ciruclus mythologicus and shape the story’s dramatic envelope. The solar year—halved by solstices, quartered by equinoxes, inter–cardinal intervals bisected again— is contained by eight nodes, a vision of the annual cycle typical of post– Neolithic agrarian societies. An ogdaodic division of the planetary ellipse is deﬁned. The Celt’s sacred solar calendar, for instance, while observing the solstitial and equinoctial, celebrates their intermediates as true thresholds of change: Beltine (Walpurgisnacht, or, in the East, St. George’s Eve) signals the season of light’s arrival, Samhain (Hallowe’en and All Souls), the dark’s. Mid-summer was observed in August, at Lughnasadh; mid–winter, in Feb- ruary, at Imbolic. The month of 30 or 31 days is, nevertheless, pure paradox, being a solar, sun–deﬁned metric rather than a true lunar, moon-dictated month. Yet it is repeatedly stressed that the Vampire is sensitive to both solar and tidal, hence lunar, ﬂuctuations. Through a tactic to which he makes repeated recourse, Stoker, using the voice of Seward in this instance, poses a rhetorical question: “Can it be that there is a malign inﬂuence of the sun at periods which affects certain natures—as at times the moon does others?” (110). The answer even- tually provided suggests that times of close coincidence between lunar and solar calendars, the former retained in liturgical affairs, provide conjunctive opportunities that Stoker is particularly keen to exploit. According to the lunar-driven calendar promulgated by the Book of Common Prayer, in the Christian era Beltine, or “Summer’s Day,” also accommodates Whitsun or Pentecost, the feast that commemorates the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles seven Sundays after Jesus’ Passover self–sacriﬁce on the cross and Revolution 95

His ensuing Resurrection. More often than not, dependant on the alignment of solar and lunar calendars, Whitsun, the traditional occasion for baptizing professing Christians during historical periods in which infants were consid- ered volitionally inept for sacramental life, follows upon St. George’s Day. Since Englishman Jonathan arrives at Castle Dracula upon St. George’s, the timing of his shaving accident or his encounter with lamiae may very well have coincided with Whitsun as the moment of Jonathan’s “baptism of blood” (297). What can be stated deﬁnitively is that Dracula’s central event is precisely pegged to the novel’s temporal midpoint, Lughsnasadh. On 7 August at Whitby, “shortly before ten o’clock the stillness of the air grew quite oppressive, and the silence was so marked that the bleating of a sheep inland or the barking of a dog in the town was distinctly heard, and the band on the pier, with its lively French air, was like a discord in the great harmony of nature’s silence. A little after midnight came a strange sound from over the sea, and high over- head the air began to carry a strange, faint, hollow booming” (76). A crewless ship, carrying in her hold 50 cases of earth—listed on the shipping bill as an agricultural experiment—soon appeared out of the storm to run aground miraculously at East Pier. 96 The Theology of Dracula The solar cycle and Dracula. © Rarignac

Stoker names his ghost ship The Demeter after the dark goddess wor- shipped at Chthonia; the 50 cases she transports contain consecrated soil from Castle Dracula and the remains of its lord. Demeter—mater and matter, The Mother and the material—births the Vampire. Iconographically associated with wheat fronds and snakes, theologically with fertility, mythically con- structed as the fruit of incest, she accepts blood sacriﬁce to graciously assure agricultural abundance and fertility. The Mother’s daughter, Persephone, embodies her spiritual dimension. Virgin bride of Plouton, Persephone rules over the realm of the dead, but resumes earthly life each spring, returning from Hades with the blossoming vegetation when the ﬂowers appear. Ironi- cally, it was as Persephone gathered spring ﬂowers that the lord of the under- world, hidden within the earth, appeared to ravage her and make her his queen. Demeter and Persephone jointly bestow the secret to eternal life to those who undergo the Eleusinian Rites. One secret that must ﬁgure promi- nently amongst those they reveal is that Plouton, whose unrepresentable visage is reserved for Hades, lurks behind Dionysus’s masks. Near the summer solstice, a half-season prior to The Demeter’s ground- ing, Mina had traveled to Whitby to visit her friend Lucy. Together, the two witnessed the scene of shipwreck. Three months later—that is, a half-season after the mysterious grounding, as the autumnal equinox neared—a wave of death swept across Britain that claimed bride-to-be Lucy. Preceding Lucy below by mere hours were her mother, her ﬁancé’s father, orphans Mina and Jonathan’s benefactor and Jonathan’s partner and virtual adoptive father—all simultaneously dispatched to the underworld. The peeling away of a ripened, elder generation, and the offering of a sacriﬁcial lamb, served to render neo- phytes initiates. Death and the rites it requires brought together the story’s various strands in the persons of the novel’s diarists and chroniclers. Death granted them awareness, gnosis. Through Lucy’s funeral, Helsing discovers Mina, accesses her knowledge of Lucy’s vampire contacts, obtains Jonathan’s Transylvanian journal, and initiates the ordering of the papers. Communally, Lucy’s orphaned friends could penetrate the mystery of her demise and res- urrection, deﬁning her relationship to a many-named lord who, questing for his queen, suddenly appeared from out of the earth in Lucy’s garden. Time would be needed for the vampire hunters to form a posse, but on 25 Septem- ber, the date of the Eleusinian Mysteries, they dedicate themselves to hunting down and destroying the Vampire. Although the tale begun on St. George’s ends six months later, the 183- day luminous half-year running from 5 May to 5 November projects a shadow-obscured Other, its dark double occupying the void between 5 November and 5 May. Metaphorically, the agrarian universe is contained by “a small octagonal room lit by a single lamp” (22), life-without–end turning Revolution 97

with the seasons. As Jonathan observes, we are always “simply going over and over the same ground again” (18). The oracular Pythian Temple at Delphi was time-shared, Apollo seizing priority during the annual period of Dionysian absence, when, the 53rd Orphic Hymn tells us, he withdrew to Persephone’s Hadean abode. Walter Otto notes that “we can even talk of a speciﬁc date, the eighth of November, as the day of his awakening” (194). Stoker suggests that that date is a bit off; the Dionysian renaissance should occur on 5 November, 40 days after the Mysteries’ conclusion. Stoker’s is a story of the Dionysian setting off to conquer the Apollonian, Dracula audaciously risking visibility for the possibility of triumphing over Light. During the season of light, Count Dracula, Plutonian avatar of a Dionysian god, remained visible to his pursuers, hunters of the hunter, who were themselves conﬁned by sun’s light. Dracula disappeared from the Apollonian as Dionysus ascended the Delphic throne to reign over darkness, until, come spring, he must return to Hades to rule during Perse- phone’s hiatus. While it is often remarked in the critical literature that Lucy Westenra’s name evokes “sunset,” the sustained interplay between light and darkness Stoker invested in his novel remains little discussed, beyond being reduced 98 The Theology of Dracula The Octagonal Room. © Rarignac

to simple polarities yoked to ideological readings. Like much vampire ﬁction, Dracula—hardly Gothic—is less about the deathless body than the encapsu- lated soul. The well-chosen name Stoker bestowed on the vessel communi- cating Dracula to England furnishes means of understanding one of Helsing’s otherwise incomprehensible speeches: When the corn is grown, even before it has ripened—while the milk of its mother-earth is in him, and the sunshine has not yet begun to paint him with his gold, the husbandman he pull the ear and rub him between his rough hands, and blow away the green chaff, and say to you: “Look! he’s good corn; he will make good crop when the time comes” [111]. When Seward complains of the obscurity of these remarks, Helsing offers continuation in way of clariﬁcation: The good husbandman tell you so then because he knows, but not till then. But you do not ﬁnd the good husbandman dig up his planted corn to see if he grow; that is for the children who play at husbandry, and not for those who take it as of the work of their life [111–12]. This, what seemed to Seward a perplexing discourse, is founded on several classical references. The discourse on the husbandman versus the child seeking amusement recalls Plato’s Phaedrus. That the farmer becomes “the good hus- bandsman” (111) aligns the Socratic speech with Jesus’ proverbial shepherd. The ear of corn clearly indexes the Mysteries of Eleusis, their initiative rites and the gestures that accompanied the mystogogues’s prayer: “Let it rain, and bear fruit!” From the sewing of seed to the threshing of grain, Dracula reports on events across the season of light. Yet by 4 November, it is “so cold that the grey heavy sky is full of snow, which when it falls will settle for all winter as the ground is hardening to receive it” (313). As the ﬁrst ﬂakes announced the end of Transylvania’s period of fertility and the sun’s last rays birthed Samhain, Dracula’s end came: “It was like a miracle; but before our very eyes, and almost in the drawing of a breath, the whole body crumbled into dust and passed from our sight” (325). Crossing the threshold from light into shade, the forces of darkness attain invisibility and, like Dionysus, perhaps only seemingly disappear. Shadow, so strong that it projects through solid objects, so uncanny it can lie undetected in the dark, reveals itself only to Light. According to Plutarch, the Phrygians believed that their god slept in winter, and woke in summer; it would seem that Dracula is that god’s antithesis. Stoker has Jonathan Harker rhetorically wonder of his own nemesis, “Can it be that he sleeps when others waken that he may be awake whilst they sleep?” (49). Demonstrating deep concern for the cyclic, Stoker sacriﬁces one crusad- ing vampire hunter on that 5 November that the Vampire was cut down— Revolution 99

Quincey Morris succumbs to wounds suffered in action. Seven years later, the Harkers report in postscript that on 5 November of the year following Morris’s death, Mina gave birth to a boy who was called “Quincey,” the trans- migration of a regal soul being implicit in their “Note.” Death had given rise to life. It may be prudent, however, to recall that Dracula crumbled into dust nearly at the instant of Morris’s death and that the infant was certainly con- ceived at the antipodes of the anniversary of Demeter’s arrival at Whitby. Jonathan concludes by acknowledging that “among the masses of material of which the record is composed, there is hardly one authentic document” (326), thereby undermining his own prefatory comments. Jonathan then appends his notarial signature to a prophecy that the son born to Mina would “some day know what a brave and gallant woman his mother is” and “how some men so loved her, that they did dare much for her sake” (327). The cases of soil that Demeter, The Mother, carried westward contained, rather than simple dirt, the Earth itself; the treasure blooming in the bosom of the Earth and revealed to favored mortal Jonathan on St. George’s Eve was a vam- pire who sought to replace Green George with his darkling self. God of death, chthonic Dracula—his luggage composed of boxes of earth—will rule the underworld alone during Persephone’s foray into the Apollonian solar world come St. George’s Day next. 100 The Theology of Dracula

Syzygy “Then came another rush of sea-fog, greater than any hith- erto—a mass of dank mist, which seemed to close on all things, like a grey pall, and left available to men only the organ of hear- ing.” (77). Ernest Jones, James B. Twitchell, and a host of others would cast the Vampire Tale as a “crime and punishment” fantasy that both expresses incest yearnings and—accommodating associated guilt—serves to effect their repres- sion. This template is so solidly established that the ageless monster that preys on adolescents freshly initiated into sexuality has become a perennial Holly- wood revenant, from Count Dracula to Jason Voorhees to Freddy Krueger to Leatherface. David J. Skal and Elias Savada claim that it was precisely the dichotomous interplay of desire and repression that attracted Tod Browning to undertake the ﬁlming of Balderston and Deane’s Broadway Dracula when Universal’s Junior Laemmle acquired the rights—Browning enjoyed playing “not only to the public’s appetite for extravagant sex fantasy but to its puri- tanical resistance as well” (93). Lorne MacDonald encapsulates the psycho- analytical take on the vampire qua universal ﬁgure of consciousness’s underworld: In Stoker’s novel, what opposes the evil power of sex is the pure power of love...: Mina, as an object of love, is opposed to the demons of the Pit, objects of desire [the lamiæ].... The novel articulates the split between affectionate and sensual feelings, between sacred and profane love, which Freud saw as endemic in civilized men. Freud attributed this split to the prohibition of incest, which forces desire away from the primary object of affection. (He considered that the psychopathology of civilized women was slightly different in this respect—that they were attracted to the forbidden, rather than to the degraded. This, as well as the identiﬁcations of male authors, may explain why female vampires, the objects of masculine desire, are notably more degraded than male ones, the merely forbidden objects of feminine desire.) And the idea of contagion symbolically restores the 101

element of incest onto vampiric eroticism: since Dracula’s victims are reborn as vampires, he is their father (and even, as the scene of Mina’s bap- tism suggests, their mother) as well as their lover. The ever-widening con- spiracy of vampires is a league of incest [202]. The charge of a conspiratorial “league of incest” echoes the accusation Byron believed Robert Southey* leveled against Shelley, Polidori, Mary Godwin, Clair Clairmont, and himself in an infamous commentary on the stormy May night that indirectly gave rise to The Vampyre, A Tale..., Frankenstein, etc.: “Extracts of a Letter from Geneva.” Its author, vaguely correct (though, as Byron insisted to John Murray, stepsisters Mary and Clair were not genetically related), nevertheless allows righteous ire to blind him to artistic merit in the works that the league generated. Incest may well be the constant on which horror generically functions, but forcing the Vampire, and Dracula in particular, into this horriﬁed interpretative frame limits our capacity to discern other layers of meaning ger- mane to the Vampire, other efforts at signiﬁcation that, even when considering blood, engage something more than simple consanguinity. Dracula is written, in Helsing’s phrase, in “the language that was of bloom and blood” (277), Perse- phone and Dionysus, resurrection and cruciﬁxion; as with Polidori’s début-de- siècle Vampyre, Stoker’s ﬁn-de-siècle novel’s ultimate concern is fertility, the cyclical, the soul, the sacred and gnosis, rather than taboo violated. It offers laconic as a keyword, though its evangelists be many. “They say much of blood and bloom and of others which I comprehend not, though I guess what they mean; but nevertheless they tell us all the things we want to know” (276). The Vampire Tale’s truest sense escapes the attention of those who insist on interpreting the story as mythic and end up with Freud. Mircea Eliade terms the underlying mythos “renewal.” Incest, a given of renewal in Demeter myths and Isiacal rites, is too narrow a frame to produce a larger understanding of these works, even as their plots expose unfolding rites of initiation and spiritual metamorphoses. Therefore, we must approach the text of Dracula as Helsing might, that is, “have an open mind, and [deny] let a little bit of truth check the rush of a big truth” (172), consider “big and little...; perhaps at the end the little things may teach us most” (253). In applying that method, Hels- ing could triumphantly report, “I did not look for any speciﬁc thing. I only hoped to ﬁnd, and ﬁnd I have” (148). Having considered Dracula’s temporal similarities to The Vampires of Dumas, Nodier, and Polidori, further penetration into the mysteries “conﬁned within the limitations of [Dracula’s] earthly envelope” (255) becomes possible. 102 The Theology of Dracula *Byron suspected Robert Southey, who crossed paths with the Cologny group at the Hôtel de l’An- gleterre, of having penned the “Extracts of a Letter from Geneva...” which was used as a preface to Polidori’s The Vampyre as well as of “Account of Lord Byron’s Residence at Mitylene,” from William Blake’s “Auguries of Innocence.”

Excepting Planché’s discrepant contribution, since The Vampyre of Polidori— whose Aubrey siblings are orphans, and whose Ianthe becomes orphaned due to her encounter with Ruthven—the Vampire Tale begins with the parentless child. Stoker, too, creates a heroic couple whose members are obliged to fend for themselves in the world. Jonathan Harker has no parents, though his employer and mentor, Peter Hawkins, treats him in a caring, even paternal way; Mina Murray, who becomes Madam Harker when she weds Jonathan about one-third of the way into the text, “never knew father or mother” (143). The critical act of being united as husband and wife is far from the only rite to which these young people will be subjected, though it may be the most important. With plot ﬁxing rites of transformation that the main character— the couple or syzygy—must undertake, the complex initiation imposed will repeatedly try Jonathan and Mina’s commitment to each other. The mysteries of sensual love seem scarcely to be their problem as they are examined and tested. While their ordeals are parallel, the timing of their individual trials and the sequencing of rites undergone are often sympathetically inverted or reversed to accommodate their respective genders. Stoker opens his novel with Jonathan, traveling with the de rigueur image of Mina, off on a career-establishing mission. He is to rendezvous at midnight with a Transylvanian nobleman. Expository dialogue set down as a journal entry has an old woman engage the youth as he prepares to set out on what seems to be the last stage of his journey. When she asks Jonathan if he knows the day, and he replies, “The fourth of May,” she nearly scolds him: “Oh yes! I know that, I know that! but do you know what day it is?” On my saying that I did not understand, she went on: “It is the eve of St. George’s Day. Do you not know that to-night, when the clock strikes midnight, all the evil things in the world will have full sway? Do you know where you are going, and what you are going to?” She was in such evident distress that I tried to comfort her, but without effect. Finally she went down on her knees and implored me not to go; at least to wait a day or two before starting. It was all very ridiculous, but I did not feel comfortable. However, there was business to be done, and I could allow nothing to interfere with it. I therefore tried to raise her up, and said, as gravely as I could that I thanked her, but my duty was imperative, and that I must go. She then rose and dried her eyes, and taking a cruciﬁx from her neck offered it to me. I did not know what to do, for, as an English Churchman, I have been taught to regard such things as in some measure idolatrous, and yet it seemed so ungracious to refuse an old lady meaning so well and in such a state of mind. She saw, I suppose, the doubt in my face, for she put the rosary round my neck, and said, “For your mother’s sake,” and went out of the room [5]. This, the ﬁrst represented act of Jonathan’s initiation (though we know that he was previously dispatched to undertake the mission), places an “old woman” Syzygy 103

“on her knees” before him, in order to challenge his will. In accepting her gift, he in part accepts her theology. The cross, offered as antithetical to “all evil things in the world,” is to be worn for “your mother’s sake.” Considering that Jonathan is an orphan, the mother referenced is necessarily his and our spiritual mother, Magna Mater, Notre Dame. Jonathan’s eastward procession leads him to an encounter with a hiero- phantic ﬁgure who will lead him through a portal, or cleft, “separating two atmospheres” (16) in the mountainous steeps of “God’s seat” (14) at that inde- terminate moment of hesitation between days old and new: midnight. As the disquiet of St. George’s Eve expires, Jonathan is rushed through the gates of Castle Dracula and confronted by an ancient warrior who invites him to enter his abode. Harker has little choice but to obey the command to “enter freely,” for, as the count stridently reminds him, he has been indentured by his sur- rogate father: “When your master, employer, what you will, engaged that someone should come on his behalf, it was understood that my needs only were to be consulted” (37). The exchange between new master and neophyte is initially stimulating, Dracula being “like a king speaking” (33). “I wish I could put down all he said exactly as he said it, for to me it was most fasci- nating” (33). The empirically-led, sober, fashionable young man of law and property who entered the castle sure of his world, is soon shifting, considering that “unless my senses deceive me, the old centuries had, and have, powers of their own which mere ‘modernity’ cannot kill” (41). Jonathan is soon con- trasting “bare, meagre facts, veriﬁed by books and ﬁgures” with “experiences which will have to rest on my own observation or my memory of them” (35– 36). So many of the givens of Jonathan’s conceptual frame have been chal- lenged that as the long evening abruptly ends at dawn he confesses to discovering, or losing himself “all in a sea of wonders” (24). Jonathan awakes and arises to ﬁnd himself alone. When he is at last joined by the lord of the domain, the Count expresses his desire to master Jonathan’s “tongue” and contends that he is “but a little way on the road I would travel” (26). He indeed dictates to Jonathan what he is to say to those who may be con- cerned about him to rationalize a prolonged absence. The solicitor, functioning as scribe, writes and postdates his letters according to the Count’s calculations. Dracula informs Jonathan, “You may go anywhere you wish in the castle, except where the doors are locked, where of course you will not wish to go. There is reason that all things are as they are, and did you see with my eyes and know with my knowledge, you would perhaps better understand” (26). The youth is particularly cautioned to “not by any chance go to sleep in any other part of the castle. It is old, and has many memories, and there are bad dreams for those who sleep unwisely” (38). As Jonathan soon realizes, he has become its prisoner. On 8 May, Jonathan is startled when shaving by the sudden awareness 104 The Theology of Dracula

of a hand on his shoulder and a voice speaking in his ear, much like Aubray’s uncanny experience at the drawing room on his return to London. Jonathan’s start, due to the fact that he had heard nothing and had seen nothing in the mirror that reﬂected the whole room, results in his cutting himself. The blood sets Dracula’s eyes ablaze “with demoniac fury” (31), a fury so consuming that “he suddenly made a grab” at Harker’s throat, that is, until his hand made contact with the rosary that Jonathan was wearing, that sign of the Sacred Mother—habitually recalled as “Ste Mary” in Stoker’s text. Bless that good, good woman who hung the cruciﬁx around my neck! For it is a comfort and a strength to me whenever I touch it. It is odd that a thing which I have been taught to regard with disfavour and as idolatrous should in a time of loneliness and trouble be of help. Is it that there is something in the essence of the thing itself, or that it is a medium, a tangi- ble help, in conveying memories of sympathy and comfort? [33]. It is, tangibly and inherently, no simple cruciﬁx hung on a necklace of beads; it is a rosary, a prayerful cycle designed to mediate and to connect a petitioning soul—through the Virgin Mother—to the Son of Man and God the Father, and a meditation on a series of mysteries: Joyous, Luminous, Sor- rowful, Glorious. Heaven knows, Jonathan requires comforting, for he is deeply afraid. “I am, I know, either being deceived, like a baby, by my own fears, or else I am in desperate straits” (32). “I start at my own shadow, and am full of all sorts of horrible imaginings” (38). Convinced that he is in the presence of Evil, Harker concludes that unless he acts, his days are few and limited to the dates already numbered and dictated by the count. One evening, Jonathan accidentally learns more of the Count’s ways as he looks out a window. To evacuate his sealed castle and grandiose cofﬁn, and in order to access the exterior world, the count slithers headlong down the walls of his battlements like a lizard. Assured that his tormentor has departed, the neophyte solicitor slips out of his rooms to discover a more appropriate means to escape his fortress-prison. He descends a long ﬂight of stairs into the Vampire’s netherworld: “doors, doors, doors everywhere, and all locked and bolted” (31–2). He ﬁnds a stairway rising into a distant wing of the structure. “At last ... I found one door at the top of a stairway which, though it seemed to be locked, gave a little under pressure. I tried it harder, and found that it was not really locked, but that the resistance came from the fact that the hinges had fallen somewhat and the heavy door rested on the ﬂoor” (40). He enters what he assumes was a room frequented by long- departed, courtly ladies. Installing himself at a writing table, he records his day. When I had written in my diary.... I felt sleepy. The Count’s warning came into my mind, but I took a pleasure in disobeying it. The sense of sleep was upon me, and with it the obstinacy which sleep brings as outrider. The Syzygy 105

soft moonlight soothed, and the wide expanse without gave a sense of free- dom which refreshed me. I determined not to return tonight to the gloom- haunted rooms, but to sleep here, where of old ladies had sat and sung and lived sweet lives whilst their gentle breasts were sad for their menfolk away in the midst of remorseless wars. I drew a great couch out of its place near the corner, so that, as I lay, I could look at the lovely view to east and south, and unthinking of and uncaring for the dust, composed myself for sleep. I suppose I must have fallen asleep; I hope so, but I fear, for all that fol- lowed was startlingly real—sitting here in the broad, full sunlight of the morning, I cannot in the least believe that it was all sleep. I was not alone. The room was the same, unchanged in any way since I came into it; I could see along the ﬂoor, in the brilliant moonlight, my own footsteps marked where I had disturbed the long accumulation of dust. In the moonlight opposite me were three young women, ladies by their dress and manner. I thought at the time that I must be dreaming when I saw them, for, though the moonlight was behind them, they threw no shadow on the ﬂoor. They came close to me and looked at me for some time, and then whispered together. Two were dark.... The other was fair, as fair as can be, with great wavy masses of golden hair and eyes like pale sap- phires. I seemed to know her face, and to know it in connection with some dreamy fear, but I could not recollect at the moment how or where. All three had brilliant white teeth, that shone like pearls against the ruby of their voluptuous lips [41–2]. Jonathan is a victim of succubae. The fair girl shook her head coquettishly, and the other two urged her on. One said: —“Go on! You are ﬁrst, and we shall follow; yours is the right to begin.” The other added: —“He is young and strong; there are kisses for us all.” I lay quiet, looking out under my eyelashes in an agony of delightful antic- ipation [42]. Back from posting Jonathan’s letters at Bistritz, Dracula sweeps into the room like a summer storm, disengaging lamiæ and sending them off in a fury amidst a hail of accusatory words on the subject of love. When the lamiae beg for sustenance, the Count motions to a sack containing, it is suggested, a suckling babe torn from its mother’s breast. He promises to surrender Jonathan to their appetites shortly, once he has ﬁnished with him. Morning dawns on Jonathan in his habitual bed, doubting his recollection of the pre- vious evening, searching anew for documentary evidence. Later, Jonathan again witnesses “something coming out of the Count’s window” (47), wearing “the suit of clothes which I had worn whilst travelling here, and slung over his shoulder the terrible bag I had seen the women take 106 The Theology of Dracula

away” (47). Within a matter of hours, an “agonized cry of a woman” (48) draws him again to his window. In the courtyard below, a Madonna dolorosa spies him; falling to her knees, she franticly implores him to return her child, accusing him of having stolen an infant, no doubt a child the Count and the voluptuous lamiae had feasted on. At a signal from the Count, wolves slink into the courtyard to end the mother’s mortal ordeal. Count Dracula eagerly prepares to depart and take possession of his new estates in England, where Mina, visiting with her bosom friend Lucy, anxiously awaits word from her ﬁancé. Before the Count is carted off, however, Jonathan steals into the chapel crypt to open his cofﬁn and search his person for a key. It seemed as if the whole awful creature were simply gorged with blood; he lay like a ﬁlthy leech, exhausted with his repletion. I shuddered as I bent over to touch him, and every sense in me revolted at the contact; but I had to search, or I was lost. The coming night might see my own body a ban- quet in a similar way to those horrid three. I felt all over the body, but no sign could I ﬁnd of the key. Then I stopped and looked at the Count. There was a mocking smile on the bloated face which seemed to drive me mad. This was the being I was helping to transfer to London, where, per- haps, for centuries to come he might, amongst its teeming millions, satiate his lust for blood, and create a new and ever-widening circle of semi- demons to batten on the helpless. ... A terrible desire came upon me to rid the world of such a monster. There was no lethal weapon at hand, but I seized a shovel which the workmen had been using to ﬁll the cases, and lifting it high struck, with the edge downward, at the hateful face. But as I did so the head turned, and the eyes fell full upon me, with all their blaze of basilisk horror. The sight seemed to paralyse me, and the shovel turned in my hand and glanced from the face, merely making a deep gash above the forehead. The shovel fell from my hand across the box, and as I pulled it away the ﬂange of the blade caught the edge of the lid, which fell over again, and hid the horrid thing from my sight [53–4]. This assault leaves an angry red wound, mark of Cain, upon the Count’s fore- head, and Jonathan is more desperate than ever to escape, imitating the Count’s headlong descent of the castle walls as he sets off towards an unknowable future. Directly or indirectly, the plot has: dispatched the initiate under order of his superior; required his wilful threshold surrender of volition; enforced the initiate’s sequestration; established an unjustiﬁed taboo; provoked an inci- dent generating motivational bloodshed; introduced a spiritual guide; pro- duced a providentially revealed cruciﬁx; encouraged the initiate to lose consciousness; admitted a misting fog and allowed for the materialization of evil; engaged a terrifying act of initiation; imposed the appearance of an authority-asserting dominant male; portrayed, through the distribution of communion, his assumption of a priestly role; promulgated a confusion of Syzygy 107

identities that should lead to the initiate’s inevitable death and rebirth in a transformed state. To see a world in a grain of sand And a heaven in a wild ﬂower, Hold inﬁnity in the palm of your hand And eternity in an hour [William Blake, “Auguries of Innocence”]. Dracula is a story of becoming that traces the symmetrical ritual paths taken by Jonathan and Mina as they are conjointly transformed into New Man and New Woman. The manifold symmetrical aspects of the novel— from the opposing hierophantic roles of Dracula and Helsing, and dual fem- inine ﬁgures of Lucy and Mina, to the balanced East-West-East itinerary of plot, its temporal design and solar equilibrium—extend into the plot’s ritual aspects. Whereas Jonathan encountered an old woman who foretold danger and provided protection from evil in the name of the Mother, life-giving force, Mina comes upon a man with “a face all gnarled and twisted like the bark of a tree” (64), Sir Oracle (65), on her ﬁrst day at Lucy’s residence at Whitby. No doubt inspired by Coleridge’s “Rime,” this Ancient Mariner takes Mina as the wedding-guest in seating her on the stone of St. Mary’s churchyard. Concerned with life’s ends, Sir Oracle, or Swales, holds court in a grave- yard situated high upon East Cliff, overlooking the grounds of an ancient abbey and the bay. His ﬁrst meditation, “a sort of sermon” (65), is on dualism and the falseness of death, which leads him to cast aspersions on the veracity of the surrounding gravestones, “simply tumblin’ down with the weight o’ the lies wrote on them, ‘Here lies the body’ or ‘Sacred to the memory’ wrote on all of them, an’ yet in nigh half of them there bean’t no bodies at all” (65). He later speaks on the conduct of Judgment Day, envisioning the truth of men’s lives as cut in stone on their graves, each soul struggling to bear the weight of the heavy truth of his mortal existence. His Geordie manner of pro- nouncing the word tombstone forces it to approach the sound of “tomb stain.” On a third occasion he concentrates on death’s arrival and the trumpet call for the soul’s surrender, saying, “For life be, after all, only a waitin’ for some- thin’ else than what we’re doin’; and death be all that we can rightly depend on” (74). Claiming to be ready to heed the call, he closes the interview by blessing Mina. A week after meeting Mina, on the night The Demeter delivers Count Dracula to England’s shores, Sir Oracle dies. His distorted features lead Mina to speculate that “he had seen Death with his dying eyes!” (85). Yet, as with the comfort that the old woman’s rosary brought Jonathan long after she was distant, the oracle had not yet issued his last, unspoken word. It awaits his funeral.
