The stone bench, mercy seat, on which Mina and Lucy would sit 108 The Theology of Dracula

listening to him hold forth while enjoying the view was, according to Swales, part of a suicide’s grave, that of a man named Canon, only son of a widow, who killed himself to spite his very own pious, holy mother. From this spot of seeing and hearing, Mina watched the funeral cortège of The Demeter’s captain approach, climbing the hundreds of steps, even as a maritime pro- cession honored the sailor on the waterway below. Swales, too, was to be interred by the East Cliff bench, and it seems that the identities of Swales and The Demeter’s captain are somehow strangely combined. In fact, it was pre- cisely there, on that seat, that Swales had died. One of the oracle’s mates, a mild and silent man with a devoted dog, joined Lucy and Mina at the bench during the funeral service, but the dog kept its distance, howling in fright and alarm. When the man, seeking to control his dog, took it by the scruff of its neck and placed it upon the bench beside him, it cowered and trembled in fright and would not be calmed—apparently terror-stricken by its prox- imity to Lucy. In Ste Mary’s East Cliff churchyard, Lucy, locked in a somnambulistic tryst with the Count, had also and already sprinkled her blood upon that bench and literal tomb stain. She described the encounter to Mina in ﬂuid images: A ﬁsh leaped as I went by, and I leaned over to look at it, and I heard a lot of dogs howling—the whole town seemed as if it must be full of dogs all howling at once—as I went up the steps. Then I have a vague memory of something long and dark with red eyes, just as we saw in the sunset, and something very sweet and very bitter all around me at once; and then I seemed sinking into deep green water, and there was a singing in my ears, as passing away from me; my soul seemed to go out from my body and ﬂoat about the air. I seemed to remember that once the West Lighthouse was right under me, and then there was a sort of agonizing feeling, as if I were in an earthquake, and I came back and found you shaking my body. I saw you do it before I felt you [94]. Despite the blood spilt, with word of Jonathan arriving from the East, Mina bids Lucy farewell and hurries off to join her ﬁancé. The two orphans, Jonathan and Mina, become one in the double city Buda-Pesht’s Convent of Saint Joseph and Saint Mary, to which Mina was summoned in the name of “God and St Joseph and Ste Mary” (95). Mina tells Jonathan, “You are nearest and dearest and all the world to me; our souls are knit into one, for all life and all time” (287). Just prior to the marriage ceremony, Jonathan presents her with his Transylvanian diary as if it is his very soul. In accepting it, she takes possession of his nightmares, and, using her wedding band as signet ring, seals the document with a sky-blue ribbon and wax (100), the transaction with a kiss. “And ... when he kissed me, and drew me to him with his poor weak hands, it was like a very solemn pledge between us” (101). Syzygy 109

This holy unity of man and woman gains in status and wealth, prospering due to Jonathan’s Transylvanian initiation. On 17 September, Mina writes to an already dying Lucy to tell her that Mr. Hawkins had named the newlyweds his heirs, and to announce a recently-formed partnership, “the important ﬁrm of Hawkins & Harker” (141). The ﬁrm’s name, deliberately communicating the sense of “eyes and ears,” “sights and sounds,” calls attention to a constant representational gambit: Throughout the text the sensory and extrasensory are given contrasting play—particularly communicative acts that confound the senses (hearing what was to be seen, or seeing that which should have been entendu, and, of course, being visited by visions). Reality, however, often exceeds fantasy in embracing ironic happenings. No sooner had Mina ﬁnished posting her letter than Death initiated youth into maturity, for on the day following the writing of Mina’s letter Mr. Hawkins unexpectedly dies at the height of a deadly harvest season in which “the Aud Man” (74) claims Lucy, Mrs. Westenra, and, at Ring, Lord Godalming, Arthur’s father. Now a man of property, Jonathan is more confused than on the day he arrived in Transylvania. He “begins to doubt himself” (141) and confesses that he no longer knows “what to trust, even the evidence of my own senses” (168). ‘It was the doubt as to the reality of the whole thing that knocked’ (168) cer- titude from him. Jonathan mostly doubts his own sanity, judgment, and abil- ities. In London, while returning from Mr. Hawkins’ funeral, he becomes distraught as he observes a man who strongly resembles the Count as he might look renewed and rejuvenated. Troubled by the effect the tall, thin, cruel- faced man spied in a London street has had on her husband’s psyche, Mina decides to “take the foreign journal, and lock myself up in my room and read it” (161) once they return home. Mina, describing the silent abode that welcomed them in Exeter as a “house empty of the dear soul” (156), exploits symbolic language Polidori once employed to suggest mortal coils sloughed off. In this void, at this barren pass in the mountains, she receives a request from a stranger, one Dr. Abraham Van Helsing, for a meeting to discuss Lucy’s death. While he is speciﬁcally interested in Mina’s Whitby diary, she cannot avoid questioning an authority on “therapeutics ... of the continuous evolution of brain-matter” (215) on the record of her husband’s Transylvanian experiences. Within a short period of time, joining West and East, Helsing determines that Lucy’s death and Jonathan’s diary are intimately related, writing to Mina, “You may sleep with- out doubt” (167), and vouching for Jonathan’s sanity and capacity to recover from the shocks he has suffered. Jonathan conﬁdes to his journal that when Mina “showed me in the doctor’s letter that all I wrote down was true ... [it] made a new man of me” (168). If previously he had “felt impotent and in the dark,” he was now conﬁdently predicting that “Van Helsing is the man to 110 The Theology of Dracula

unmask” (168) the Count. The couple joins Helsing at his protégé Seward’s asylum. In joining together Lucy’s diary and correspondence with the Harkers’ personal papers, Helsing also gathers the journals’ authors and the personalities that enliven their pages. As Jonathan was surrounded by the Count and his three ladies in Transylvania, Mina will be by Helsing and his three gentlemen in Britain. These latter, Lucy’s former suitors all, will embrace Mina nearly as they had Lucy. Mina, who knows of them through Lucy, solicitously extends to them her heart, she; afﬁrms to Jack Seward, “You will let me help you, will you not?” (197) she explains to Art Holmwood that she and Lucy “were like sisters; and now she is gone, will you not let me be like a sister to you in your trouble?” (203); and she asks Quincey Morris, “Will you let me be your friend, and will you come to me for comfort if you need it?” (204). At their ﬁrst meeting, “The Professor stood up and, after laying his golden cruciﬁx on the table, held out his hand on either side. I took his right hand, and Lord Godalming his left; Jonathan held my right with his left and stretched across to Mr. Morris. So as we all took hands our solemn compact was made,” another “transaction of life” (210), joining the couple to Helsing’s band. Despite oaths of solidarity and joining of hands, Mina is soon isolated, not by the walls of a material fortress but by gender—the surrounding band of men think her participation inappropriate and dangerous. For Mina, “to accept their chivalrous care” (214) was “a bitter pill” (214). Although she is physically present at Seward’s asylum, she is for Jonathan as much an image as she had been when he was in Transylvania. For noble-sounding, deceit-jus- tifying paternalistic reasons he strives to exclude her from sharing in the group’s collective knowledge. His reports reﬂect the depth of his gender chauvinism: I could not tell the others of the day’s discovery till we were alone; so after dinner—followed by a little music to save appearances even amongst our- selves—I took Mina to her room and left her to go to bed. The dear girl was more affectionate with me than ever, and clung to me as though she would detain me; but there was much to be talked of and I came away. Thank God, the ceasing of telling things had made no difference between us [234]. Drawing a curtain that partitions their covenant, an initial foray into the count’s demesne was launched without Mina’s knowledge. Mina stoically accepts the situation. “Manlike, they have told me to go to bed and sleep; as if a woman can sleep when those she loves are in danger! I shall lie down and pretend to sleep, lest Jonathan have added anxiety about me when he returns” (214). While menfolk conspired and advanced against the Count’s territory, the Count made their asylum his sanctuary, seeking out, “as though he owned the whole place” (245), its chamber of courtly ladies. The returning men were jubilant: “More that all do I rejoice that this, Syzygy 111

our ﬁrst—and perhaps our most difﬁcult and dangerous—step has been accomplished without the bringing thereinto our most sweet Madam Mina or troubling her waking or sleeping thoughts with sights and sounds and smells of horror which she might never forget” (223), was Helsing’s optimistic assessment of the foray he had led. Jonathan bade his comrades good-night and “came tiptoe” to ﬁnd “Mina asleep, breathing so softly that I had to put my ear down to hear it. She looks paler than usual. I hope the meeting tonight has not upset her. I am truly thankful that she is to be left out of our future work, and even of our deliberations. It is too great a strain for a woman to bear. ... Henceforth our work is to be a sealed book to her, till at least such time as we can tell her that all is ﬁnished” (223). Mina’s unsealing of Jonathan’s book brought together Helsing’s forces; the band’s sealing off and cloistering of Mina has prepared her for initiation. Despite Jonathan’s innocent willingness to cross Castle Dracula’s thresh- old, it was Mr. Hawkins who engaged the ﬂedgling solicitor’s volition by dis- patching him to Transylvania in his stead; similarly, it is Mr. Renﬁeld, “mouth ... nauseous with ... ﬂies and insects” (225), who places Mina within the Vam- pire’s grasp via his willingness to welcome the Count to his cell. In designating these particular wilful agents, Stoker, who had earlier proclaimed that “the God created from human vanity sees no difference between an eagle and a sparrow” (96), contrasts the mighty hawk (albeit, a hawk with “neither chick nor child” (140)) and the humble wren, picturing the former emerging “from under the shadow of your beautiful cathedral at Exeter” (36) while situating the latter merely “somewhere under this” (226)—that is, in a place beneath us. “[W]ith his ﬂy business” (169), Renﬁeld, variously depicted as disgorging “a whole lot of feathers” (71) and “singing gaily as he used to do” (239), is cajoled by Dr. Seward with images of ﬂight and freedom from the bars of his conﬁning cage: “A nice time you’ll have some time when you’re ﬂying out there” (237), his status suddenly elevated. Seward duly reports: “He did not care for any of the things of mere earth; he was in the clouds and looked down on all the weaknesses and wants of us poor mortals” (235); yet: “Our bird when he found the cage open would not ﬂy” (102). In choosing his birds, Stoker has perhaps borrowed imagery from Shakespeare’s Richard III, Act I- 3 or King Lear, Act IV-6, while equally attaching his work to couplets of the great mystic artist William Blake’s “Auguries of Innocence.” Renﬁeld, a legally-constituted madman, is bribed by an implicit promise of the provision of millions of lives for his consumption—a bribe expressed, he makes clear, through gesture only. He admits the Vampire into the asylum: He slid into the room through the sash, though it was only open an inch wide—just as the Moon herself has often come in through the tiniest crack, and has stood before me in all her size and splendour [245]. 112 The Theology of Dracula

Lunatic, devotee of the moon, Renﬁeld claims he has previously been visited by Artemis–Hekate; he also “thought that somehow Mrs Harker had come into the room” (245). On the occasion of her ﬁrst visit, “[s]he came into the room with an easy gracefulness which would at once command the respect of any lunatic.... She walked over to him, smiling pleasantly, and held out her hand.” Before he could speak she said to him, “‘Good evening, Mr Renﬁeld’” (205). One persistently posed question in Dracula is whether Mina, the only woman represented as appearing in Renﬁeld’s cell, will be ﬁgured as queen of night or of day. Madam Mina—that is, “My Lady Love”—is often por- trayed as a celestial guide, pointing the way through darkness, “with such spiritual intensity that her eyes were like pole stars” (283); her given name, Wilhelmina, suggests “wilful (or desirous) protectress (or shield) of love.” Unlike “radiantly beautiful” (179) Lucy Westenra, ruddy Light of the West, whose hair spreads in “sunny ripples” (146), Mina is constant and enduring. Addressing Mina, Helsing proclaims, “there are darknesses in life, and there are lights; you are one of the lights” (165), but she seems a light in contrast to darkness, as if a star in the night sky, or, indeed, the moon, seat of feminine fertility. Although it appears at times that Mina is diurnal as she confesses, “I do not understand Lucy’s fading away as she is doing” (92), she seems unfamiliar with Lucy’s brilliant habits; moreover, she guardedly controls access to the nocturnal world, repeatedly noting, “I keep the key of our door always fastened to my wrist at night” (92). One often suspects that Mina is an Anglicized expression of Luna. Equally at home by day and night, “sweet” and “appealing” are adjectives repeatedly summoned to render “our sweet Madam Mina” (223): “She looked so appealing and so pretty” (205), “a sweet-faced, dainty-looking girl” (194). “So true, so sweet, so noble, so little an egotist” (169) that Renﬁeld bids her farewell saying: “I pray God I may never see your sweet face again” (207). The thoughts of “her man’s brain” become “her sweeter counsels” (269). She can also be brilliant and her happiness is shown in her “bright smile” (208). “Her lips are curved and the face beams with happiness” (282), and she “will not be content, I know, to remain in the dark” (197). Of herself, she reports: “I always used to make up the timetables, so as to be helpful to my husband” (293) (he is described as being full of energy “like a living ﬂame.” [263]), though she “shall not wonder if at ﬁrst he mixes up not only the month, but the year” (100); it is Mina, with her husband’s help, who organizes the dates and puts “all the papers into order” (202). Unsurprisingly, another word used in conjunction with Mina is “phase”: “The new phases of things leave my mind in a state of wonder” (282). “If this new phase was spontaneous, or in any way due to her unconscious inﬂuence, she must have some rare gift or Syzygy 113

power” (206). “She seemed brighter and better than she has been for days” (292). Yet, on another occasion she self–consciously writes: “When coming home—it was then bright moonlight, so bright that, though the front of our part of the Crescent was in shadow, everything could be well seen” (91). Lunar Mina mediates what is there to be seen and that which is not visible, the bright and the dark faces of the cosmos. The bat that ﬂits at close of eve Has left the brain that won’t believe. The owl that calls upon the night Speaks the unbeliever’s fright. He who shall hurt the little wren Shall never be beloved by men. He who the ox to wrath has moved Shall never be by woman loved. The wanton boy that kills the ﬂy Shall feel the spider’s enmity [Blake, “Auguries of Innocence”]. On the evening of 2 October, the Count, not Hekate, appears to Renﬁeld. Despite Renﬁeld’s most strenuous efforts, and at the cost of his life, the Count penetrates the Harkers’ bedroom to conduct Mina’s initiation. Through a dying Renﬁeld, Helsing, Seward, Quincey, and Art learn of Count Dracula’s presence in the asylum, and rush to the Harkers’ room. When they ﬁnally penetrate the sealed chamber a rite of initiation is nearly complete and the moon has arrived. The moonlight was so bright that through the thick yellow blind the room was light enough to see. On the bed beside the windows lay Jonathan Harker, his face ﬂushed and breathing heavily as though in a stupor. Kneeling on the near edge of the bed facing outwards was the white-clad ﬁgure of his wife. By her side stood a tall, thin man, clad in black. His face was turned from us, but the instant we saw we all recognized the Count— in every way, even to the scar on his forehead. With his left hand he held both Mrs Harker’s hands, keeping them away with her arms at full tension; his right hand gripped her by the back of the neck, forcing her face down on his bosom. Her white nightdress was smeared with blood, and a thin stream trickled down the man’s bare breast which was shown by his torn- open-dress [246–47]. Despite the room’s “thick yellow blind,” the moonlight is brilliantly illumi- nating, as if the light were generated by Lady Love herself. The kneeling ini- tiate is, like the White Goddess, “white-clad”; the standing priest, “clad in black,” is lost in night. His dress, however, is torn open like his ﬂesh and the initiate is partaking of his body and blood. Although Helsing misleadingly 114 The Theology of Dracula

terms this “the Vampire’s baptism of blood” (280), unlike Lucy’s baptism— which she described as “sinking into deep green water, and there was a singing in my ears, as I have heard there is to drowning men”—it is given the form and the discourse of a Communion. Forced to taste the Count’s blood, Madam Harker has become one with him, and he claims her as “ﬂesh of my ﬂesh; blood of my blood, kin of my kin” (252). This profaning act of Communion, de facto Marriage in which lunar Mina is wed to a being we believe to be one with the Night even as her ﬂush-faced Apollonian husband silently, impotently witnesses by her side, is still far from the ultimate ordeal Mina shall undergo. Helsing, noting that Mina is safe until sunset, lovingly seeks to protect her further by blessing her with the Eucharistic Host. He solemnly intones, “On your forehead I touch this piece of Sacred Wafer in the name of the Father, the Son, and—“ (258), at which point Mina completes her interrupted Persephone-like “scream, so wild, so ear-piercing, so despairing that it seems ... it will ring” forever (247), for “[a]s he had placed the Wafer on Mina’s forehead, it had seared it—had burned into the ﬂesh as though it had been a piece of white-hot metal” (258–9). As Jonathan was returned to health by the sisterhood of the Convent of St. Joseph and St. Mary, Mina will be defended by a brotherhood, “ministers of God’s own wish” (278) that Helsing construes “as the old knights of the Cross” (278). The Brotherhood’s pledge, “to peril even our own souls for the safety of one we love—for the good of mankind, and for the honour and glory of God” (279), is solemnly renewed and a new covenant founded. Hels- ing, presiding over the Brotherhood in a priestly manner, counsels Mina: “You must struggle and strive to live, though death would seem a boon unspeakable. You must ﬁght Death himself, though he come to you in pain or in joy; by the day, or the night; in safety or in peril! On your living soul I charge you that you do not die—nay nor think of death—till this great evil be past” (254). The brothers struggle and strive to re–sanctify the profaned consecrated earth of the Count’s many transient resting places, gathered in a disused chapel that “smelled ole Jerusalem in it” (201). Helsing, rephrasing the Ophite’s Gnostic phrase “The beginning of perfection is the knowledge of man, but absolute perfection is the knowledge of God” (King, 19), eluci- dates the theology of their mission: “It was sanctiﬁed to such use of man, now we sanctify it to God” (260), for “[i]t seemed as though corruption had become itself corrupt” (221)—blackness had become blacker than black. As consecrated ground corrupted requires renewed sanctiﬁcation, Mina, aggrieved by her innocently-acquired pollution, becomes the object of a par- ticularly solemn sacramental ceremony dominated by her volition. Mina tells her husband, “I want you to read the Burial Service” (288). “Oh, my wife, must I read it?” he asks. “It would comfort me, my husband!” (288), says she. Syzygy 115

The formality of their exchange resounds with scriptural overtones. The old woman that was Mina must die to permit Mina’s rebirth as a New Woman, and her husband must pray for her soul as Helsing had once done for Lucy’s. This was soon undertaken; the prayerful source? The Book of Common Prayer or, considering Helsing’s spiritual role, The Sarum Missal. The caterpillar on the leaf Repeats to thee thy mother’s grief. Kill not the moth nor butterﬂy, For the Last Judgment draweth nigh [Blake, “Auguries of Innocence”]. The Brotherhood, its core composed of hunters of beasts rather than ﬁshers of men, is formal, and is given the shape of a hand, Helsing and his “rude four-in-hand” (313); ﬁve men, repeatedly described as brave and strong, earnest and good, constitute its explicitly secret organization: “We are pledged to set the world free. Our toil must be in silence, and our efforts all in secret; for in this enlightened age, when men believe not even what they see, the doubting of wise men would be his greatest strength” (279). Comprised of “gentlemen, who by nationality, by heredity, or by the possession of natural gifts, are ﬁtted to hold ... respective places in the moving world” (215), it con- stitutes an elect. Mina is central to the Brotherhood, not as a member but as its object of devotion, Helsing elevating her to nearly divine status: “We are men, and are able to bear; but you,” he says, addressing Mina, “must be our star and our hope” (214). Her stigmata, characterized by Helsing as a cross to bear, cause the knights to gather around her and swear themselves to her sacred cause. “We men pledged ourselves to raise the veil of sorrow from the head of her whom, each in his own way, we loved; and we prayed for help and guidance in the terrible task which lay before us” (259). For “it may be that we are chosen instruments of His good pleasure, and that we ascend to His bidding as that other through stripes and shame; through tears and blood; through doubts and fears, and all that makes the difference between God and man” (259). She, tired of being “kept in the dark” (225), insists: “There must be no more concealment” (253). Jonathan recovered rapidly from his “brain fever” (100) after Helsing made of him a New Man, but once Mina’s ﬂesh was corrupted by the Count, he becomes destabilized in a different way: rushed, rash, vengeful, the man who pledged himself “heart and soul” (169) to the defeat of the Count pro- claims himself ready to “sell [his] soul” (265) to destroy him. He is called back from this new malady by Abraham, who would protect his soul, and Mina, who would save the souls of all the afﬂicted, including her husband’s. They each implore him, “Oh hush!” (265, 269) in the name of God. Mina 116 The Theology of Dracula

argues for compassion for the accursed Count and his kind, and for forgiveness. In her generous celestial spirit, Mina approaches the Holy Mother, modestly asserting that “women have something of the mother in us that makes us rise above smaller matters when the mother-spirit is invoked” (203). Indeed, Mina is celebrated for her goodness—Helsing proclaims her exemplar of the good woman and deﬁnes “good women” as those “whose lives and whose truths may make good lesson for the children that are to be” (166). The ﬁnal hunt is engaged neither to avenge Lucy, nor to rid the world of a monster, but to purge Mina of a pollutant within her that came of the impure “baptism of blood.” Mina confessing to sensing “some of the taste of the original apple that remains still in our mouths” (164). Mina herself casts this hunt as a question of uncovering true selves, of locating a singular truth within a duality and a light within darkness, encouraging her heroes: “you must destroy even as you destroyed the false Lucy so that the true Lucy might live hereafter; but it is not a work of hate” (269). In deﬁning their mission, Mina’s mention of Lucy necessarily refers to light. High mysticism resides in Stoker’s text beyond its constant references to light and dark. Helsing, who becomes “The Professor” in a very evangelical way, assumes a priestly function in his distribution of sacred Hosts, theological and metaphysical discourse, and role as father ﬁgure to the entire order. Hail- ing from Holland, Low Countries or the Netherlands, Abraham—in contact with the underworld, but “come ... to do what [he] can of good” (184)—is prophetic, declaring, for example: “He have gone back to his Castle in Tran- sylvania. I know it so well, as if a great hand of ﬁre wrote it on the wall” (274). The Professor’s very work is to arrive at profound understandings of things that at ﬁrst glimpse seem transparently simple, to read with a “man brain” instead of a “child brain.” As he says, ‘‘He have been blind somewhat; blind after the manner of men, since when we can look back we see what we might have seen looking forward if we had been able to see what we might have seen!” (273). He comes to see more clearly when “our dear Madam Mina is once more our teacher. Her eyes have seen where we were blinded” (306). His speech seems moreover prophetic to his companions: Then Van Helsing turned and said gravely; so gravely that I could not help feeling that he was in some way inspired, and was stating things outside himself:— “It may be that you may have to bear that mark till God himself see ﬁt, as He most surely shall on the Judgment Day to redress all wrongs of the earth and of His children that He has placed thereon. And oh, Madam Mina, my dear, my dear, may we who love you be there to see, when that red scar, the sign of God’s knowledge of what has been, shall pass away and leave your forehead as pure as the heart we know” [259]. Syzygy 117

He who mocks the infant’s faith Shall be mocked in age and death. He who shall teach the child to doubt The rotting grave shall ne’er get out. He who respects the infant’s faith Triumphs over hell and death [Blake, “Auguries of Innocence”]. They are all present, a glowing “hand of ﬁre” (274), when in the East the sun sets on Judgment Day. Dracula’s East-West opposition has been remarked upon by several commentators and understood in colonial, racial, anti–Semitic, anti–Slav, or other xenophobic terms; it more rightly should be seen as scriptural discourse. What began with the arrival at Castle Dracula on Saint George’s Eve reaches a Western nadir with the death—on the western isle and land of Saint George—of Lucy Westenra, but the solar circuit must be completed, concluding in the East again. When Jonathan reports, “We left Charing Cross on the morning of the 12th, got to Paris the same night, and took the places secured for us in the Orient Express” (289), we are invited to picture their departing from Charing Cross, heading east, expressly, inevitably, on a spiritual journey towards the Orient where they are to assume their divinely assigned places. Charing Cross is not merely the name of a London train station but of London’s historic omphalos and the axis mundi from which emanate all geo- graphical measurements in the British vernacular. The word “Charing” is said to be a corruption of the French chère reine, marking the location as the place bearing the “cross of the dearest queen,” as this site was ﬁxed by a cenotaphic monument erected in honor of the beloved Eleanor of Castile, queen to Edward I. It was the last of 12 “Eleanor crosses” erected at the places of rest attained over a nearly two week period by Eleanor’s funeral procession as the bier wended its way from the northern city of Lincoln, where she had died, to the capital. No simple cross, this multi-tiered, four-faced and octagonal monument can be further seen through its geographic function as the embod- iment of Stoker’s precious Quatre Faces. Since from Carfax the Count entered London through King’s Cross station, it is only ﬁtting that Mina would leave London through Cross of the Dearest Queen. Time and space become confounded in Stoker’s transcendental, transcon- tinental journey, the Professor expressing the ﬁnal stage of their restless east- ward voyage in cosmic terms: “For we are going up, and up; and all is oh! so wild and rocky, as though it were the end of the world” (316). The end of the world will coincide with the end of time. As the Professor foretold of Mina and as she herself had promised: “I must bear this mark of shame upon my forehead until the Judgment Day” (259). In her mark of shame, the circular 118 The Theology of Dracula

scar seared into the ﬂesh of her brow even as she had sealed Jonathan’s journal with her wedding band, the Charing Cross is manifested. Mina processes towards Castle Dracula as Jonathan once had, but with the Professor rather than the Count serving as coachman. Arriving to await Judgment Day in the shadow of the Count’s Transylvanian retreat, Helsing shelters Mina as night descends, enclosing her within a lunar disc whose perimeter he marks with fragments of Sacred Host, situating her now as if within the Host itself, “the Holy Circle” (318) being the Professor’s term, her person incarnating the Holy Spirit. Although he asks her to move beyond the ring, Mina is unable: “I rejoiced, for I knew that what she could not, none of those that we dreaded could. Though there might be danger to her body, yet her soul was safe!” (316). Seasons have been reversed since Jonathan faced a ring of wolves in the same spot, and in the gloom, “the snow ﬂakes and the mist began to wheel and circle round, till I could get as though a shadowy glimpse of those women that would have kissed” (317) Jonathan. Now they call to Mina, as Juana and Hélène once called to Antonia: “Come, sister. Come to us. Come!” (317) mistaking her for their sister, but “God be thanked she was not, yet, of them” and they “could not approach ... Madam Mina whilst she remained within the ring which she could not leave” (317). The symbol of the ring has been a constant across plot, surrounding Jonathan with a lupine “living ring of terror” (20), marking out the Count’s English domains, sealing Jonathan’s diary, ennobling Lord Godalming, sus- taining the agonized sound of Mina’s passion, marshaling the Syzygy that will cost Quincey Morris his life, joining the Brotherhood as a band, and securing its jewel: Mina. “And so the circle goes on ever widening” (190). Her spiritual transformation is complete when she is purged of evil through Dracula’s death, that is, upon the perfection, conﬁrmation of the sacrament that the Professor initiated but which was suspended when it resulted in Mina’s branding. Yet to be cleansed of evil unavoidably requires the death of purity, embodied by Quincey, who, hurried in his “lonely walk between this and Kingdom Come” (60), sacriﬁces himself for the sake of Lady Love: With a sigh he took, with a feeble effort, my hand in that of his own which was unstained. He must have seen the anguish of my heart in my face, for he smiled at me and said:—“I am only too happy to have been of any serv- ice! Oh, God!” He cried suddenly, struggling up to a sitting posture and pointing to me, “It was worth this to die!—Look! Look!” [326]. The genesis of Mina’s stigmata, rooted in a verbally-rendered Sign of the Cross, meets its ends in a cathartic rose light: “The sun was now right down upon the mountaintop, and the red gleams fell upon my face, so that it was bathed in rosy light” (326). After having skirted the Black Sea to attain a point east of our “Dearest Queen’s Cross,” Mina is reunited with Lucy Syzygy 119

Westenra, rosy Light of the West, Stoker attributing, perhaps, a new sense to Charing Cross derived from “charring in the ﬁre” (190): “the charred, burnt or branding cross,” or even, “Cross of the Char Ring.” Helsing was right: the Host had protected Mina until sunset, now ﬁnally come. As day gives way to endless night, queenly Mina is liberated. Mina’s forehead, like Jonathan’s hair, ﬁnds a white purity through her contact with the Vampire; having been stained by sin and re-sanctiﬁed, she, New Woman, can, in full knowledge of good and evil, claim true purity. Every night and every morn Some to misery are born. Every morn and every night Some are born to sweet delight. Some are born to sweet delight, Some are born to endless night. We are led to believe a lie When we see not through the eye Which was born in a night to perish in a night, When the soul slept in beams of light. God appears, and God is light To those poor souls who dwell in night, But does a human form display To those who dwell in realms of day [Blake, “Auguries of Innocence”]. Through long sections of the novel, Mina—the novel’s “ﬁxed point” through which “the centripetal force is balanced with the centrifugal” (62)— is necessarily an ambiguous and divided ﬁgure, a woman united at once to a man in holy matrimony and a corpse in unholy servitude. Ambiguity also describes Messrs Hawkins and Renﬁeld, to whom Stoker was required to attribute mixed functions in order to perfectly balance his symmetrical com- position. Renﬁeld’s dual role is particularly complex, not merely a John the Baptist to diabolical Dracula, but a man for whom the struggle between light and dark is lived daily as his insanity, yet who, knowingly and courageously, deﬁes the count to protect Madam Mina. He selﬂessly serves the Brotherhood, which nevertheless fails to count him “amongst the best and truest of ... friends” (216). Sharing a priestly function with the Count, the lunatic-wed- ded-to-wisdom Renﬁeld counterbalances the sage-wedded-to-folly (see 158) Helsing. When Helsing muses “Perhaps I may gain more knowledge out of the folly of this madman than I shall from the teaching of the most wise” (225), he is rightly greeted by Renﬁeld as “the old fool Van Helsing” (225). Speaking as a Baptist-like ﬁgure, Renﬁeld transforms John 3:29’s metaphor of a marriage scene by substituting senses—sight for sound, watching for 120 The Theology of Dracula

harking—and focus—feminine for masculine, deception for joy: “The Bride maidens rejoice the eyes that wait the coming of the bride. But when the bride draweth nigh, then the maidens shine not to the eyes that are ﬁlled” (96–7). The Professor, too, calls attention to this confounding of eye and ear, exclaiming as Thomas: “I could not have believe until such time as that fact thunder on my ear. See! see!” (209)—though the Professor also connects hand to foot, looking forward and moving back, admonishing “once our feet are on the ploughshare, we must not draw back” (193). Stoker confronts several other scriptural sources, calling repeatedly on the Old Testament’s ﬁrst books, Genesis, Exodus, Numbers, and the apoc- rypha. His conceit turns on Genesis 9’s command to Noah: “Every creature that moves and lives shall be food for you; as I gave you the green plants, I give you everything. But the ﬂesh with its life—that is, its blood—you shall not eat” (Genesis 9:3–4). Renﬁeld confesses, “I used to fancy that life was a positive and perpetual entity, and that by consuming a multitude of live things, no matter how low in the scale of creation, one might indeﬁnitely prolong life.... ‘For the blood is the Life’” (206). Yet Enoch becomes his model “because he walked with God” (Genesis 5). To Renﬁeld’s evocation of Enoch, Seward, too, confounds eye and ear, claiming “I could not see the analogy ... so I harked back to what he had denied” (236). According to Genesis 9, it is Noah, great-grandson of Enoch, who was said to “Walk with God.” Stoker has Renﬁeld refer to the Book of Enoch (published in translation from Ethiopic by Robert Henry Charles in 1893), a text in which apocalyptic depictions of the end time are rendered and scriptural and psychoanalytic imaginations coincide. Enoch “the scribe” begins by saluting the elect and the righteous. He explains that, charged with petitioning the Divine on behalf of “the Watchers,” he has seen and heard remote generations to come. The Watchers are archangels who, having formed a compact to defy the Great Glory, abandoned their heavenly home to descend to Earth and fornicate with the comely daugh- ters of man, begetting a race of sinful monsters. Seeking redemption, they have engaged Enoch to record their petition. Enoch receives visions in his sleep that constitute the divine response to the Watchers’ prayers. His dreams take the form of astral voyages through the elements in their wildest expres- sions, the bitter and the sweet, that take him west, to the place of heavenly lights; to the sacred omphalos, Jerusalem; and to the east where, beyond its deserts, a fertile land rises in far off mountains. He visits the Great Glory who charges the eternal Watchers with deﬁling themselves with the blood of women and with mortal ﬂesh. Enoch is shown the ﬁery abyss in which the evil ones will pass aeons. In their transgressions, the Watchers have introduced mankind to knowledge Syzygy 121

and sin. The petition that Enoch has scribed will not be granted, but the Watchers shall be known as evil spirits, and conﬁned to the earth until they are destroyed with the ungodly while the elect “shall inherit the earth.” Enoch is to inform the Watchers that they know not the true mysteries, only worthless ones, and to alert his grandson Noah to prepare for a purgative deluge. Several parables follow that sketch out an elect dominated by the Elect One, or Son of Man, ﬁnal judge of all ﬂesh, and particularly the judge of the mighty of the world. In a last section, great attention is paid to the movement of the sun, stars and heavenly lights in time, and the according divisions of time, Enoch arguing for solar rather than lunar division of the year. Stoker, confounding eye and ear, replaces angelic Watchers with human (scribe and solicitor) Harkers. He also has Renﬁeld comment on the Elect of the Purﬂeet Brotherhood as he is introduced to them, and this seems to suggest that they represent four iterations of New Man: Jesus, Adam, Abraham, and Moses—the ﬁrst being son of the Lord Godalming; second, author of political fable; third, ﬁrst of his kind and holder of “an Indulgence” (187); and last, guide dear to all seekers of asylum and one ﬁt to lead “well to seaward” (76). The justice of this reading is supported through Stoker’s Notes, which suggest “Quincey P. Adams” as the name for one of the principals (91). Helsing, “having something of angels’ eyes” (165), pledged that the activ- ities of the brotherhood should in no way be incompatible with the Christian faith or gentlemanly honor (182); they are not, though the Church of Rome seems to be portrayed as a “worthless wretch who stole” the golden cross: “She knew not altogether what she did” (150). The Professor’s pronouncements endow the Brotherhood with Rosicrucian, mystic, and Gnostic overtones: “There are always mysteries in life” (171), “mysteries which men can only guess at, which age by age they may solve only in part” (183); “we see around us every day the growth of new beliefs, which think themselves new; and which are yet but the old, which pretend to be young—like the ﬁne ladies at the opera” (171). Even scientist Seward’s proclamation that “Transcendentalism is a beacon to the angels, even if it be a will-o’-the-wisp to man” (293) expresses Thomas Taylor-inﬂuenced religious themes that propose a return to ancient rites of renewal previously placed at the center of the Vampire Tale. The old-beliefs-growing-as-new however give form to Dracula’s subject: “We seem to be drifting into unknown places and unknown ways; into a whole world of dark and dreadful things. Godalming is shutting the furnace door” (310). A new era may be dawning in which Hell’s ﬁres are less all-con- suming and forgiveness is possible. Adam has sacriﬁced himself and died with clean hands—“unstained” (326) is the word Mina chooses. Even the Vampire, released from its body, knows peace and felicity. When Dracula was beheaded, Mina commented: “I shall be glad as long 122 The Theology of Dracula

as I live that even in that moment of ﬁnal dissolution, there was in the face a look of peace, such as I never could have imagined might have rested there” (325). In the case of Lucy: “One and all we felt that the holy calm that lay like sunshine over the wasted face and form was only an earthly token and symbol of the calm that was to reign forever” (192). Of the three lamiae, Hels- ing confessed: “It was butcher work; had I not been nerved by thoughts of other dead, and of the living over whom hung such a pall of fear, I could not have gone on.... God be thanked, my nerve did stand. Had I not seen the repose in the ﬁrst face, and the gladness that stole over it just ere the ﬁnal dissolution came, as realization that the soul had been won, I could not have gone further with my butchery” (320). In every case, true death sparks a “holy ray of light” (198) that is felicity. The false Lucy is executed so that the true Lucy may shine. Stoker’s symmetry has resolved the conﬂict between good and evil, day and night, and it is espe- cially the New Woman that serves as polestar for learning forgiveness. “She is one of God’s women, fashioned by His own hand to show us men and other women that there is a heaven where we can enter, and that its light can be here on earth” (169). The elect not only save themselves, but the damned. As the sweeping away of Mr. Hawkins and Lord Godalming by the “scythe- man” (216) gave birth to New Men, the harvest of the Un-Dead makes of Mina a New Woman. Feet planted on the Earth, silhouetted against a dark- ening night sky that glitters with its brilliant inhabitants, crushed serpent, Little Dragon, at her feet, Mina presents an Isian or Marian ﬁgure and returns the narrative to its beginning and the rosary. Jonathan, who had asked Mina “to share [his] ignorance” (100), is com- pelled by his wife to share knowledge, gnosis. The Professor instructs the notary’s wife: “You must be scribe and write him all down, so that when the others return from their work you can give it to them; then they shall know as we do” (297). The ﬁnal sacramental transformation reserved for the Harkers occurs when the orphans become themselves parents. Lady Love is transformed into The Mother, and the knowing syzygy has answered Sister Agatha’s request to come together “in the name of God and Saint Mary and Saint Joseph” and has brought forth a new generation to take the place of the old. In the end, Mr. Hawkins’ place is occupied by Abraham; he who had lost a son (157) has found a progeny through orphans Jonathan and Mina. Syzygy 123

The Children of Night “It struck me as curious that the moment she became conscious she pressed the garlic ﬂowers close to her. It was certainly odd that whenever she got into that lethargic state, with the ster- torous breathing, she put the ﬂowers from her; but that when she waked she clutched them close. There was no possibility of making any mistake about this, for in the long hours that fol- lowed, she had many spells of sleeping and waking and repeated both actions many times” [145]. Stoker claimed, perhaps facetiously, that dream-life—nightmare— inspired Dracula, attributing the novel’s genesis to ill-digested dressed crab. He apparently envisioned the Count scurrying, crab-like, down precipitous castle walls. Perhaps being introduced to the Count in dream-life helped frame the novel, for its conceit is fuelled by somnambulism, hypnotism, and opiates. Although dragged-about babes are always to be seen, despite the roughness of their treatment, fast asleep, and though sleep-induction seems to be one of the count’s many charms, it is exclusively within the realm of Dreams that he holds absolute sway and is able to enter into his victim’s life-ﬂow, siphon off their anima, and effect his own renewal. The foster-father of Romantic vampire ﬁction, John William Polidori, submits that dreams are “for the convenience of souls having converse with dead or distant friends” (tr. qtd. Macdonald 39). As a romantic, he embraced the age-old view of the dream as a window on an “otherworld” of ancestors, shades, and divinities; as a Doctor of Medicine, his dissertation “Disputatio Medica Inauguralis quaedam de Morbo, Oneirodynia Dicto, Complectens” determines with a shrug that “the actions of the soul, and of external bodies, on the organic body are so obscure, that it seems we shall never know the cause of things. For when in chemistry and even in mechanics we are ignorant of many and great things, how are we to believe that we shall come near to grasping the principles of vegetable life, much less those of animal life and of 124

the soul?” (tr. qtd. Macdonald 39). Dreams, it would seem, are native to the soul and intrinsic to soul-life. Had Polidori author of Ximenes, or, the Modern Abraham and Ernestus Brechtold, or, the Modern Œdipus, been granted the possibility of subtitling his Vampyre, he may well have connected it to the Modern Dionysus, that masked divinity of theatre and aesthetics, disguised lord of the underworld, dark groom of Persephone, whose characteristics he assigns to Lord Ruthven. Abraham Stoker, having had occasion to subtitle Dracula, subtly suggests “The Modern Morpheus” (97) for his own novel, a name stamped from a mythological die that is particularly germane to Count Dracula. It is imma- terial whether the Count assumes Morpheus’s characteristics or the latter mim- ics the former’s traits: Morpheus inhabits the novel. As Oscar warned in Nodier’s melodrama, it is through dreams that the Vampire overcomes his victim, a warning the count himself sternly reiterates, promising that bad dreams await “those who sleep unwisely” (38). Establishing Morpheus as antithetical to Light, Stoker introduces him by name in having Seward pledge “not to dishonour Lucy by mixing the two” (97). In rejecting Morpheus, Seward adds: “If need be, tonight shall be sleepless” (97). God of dreams, shape-shifting actor able to imitate in walk, voice, and gesture any human form, Morpheus is, according to Cicero, the son of Night (Nocte) and Darkness (Erebo). (Fomenting genealogical obscurity, Ovid pres- ents Morpheus, Icelos and Phantasus, respectively imitators of humans, beasts, and inanimate objects, as the sons of Hypnos.) Although Morpheus has count- less siblings among the great brood of “children of the Night,” that is, of Night herself, only his relationship with twin brothers Hypnos (Sleep) and Thanatos (Death) directly concerns Stoker, who pointedly salutes the twins in excerpting Thomas Hood’s paean to their honor, “The Death-bed”: “We thought her dying whilst she slept, And sleeping when she died” (147). Victorian graveyard statuary represents Sleep as a dozing cherub whose gracefully splayed ﬁngers and outstretched arm rest lightly on an overturned antique lamp. Through this device, Sleep—in whose empty grasp the invisible becomes visible while the ordinarily visible is not to be seen—is ﬁgured upset- ting the norms of everyday life. The extinguished, overturned lamp also speaks to the forgetfulness that comes with sleep, the drowsing cherub seemingly having lost control over his own plump hand. The fact that such sculptures nearly always appear in cemeteries evidences the indissoluble association join- ing Sleep to Death, for the overturned lamp was previously lit by the ﬂame of Life. The twins are so alike that the Victorian preferred substituting one for the other, no doubt with the idea of establishing the graveyard as a place of eternal rest and encouraging thoughts of an otherworldly awakening. Since it is Sleep that affords Morpheus opportunity to hold sway and The Children of Night 125

inevitably provoke a kind of death, Dracula, though chronicling the mercurial activities of Morpheus, is concerned ﬁrst and foremost with accomplices Hyp- nos and Thanatos, for it is Hypnos who opens the way for Morpheus, Thanatos who appears in his wake. Dracula is thus a story about sleeping and guarding against sleep in order to prevent dream-laden Sleep from becoming Death. “Oh, but I am tired! If it were not that I had made my diary a duty I should not open it tonight!” (86) is a typical diarist’s plaint that underscores the dogged commitment of the scribes. Seward’s dictum “Cannot eat, cannot rest, so diary instead” (61) contrasts physical need with epistemological imper- ative. The record the writers dutifully assemble is obsessively concerned with sleeping, the travails that come from losing consciousness, and the superhuman burden assumed by those charged with maintaining watch—eloquently artic- ulated in the occulted addendum to The Demeter’s captain’s log. The diarists catalogue where and under what conditions sleep occurs, and enumerate the extravagant efforts undertaken to prevent its onset and to defend against unwanted dreams—i.e., the steady stream of ﬂowers from the Netherlands whose ﬂow is compared to “the waters of [the] Lethe” (120), and the sacred symbols of the celestial Lord that are engraved upon persons, places, things, and even the Earth herself. The journalists also chronicle their chagrin and frustration when undesired lapses of consciousness allow Morpheus to sneak past their guard, enter into a sleeper’s spirit, and gain dominion over volition. Morpheus is said to set off at dusk from his mansion in the form of a bat. It is also claimed that once Hypnos has gained the upper hand over a human soul, putting it to sleep, Morpheus soundlessly glides into the spirit of the unprotected sleeper on the wings of the butterﬂy, like the wings Renﬁeld refer- ences in his discussion of “the aerial powers of the psychic faculties” (235). These various rumors of transforming wings are strongly reminiscent of Mélusinian legends, the Welch night-hag Gwrach-y-Rhybyn, and Dumas’ claim that ghouls put their victims “to sleep with the whisper of their great wings” (428) in order to suck their handsome youth’s life’s blood in a deadly embrace. Only in bringing sleep about with the ﬂuttering of wings, are the Ghoul and Vam- pire able to purloin their victim’s anima mundi, that is, the soul—blood and soul being symbolic equivalents since the blood contains and circulates the anima. The soul, like the Paraclete, is pictured as a winged thing. Renﬁeld’s further comment that “the ancients did well when they typiﬁed the soul as a butterﬂy!” (235) is therefore piercingly to the point. Morpheus’s stealing the sleeper’s soul away enables his further predatory ﬂights of fancy through the use of the wings of the newly stolen soul. Stoker’s Count, however, always setting out for conquest, is only, though repeatedly, represented as “a big bat” (213), a changeless, liminal creature, a ﬂying mammal known for its nocturnal habits, its penchant for living upside-down, and, in three of its 126 The Theology of Dracula

species, an appetite for blood. Polidori’s Persephone-like Ianthe, Ruthven’s original victim, truly was characterized as a butterﬂy, “a Kashmere butterﬂy” (270)—a gentle, benign creature celebrated for representing spiritual meta- morphosis. She was doomed to forever ﬂutter about certain Attic precincts. Through these winged representational idioms, the poetic image of the Vam- pire collides with Freudian dogma, the shock of their impact solidifying the clichés of horror. To Freud disciple Ernest Jones, “the appearance of the Vam- pire in animal form, particularly in that of a butterﬂy or snake—two of the commonest Oriental representatives of the father, is one of the many charac- teristic features of this origin [in incest yearnings], as again is the fact that [the vampire’s] activities are altogether characterized by every possible infantile perversion” (130). It is difﬁcult not to regret the stridency of the Freudians’ incest ﬁxation. While Stoker may have been aware of Freud’s gestating theories during Drac- ula’s writing through his attendance of the Society for Psychical Research lec- ture series (Belford 212–13) and attendant interest in Freud mentor Jean-Martin Charcot, Freud exerted no apparent inﬂuence on the novel’s con- tent. It is thus odd that, though Die Traumdeutung only appeared several years after Dracula’s publication, Freud has provided the sense-producing ﬁlter that has most consistently been applied to Stoker’s novel, so much so that the Freudian “latent content” has come to mask Dracula’s veritable deep text. Dismissing Polidori’s thesis, Freud subjects the dream processes of Romantic expression to “scientiﬁc” examination to conclude that dreams arise from unrealized wishes. Through dreams, he elaborates a theory of mind that furnishes an overarching explanation to human intellectual and cultural life, claiming to uncover socio-neural phenomena whose simple exposition could make bafﬂing dreams and the intellectual processes that produced them intel- ligible to their authors. Dreams, like magic inverted, are rhetorical entities dependent on metaphor and metonymy, working through narrative techniques of condensation, displacement, ﬁguration—the poet’s, and Stoker’s, very tools. Freud, however, considering the dreamer as a social creature, concerns himself more with the editorial and publishing aspects of dreams—their auto- representation to the self—than with their poetics sensu stricto, leading him to integrate into his theory anthropological notions of taboo, norms of social and moral behavior, and, borrowing from Charcot, the interplay of conscious and unconscious functions of mind. In Freud’s wish-fulﬁlment scheme, the greater the taboo associated with dreamt wishes, the more aggressively “the dream-work,” the mind’s obscuring poetic function, disguises the wishes rep- resented, legibility operating in inverse proportion to acceptability by the conscious self; manifest content masks latent content, with the latter speaking to the motivating cause of the representation. The incest taboo, the primordial The Children of Night 127

social constraint, is the mighty psycho-sexual source feeding the great sub- terranean river of the unconscious’s wishes, which periodically bubbles to the surface through dreams. The temptation to dispose of the complexities of Dracula, an admittedly enigmatic, profound, and often disturbing work, with a ready-made cognitive template is understandable. Freudian analysis seems particularly apt in light of Stoker’s insistent concentration on tensions between conscious and uncon- scious selves, such as the alternation observed in Lucy, who accepts and then rejects bouquets of garlic according to her ﬂuctuating state of consciousness. Fundamental differences between Freud’s notion of consciousness and Stoker’s are critical. The Freudian self, a two-tiered mind that is termed “psy- che” but does not mean “soul,” is constituted a bit like the American government, with components of a tripartite structure—ego, id, superego —dynamically vying for power and dominance. Consciousness for Freud is ruled by the self ’s rational, cognitive elements, the ego and superego. For Stoker, consciousness is simply wilful self–awareness, a recollection of ﬁnalities and beginnings: the dust of mortality and the Light of the divine. Freud’s and Stoker’s views of the unconscious contrast even more sharply. In Freudian usage, the uncon- scious allows the consciously-censored id freer rein to indulge repressed wishes, exercise sublimated drives, indulge traumatic memories; in Stoker’s, it is simply the surrender, even the unwitting surrender, of volition, thus losing sight of ends and beginnings due to the distractions of what is termed the moving world, that is, the forgetting of God. It is also rational, “unconscious cere- bration” (69, 237), “brother” (70) to conscious thought, playing a major role in logical problem-solving and cognitive elaboration. Mental activities that are consciously undertaken in Freudian terms can be perfectly unconscious in Stoker’s, and vice versa. Freud’s psyche, the mind, and Stoker’s, the soul, are incongruous, incom- patible. The same must be said for Dracula: Freud’s Dracula is not Stoker’s. This is not to disparage the brilliant Viennese analyst and theoretician, to challenge the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society, or to seek some other psychoanalytic ﬁlter; it is merely to liberate Dracula and return it to the frame that Polidori suggests and Stoker embraces. As Freud’s colleague Carl Gustave Jung writes: If we assume with [Freud] that the incest motif is the source of all modern man’s psychological problems as well as of alchemical symbolism, this gets us nowhere as regards the meaning of the symbols. On the contrary, we have landed ourselves in a blind alley, for we shall only be able to say that all symbolism, present and future, derives from the primal incest. That is what Freud actually thought, for he once said to me: “I only wonder what neurotics will do in the future when it is generally known what their sym- bols mean” [14: 302]. 128 The Theology of Dracula

The one work on dreams that appearing in the Notes, Rosenbach #66, is a work by Robert Gray ill-referenced by Stoker under the name of its pub- lisher, Rivington (235). This work considered dreams, very much within the Polidorian soul-life context, as being oracular, visionary, or requiring hermeneutical interpretation. Gray considers famous examples of profane and sacred dreams as they were recorded in well-known texts—from antiquity, citing classical and Biblical sources, to more recent dreams of well-known ﬁgures such as Lorenzo di Medici. Gray dedicates several pages to Ovid’s account of Morpheus (94–96), and a chapter to “Inspired Dreams which Contributed to the Conﬁrmation and Advancement of the Gospel.” Cicero’s Morpheus is granted consideration in a second tome whose most interesting aspect may be the ﬁnal chapter title, “The Use of Fictitious Dreams in Lit- erature.” The Notes show that Stoker found little of interest in Gray, and no doubt continued his research through other means. Despite Stoker’s classical use of dreams, the fact that the Count is iden- tiﬁed as the Vampire and that he reveals himself to his victims exclusively through dreams make Dracula understandably and irresistibly attractive to Freudians. Applying psychoanalytic principle to the vampire–inhabited terrain of nightmare and advancing Freud’s theory one step further, Ernest Jones per- ceives nightmare as a psychic guillotine, an angst-infested reverie serving to vent the id’s taboo desires in order to assure their continued repression. While such a frame seems to contain Dracula perfectly (does not the Vampire lose his head in the end?), closer examination shows Stoker intends Dracula’s occulted content to triumph in the rosy light of the illuminating moment of judgment. The ambitions of Stoker’s text ﬂatly contradict Freud’s hypothe- sis. Complicating this situation, however, is the history of the Vampire con- struct itself. Knowing that folklore’s vampire only troubles his intimate and familial relations, Stoker duly indulges the incest paradigm, as father-ﬁgure Abraham humorously concedes: “Then this so sweet maid is a polyandrist, and me ... am bigamist” (158). Indeed Stoker does everything possible to indulge yet dismissively expose the ﬂimsiness of the garden variety incest trope, with Helsing’s burning candle, angled “so that he could read the cofﬁn plates, and so holding it that the sperm dropped in white patches which con- gealed as they touched the metal” (176), rendering a parody of sepulchral Sleep. To drive the point home, all tools become phallic: “Another search in his bag, and he took out a turnscrew” (176). From turnscrew to the wooden stakes, the phallic tools ﬂirt with parody. The Professor’s further comment, “And so the circle goes on ever widening” (190), manifestly refers to the con- tagious aspect of the metaphysical malady he is trying to stamp out, while latently projecting a spreading incestuous tsunami. Lucy even wonders, “Why The Children of Night 129

can’t they let a girl marry three men, or as many as want her, and save all this trouble?” before adding “But this is heresy, and I must not say it” (60). Dracula is a sacred, but not a sanctimonious text; its interest in incest, however, is not where the Freudian ﬁnds it. Jones’s great work On the Nightmare is nevertheless relevant for its survey of literature on the nightmare phenomenon, some portion of which may have actually inﬂuenced Stoker. Jones assembles symptomatic descriptions of the condition as reported by medical doctors who suffered from it; for instance, the 1753 “Observations on the Incubus, or night-mare” of Dr. John Bond: The Nightmare generally seizes people sleeping on their backs, and often begins with frightful dreams, which are soon succeeded by a difﬁcult respi- ration, a violent oppression on the breast, and a total privation of voluntary motion. In this agony they sigh, groan, utter indistinct sounds, and remain in the jaws of death [Jones 16]. According to Dr. Woldemar Cubasch, “some kind of Being, most often a shaggy animal, or else a hideous human form presses on the sleeper’s breast, or pinions his throat and tries to strangle him. The terror increases with the suffocation, every effort at defence is impossible, since all his limbs are par- alyzed as though by magical power” (Jones 24). This terror is imbued with an erotic content however: “With women, the Bogey ... does not suddenly throw himself on his victim, but often enters the room gently and just as gently climbs on to the couch, so as to become a love partner of the sleeper” (Jones 47). Dr. Johann Boerner elaborates: “Sometimes voluptuous feelings are coupled with those of Angst; especially with women, who often believe that the night-ﬁend has copulated with them” (Jones 50). Dr. Jules Delassus insists that one who senses the approach of Incubus or Succubus is seized with an intense angst. The throat tightens, initiating a feeling of suffocation, all the while the mucous membranes are caressed in voluptuous titillation, as if an extraordinarily expert lover were enveloping you, penetrating you, melting within you. The orgasm is wild; the nervous expenditure, terrible (Jones 47). Nightmare’s terrifying and erotic elements are inseparable. In a dictionary entry, Dr. Auguste Motet asserts that the most difﬁcult aspect for the dreamer incapable of stopping the transformational creature from enforcing its will is the feeling of impotence (Jones 19). For many, including Dr. Robert Macnish, whose ideas will be considered in more detail, the angst that accompanies the impression of impotence is far worse still. Jones concludes that “resemblances between the beliefs relating to Devil, Witch, Incubus, and Night-bogey (Alp) and Night-hag (Mahre) are so intimate that they may be said to present merely different aspects of the same theme” (232). “The Vampire superstition is evidently closely allied to that of the 130 The Theology of Dracula

Incubus and Succubus” (125). “The main differences are that hate and guilt play a far larger part in the Vampire than in the Incubus belief” (130). “The very fact that the Vampire is a revenant is decisive here, for we have already traced this conception to the incest complex” (127). While the apparent cer- titude of these opinions tends to place them beyond reach of judicious appeal, examination of Jones’s sources shows that nearly all are exclusively concerned with Incubi and Succubi, hence eroticized nightmare. In Stoker’s work there is need for some other context, some other asylum for the Count, because, in Dracula, instead of the dream being something produced by the uncon- scious it is itself a means of producing unconsciousness, that is, a means of accessing some Otherworld that is both underworldly and celestial, and in which the abandonment of volition can quickly become fatal. The question of how to bring worlds visible and obscure into disbelief- suspensive contact must have presented Stoker with a signiﬁcant strategic challenge. Some mechanism, some effective interface between realms, was required to sustain his ﬁction so that “there seems to be through it all some thread of continuity” (Stoker 161). While Belford suggests that the tarot may have been considered as that mechanism (214), ancient Morpheus and his clan offered a far more appropriate option. Pythagorean and phrenologist Robert Macnish, who begins his 1838 A Philosophy of Sleep with the assertion that “Sleep is the intermediate state between wakefulness and Death” (1), drafts a virtual road map to effecting Morpheus’s integration into Stoker’s “wide world.” Macnish’s description of nightmare is particularly apropos: “The whole mind, during the paroxysm, is wrought up to a pitch of unut- terable despair; a spell is laid upon the faculties, which freezes them in to inaction; and the wretched victim feels as if pent alive in his cofﬁn” (123). Nightmare, described as having “a connection with physical disorder, ranging along the gloomy conﬁnes of terror, holding communication with hell and the grave, and throwing a discolouring shade over human life” (2– 3), seems wilfully autonomous, the dreamer being, as one under a spell, a pure victim of gratuitous terror. Dr. Macnish, author of “The Metempsy- chosis” and other quite successful, light, occult-themed ﬁction, paints a picture evocative of Fuseli’s most celebrated image: Sometimes he is involved in the coils of a horrid, slimy monster, whose eyes have the phosphorescent glare of the sepulchre, and whose breath is poisonous ... he is hissed at by serpents, tortured by demons, stunned by the hollow voices and cold touch of apparitions ... the unearthly shrieks and gibberish of hags, witches, and ﬁends ﬂoat around him.... At one moment he may have the consciousness of a malignant demon being at his side.... Or, he may have the idea of a monstrous hag squatted upon his breast ... an incarnation of the evil spirit ... or he is entombed alive in a sepulchre, beside the mouldering dead [122–25]. The Children of Night 131

Not limited to a consideration of incubi, A Philosophy of Sleep opens out onto a far vaster mindscape that constitutes a ready-made guide to the realm of sleep and its variegated states of consciousness, offering chapters on among other topics, “Night-Mare,” “Spectral Illusions,” “Sleep-Walking,” “Sleep- Talking,” “Trance,” “Induction of Sleep through Opiates,” “Day-Mare,” “Prophetic Dreams,” “Reverie” and “Abstraction” (vii-viii). Stoker, following in Macnish’s shadow, pursues all these phenomena. While Macnish notes that the somnambulist “may safely return, even over the most dangerous precipices ... to his bed” (188) and advises “that sleep-walking is sometimes hereditary” (164), Stoker writes that “Mrs Westenra has got an idea that sleep-walkers always go out on roofs of houses and along the edge of cliffs.... Poor dear, she is naturally anxious about Lucy, and she tells me that her husband, Lucy’s father, had the same habit; that he would get up in the night and dress himself and go out, if he were not stopped” (72). While Macnish maintains that “somnambulism as well as lunacy, sometimes bestows supernatural strength upon the individual” (173), Stoker has Renﬁeld declare, “I had heard that madmen have unnatural strength” (245). Ultimately, Macnish authors Hels- ing’s suspect formula: “Decomposition is the only infallible mark that existence is at an end, and that the grave has triumphed” (237). He goes so far as to describe the glazed eyes and shrinking visage of the already dead, useful to contrast with the Un-Dead resting in their cofﬁns. Macnish, whose uncom- promising scepticism of premonitory dreams in the modern world comple- ments Dom Augustin Calmet’s views on the likelihood of the existence of vampires, compresses the human life cycle into a philosophy of sleep that unites the physic and psychic under the auspices of a benevolent God in a manner bound to appeal to Stoker. Freud’s obscure cave of the unconscious, abode of the primordial psy- chological being, is hollowed out of emotional bedrock during pre–verbal times. Along its labyrinthine ways uncharted passages link dreams, the realm of individual imaginings, and myth realm of the archetypal image. As dream- life reﬂects myth, dream time approaches mythic time, the cyclical, spiraling realm of continuity and repetition that reaches back to the timeless moment before the beginning. The two conjointly deﬁne a locus where Stoker and Freud can momentarily pause and join in admiration for the work of social anthropologist J. G. Frazer before parting ways. For it is here that the psy- choanalytical, focusing on projected assumptions of a libidinous human econ- omy anchored in “infantile perversions,” assigns the archetypal to the individual, alienating myth’s sense and purpose by denying or ignoring myth’s communal, spiritual origins; it is here where Freud’s psyche, the mind, and Stoker’s psyche, the soul, irreversibly diverge. The Freudian seeks to offer sci- entiﬁc help to those with problems of the mind; Stoker is concerned with 132 The Theology of Dracula

depicting the sacred and discoursing on the problems of the soul. Jung will eventually make an awkward attempt to bridge the divide, but in 1897 the chasm is dauntingly real. Anthropology views the mythic soul rising from two possible sources, the shadow and the breath. The ﬁrst yields the underworldly chthonic soul; the second, the celestial. From a psychoanalytical perspective, the shadow- soul (a projected though insubstantial image) is proper to the dream, yet the Count, while dependent in chthonian fashion on “sleeping” in his consecrated native soil, casts no shadow, returns no reﬂection. This, according to Stoker’s notes, is among the ﬁrst of the Count’s attributes to be established, shadow being, after all, useless to those inhabiting darkness. It is the breath soul that is at play in Dracula. The breath soul is moreover encoded in the ﬁnality of the Vampire. To prevent the reanimation of Lucy’s corpse, Helsing “took ... a little gold cruciﬁx, and placed it over the mouth” (149). To be spiritually released from the binds of the material, the Vampire’s head must be severed, mouth ﬁlled with garlic, etc.; only when the breath has been surrendered does the Vampire ﬁnd felicitous, true death. Rather than being an immaterial spirit or shade, Stoker’s corporeal Un- Dead hungers for spirits, souls, and yearns to consume them; it is not the blood that is the life, but the soul. Seward suggests as much to Renﬁeld, asking “But ... how are we to get the life without getting the soul also?” (237), thereby presenting the Count’s John the Baptist with a wrenching and unanticipated moral dilemma that results in his conversion to a less sanguine faith. The Professor, expert on “obscure diseases” (105), leaves no doubt, in explaining to Mina the peril of dying in her unclean state, that vampirism’s danger is to the soul, not the body. This also clariﬁes why the Vampire’s victims would be described as feeling “down in the spirit” (107), or would report of themselves that “sleep has not refreshed me, for today I feel terribly weak and spiritless” (228)—the spirit having been drawn off overnight. To appreciate the oral, celestial soul beyond brute “psycho-sexual instinct” an authentically Gothic representation is instructive and perhaps illuminating of the Vampire’s habit of searching out its victim’s throat. Lucy, describing her primary symptom, writes, “my throat pains me. It must be something wrong with my lungs, for I don’t seem ever to get air enough” (104). A chapel in the western transept of the Abbatial church of Mont-Saint- Michel contains a polychromed 15th–century alabaster relief produced in Not- tingham, England, narrating the Betrayal, Passion, Cruciﬁxion, Burial, and Resurrection in ﬁve frames, based principally on the Gospels of Luke and John. The central panel of this retable, representing Christ on the cross, is substantially larger than the others. At its center, Jesus is stretched upon his cross atop Golgatha; His head, fallen limp, rests on His shoulder—as the The Children of Night 133

central image of the central panel, it is key to the artwork’s symmetric con- ceptual and spatial organization. Two thieves, one to Jesus’ left, the other His right, are dying. To the left of the Cross, Jesus’ right hand side, His Mother Mary, His aunt Anne, Mary wife of Cleophus, Mary Magdalene, and others bear witness; to His right, Roman soldiers wile away their time. The thieves are being punished for crimes of property; Jesus, for a crime of words: In not denying His purported divinity to the Roman consul, He has blasphemed. Something fabulously original animates the iconography of the Cruciﬁx- ion scene: Babes are being born from the open mouths of the dying thieves. Each thief—head forced back, mouth agape—is, in giving up his own corporal existence, bringing forth a new being, a spiritual life: a soul. In this fantastic metaphor, the mouth becomes a vaginal construct; the lungs and larynx, the womb of the spirit. Above each thief, delivering the newborns like midwives, an angel hovers: Saint Michel draws the infant/soul from the thief who dies on the right-hand side of Jesus; Lucifer pulls on the body of the new life that emerges from the mouth of the thief who expires on the left (right side of panel). Saint Michel claims the soul of the thief who, according to Luke, indi- cated in words that he accepted the divinity of Jesus; Lucifer, that of the thief who mocked Him. It is curious that the Gospel of John states so clearly that in the beginning was the Word, while the ﬁrst book of Moses, Genesis, describes the beginning so differently. John seems more concerned with volition and the realization of the promises of the Old Testament, Genesis with the construction of a material reality, with corporeality. Genesis claims that God created the 134 The Theology of Dracula Saint- Michel Retable. © Centre des monuments nationaux, Paris, Etienne Revault

universe out of a void, dividing element from element in a dialectical process, identifying binary components of light and dark, solid and liquid, separating one thing from the other by the assignation of names. This universe of Moses is created through performative language: God said, “Let there be light; and there was light” (1:3). Remarkably, Genesis then reports that God observed the material effect of his proclamation: “And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night” (1:5). Thus in a substantial sense, the Word was the beginning. The identiﬁcation of separate aspects of existence, the merging of a phenomenon with the idea of the phenomenon is achieved through the attachment of a name to a thing. John, clearly referring to the account of Genesis, proclaims that in Him (meaning God, hence the Word) was life; “and the life was the light of men. And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not” (1:5). The Word, formed of the breath, is constitutive of the soul. As Sir Oracle observed and insisted, it is the words that are attached to the deceased that will be critical on Judgment Day. These pivotal authors of the Old and New Testaments return to mythic time in their introductory statements, a moment not simply preceding history, but creation. It is a time that repeats cyclically, even as the Betrayal, Passion, Cruciﬁxion, Burial, and Resurrection of the Mont-Saint-Michel Retable are The Children of Night 135 The taking of the souls: detail, Mont- Saint- Michel Retable. © Centre des mon- uments nationaux, Paris, Etienne Revault

reviviﬁed each time the act of transubstantiation, the miraculous investment of Christ into the unleavened bread of Communion, occurs before it. Morpheus ﬁrst appears in a sacred text whose portrayal of the beginning is reminiscent of Genesis’s bifurcating process of material creation: Hesiod’s Theogony. The fertile divine persona it introduces come into being through a mitotic, procreative process: Verily at the ﬁrst Chaos came to be, but next wide-bosomed Earth, the ever-sure foundations of all the deathless ones who hold the peaks of snowy Olympus, and dim Tartarus in the depth of the wide-pathed Earth, and Eros (Love), fairest among the deathless gods, who unnerves the limbs and overcomes the mind and wise counsels of all gods and all men within them. From Chaos came forth Erebus and black Night; but of Night were born Aether and Day, whom she conceived and bare from union in love with Erebus [¶116–138]. And from these latter did Morpheus and his kind derive. The Chaos that birthed Night and Erebus is akin to the Néant that claimed Ruthven, but what, it must be asked, and Stoker insists on it, came before the “Chaos came to be”? The divine realm of the soul. As will be seen, philosophy rather than theology will help Stoker probe the question of unbegottenness, for the dialectical divisions of the Old Tes- tament are no more the crux of The Book of Stoker than the genealogy of Hesiod’s Theogony, though both contribute to its sacred discourse. Morpheus and dream-life, Genesis and Exodus are harnessed to facilitate art. Intersect- ing, ecliptic mythological discourses and pagan temporal ordering offered Stoker great integrative possibilities, and, one might suspect, speak to a syn- cretic mode of seeing mankind’s spiritual quest that pleased him. Drawing on the antique and the prophetic while maintaining a disciplined focus on the topical, technological, and contemporary, Stoker integrates the pagan and Christian with no more conﬂict than Lazarus encountered when summoning guides at the inn. Antique gods, Children of Night, interact with humans as “Watchers” of mythic time once did. In Dracula, however, the scribing Hark- ers work to petition God in the name of mankind. Stoker’s creative and spir- itual vision foresees nothing less than the establishment of a New Jerusalem by a New Woman and New Man who conjointly form an aware and knowing syzygy within an eternal divine. To clearly perceive the functioning of Stoker’s vampire as a haunter of dreams, an invader scaling the broken battlements of consciousness, it is instructive to look closely and discover traces of Morpheus’s presence within the novel’s earliest énoncés: I did not sleep well, though my bed was comfortable enough, for I had all sorts of queer dreams. There was a dog howling all night under my window, 136 The Theology of Dracula

which may have had something to do with it.... Towards morning I slept and was wakened by the continuous knocking at my door, so I must have been sleeping [10]. Sleep and dreams are encountered prior to any direct encounter with the Count, whose subtle introduction, beyond the barking of dogs and visitations by queer dreams, is given form in his only textual contribution to the cento. My FRIEND,—Welcome to the Carpathians. I am anxiously expecting you. Sleep well tonight [12].
