A secondary focus on the Word and on writing arises soon thereafter, positioning the preserved, conscious, written word as antithetical to the uncon- scious-yet-vividly-experienced dream, an opposition that is ﬁercely sustained throughout the novel, whether expressed by Mina who notes, “No sleep now, so I may as well write” (87), or by Dracula, executing his scorched word policy, burning “the manuscript” (249) as he ﬂees his tormentors. These con- trasting poles are ﬁxed by Jonathan as natural at the beginning: I am not sleepy, and, as I am not to be called till I awake, naturally I write till sleep comes. There are many odd things to put down [13]. These comments anticipate the physical imposition of the octagonal room that separates the count’s library and Jonathan’s sleeping chamber. Among the many “odd things” needing to be put down, Jonathan writes of having experienced “a queer sting on the tongue” (13), and as hearing “a lot of words often repeated, queer words” (13) from people of many nations seated on a “word-bearer.” Before separating from Jonathan, society hands him a rosary, “gifts ... of an odd and varied kind ... given in simple good faith, and a kindly word, and a blessing, and that strange mixture of fear-meaning movements which I had seen outside the hotel at Bistritz—the sign of the cross and the guard against the evil eye” (16), along with a warning from the driver: “No, no,” he said; “you must not walk here; the dogs are too ﬁerce”; and then he added, with what he evidently meant for grim pleasantry—for he looked round to catch the approving smile of the rest—“and you may have enough of such matters before you go to sleep” [16]. Ultimately, “bad dreams for those who sleep unwisely” (38) and “the good practice” (112) of writing, those embodiments of unconscious and con- scious representation respectively, prove to enjoy a conﬂictive yet ultimately symbiotic relationship. To understand, and following Ernest Jones’s method- ology, it should be fruitful to extract and consider from the collected state- ments that make up Dracula several individuals’ reports on the invasion of their dreams, noting their coincidence. The ﬁrst to encounter Morpheus is Jonathan: The Children of Night 137

Something made me start up, a low, piteous howling of dogs somewhere far below in the valley, which was hidden from my sight. Louder it seemed to ring in my ears, and the ﬂoating moats of dust to take new shapes to the sound as they danced in the moonlight. I felt myself struggling to awake to some call of my instincts. Nay, my very soul was struggling, and my half- remembered sensibilities were striving to answer the call. I was becoming hypnotised! Quicker and quicker danced the dust. The moonbeams seemed to quiver as they went by me into the mass of gloom beyond. More and more they gathered till they seemed to take dim phantom shapes. And then I started, broad awake and in full possession of my senses, and ran scream- ing from the place. The phantom shapes, which were becoming gradually materialised from the moonbeams, were those three ghostly women to whom I was doomed [48]. Lucy, Morpheus’s next acquaintance, reluctant to believe that he had indeed come to know her, stridently disbelieves, confounding the conscious and unconscious. “I didn’t quite dream,” she insists, in that “it all seemed to be real” (94). She felt a fear-driven impulse to attain the bench of Sir Oracle, without knowing why or of what she should have been afraid. She had, but a few days earlier, daydreamed of taking her ﬁancé “up to the seat on the churchyard cliff and showing him the beauty of Whitby” (72). Now she, the Beauty of Whitby, imagines that she must have gone there while sleepwalking, though she recalls, I heard a lot of dogs howling—the whole town seemed as if it must be full of dogs all howling at once, as I went up the steps. Then I had a vague memory of something long and dark with red eyes, just as we saw in the sunset, and something very sweet and very bitter all around me at once. And then I seemed sinking into deep green water, and there was a singing in my ears, as I have heard there is to drowning men, and then everything seemed passing away from me [94]. The most startling portion of her report, however, concerns her soul: “My soul seemed to go out from my body and ﬂoat about the air. I seem to remem- ber that once the West Lighthouse was right under me, and then there was a sort of agonizing feeling, as if I were in an earthquake, and I came back and found you shaking my body. I saw you do it before I felt you” (94). In other words, she returned from some otherworld to her body and found it being shaken. As Macnish warns, the somnambulist may “be insensible not only to a slight touch, but a severe shaking of the limbs” (188). When after a similar ordeal she once again returned to “consciousness” she was aware that an indeterminate amount of time had passed during which she was exterior to herself. Still, “dogs all round the neighbourhood were howling, and in our shrubbery, seemingly just outside, a nightingale was singing. I was dazed and stupid with pain and terror and weakness, but the 138 The Theology of Dracula

sound of the nightingale seemed like the voice of my dead mother come back to comfort me” (132). Like Jonathan, Lucy too is drawn in and amazed by a queer phenomenon, the appearance of a vortex of materialization: “The air seems full of specks, ﬂoating and circling in the draught from the window, and the lights burn blue and dim” (132). Dr. Seward, man of science, refused to acquiesce to Morpheus. He nev- ertheless witnessed the nightmare spectacle of the graveyard where the decep- tively cherubic Sleep most particularly holds sway at midnight. “Never did bough creak so mysteriously, and never did the far-away howling of dogs send such a woeful presage through the night,” he records. As he waited in the night, “a long spell of silence” (187) produced a “big, aching, void” (187) only ﬁlled by a signal from the Professor. Looking far down the avenue of yews we saw a white ﬁgure advance, a dim white ﬁgure, which held something dark at its breast. The ﬁgure stopped, and at the moment a ray of moonlight fell upon the masses of driving clouds, and showed in startling prominence a dark-haired woman, dressed in the cere- ments of the grave. We could not see the face, for it was bent down over what we saw to be a fair-haired child. There was a pause and a sharp little cry, such as a child gives in sleep, or a dog as it lies before the ﬁre and dreams [187]. Mina was pointedly linked to Morpheus in having her initiation rite interrupted. When asked to recall the particulars of one encounter with Mor- pheus, she replied, “I can’t quite remember how I fell asleep last night. I remember hearing the sudden barking of the dogs and a lot of queer sounds, like praying on a very tumultuous scale, from Mr Renﬁeld’s room.... And then there was silence over everything, silence so profound that it startled me, and I got up and looked out of the window” (227). What she saw and heard was an absence of anything to see or hear, for everything was “dark and silent, the black shadows thrown by the moonlight seeming full of a silent mystery of their own. Not a thing seemed to be stirring, but all to be grim and ﬁxed as death or fate, so that a thin streak of white mist, that crept with almost imperceptible slowness across the grass towards the house, seemed to have a sentience and a vitality of its own” (227). Death and fate having mated, a lifeless vitality—a seeming consciousness—stealthily advanced towards her abode, that being, as always, her bodily living self. Somehow the curious serpentine mist brought not only a reassuring com- fort but a growing languorous lethargy that forced Mina to take to her bed again. “I lay a while, but could not quite sleep, so I got out and looked out of the window again. The mist was spreading, and was now close up to the house, so that I could see it lying thick against the wall, as though it were stealing up to the windows” (227). Renﬁeld’s cries kept growing louder as the mist approached his window. Mina claims that though she was unable to The Children of Night 139

understand his words, his tone communicated “some passionate entreaty” (227) that approached the desperate and left her so distraught by the com- motion beneath her that she retreated under the covers with her ﬁngers in her ears, attempting to deny her very role as a Harker. The next thing she recalled was awakening, even though the last thing she remembered prior to waking was not being sleepy. “I think that it took me an effort and a little time to realize where I was, and that it was Jonathan who was bending over me. My dream was very peculiar, and was almost typical of the way that waking thoughts become merged in, or continued in, dreams” (227). Mina, too, perceives whirling forms, but with several signiﬁcant differ- ences from the spiraling “simoom in the desert” (131) that Jonathan, Lucy, and the Professor report. First, she establishes a parallel between her inner, conscious self, and an external quasi-unconscious world: “Things began to whirl through my brain just as the cloudy column was now whirling in the room, and through it all came the scriptural words ‘a pillar of cloud by day and of ﬁre by night’ Was it indeed such spiritual guidance that was coming to me in my sleep?” (227), she asks herself, exercising her critical capacities. Then, accenting the un–Freudian nature of consciousness in Dracula, Mina’s oneiric ordeal causes her to lose consciousness even as she sleeps and dreams. She recalls Jonathan’s ordeal at Castle Dracula: “Suddenly the horror burst upon me that it was thus that Jonathan had seen those awful women growing into reality through the whirling mist in the moonlight, and in my dream I must have fainted, for all became black darkness” (227). Finally, having described the loss of consciousness in a dream, she ends her session with the Professor as if emerging from an exercise in hypnosis, retracing her return to consciousness. “The last conscious effort which imagination made was to show me a livid white face bending over me out of the mist. I must be careful of such dreams, for they would unseat one’s reason if there were too much of them” (227–28). Mina, having entered a spiritual desert, is being divinely led, day and night. This lesson of Exodus, journal of the trials of those being led from one state into another, promises that faith will indicate her way: “So we came down this road; when we meet other ways—not always were we sure that they were roads at all ... the horses know and they only. I give rein to them, and they go on so patient” (314). Renﬁeld, whose ambivalent role has already been discussed, was not hos- tile to the Count. He reports his accession to him in familiar terms: “Then the dogs howled, away beyond the dark trees in His house. He beckoned me to the window” (244). This “beckoning” is evidently an image of the mist. The collation of the various reports has Mina, above, retreating to her bed as Renﬁeld, below, rises from his. “I got up and looked out,” reports Renﬁeld, 140 The Theology of Dracula

and He raised his hands, and seemed to call out without using any words. A dark mass spread over the grass, coming on like the shape of a ﬂame of ﬁre. And then He moved the mist to the right and left, and I could see that there were thousands of rats with their eyes blazing red, like His only smaller. He held up his hand, and they all stopped, and I thought he seemed to be saying, “All these lives will I give you, ay, and many more and greater, through countless ages, if you will fall down and worship me!” And then a red cloud, like the colour of blood, seemed to close over my eyes, and before I knew what I was doing, I found myself opening the sash and saying to Him, “Come in, Lord and Master!” [244–45]. The use of capitals indicates the divine role ascribed to Morpheus by the Lunatic. The barking dogs, sonic commotion and clamoring tongues, the rustling trees, and the plunging sensation are constants that to each individual seem so unlike a dream that they feel compelled to note the confounding, disori- enting impression. Through dream life, they have tumbled into liquid, mythic depths. Two clashing realms that work to negate each other are reﬂected in the imagery: the “wide world” we inhabit and the mysterious mansion of Sleep in which dwells Morpheus. Edith Hamilton, paraphrasing Ovid’s Metamor- phoses XI, describes that noble dwelling to which Morpheus drags back souls as near the black country of the Cimmerians, in a deep valley where the sun never shines and dusky twilight wraps all things in shadows. No cock crows there; no watchdog breaks the silence; no branches rustle in the breeze; no clamour of tongues disturbs the peace. The only sound comes from the gently ﬂowing stream of Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, where the waters murmuring entice to sleep. Before the door poppies bloom, and other drowsy herbs [107]. In Dryden and Garth’s verse translation: Near the Cymmerians, in his dark abode, Deep in a cavern, dwells the drowsy God; Whose gloomy mansion nor the rising sun, Nor setting, visits, nor the lightsome noon; But lazy vapours round the region ﬂy, Perpetual twilight, and a doubtful sky: No crowing cock does there his wings display, Nor with his horny bill provoke the day; Nor watchful dogs, nor the more wakeful geese, Disturb with nightly noise the sacred peace; Nor beast of Nature, nor the tame are nigh, Nor trees with tempests rock’d, nor human cry; But safe repose without an air of breath Dwells here, and a dumb quiet next to death [Ovid XI]. Within the various dream testimonies, the barking dogs, cacophonous prayers The Children of Night 141

and trembling branches depict the moment of Morpheus’s arrival in an alien land where “Sleep has no place it can call its own” (272). The dogs, like that of Swale’s silent friend, are alarmed—as is all nature—due to the Count’s presence. Rather than being commanded by the Count, they, “the best and truest of friends” (216), betray him by sounding the alert. When Helsing, seeking to administer an “injection of morphia” (119) into plot, speaks of “the waters of Lethe” and “Lotus ﬂowers” (120), he—rummaging within Ovid’s account of Morpheus—consciously dispatches his patient to the land of Hyp- nos. Entwined within his hybrid text mixing mythology, classical poetry, and Platonic dialogue, Stoker encloses more contemporaneous musings: Keats’s “Nightingale” singing to redeem Mrs. Westenra’s immortal soul, summer’s departed days, and the terrible terrain where dream dreamt and life lived have become indistinguishable. Stoker’s dream-like, interweaving organization is typical of both the Vampire Tale and of scripture, in which the New Testament reiterates much of the Old while transforming it through a new signiﬁcance. Reaching beyond the merely organic in assembling Morpheus’s extended clan, Stoker atomizes sleep into ﬁner components than those dozen phenom- ena Macnish marshals into his philosophy, representing: dizziness, fainting, stupor, drowsiness, fatigue, sleep deprivation, insomnia, falling asleep both voluntarily and involuntarily, sleep, nightmare, paralysis and petrifaction, somnambulism, sleep-talking, premonition, prophecy, somniphobia, narcotic sedation, trance, hypnosis, hallucination, insanity, astral projection, telepathy, materialisation, forgetfulness, obliviousness, amnesia, death, anamnesis, awak- ening, and felicity—conditions that frequently accumulate into multi–faceted metaphysical experiences. While their combined effects occasionally give rise to a sleep that is purely physical, it is more frequently richly psychic. Lucy’s experience, perhaps based on the Republic’s Platonic parable of Er, includes an episode of astral projection that accentuates Stoker’s East–West–East motif, as she passes from East Cliff to West Lighthouse and back again, Stoker— always concerned with symmetry and solar movement, makes great effort to inform his reader of a light that had just been installed on East Cliff. When describing their states of consciousness during their respective ini- tiations, the Harkers make similar statements, both describing their encounters with the Vampire as something seen despite closed eyelids. Mina reports: “I closed my eyes, but could see through my eyelids” (227); Jonathan: “I was afraid to raise my eyelids, but looked out and saw perfectly under the lashes” (42). Jonathan also describes a thrall he experienced, which, perceived as a form of hypnosis, he battled to resist: “I felt myself struggling to awake to some call of my instincts. Nay, my very soul was struggling, and my half- remembered sensibilities were striving to answer the call. I was becoming 142 The Theology of Dracula

hypnotised!” (48). In contrast, Mina actively seeks out hypnosis: “I have an idea.... He must hypnotize me before the dawn, and then I shall be able to speak” (271) (though how she knows of the Professor’s interest in Charcot remains a mystery). Whereas Mina’s hypnosis opens telepathic links to the Count, Jonathan’s fear of the hypnotic-as-forgetfulness opens a connection to a central aspect of theme, forgetfulness being instrumental to theme the way Mina’s telepathic link with the Count is to plot. In Jonathan’s written statement, he amends his initial phrase, revising his thought to contradict himself. He writes ﬁrst of awakening an instinct. Then, correcting that, insists that it was in fact not instinct, that canny animal intelligence, but his “very soul” that was called on to battle the forces of Hyp- nos, volition summoning ‘half-remembered sensibilities’; sensibilities half-, and no doubt nearly entirely-forgotten. What Thanatos is to the material, Hypnos is to the spiritual, a force of corporal domination and psychic relax- ation which causes forgetfulness. Even Mina, though willingly submitting to hypnosis, insists, “I don’t like this lapsing into forgetfulness” (156). In the logic of myth, to forget is to endanger the soul and the accom- plishment of life’s sacred mission: the return of the soul, enriched, renewed, to the point before the beginning, the moment before Hesiod and Moses begin their accounts of creation. In the aftermath of their encounters with Morpheus, Dracula’s characters are unable to remember what has happened to them, recalling only their fear and accompanying angst. Forgetfulness char- acterizes them all, consigning those who have dreamt unwisely to a repast of Lotus blossoms washed down with the waters of the Lethe. Those assigned to watch over the dreamers are forbidden sleep in order to protect the dreams of those they guard, a chore that is in and of itself a nightmare; as the Professor, eerily sounding like the Count, warns his student, “Remember, she is your charge. If you leave her, and harm befall, you shall not sleep easy hereafter!” (116). Omnipresent Nightmare ﬁnds Dracula’s protagonists reporting classic symptoms: “I was powerless to act, my feet, and my hands, and my brain were weighted, so that nothing could proceed at the usual pace” (227); “For an instant my heart stood still, and I would have screamed out, only that I was paralysed” (251); “it seemed to me as if my feet were weighted with lead, and as though every joint in my body were rusty” (88). Nightmare is notably omnipresent until the Count takes ﬂight, with amnesiac sleepers reluctant or incapable of recalling their guillotine dreams. “More bad dreams. I wish I could remember them” (103), is Lucy’s halfhearted regret. Jonathan, according to Mina, “does not remember anything that has happened to him for a long time past. At least, he wants me to believe so, and I shall never ask” (99). Seward observes that even Mrs Harker seems to lose sight of her trouble for The Children of Night 143

whole spells” (280). At last, Renﬁeld, “working in the interval” and encouraged to “tell us your dream” (243), confronts truth: “I must not deceive myself. It was no dream, but all a grim reality” (243). Through this announcement, Renﬁeld marks the turning point of plot. Dracula’s entire population of Britons, with the exception of oracular Swales, is swept up by the glamour of what is repeatedly called either “the wide world” (62, 100, 152, 184, etc.), or, variously, “the moving world” (215), “the world ... at movement” (256), “world of life” (100), and even “the brute world” (223), and thus in their distraction forget themselves. The Professor from the Low Countries, too, momentarily (if only occasionally) forgets him- self: “But presently I forget all of watching; and when I sudden remember that I watch, I ﬁnd her lying quiet, but awake, and looking at me with so bright eyes” (315). The others forget themselves blindly. The young men, captivated by Lucy, world of light and light of the world, become lovers and so enamored of the moment as to be forgetful of the Otherworld to which their own soul-life belongs, so enmeshed in the web of linear, historic time that they lose sight of the ultimate cyclic force of returning that inevitably deﬁnes their adventure. Those disappointed in love, attempting to lose themselves through other means—through work on Seward’s part, adventure on Quincey’s—fail to recall themselves in their melancholy. This is how and why, as Mircea Eliade remarks, “‘forgetfulness is assimilated to death” (115), meaning spiritual death, the extinction of the soul. The soul of Stoker’s Dracula is the Platonic soul, recalled by the Vampire due to its loss and an undying, Un-Dead hunger to recover it. Socrates’ turn- ing analysis of the moving world in the Phaedrus seems to have been partic- ularly inﬂuential upon Stoker, contrasting the volitional, self–moving being with the Vampire-dominated soulless body: The soul through all her being is immortal, for that which is ever in motion is immortal; but that which moves another and is moved by another, in ceasing to move ceases also to live. Only the self–moving, never leaving self, never ceases to move, and is the fountain and beginning of motion to all that moves besides. Now, the beginning is unbegotten, for that which is begotten has a beginning; but the beginning is begotten of nothing, for if it were begotten of something, then the begotten would not come from a beginning. But if unbegotten, it must also be indestructible; for if beginning were destroyed, there could be no beginning out of any- thing, nor anything out of a beginning; and all things must have a begin- ning. And therefore the self–moving is the beginning of motion; and this can neither be destroyed nor begotten, else the whole heavens and all cre- ation would collapse and stand still, and never again have motion or birth. But if the self–moving is proved to be immortal, he who afﬁrms that self– motion is the very idea and essence of the soul will not be put to confusion. 144 The Theology of Dracula

For the body which is moved from without is soulless; but that which is moved from within has a soul, for such is the nature of the soul. But if this be true, must not the soul be the self–moving, and therefore of necessity unbegotten and immortal? [Phaedrus]. The activity of the scribe, writing, established as the antidote to sleeping, allows dreamers to overcome forgetfulness. It is both an act of remembrance and recollection, and an investment in transcending the momentary. Through the witness and the witnessing of dreamers, awakening is achieved. Stepping away from rigid scepticism on letters as merely productive of the show of wis- dom without the substantative reality, and assuming a more forthrightly Gnos- tic stance, the Professor instructs his former student Seward: “Remember, my friend, that knowledge is stronger than memory, and we should not trust the weaker” (112). He counsels to commit all observations great and small to writ- ing, sustaining the Platonic belief that the living word of knowledge has a soul whose image can be contained, however imperfectly, by the written word. The Professor, having listened to Mina’s analysis of the Vampire’s con- sciousness and diagnosis of his fatal conceptual ﬂaws, somewhat mystifyingly announces: “‘Dos pou sto,’ said Archimedes. ‘Give me a fulcrum, and I shall move the world!’” (296). This comment—promising to move away from pas- sivity, from being hypnotized by the moving world, towards activity, that is, towards being the engaged force that sets the world to moving—seems to mark Dracula’s epistemological turning point, for the text suddenly becomes clogged with such un–scientiﬁc terms as “child-brain” (264), “man-brain” (294), “child-thought” (295), “man-thought” (295), and “half-thought” (295). The Professor has understood that the archaic fallen angel is unaware of the new context of the transformed contemporary world. In terms of Watch- ers, and by analogy Harkers, that new context was born in Bethlehem to come to maturity in Jerusalem with the Cruciﬁxion and Resurrection. The Dutch- man proposes to move the world forward in overcoming superior force through the application of knowledge, gnosis. Yet the question of what the Professor intends to leverage remains not entirely clear, leaving the reader to surmise that he intends to exploit the Count’s cognitive limitations to effect the Vam- pire’s destruction. What the Professor celebrates no doubt is his knowledge of the Count’s ignorance and the Count’s ignorance of his knowledge: Such it would seem is his lever. Mina distils the Professor’s arguments, noting that the strategies of Evil, rooted in things of the earth, the material, and of present time, are forever the same, though the spirit of volitional freemen progresses and evolves due to the self–moving soul. Thus the Vampire, having no soul of its own, is incapable of advancing, for what “advancing” truly means in the dream-logic, mytho- logic of Dracula, is “returning,” returning to God and to the unbegotten state The Children of Night 145

existing beyond matter and beyond time, that timeless moment before cosmic infancy. For John the Evangelist, the Word is key to the recovery of a glimpse of what was before the beginning. For Hesiod, the ineffable and eternal is accessed through the story told by the Muses, daughters of omniscient Mnemosyne, who sing of the castration of the Father of fathers and Kronos’s beginning of Time, the declination of the gods, and birth of the Children of Night. Jean-Pierre Ver- nant, considering the ontological function of myth, regardless its tradition, writes: “The past thus revealed is much more than the antecedent of the present; it is its source. In going back to it, recollection does not seek to situate events in a temporal frame but to reach the depths of being, to discover the original, the primordial reality from which the cosmos issued and which makes it possible to understand becoming as a whole”* (qtd. in Eliade 120). Yet for the volitional being, having forgotten the self–moving soul, having been distracted by the fogs and mists of the world whose reality is the ultimate source of illusion, is it not possible that in the universe of Dracula the fulcrum that has appeared to set the world in motion anew, by creating New Woman and New Man, is the Count? That is, in terms of plot, the Professor leverages the Count’s epistemological limitations against the Vampire; but in thematic terms, Stoker leverages the Count to move his protagonists towards the sacred and their own puriﬁcation. The Count’s role is thus to awaken his victims profoundly, ﬁrst by sub- jecting them to forgetfulness and then by horrifyingly calling them to themselves when the spiritual enjeu becomes clearly deﬁned. To Jonathan and Mina he is as much a spiritual guide as the Professor, albeit one who leads with the stick rather than the carrot. He is moreover a being that deﬁes the image in that he lacks the Imago Dei. Returning to Plato’s “Phaedrus,” Socrates maintains that every soul of man has in the way of nature beheld true being; this was the condition of her passing into the form of man. But all souls do not easily recall the things of the other world; they may have seen them for a short time only, or they may have been unfortunate in their earthly lot, and, hav- ing had their hearts turned to unrighteousness through some corrupting inﬂuence, they may have lost the memory of the holy things which once they saw. Few only retain an adequate remembrance of them; and they, when they behold here any image of that other world, are rapt in amazement; but they are ignorant of what this rapture means, because they do not clearly perceive. For there is no light of justice or temperance or any of the higher ideas which are precious to souls in the earthly copies of them: they are seen through a glass dimly; and there are few who, going to the images, behold in them the realities, and these only with difﬁculty [Phaedrus]. The Count establishes the dangers of the mortal world when, upon his 146 The Theology of Dracula *From article “Aspects mythiques de la mémoire en Grèce,” in Journal de Psychologie (1959), p. 7.

sudden appearance, Jonathan is surprised by what he has failed to see reﬂected in his shaving mirror, as if that which the looking glass contained was identical to the real. His surprise and disorientation cause him to cut himself and his life’s blood to ﬂow. The Count seizes Jonathan’s shaving glass, saying: “‘And this is the wretched thing that has done the mischief. It is a foul bauble of man’s vanity. Away with it!’ And opening the heavy window with one wrench of his terrible hand, he ﬂung out the glass, which was shattered into a thousand pieces on the stones of the courtyard far below” (31). The sense of the Count’s warning is of course not understood by Jonathan, but it should be clear that Stoker truly is asserting that man’s vanity deceives him into believing the illu- sory to be the real, confounding the image and the substance, even when it is the substance of the insubstantial. Stoker leads his reader into the forgetfulness of plot with a frantic coach ride, the driver determined to have his horses seize from space what he would redeem from Time and steal away from the evening when all evil things in the world hold sway. As Jonathan catches occasional glimpses of “God’s seat” through the trees, and spring blossoms brighten the fading day, he notices wayside shrines. “By the roadside were many crosses, and as we swept by, my companions all crossed themselves. Here and there was a peasant man or woman kneeling before a shrine, who did not even turn round as we approached, but seemed in the self–surrender of devotion to have neither eyes nor ears for the outer world” (15). The devout may not be distracted by the outer world that rushes by in full movement, but for the rest of us, approaching evil may serve to intensify spiritual awareness, forcing us to realize that we existed within Mythic Time before being born to the historic, that our exis- tence therein shall endure when History has been dissolved and atomized, and that our psyche entails more than organic mind. Without awakening, sleep gives way to death, Hypnos becoming Thanatos. In the Theology of Dracula, as we have been uncovering it, anam- nesis, the recalling and awakening, is the ultimate spiritual act; it is the Living Ofﬁce of the Dead, dealt with repeatedly in scripture, for gnosis comes from being alert, conscious, and aware. As Mina exclaims when she comes to Jonathan and ﬁnds him asleep: “He is waking!” (99). In awakening, we are recalled to ourselves as spiritual beings and brought into a useful relationship with the knowledge we have gained. Repeated Pla- tonic references mark Stoker’s Dracula, this magnum opus that calls so fully on Stoker’s life experience, from his clerical duties in Dublin’s Court of Petty Sessions, to his role as president of “The Phil,” Trinity University’s philo- sophical society. It is Phaedrus that is most often suggested; when, of Renﬁeld it is said, “He did not care for any of the things of mere earth; he was in the clouds and looked down on all the weaknesses and wants of us poor mortals” The Children of Night 147

(235), Phaedrus seems clearly indicated, as it is through the various discourses on madness. “All men are mad in some way or the other; and inasmuch as you deal discreetly with your madmen, so deal with God’s madmen, too— the rest of the world” (111). As the Professor tries to explain with his King Laugh speech, as Renﬁeld serves to illustrate in his very being, true awareness is madness: the fourth and last kind of madness, which is imputed to him who, when he sees the beauty of earth, is transported with the recollection of the true beauty; he would like to ﬂy away, but he cannot; he is like a bird ﬂuttering and looking upward and careless of the world below; and he is therefore thought to be mad. And I have shown this of all inspirations to be the noblest and highest and the offspring of the highest to him who has or shares in it, and that he who loves the beautiful is called a lover because he partakes of it. ... There was a time when with the rest of the happy band they saw beauty shining in brightness,—we philosophers following in the train of Zeus, others in company with other gods; and then we beheld the beatiﬁc vision and were initiated into a mystery which may be truly called most blessed, celebrated by us in our state of innocence, before we had any experience of evils to come, when we were admitted to the sight of appari- tions innocent and simple and calm and happy, which we beheld shining in pure light, pure ourselves and not yet enshrined in that living tomb which we carry about, now that we are imprisoned in the body, like an oyster in his shell. Let me linger over the memory of scenes which have passed away [The Phaedrus]. We are imprisoned in the body, like an oyster in his shell. Let us linger over the memory of scenes which have passed away! The Children of Night 149

Kingdom Come “The girl is dead. Why mutilate her poor body without need? And if there is no necessity for a post–mortem and nothing to gain by it—no good to her, to us, to science, to human knowl- edge—why do it? Without such it is monstrous” [149]. On the eve of Dracula’s publication Bram Stoker took time to draft a note to former British Prime Minister William Gladstone in which he pledged that there was “nothing base in the book” about to appear, then added, “and ... I hope it is not irreverent” (letter of 24 May 1897, British Library Mss. 44525, 221–22, reproduced in Journal of Dracula Studies 1 [1999]:48). As there is no reason to doubt that Stoker made these comments earnestly and with perfect sincerity, it is ironic that Dracula in all its incarnations is forever recalled by enthusiasts and detractors alike as a scandalous and sordid tale of questionable interest and poor taste, featuring perversion, depravity, sexism, intolerance, xenophobia, incest, and boundless variations on moral deviance couched in melodramatic language and coated with a thickly applied glaze of genteel sentimentality of perfectly Victorian fabrication and quasi-parodic magnitude. While it may be difﬁcult to square Stoker’s pledge with representations of deathless beings that nourish themselves on the blood of innocent human life, the most perverse feature of Dracula may be the elevated position that academia has of late bestowed upon it; the novel’s attainment of respectability and canonical status is largely due to the very reasons for which it had for generations been shunned. Dracula’s ruby-lipped embrace by a cadre of new women and men pur- suing new orientations in the humanities, a ﬁeld of endeavor for identity- afﬁrming critical approaches that set practitioners busily unpacking dedicated theoretical objects from Stoker’s textual cornucopia to thrive on notions of “excess” and “transgression” (particularly politico–sexual excess and transgression), 150

“effaced” boundaries (particularly politico–sexual boundaries), and boundless conﬁgurations of “Otherness,” is frankly comic in its irony, since these projects necessarily grate against the author’s stated intent, which—classical and cathartic in the deepest sense—is to purify. Stoker’s own intense concern with the Other was uniquely invested in the dichotomous nature of being in all its dimensions and deﬁnitions, “some dual life that is not as the common” (179). Determined to produce a sacred text, ill at ease with the usage he, in the weaving of his narrative, had made of superstition, yet realizing that a work founded upon a superstition could hardly avoid some commerce in it, Stoker found solace in his belief that the book was “calculated to cleanse the mind by pity and terror” (Stoker-Gladstone letter). In monstrous fashion, and per- haps at the root of Dracula’s confusing aesthetic position, he took an Aris- totelian end and assigned it to a thoroughly Platonic undertaking. Sylvia Starshine, considering the rushed theatrical adaptation that Stoker made of Dracula for its unique and pro-forma 18 May 1897 Lyceum perform- ance as The Un-Dead, notes the importance of the Platonic by signaling Stoker’s concern with the position of the Professor: “Stoker was a busy man with a demanding job, and it soon becomes obvious that the initial creative intent to dramatise the novel properly soon gave way to the imperative of moving the plot along. There is also a favouring in the amount of stage time given to Van Helsing, suggesting that Stoker was rather preoccupied with the good doctor’s ideas and thoughts” (xii). The Professor is so thoroughly Stoker’s principal Platonic conduit that he appears to have been summoned from the most hellishly infernal regions of the Low Countries exclusively to profess a mystic’s view through the all-enveloping parable of the Vampire and original demonstrations of the force of the Eucharistic Host. Yet while the Professor does not immediately respond to his student’s “Why do it?” interrogation on Lucy’s post–mortem, the response he eventually provides shows that Dracula’s raison d’être is in fact to contribute to human knowledge, gnosis; the professor so signals with a question of his own: “Do you know all the mystery of life and death?” (171). Stoker’s spiritual investment in Dracula seems so transparently central to the work that, were it not for the fact that it has hardly ever been considered, it would seem almost pointless to call attention to it. However it may be read and whatever it might represent to today’s identity-centric critical reader or become for tomorrow’s scholar, Stoker’s Dracula is not a book about homo- sexuality. It is not about syphilis or STDs. It is not about incest, though the author indicates an awareness of the potential to read its knotted relations through that prism. It is about colonialism only in the most remote and abstract way, in that it is about a wide world where all cultures and societies exert inﬂuence on all others as they attempt to return through myth and rite Kingdom Come 151

to the primordial moment and that which always preceded it. It is about the world and the empire not of this world. While absolutely concerned with the Alpha and the Omega, it is scarcely a piece of proselytization for some exotic religious movement, though it deﬁnitely embraces a syncretic from-Renﬁeld- to-Professor-expressed vision of being. A sacred work of art, yes, but not from any one clear tradition that would guide exegetic efforts like a compass. While many have speculated upon Stoker’s connection to the late 19th, early 20th-century magical order recalled as the Golden Dawn, no evidence has been produced to support any ﬁrm linkage—perhaps Douglas Menville’s unsubstantiated contention “that Stoker was probably a member of a splinter group of the famous occult society, the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn” (qtd. by Hennelly) is justiﬁable, though it seems most likely Mr. Stoker formed a group of one. He has, at any rate, created a complex theological statement that—put to parchment with the sharp edge of a shovel, then locked within boxes, entombed, enclosed and immured—truly requires intensive unpacking. In its mission, it fully interacts with Stoker’s own Victorian period and social milieu, replete with a clin d’oeil directed at “Ellen Terry” (160), but surely the author considered, even in writing to former Prime Minister Gladstone, that he was addressing the historically atemporal with a parabolic discourse on the ineffable. In light of the immensity of his ambitions, and resigning himself to the reach of the possible, Stoker contented himself with the simple project of rep- resenting evil as bafﬂed: “It would be impossible to describe the expression of hate and bafﬂed malignity—of anger and hellish rage—which came over the Count’s face” (267); “Never did I see such bafﬂed malice on a face; and never, I trust, shall such ever be seen again by mortal eyes” (188). The Demeter’s cap- tain sets the course: “But I shall bafﬂe this ﬁend or monster, for I shall tie my hands to the wheel when my strength begins to fail, and along with them I shall tie that which He—It!—dare not touch; and then, come good wind or foul, I shall save my soul, and my honour as a captain” (84). The Notes show that as his text evolved from an ill-deﬁned story of a “Young man” and an “Old man” (Rosenbach # 35, Notes 17) into the epic that ﬁnally reached the public in 1897, Stoker was guided by an idea that materi- alized from dust and mist; he was very willing to jettison or modify certain of his earliest ideas while ferociously refusing to let go of others. Structure and polarity seem to be more rigidly ﬁxed entities, the detail of contents far more ﬂuid. As an example of an idea modiﬁed, Stoker considered, early on, afﬁxing the name “Abraham Aaronson” to the solicitor he eventually christens Peter Hawkins. He wished Abraham Aaronson to be identiﬁed as a member of “the Incorporated Law Society,” an organization Stoker sought to feature from 152 The Theology of Dracula

Dracula’s genesis. Reference to Exodus, Mosaic law, eloquent pleading, mag- ical accomplishment, and the golden calf—that is, law, magic, transgression, idolatry—seem intended through the Aaronson appellation. “Abraham,” was readily available to serve whatever character was to be cast as the founding pillar of a new faith and humanitarian age, a father ﬁgure, and alter ego of Stoker himself; thus the name “Abraham” along with much of solicitor Aaron- son’s symbolic function, were attributed to Helsing, with a fainter echo being heard in the person of seaman Abramoff, one of a number of ill-fated sailors with prophetic or apostolic names that set off on The Demeter, that vessel with a religious but anonymous captain. Retained ideas are plentiful. Stoker, from the very beginning, envisages the Count claiming Jonathan as his own man with the transformed Nodier- like phrase “This man belongs to me” (Notes 17, 29, 39). He places great stock in having a Texan and a “Silent Man” among his cast of characters; in incor- porating consecrated grounds and zoological gardens into his roster of dra- matical loci; in endowing a lordly Un-Dead with certain uncanny powers and compensatory limitations based on the interplay of light and darkness; and in featuring, as in previous vampire texts, a promise that he terms “The Vow.” Rather than giving the “Silent Man” to the Count as a servant, as initially planned, Stoker winds up assigning him and an eloquent dog to Mr. Swales as boon companions. Page 8 of the Notes, Rosenbach #2 (29), setting out a relatively complete outline of the novel’s structure and a primitive ébauche of its prospective contents, instructs, “Texan to go to Transylvania,” remarking later, “On the track—Texan in Transylvania.” The outline concludes, but a phrase manifestly added later is penciled in at the bottom of its last page, “Bring in the Texan”; from these words a vertical line emanates and rises before trailing off, assigning the idea to an indeterminate place somewhere in the latter part of the concluding Book IV. Despite numerous discarded incar- nations, the Texan, evidently intended to trigger a cataclysmic ending, survives and dies in the person of Quincey Morris. Elizabeth Miller, in “The Dracula We Might Have Read: What Stoker Cut from His Manuscript,” duly observes that Stoker’s Notes reveal that an explosive ending, with Castle Dracula being struck by lightning, shaken by an erupting volcano, and rattled by earthquake as a “Texan” ﬁres away with a “maxim gun” (Notes 117), was at one point intended, Stoker ending his novel with the néant ﬁrst imagined by Charles Nodier. A typewritten draft in the possession of a collector includes the apocalyptic scene along with an editor’s notation for cutting it: a boxed section of text barred vertically. Both Peter Haining and Barbara Belford have written on this suppressed end- ing, and Elizabeth Miller (“Dracula 2: The Sequel?”) has assayed their argu- ments: Kingdom Come 153

The published novel contains this sentence: “The Castle of Dracula now stood out against the red sky” .... According to the typescript, that line was originally to have been followed by this passage, which was deleted before publication: —As we looked there came a terrible convulsion of the earth so that we seemed to rock to and fro and fell to our knees. At the same moment with a roar which seemed to shake the very heavens the whole castle and the rock and even the hill on which it stood seemed to rise into the air and scatter in fragments while a mighty cloud of black and yellow smoke volume on volume in rolling grandeur was shot upwards with inconceiv- able rapidity. —Then there was a stillness in nature as the echoes of that thunderous report seemed to come as with the hollow boom of a thunder-clap—the long reverberating roll which seems as though the ﬂoors of heaven shook. Then down in a mighty ruin falling whence they rose came the fragments that had been tossed skywards in the cataclysm. —From where we stood it seemed as though the one ﬁerce volcano burst had satisﬁed the need of nature and that the castle and the structure of the hill had sunk again into the void. We were so appalled with the sud- denness and the grandeur that we forgot to think of ourselves [qtd. in Belford 267]. Offering facsimile pages of a typewritten text with handwritten emendations (266–67), Belford claims that this cataclysmic ﬁnale made it through into the typesetter’s proof before being deleted in extremis, and wonders whether the change was implemented to set the scene for a sequel. Should Stoker have been intent on authoring sequels, Dracula’s every conceivable ending could offer the potential for new beginnings. In a text ﬁlled with examples of the atomized Vampire materializing from dust, fog, and mist, the disintegration of an Un-Dead’s body or a granite fortress hardly guarantees that along its dust-to-dust continuum no further materialization will occur. Such an outcome, however, would impose an absurdist’s viewpoint on an author believing in God, the possibility of human perfectibility and the promise of material progress. While the facsimile appears to be made from a working draft in an indeterminate state of development, the modiﬁcations to the text seem likely due to no commercial consideration but to Stoker’s own evolving understanding of the theological rock on which his text reposed. Not generated as a commodity but as a prayer, Dracula’s creation necessarily involved true inspiration—the work, taking on a life of its own, contributed to its own development. The novel’s intended ﬁnal destination is retained in its beginning, as it traces the progress of that coach ﬂying over a paradisiacal land beyond the forests. There was everywhere a bewildering mass of fruit blossom—apple, plum, 154 The Theology of Dracula

pear, cherry; and as we drove by I could see the green grass under the trees spangled with the fallen petals. In and out among these green hills of what they call here the “Mittel Land” ran the road, losing itself as it swept round the grassy curve, or was shut out by the straggling ends of pine woods, which here and there ran down the hillside like tongues of ﬂame. The road was rugged, but still we seemed to ﬂy over it with a feverish haste. I could not understand then what the haste meant, but the driver was evidently bent on losing no time in reaching Borgo Prund [14]. Jonathan Harker, accompanied by people of many nations, sun setting directly behind them, charges eastward. “Beyond the green swelling hills of the Mittel Land rose mighty slopes of forest up to the lofty steeps of the Carpathians themselves” (15). A passenger cried out, “‘Look! Isten szek!’—‘God’s seat!’— and he crossed himself reverently. As we wound on our endless way, and the sun sank lower and lower behind us, the shadows of the evening began to creep round us” (15). At mid–spring they traverse the Mittel Land, a place of greenery, fruitfulness, and sharply differentiated seasons. Flower petals replace snowﬂakes, but the road is not yet at its summertime state of repair. The road, described as an “endless way,” has of course a ﬁnality as yet unseen, and it shall inevitably lead the reader thither. Mittel Land, or Midgard as it is called elsewhere, signifying middle gar- den or middle enclosure and referring to the world of our quotidian reality, is a cosmologically loaded term. Derived from Norse saga, it is present in all Teutonic as well as in many Celtic peoples’ mythologies and has been inserted into popular virtual mythologies of modernity’s manufacture through the myth-raiding efforts of writers of fantasy ﬁction. Midgard, according to The Prose Edda, was formed by Odin and his brothers out of the brow of the giant Ymer; they then formed man and woman out of two trees. In the Old English Beowulf the world we inhabit, embodied as “middangeard,” originates in a fraternal mythos. Having used the term Mittel Land, Stoker is nearly required to provide an apocalyptic debouchment, in that its use establishes contrast with other realms of being and inevitably leads towards the dissolution of this world at the moment of judgment. “Ragnarök” is the Eddic name for the end conﬂict. The wolf, chained to the mountain of Odin, devourer of Sun and Moon, is to be the great god’s bane. Once the Sun has turned black, hammer-bearing Thor kills the great serpent Jormungandr. The world and Yggdrasil tremble and the earth sinks into the sea. Aspects of the Christian apocalypse were eventually incorporated into Ragnarök in various traditions to live on in folk- lore. This template accommodates the unmoored ship careening through great storms and many other details that do ﬁgure prominently in Dracula. One suspects that additional elements woven into Stoker’s nexus derived from Kingdom Come 155

variations crafted to ﬁll the formal requirements of Wagnerian opera. In a chapter on the occult, though primarily concerned with Stoker’s vacations, Belford reports that the Stokers “attended the Wagner cycle in Bayreuth” (220), and one can hear in Lord Godalming of Ring a queer resonance with Wagner’s Götterdämmerung. Mark M. Hennelly, Jr., reading Stoker plainly, perceives this very image: “The four horsemen (Harker, Morris, Godalming, and Seward) climactically ‘rid[e] at break-neck speed’ from north and south in order to seize Dracula’s four-sided cart (cf. quatre) and unseal his cofﬁn before sunset ... suggesting the liminal value of the apocalyptic Seventh Seal, as well as dramatizing a ﬁn de siècle version of Götterdämmerung (from ‘Betwixt Sunset and Sunrise’).” His article “Gnostic Quest and Victorian Wasteland,” dating to the threshold moment of Dracula’s 1970s academic canonization, considers the evident pro- gnostic-ations of Helsing—or “Hell-sing” (22), as Hennelly puts it—as a generic marker. Concerned primarily with considering Dracula against a back- drop of Victorian societal and literary currents, Hennelly nonetheless notes a “consistently-stressed analogy between vampirism and Christianity” (18) established through three contentious parallels: zoophagy and transubstanti- ation, chthonic versus celestial rituals; and sublimated theomachy through conﬂicting symbolic and iconographic displays. Prior to focusing on exogenous literary questions, Hennelly asserts that the engagement of a gnostic quest, indeed a complex of competing gnostic quests, sustains the novel. In “Betwixt Sunset and Sunrise” the notion of “gnostic quest” is pursued as Hennelly offers a study of liminality in Dracula, its impact on and expression through the threshold status of its neophytes as they gain in knowledge. The observation that a race for gnosis animates the novel opens an efﬁ- cient avenue of approach to the enigmatic novel’s core. Such a quest sends the Professor to Exeter to appear at the Harkers’ door, integrates the Harkers into the circle of the Purﬂeet Brotherhood, and ultimately justiﬁes the com- pilation of the text itself, the text embodying the fruit of a collective “gnostic quest.” This quest lends an essential dimension to the great chase from Charing Cross to Castle Dracula, taking over plot to such an extent that the Professor’s posse, obsessively focused on liminality, spends anxious days waiting around the Black Sea hypnotizing Mina and interrogating petty ofﬁcials when they might have less stressfully gone directly to the castle, sanitized the sacred earth of the Vampire’s ﬁnal resting place and patiently awaited the Count’s return. Like the dragon who displays the attributes of all animal classes—bird, serpent, ﬁsh, amphibian, carnivorous beast—yet conforms to none, the Vam- pire is a classiﬁcation-defeating entity. It apparently exists in a liminal zone in which taboo is dissolved, boundaries are eradicated, deﬁnition, hence order, is deﬁed and the sacred deﬁled, but Dracula’s little dragon may be more of a 156 The Theology of Dracula

red herring than anything else. What the Professor’s posse is most stridently concerned with sounding through the liminal-dwelling Vampire and all epis- temological means available, is the unknowable realm of the True-Dead, oth- erworld of the spirit; that is, they are interested in performing an epistemological post–mortem. Their extravagant pursuit—not even discov- ering what it’s like to be a bat—merely ends up tracking a package. The false gnosis of the apparent liminal and monstrous distracts from a True Gnostic quest and cathartic odyssey towards Sophia and the Son of Man. And it is this, this interior-penetrating Gnostic quest, that likely motivated Stoker to write the book in the ﬁrst place. In drafting his magnum opus, in wrestling with the theological considerations it contains, Stoker gained spir- itual insight. No longer dependent on a scheme borrowed from Teutonic and Neolithic mythologies, he was freed to abandon a Ragnarök-dictated ending for something ﬁnally quieter, simpler, truer, newer—spectacular volcanic eruptions becoming vulgar and superﬂuous. To expropriate Ernest Jones’s phraseology, the very fact that the Vampire is Un-Dead is decisive here, for this concept is necessarily linked to liminality. It is therefore to be expected that Stoker will meticulously mark the crossing of thresholds, limit the Count by the extremes of the tides and apparent solar movements, and, conversely, have Mina feel her autonomy buttressed by those same forces. Mme. Blatovsky’s Victorian age Theosophical dogma rested on “the absolute universality of that law of periodicity, of ﬂux and reﬂux, ebb and ﬂow, which physical science has observed and recorded in all departments of nature. An alternation such as that of Day and Night, Life and Death, Sleeping and Waking, is a fact so common, so perfectly universal and without exception, that it is easy to comprehend that in it we see one of the absolutely fundamental laws of the universe” (4). Trinitarian tensions between Sun, Moon, and Earth author these phe- nomena that are experienced as binary universals. Dracula’s assemblage of characters is speciﬁcally limited, or not, by the forces of sun and moon and notions of residence, attachments to Earth. Liminality, rather than a speciﬁc status-obscuring condition impacting particular persons, actions, gestures, situations, forms a central, enveloping theme that seeps into and saturates the ﬁction’s every aspect. Notably, it marks the plot’s temporal extremities and dramatic limits as particularly signiﬁcant—indeed so signiﬁcant as to require textual addenda as special markers—, for on the other side of the threshold of the novel’s plot lies the unexplored silence of Winter’s half-year of darkness and the ﬁnal chilling destination of every character. The novel, rather than testing, pushing, or challenging boundaries, as it seemingly does, works to reinforce and delineate boundaries and their ﬁnalities while amalgamating everything seen, from May to November, and unseen from, November to May, into a Kingdom Come 157

great circular ring that melds time and space. It accomplishes this not through repression but through dissolution, atomization. Even in planning the novel, Stoker portrayed the Count as falsely liminal: “Dracula visits asylum. Stumbles on threshold” (Rosenbach #16 Notes 55). Yet, in truth, if the Count is falsely liminal it is because, and only because, in the logic of myth he is also truly liminal. To dispose of the problem, under Stoker’s pen thresholds are conve- niently converted to “joinings” (227). Rather than engaging the simple gnostic quest of the detective story or spy novel genres, Stoker dispatches his protagonists into the ﬁeld “armed against ghostly as well as carnal attack” (258), “against evil things, spiritual as well as physical” (282), and sustains them through Hebraic scripture and Christian and Gnostic symbology. When Abraham proclaims, “And then begins our great quest” (193), he rallies a freshly matured generation to set out upon a veritable crusade. Providing Arthurian images of a search for the Holy Grail and True Cross, young Lord Godalming’s given name, Arthur Holmwood, expresses the quest’s religious nature. They set off chivalrously pledging themselves to Madam Mina. The Professor’s theory, Stoker’s, is that the Kingdom is within and acces- sible to those who actively strive to defeat evil. The novel’s end comes as a moment of confrontation, judgment, and victory, less an occasion of divine retribution than an instance of the triumph of human volition and the capacity of a community of dedicated souls to reject evil and do good. The vicinity of Castle Dracula, God’s seat, becomes the seat of judgment for Jonathan, Mina, the Professor, Quincey, Seward, the Count, Weird Sisters, and Art, Lord Godalming; the Professor deﬁnes Judgment Day as the occasion on which God “most suredly shall ... redress all wrongs of the earth and of His children that He has placed thereon” (259). The previously considered 15th–century cruciﬁxion scene of the alabaster altarpiece at Mont-Saint-Michel constitutes a judgment scene transposed. At the crest of a hill the royal judge, crown formed of thorns, having himself been subjected to trial and punishment, is, rather than seated on a throne, stretched out upon a cross. At a somewhat lower level, on the cross to the left of Jesus, a faithless thief is condemned to damnation; to his right another cruciﬁed thief, having been pardoned, has his soul led towards heaven by Saint Michael. Matthew writes: “Then the king will say to those on his right hand, ‘Come, blessed of my Father, take possession of the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world’” (25:31). Roman soldiers gathered to the right of the cross, to the left hand of Jesus, are separated from the faithful standing to the right. Soldiers, squatting on the ground, engrossed in a game of chance disputing the mantle of the dying man, will be forgiven by Jesus as ignorant and unknowing. The three Marys and the courageous faithful 158 The Theology of Dracula

are shown facing the cruciﬁed Christ on the side where the believing thief has died. The faithful are positioned on the right-hand side of Jesus, the soldiers and temporal authorities are with the blasphemous thief to his left. This is how the Judgment, like the Cruciﬁxion, is to be conducted, the moving-world stopped and arrayed in perfect symmetry. Indeed, the Cruciﬁxion accom- plishes this effect by revolutionizing the history of man. A ﬂow of successive liminal moments, felt on earth as the movement of the sun and moon, are produced by the sweep of a great cosmic pendulum ﬁxed by the terrestrial perceptive eye; sense and ﬁnalities, on the other hand, are determined by the pivot of justice’s scale, the balance of Themis. Scale and pendulum require a ﬁxed central point of equilibrium. Due to the novel’s title and a fascination with his glamor, the popular imagination places the Count at the novel’s center, resulting in meaning being consigned to the dark season and thus going unseen. If the novel’s title was intended to be indicative of a principal character, that singular, indexical, transformational entity ensconced at plot’s center, it should read Wilhelmina. She is Dracula’s true personiﬁcation of liminality, ready to shift as a bascule in one direction or another, and, with polestars in her eyes, is its stable and guiding center. When she identiﬁes the Count as “the Thing” (202, 322), an object rather than a subject, it is not without larger signiﬁcance. When she graciously maintains, “It was my privilege to be your friend and guide” (101), she could be addressing us all. Dracula’s plot largely concerns itself with gaining knowledge of the jour- ney of the dead, physically expressed in the shipment of a half-century of wooden cases, geometric sarcophagi, later reduced to a single cofﬁn. A man named Smollet supplies information on the progress of this odyssey and pro- vides an early key to tracking it. “He remembered all about the incident of the boxes, and from a wonderful dog’s-eared notebook, which he produced from some mysterious receptacle about the seat of his trousers, and which had hieroglyphical entries in thick half-obliterated pencil, he gave me the desti- nations” (229). This evocation of half-obliterated hieroglyphics that retrace the journey of the dead connects the quest to a 3000-year-old Egyptian image. “Spells for Setting Forth by Day,” recalled as The Egyptian Book of the Dead, was translated in large part from the scroll The Papyrus of Ani, purchased and housed at the British Library in 1888. Stoker owned a copy of the book. Accompanying its hieroglyphs, a vignette depicts Psychostasia, that is, the weighing of his heart or soul. The scroll of Hunefer, a section of which is reproduced below, contains remarkably similar images. Not unlike the Mont- Saint-Michel Retable in composition, the image shows the scale of divine jus- tice as the gods evaluate the life of Hunefer as his soul sets forth at harvest time. Above the weighing ﬂoor a panel of gods form a jury, half manifest the Kingdom Come 159

ankh or crux ansata, graphically echoing the cruciform of the scale; half do not. The scale, its centrality, symmetry and geometry are striking. To the right of the scale in the image, we see Toth with the head of an Ibis, stylus in hand, ready to assume his role as scribe, recording angel. Anubis ﬁxes the pointer of the scale while a monstrous beast with the head of a jackal, soul-eating Amemit the Devourer, awaits the verdict. Hunefer’s heart is posed on the left-side basket; on the right is placed the unit of divine justice: an ostrich feather belonging to the goddess Ma’at. The departed, Hunefer, is seen twice, or rather in two different states of being. On the left of the image, an ankh-bearing, jackal-headed divine leads him to his trial; to the right of the scale, Horus awaits to present Hunefer to Osiris who, in a further portion of the vignette not reproduced here, is seen on his throne, Isis standing behind him and a third avatar of Hunefer, his hair now whitened, kneeling before him. Returning to the persistent rumors tying Stoker to the Golden Dawn, Mina Mathers, wife of Samuel Liddel “MacGregor” Mathers, the order’s chief of the 1890s, echoed the phrase of the Tyrolean seer of Nodier’s roman, and maintained that the Hermetic Order based their rites “on the ancient mysteries, chieﬂy those of Egypt, Chaldea and Greece” (Gilbert 117). More generally, Victorian armchair anthropologists, mythographers, theosophists, and occultists consistently pursued the notion of a world-binding universal the- ology, a myth-led Neolithic belief system, ﬁnding unique expressions within 160 The Theology of Dracula The Weighing of the Heart, from Book of the Dead of Hunefer. ©The Trustees of the British Museum.

each tribal order, but bridging the globe through shared common macro- structures. We ﬁnd that notion expressed by Jacob Grimm, J. G. Frazer, Sabine Baring-Gould, and other writers with whom Stoker was familiar. As the keeper Thomas Bilder establishes equivalency between jackals, hyenas and wolves, (“I gives the wolves and the jackals and the hyenas in all our section their tea afore I begins to arsk them questions” [123]), Stoker, concentrating largely on Teutonic myths, Transylvanian superstitions, Roman Catholic liturgy and iconography, and Gnostic rites, is more apt to work with the lycanthropic than jackal-headed ﬁgures, but the image of the cross-as-scale and the com- position so similar to the Mont-Saint-Michel Retable seem to illustrate the structural basis of Stoker’s four-part novel and speak to his myth-inspired plot. Life, possessed of an inescapable symmetry and balance expressed through the tides and daily and seasonal solar cycles, provides Stoker with his grand metaphor and underlying structure. The general palindromic A-B-C— C-B-A scheme is easy to perceive: A mid–spring coach ride leads a neophyte (male) to Castle Dracula; the youth is soon initiated within; an infant and its mother are sacriﬁced. A ship sails west with the Vampire aboard; at its (white) destination one young woman is initiated (destroyed); a mother and her child are sacriﬁced. The Ofﬁce of the Dead is read for the previously ini- tiated girl; a vampire is destroyed (initiated). Another young woman is initiated Kingdom Come 161 The Papyrus of Hunefer cruciform scale. © Rarignac

(nearly destroyed); the Ofﬁce of the Dead is read for the second girl. A ship sails east with the Vampire aboard to its destination (black). A mid–autumn coach ride leads an initiate (female) to Castle Dracula; vampires are destroyed (initiated). The initiate is perfected. While beyond “that interesting place” (11) “to the dark side of twilight” (11) the “moving world” may offer the illusion of deﬁnitive states of being— darkling night, luminous day—life is mostly lived as a passing along a chain of liminal moments, times of uncertain status succeeding each other like beads on a rosary; we are seemingly poised at the verge of change without end until, at last, death intervenes. Celestial and earthly balance, symmetries wrought by compensatory shifting elements, percuss through men on planes “carnal” (190, 258) (the body which imprisons the soul) and spiritual (represented as consisting of soul, mind, mood, strength, and volition) until death rives the duality and the soul is freed. A moment near the autumnal equinox ﬁnds numerous grief-crippled protagonists experiencing a spiritual low tide, lacking robustness in their will to persevere. Jonathan is “so injured that the very essence of its strength is gone” (143); Seward, “too miserable, too low-spirited, too sick of the world and all that is in it, including life itself, that [he] would not care if [he] heard this moment the ﬂapping of the wings of the angel of death” (144); and Arthur asking himself, “What shall I do? The whole of life seems gone from me all at once, and there is nothing in the wide world for me to live for” (152). Feel- ings of hopelessness and fatalism pervade the season “to the dark side of” equinox, and “it all seems like a horrible tragedy, with fate pressing on relent- lessly to some destined end. Everything that one does seems, no matter how right it may be, to bring on the very thing which is most to be deplored” (226). Seward, reﬂecting on despair and the obligation to maintain faith in life regardless of the tribulations faced, dictates: “To me it seems only yesterday that my whole life ended with my new hope, and that truly I began a new record. So it will be until the Great Recorder sums me up and closes my ledger account with a balance to proﬁt or loss” (71). Faith dictates that man go for- ward with courage, “for none of us can tell what, or when, or how, the end may be” (285). In the complex universe of Dracula it is often an inversion, negation, or transformation rather than identical elements that are placed in the balance, heavy heart being tested against lightness’s very image, negative elements off- setting positive, light compensating dark: “We shall tonight play sane wits against mad ones” (102), as Seward, ﬁguring his accounts, puts it. Due to the inﬂuence of the master actor Morpheus, people, places and things are or aren’t what they seem, existing in a true state and a false one, making it difﬁcult, as Jonathan discovers, to maintain a reasonable sense of certitude. Meaning 162 The Theology of Dracula

is often dream-coded, clear statements being issued with the intent of signi- fying the reverse of their literal sense. Not only does Stoker transparently negate values—acknowledging, for instance, his debt to Wilkie Collins by having The Westminster Gazette quote a headline hawking “The Woman in Black” (159)—he portrays a world in which things become doubly reversed yet not quite restored to their original condition. Yet from prefatory statement to closing “Note,” from the sequence of actions to the intersecting personalities that accomplish them, a meticulous balance is in all ways maintained as Stoker piles element after element in the baskets of his cruciform scale. This promotes a deliberate homogenizing effect from the earliest pages. For instance, the cunning Count perniciously imper- sonates his prisoner by wearing Jonathan’s clothes to Bistritz, the center of human habitation closest to his dwelling place, where he is able to post letters, abduct babies, and, while he’s at it, to inculpate Jonathan. The second skin of clothing sufﬁciently approaches the living and the Un-Dead in appearance to cause an aggrieved mother to mistake one for the other just as Léoniti had mistaken Aubray for Ruthwen. Flushed-face, Apollonian Jonathan may indeed be more like the black- as-night habited Count than is immediately apparent. When Jonathan pen- etrates the Count’s inner-sanctum, he notes, “The only thing I found was a heap of gold in one corner—gold of all kinds, Roman, and British, and Aus- trian, and Hungarian, and Greek and Turkish money, covered with a ﬁlm of dust as though it had lain long in the ground” (50); when he slashes through the Count’s black clothing at Piccadilly, “a stream of gold fell out” (266). It is said these incidents make of the Count a money bag, but the gold, like the incongruous straw hat he wears on Doolittle Warf, reveals that the Count has within a hidden solar aspect. Light-bearer Lucifer, a luminous spirit visible only at dawn and dusk, fallen in Enochian shame, contributes much to con- structing the Count, for “he is the devil in callous” (209). For imprisoned Jonathan, awash in darkness, the sun is an agent of God, indeed the Paraclete: “When the sun grew so high this morning that it struck the top of the great gateway opposite my window, the high spot which it touched seemed to me as if the dove from the ark had lighted there” (49). Stoker introduces this worshipper of light as he approaches his hotel, the Golden Krone—indexing a gold coin—where he is soon to be drinking “Golden Mediasch” and curi- ously dining on a dish taking its name from the fact that it isn’t what it seems: “Robber Steak” (13). Occasionally, Stoker attains equilibrium through displacement, as can be seen through the device of Renﬁeld’s kitten. Renﬁeld requested from Seward “a kitten, a nice little, sleek, playful kitten, that I can play with, and teach, and feed—and feed—and feed!” (70), which was denied him. Renﬁeld not Kingdom Come 163

only wants to feed it three times, he thrice repeats his always denied request. Later, when Renﬁeld escapes from the asylum to attack the carters hauling away the Count’s great cases from neighboring Carfax, the asylum’s personnel belatedly arrive to subdue the lunatic and stop his assault of the movers. The doctor in charge reports that Renﬁeld “struggled with the three of us, pulling us to and fro as if we were kittens” (142). Still, Renﬁeld’s prime task is to serve as the Count’s herald and messenger, thus the image of the kitten reappears in a description of Mina’s initiatory ordeal, which bore “a terrible resemblance to a child forcing a kitten’s nose into a saucer of milk to compel it to drink” (247). An example of contrasted equivalence resides in certain letters that com- prise the text itself: Jonathan’s ersatz letters sent by the Count to Mina are compensated by Mina’s heartfelt-but-never-received missives to Lucy, even- tually studied in post–mortem by the Professor. The Professor, of whom it is noted that Seward, Arthur, and Lucy “must accept his wishes,” and the Count, who asserts that “it was understood that my needs only were to be consulted” (37), are sufﬁciently alike to balance the narrative vessel and more. The Pro- fessor readily acknowledges their common traits: “Our old fox is wily; oh! so wily and we must follow with wile. I too am wily and I think his mind in a little while” (273). The Professor’s coming has him leave the Netherlands “to do what [he] can of good,” whereas the Count’s going signiﬁes that “the earth is free from a monster of the netherworld” (224). As earlier mentioned, Abra- ham is ﬁgured as progenitor of a new sacred order of men, yet the Professor sees the Count as potentially “the father or furtherer of a new order of beings, whose road must lead through Death, not Life” (263). While the Count, with his wolves, mountain, and leiter-wagon or leit- erwaggen, is ﬁgured in a Teutonic mode as Woden or Odin, the grandfatherly Professor, shown as a driver of wagons, wielder of a great hammer, is, in that idiom, Thor-like. The “leiter-wagon—the ordinary peasant’s cart, with its long, snake-like vertebra, calculated to suit the inequalities of the road” (15)— is described as one more curiosity in Jonathan’s travelogue, but the association of the Count with these and similar carts will be incessant; the Count, as noted, even does business with a man named Carter. That the English involved in hunting the Count down ubiquitously speak of “leiter-wagons” rather than the more familiar “cart” or “hay cart” is certainly not by accident, for the “leiter-wagon” is associated with Odin. It will be through his continual use of wagons that the Count’s movements are monitored. It further explains why he appears on Doolittle’s Warf in a cart and wearing a straw hat. Something like solar-lunar interplay is offered in feminine guise through the persons of Lucy and Mina, but their sympathetic relationship, as they admire and assist each other, reverses the enmity existing between Jonathan and the Count. Luminous Lucy virtuously claims, “I must imitate Mina” 164 The Theology of Dracula

(103), a compliment the Professor carries forth, telling Mina that Lucy wrote “in imitation of [her]” (164), and Mina unambiguously and affectionately sums up her relationship with Lucy with the declaration, “She and I were like sisters” (209). Beyond giving their hearts and blood to the same woman, Lucy’s beaux, hunting partners Quincey and Art, are so closely associated with each other that they appear in each other’s place, one speaking for the other. The major difference between them seems to be that in their pursuits of game Art takes charge of animals and Quincey of armaments and strategic planning. That they separate from each other for their ﬁnal hunt—one going by water, the other by land—seems strange, incongruous, but their separation is required to maintain balance. While all the male protagonists are hailed as noble, aris- tocratic Lord Godalming and Count Dracula share the distinction of being exceptionally landed, men of property, of the earth, even if the Transylvanian boyar be more literally so. The Count, described as “more prisoner than the slave of the galley, than the madman in his cell” (211), is further linked to both Jonathan and Renﬁeld. These latter two, beyond their quite evident shared experience of being held against their will, manifest other countervailing traits: Jonathan has “had brain fever, and that is to be mad” (99–100), while the ﬂeeting, intermittent insanity of Renﬁeld renders him a true “lunatic”; both are repeatedly depicted scribbling indecipherable records into their notebooks. They also contrast. As happened in the accident with a mirror and razor while Jonathan was shav- ing, a letting of blood occurs when Renﬁeld invades Seward’s ofﬁce and rushes at him with a dinner knife, cutting him. Whereas the Count was forced to control his appetites by the power of the rosary, Renﬁeld threw himself down onto the ﬂoor to lap up the spilt blood, chanting, “The blood is the life!” (130). In the end, however, Renﬁeld, Lazarus-like, joins Jonathan in opposing the Count; a concern for the soul has him cast his unhappy lot with the Broth- erhood, no doubt bringing salvation upon himself. The association of zoophagous Renﬁeld with the vampiric Count is estab- lished more pointedly and with greater effort at making the linkage evident: Referring to the Professor, Seward notes: “He thinks that in the meantime I should see Renﬁeld, as hitherto he has been a sort of index to the coming and going of the Count” (199). Seward expresses similar sentiments in rationalizing his own mistrust of Renﬁeld’s sanity: “He seems so mixed up with the Count in an indexy kind of way” (219). Seward, having heard Renﬁeld seek reassur- ance from the Count—“You will not pass me by, will You, dear Master, in Your distribution of things?”—perceives mercantile greed in Renﬁeld, com- menting: “He thinks of the loaves and ﬁshes even when he believes he is in a Real Presence” (98). Seward, as is often the case, may have misread the Kingdom Come 165

situation. Renﬁeld’s plea sounds more likely a transformation of the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13). In linking his inmate of the asylum to the inmate of the grave, Stoker goes so far as to have Renﬁeld complete a half-rendered portrait of the Count. At Castle Dracula, Jonathan “saw ... the Count’s head coming out from the window” (39), specifying, “I did not see the face, but I knew the man by the neck and the movement of his back and arms.” At the asylum, Renﬁeld’s guard “ran back and saw [Renﬁeld’s] feet disappear through the window” (97), Renﬁeld, like the Count, evidently going head-ﬁrst out the window. Stoker thus provides interior and exterior perspectives of a single, birth-like action, of blood-obsessed men escaping their asylums to assault the world. Jonathan confesses that his “very feelings changed to repulsion and terror when I saw the whole man slowly emerge from the window and begin to crawl down the castle wall over that dreadful abyss, face down, with his cloak spreading out around him like great wings” (39).
