Renﬁeld, too, is repeatedly represented as winged; the Notes ﬁrst envisage him as a ﬂy man who has been tied down (“ﬂy patient—bound down” [Notes 29]). Having encountered all kinds of half-human beings, including a gypsy “like a Centaur” (323), and been introduced to the law ﬁrm of “Wholeman, Sons” (150), Drs. Seward and Helsing forthrightly merge into a unitary form, the Professor urging, “Let us not be two, but one, that so we work to a good end” (150). Seward, losing autonomous critical abilities, asks: “Are you mad that speak such things, or am I mad that listen to them?” (184) Soon others join them: “Simultaneously we each took one of the old man’s hands and bent over and kissed it. Then without a word we all knelt down together, and, all holding hands, swore to be true to each other” (259). All these seemingly conﬂicting personalities, from the Count to the Harkers, are energetically amalgamated, independently of their having transfused Lucy or not, to form a singular personality incorporating conﬂicting tendencies, good and evil. Not only identity, but ideas ﬂow like water, with eddies, whirlpools and counter–currents mixing and redistributing fungible contents, streams of sym- bolic transaction meandering in serpentine fashion. The testimonies of the captain of The Demeter (Petrovsky missing, Abramoff disappeared, etc.) and Captain Donelson of The Czarina Catherine serve to balance the text, both in their relative positions across the temporal span of plot, and in the novel’s typical virtuous-vicious, positive-negative, asymmetrically-symmetric manner: All hands died on The Demeter, none on The Czarina Catherine. It is curious, moreover, to ﬁnd a man named Donelson setting off from Doolittle Warf as skipper of the Russian Czarina Catherine, since Donelson is the name of the American diplomat, nephew of Andrew Jackson, responsible for negotiating the treaty of annexation of Texas that 166 The Theology of Dracula

Renﬁeld admiringly referenced upon his introduction to Quincey. Mythical torch-bearing “Demeter” brings light to the world through her role in the Eleusinian Mysteries; Catherine the Great, native Pomeranian who was chris- tened Sophie by her Lutheran parents, became known as the Enlightener or Illuminator, and brought Russian dominance and the spark of the Orthodox faith to the Black Sea region through her victories over the Ottoman Turks. Sophie, ﬂowing from the Greek for “Wisdom,” became Catherine (also from Greek and, as with catharsis and Cathar, signifying “Pure”) upon her conversion to the Orthodox faith. Voltaire celebrated the empress as “the Star of the North,” the immutable, thereby aligning her with Mina and contrasting her with the Count as Lucifer and the morning star—visible only at dawn and dusk. “The Czarina Catherine” is ﬁttingly named for a vessel intended to transport a gnostic quest towards its ultimate ends: Wisdom and Purity. In Whitby, the Count’s agent is Billington of the Crescent; in Romania, a man of the Count’s hated “Crescent” (34), in that he appears in a fez. Billington was an important source of information on the Count’s movements, since through his billing for the work of Carter and brethren the Count’s penetration of England could be traced. Captain Donelson divulges that Count Dracula’s agent goes by the name of Immanuel Hildesheim (302), and he had already taken possession of the square box shipped to the Romanian hinterlands by London’s urbane Count de Ville. The portrayal of this “Hebrew of rather the Adelphi Theatre type” (302) is often cited as an expression of Victorian, and Stoker’s own, anti-Semitism. Matthew the Evangelist tells us that Immanuel signiﬁes “God is with us” (1:23). It twice appears in the Prophecies of Isaiah, ﬁrst when he foresees the birth to a virgin of a son, to be called Emmanuel, who knows to refuse evil and choose good (7:14), and then when Isaiah envisions Emmanuel spreading his wings across the earth (8:8). Matthew recalls Isaiah to equate Emmanuel and the Messiah, and in his depiction of an angel instructing Joseph to protect the Virgin Mary, with child by the Holy Spirit, and to name the infant to be born “Jesus.” Stoker employs the image of wings, angelic or maleﬁc, spreading over the world of men on several occasions. Seward imagines “for many a long day loneliness will sit over our roofs with brooding wings” (159), declaring, “I would not care if I heard this moment the ﬂapping of the wings of the angel of death” (144), and the Professor launches an idea as “a big swan thought that sail nobly on big wings” (295). Hildesheim is a place name denoting a town in Lower Saxony—a town Stoker no doubt passed through on his way to Bayreuth—where the Tree of Life (Irminsul, variant of Yggdrasil ) was commemorated through a stone pillar. Perhaps toppled and buried at the time of Christian conversion, this stele was Kingdom Come 167

excavated in the 13th century during the construction of Hildesheim’s Gothic Ste. Anne’s Chapel, part of the cathedral Dom Santa Maria complex, where it was installed as a pillar that also served as a central candelabra—hence a pillar of ﬁre. Though incorporated into the church, the pillar represented a defeated pagan element, the Irminsul, whose destruction by Charlemagne is commemorated on Laetarean Sunday. Immanuel Hildesheim’s ofﬁce is situated on the Burgen-strasse, a Ger- manic appellation suggesting “The Castles’ Road.” Hildesheim consigned the box directly to riverboat shipper Petrof Skinsky, who, having disposed of his charge, is soon discovered “inside the wall of St Peter’s churchyard” (303), his throat torn open as if by some wild animal. This event of the day on which The Czarina Catherine arrives at its Black Sea port provides, on one hand, counterpoint to the ancient mariner Oracle Swales’ death at Ste. Mary’s churchyard and the killing of the mastiff so savagely ripped apart on the night that The Demeter washed up at Whitby; but, on the other hand, it serves to counterbalance in a curious way the account of Petrovsky of The Demeter’s crew. Petrovsky, which can be reduced to Petr, or Peter-of-Sky, mirrors Petrof Skinsky, which in turn yields Petr, or Peter-of-Skin-Sky, celestial Peter—par- ticularly signiﬁcant when it is considered that the latter’s body is described as found in St. Peter’s churchyard, perhaps intending to evoke the Holy See and the rationale for the claim of Catholicism. Stoker worked so hard to place his Petrovsky and his Petrof Skinsky in positions of equilibrium in his text, one wonders if and how Peter indeed holds the keys to the Kingdom. The quest is often rendered concrete and made tangible, as in the search for a key whose legion referents summarize plot: “I looked for the key, but it was not in the lock, and I could not ﬁnd it anywhere” (50); “You didn’t have any key?” (232); “When the Professor locked the door he gave the key to Arthur” (193); “friend John, where are the skeleton keys?” (220); “She tries the door, and ﬁnding it locked, goes about the room searching for the key” (73); “On a table in the hall was a great bunch of keys, with a time-yellowed label on each” (220); “With a little trouble we found the key on the bunch and opened the door” (221); “Dr Van Helsing had taken the key of the hall door from the bunch, and locked the door in orthodox fashion, putting the key into his pocket when he had done” (223); “We now have a rare job on hand—unless we can ﬁnd the Count’s key basket” (235); “But think, in all probability the key of the situation is in that house in Piccadilly” (255); “Now we wish to get into the house, but we have no key; is it not so?” (256); “Then he held the door partly open, steadying it with his knees, whilst he ﬁtted a key to the lock. This he ﬁnally handed to Lord Godalming” (261); “He held up a warning hand as he spoke, for we all could hear a key softly inserted in the lock of the hall door” (266). 168 The Theology of Dracula

In initiating the quest for the key, Jonathan reveals much: “I thought he might have the keys on him, but when I went to search I saw the dead eyes, and in them, dead though they were, such a look of hate ... that I ﬂed” (51). “Then a wild desire took me to obtain that key at any risk, and I determined then and there to scale the wall again” (53). “I knew I must search the body for the key.... I searched all over the body, but no sign could I ﬁnd of the key” (53). The corpse searched is itself the key, it contains the remains of the Count’s body but no key, for the soul is no longer to be found within. The importance of this descent into the underworld is repeatedly stressed, Helsing proclaiming Jonathan “a noble fellow; and let me tell you from expe- rience of men, that one who would do as he did in going down that wall and to that room—ay, and going a second time—is not one to be injured in per- manence by a shock” (167). Seward agrees: “That going down to the vault a second time was a remarkable piece of daring” (199). The key present through its absence contains Stoker’s apophatic premise: “A key is nothing” (177). As we have heard through the Professor’s description of the Count as one less free than a prisoner, the key is indicative of the ﬁrst frankly Gnostic turn in Stoker’s theology: The body constitutes the soul’s prison. Whether or not the true key is ever found, the searched-for key is often associated with gold and material wealth, always with dust. Even more than gold, dust deﬁnes the Count’s constitution and natural environment: “He come on moonlight rays as elemental dust—as again Jonathan saw those sisters in the castle” (211); “the very moonlight alive with grisly shapes, and every speck of dust that whirls in the wind a devouring monster in embryo” (307). But the Count’s activities never disturb its accumulation as it, in turn, never registers his activities: “The whole place was thick with dust. The ﬂoor was seemingly inches deep, except where there were recent footsteps, in which on holding down my lamp I could see marks of hobnails where the dust was caked. The walls were ﬂuffy and heavy with dust” (220). More comically, it is observed: “There was dust that thick in the place that you might have slep’ on it without ‘urtin’ of yer bones” (201). Dust is merely the sign of the material, realm and essence of the Vampire—“Hardly had my knife severed the head of each, before the whole body began to melt away and crumble into its native dust” (321)—only the soul endures. It is not merely people, ideas, actions, and symbols that, full of contrasts and poetry, are made to speak in Stoker’s text, but, as was seen with the topo- graphically opposed Carpathians and the Thames tidal ﬂats, and the “chess game” (223) polarity of Whitby and the Black Sea, the landscape and the ele- ments are equally eloquent of matters that are immaterial but oh so pertinent. One senses, for instance, that Whitby’s “black mass of Kettleness” (75), presented with the evocation of a Turner painting or a Whistler nocturne, Kingdom Come 169

seeks to evoke Ceridwen’s mythic cauldron of pagan traditions. The Daily- graph clipping that describes the storm presaging The Demeter’s shipwreck reports that “some of the gossips who frequent the East Cliff churchyard, and from that commanding eminence watch the wide sweep of sea visible to the north and east, called attention to a sudden show of “‘Mares’-tails’ high in the sky” (75). Stoker, seizing on a curious ﬁgure of speech, no doubt confected this detail in full knowledge that the goddess Demeter, personiﬁed as a mare, led initiates in the annual procession to Eleusis; he had already told us that the East Cliff churchyard’s commanding eminence is Oracle Swales, the Ancient Mariner. The article’s reporting that as The Demeter approached shore “the silence was so marked that the bleating of a sheep inland or the barking of a dog in the town was distinctly heard” (76) seems intended to foretell their sacriﬁce; the dog personiﬁed in the mastiff, the lamb in Lucy. Sheep constitute a returning image, from Hildeshein’s nose to, ironically, the assembled hunters of the lupine Count, whom Stoker characterizes “like sheep in a butcher’s.” Matthew proclaims that “when the Son of Man shall come in his majesty, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on the throne of his glory; and before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will sep- arate them one from another, as the shepherd separates the sheep from the goats; and he will set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left” (25:31–33) and these will go into everlasting punishment. Most often the Word is at the origin of Stoker’s creation. He seizes on curious names for things, latches onto them for their latent, often overdeter- mined meanings, and uses them to enrich symbolic discourse, each word weighed and weighted, phonetic spellings, Scottish, Geordie, Dutch, Cockney accents, and assorted malapropisms designed to simultaneously encode and obscure meaningful information. Parabolic discourse is rampant. The Pall Mall Gazette’s report on an escaped wolf is far less concerned with communicating information than with providing readers with keys to reading. The parable of discoursing with beasts relates how animal appetites must be satisﬁed, nature gratiﬁed—metaphori- cally scratched behind the ear—before more abstract and spiritual activities can be undertaken. Thomas Bilder, an inmate of the zoo who lives with his wife in an enclosure behind the elephant house, in claiming to serve tea to wolves, jackals, and hyenas before questioning them, joins together as a uniﬁed genus beasts of the Egyptian deserts and the Nordic forests. Referred to as “the worthy Thomas” (128), he and his wife, like Mina, unable to “resist the temptation of mystifying him a bit” (164), enjoy pulling the leg of the inter- viewer. Thomas believes that the wolf will become hungry, try to steal meat from a butcher’s shop, though he “shouldn’t be surprised if the census is one baby the less” (128). To conclude the interview, the Norwegian wolf, Berserker, 170 The Theology of Dracula

returns to be received “like a sort of vulpine prodigal son” (129), being fed “a piece of meat that satisﬁed, in quantity at any rate, the elementary conditions of the fatted calf ” (129). The Pauline Epistle to the Hebrews 3:3, asserting Jesus’s superiority to Moses, claims “the worthy builder,” rather than “the worthy Thomas,” is more honored than the house he builds. But Thomas the Apostle, the Gnostic evan- gelist known as the Twin, is recalled as a master builder and preacher, bringing the gospel to Syria, Persia, and the Indian subcontinent. Engaged by an Indian maharaja to build a palace, Thomas is said to have distributed the raj’s money to the poor, explaining to the king that he was constructing a heavenly abode. It is Thomas who determined to accompany Jesus to raise Lazarus, even should it cost his own life. This incident, during which Jesus remarks, “Are there not twelve hours in the day? If a man walks in the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world. But if he walks in the night, he stum- bles, because the light is not in him” (John 11:9–10), ﬁgures predominantly in Maquet and Dumas’ Le Vampire. Thomas, who doubted Christ’s resurrec- tion, was nonetheless, alone among the apostles, chosen to witness the Virgin Mary’s Assumption. The large “man in an ofﬁce of wood so small that the man looked bigger than the ofﬁce” (275) on Doolittle’s Warf, whose treasure is kept in a tiny bag hidden in an obscure part of his person, seems to be inserted as a comment (perhaps on the overlords of theatrical box ofﬁces) on similarities between the situations of the living and the dead. Renﬁeld, in alluding to the author of the Monroe Doctrine, references the noted anti–Masonic politician John Quincy Adams, who was the son and eventual successor of President Monroe’s secretary of state and the doctrine’s author; in transforming “Quincy” to “Quincey,” Stoker enlarges his ﬁeld of referents to include Thomas de Quincey, author of a text invoking the signiﬁcance of the Ruthven family name, the debunking “Inquiry on the Origins of The Masons and Rosicruicians.” Stoker is likely cautioning the reader to not be too taken in by allusions to rosy crosses or by plot similarities to the Fama Fraternitas, for he is perhaps offering a new doctrinal statement for a New World in which hemispheric concerns, separating day and night, are dissolved. Smollett, contract shipper and hauler at times known as Jack and at others as Joseph, is hailed as “a decent, intelligent fellow, distinctly a good, reliable type of workman, and with a headpiece of his own. He remembered all about the incident of the boxes ... from a wonderful dog’s-eared notebook” (229). As with the reference to “the Woman in Black” offered in tribute to Wilkie Collins, Smollet seems destined to recall Tobias Smollet and his Count Fathom of 1753, a novel recounting the adventures of a young Hungarian rascal who invades England as Count Fathom on a wild mission of unholy Kingdom Come 171

adventure, has empty cases shipped to his dwelling to deceive neighbors into thinking him a man of property, and whose story ends in the mystical initi- ation of a quasi-divine couple of near orphans, the forgiveness of the serpent, and universal felicity. Stoker’s Smollet, through his accented phonetic spelling, also serves to teach scribe Jonathan to read in a new, less traditional manner in his search for “the depite” (230). Stoker in his gnostic quest could, along with Jonathan, say that his Church of England heart was comforted by surprisingly powerful Catholic iconography, liturgy, and theology. Yet the Pauline view of the role of woman in the Roman church, too, seems difﬁcult to reconcile with Stoker’s. The numerous, deliberate sexist touches Stoker’s male characters promulgate are intended to argue for woman’s equality, even if, it is true, an equality limited to the context of the sacred syzygy. Thus, Jonathan’s initiation, undergone as “a ‘nine days’ wonder” (80), calculated from the moment he accepted the Count’s invitation to enter his castle proprio motu, was identical to Mina’s from the time she accepted the Professor’s request to admit him as a visitor. The links and parallels between the Professor and the Count become perfectly articulated therein, and their metonymical roles as drivers on the road to the castle, Telesterion, the Count with Jonathan, the Professor with Mina, crys- tallize their unitary role: The function that one performs in the initiation of one member of the syzygy, the other assumes with that member’s mate. Only the signiﬁcance of the “castle” changes. Menfolk may indulge well-intentioned sexism, but it always serves merely to compound their problems, as Mina, sequestered, reminds them by recalling: “There was in the room the same thin white mist that I had before noticed. But I forget now if you know of this; you will ﬁnd it in my diary which I shall show you later” (251). Stoker’s discourse on phrenology and brains—reptilian, mammalian, child-like, man-like, woman-like, the Professor’s status as an expert on brain evolution and Seward’s role as director of an asylum for the mentally disturbed stimulate, it is true, certain epistemologically-rooted questions. It is worth noting, however, that in Mina’s case, her “man’s brain” (295) is both highly feminine, memorizing schedules, and maternal. “I have an idea,” she announces. “I suppose it must have come in the night, and matured without my knowing it.... Go quick, dearest; the time is getting close” (271). In urging Jonathan to react with haste and to go get the doctor, she makes it seem as if her idea were a baby come to term. The reader reaching that phrase undoubtedly recalls that the last thing to come upon Mina in the night was the Count performing the bridal chamber anti-sacrament. Appropriately, her idea is to exploit the link then established between the Count and herself through the use of hypnosis. Should, as the Professor contends, the Count have intended to perpetuate 172 The Theology of Dracula

a thriving vampire colony in London, he was demonstrably a slacker. Although Dracula fuels its progress through the shedding of cadavers, curiously few are attributable to vampirism, even in Transylvania. To render a Renﬁeld-like accounting: Jonathan’s diary informs us directly or indirectly of two outside- of-plot infant deaths; it also reports on witnessing a mother being fed to wolves, upon the Count’s command, rather than being reserved to provide nourishment for vampires; it further meditates on the journal author’s dire plight, though he nonetheless survives and thrives. Despite numerous allusions to Coleridge’s “Rime of the Ancient Mariner,” for all we know, mysterious circumstances and hysteria drive the eight-member crew of the schooner Demeter to throw themselves overboard, leaving her captain, lashed to the wheel, alone to die of unknown causes. Ancient Mariner Oracle Swales is dis- covered dead, his neck broken, on the stone bench, though it seemed to Mina that he died from having seen Death’s approach. His death is not considered suspicious. About the time of Swales’ demise, a large, half-breed mastiff was killed at Whitby, its throat ripped apart and belly torn open. Lucy is soon thereafter attacked and bled over an extended period of time, eventually dying of blood loss suffered in satisfying the Count’s appetite. Mrs. Westenra, Lord Godalming, and Peter Hawkins die without being attacked, though Mrs. Westenra’s death was hastened by fright upon seeing the Count’s lupine emis- sary. Numerous ﬂies, spiders, and birds were ingested by Renﬁeld, who sac- riﬁces himself to oppose the Count’s will. A maritime shipper in Bukovina had his throat ripped apart, as if by a wild animal, and Quincey died of a knife wound near Castle Dracula. On the other side of the ledger, Lucy, three “Weird Sisters,” and the Count are executed or true-killed by various members of the Brotherhood. The books are thus quite balanced. The Count seems clearly homicidal, but the most curious conclusion we can reach is that Stoker wished to represent him, through his victims, as effete and sterile: He is only dangerous to poten- tial brides and to seamen, that is, Swales, the men of The Demeter and, perhaps, The Czarina Catherine, and the Bukovinian shipper. Taking Mosaic Seward, seen as Seaward, as an inverted paradigm, the seamen left mysteriously dead due to coincidental contact with the count intend to speak of “semen.” Dracula is not about an exchange of bodily ﬂuids, but the depravation of ethereal “soul.” The novel’s conceit depends upon materializing the immaterial, and stig- mata, signs of suffering, allow for recognition, reversal, and catharsis, partic- ularly as it concerns the removal of Mina’s Eucharistic scar on one hand, and the disappearance of Lucy’s twin stigmata preceding her death on the other. The Phaedrus uncannily helps connect the image of the winged soul being drawn from the larynx of the dying thieves and the scars observed on the Kingdom Come 173

throats of the Vampire’s victims. Plato claims that when the soul is connected with the divine it sprouts wings. “But when she is parted from her beloved and her moisture fails, then the oriﬁces of the passage out of which the wing shoots dry up and close, and intercept the germ of the wing; which, being shut up with the emotion, throbbing as with the pulsations of an artery, pricks the aperture which is nearest, until at length the entire soul is pierced and maddened and pained.” If, for those who become infected by the Vampire, “there comes with the change the curse of immortality; they cannot die, but must go on age after age adding new victims and multiplying the evils of the world; for all that die from the preying of the Un-Dead become themselves Un-Dead” (190). As previously observed, the Count’s London gambit was a signal failure. Although Jonathan, upon his happenstance London crossing of the Count’s path, wondrously exclaims the Count “has got younger, and how?” (168), the Vampire had, at that point, only been rejuvenated through his relations with Lucy. Where, too, was the Walachian voivode’s tributary population of Tran- sylvanian vampires; where were the teeming masses of incestuous Un-Dead? The polygamous Count, depicted dutifully stealing babies with a well-used sack, apparently unable to rely on the “Weird Sisters” to help with housework during Jonathan’s stay, was hardly promiscuous. The occasion of Jonathan’s initiation concludes with an acrimonious exchange between the Un-Dead on the subject of love—past and present, though lacking a sense of futurity— the Count claiming his companions knew from prior experience that he indeed could love and had knowledge of love: “you yourselves can tell it from the past. Is it not so?” (43). It seems that these feminine ﬁgures had at one time been courted by the Count. Despite eroticization, these womanish beings are sterile lamiae, Lilith-like thieves of the lifeblood of infants. The Count’s wives, rather than enjoying a productive life within a sacred union, are condemned to purloining the fruits of the wombs of others to indulge their murderous appetites. When a true mother, spying Jonathan at his window, believes she rec- ognizes the kidnapper of her child, she throws herself “on her knees, and raising up her hands,” cries out from her prayerful position: “Monster, give me my child” (48). In response, “high overhead, probably on the tower, ... the voice of the Count ... in his harsh metallic whisper” (48) calls out to his tributary wolves, which pour in upon the distressed mother “like a pent-up dam when liberated” (49). The grieving woman meets her death in stony silence. To preserve compositional equilibrium and pave the way to Mina’s initiation, Stoker sacriﬁces a mother and child in England: Mrs. Westenra and Lucy, mother once again dying because the Count has summoned his wolf. “For a second or two she sat up, pointing at the wolf, and there was a 174 The Theology of Dracula

strange and horrible gurgling in her throat; then she fell over, as if struck with lightning, and her head hit my forehead and made me dizzy for a moment or two” (131). The mother disposed of, child unconscious, the Count drained Lucy of her illuminating soul. “The funeral was arranged for the next succeeding day, so that Lucy and her mother might be buried together” (147). The daughter was mourned not as a young woman about to be married but as “that poor lily girl” (163), “that poor dear child Lucy Westenra. ‘God! God! God!’ he said. ‘What have we done, what has this poor thing done, that we are so sore beset? Is there fate amongst us still, sent down from the pagan world of old, that such things must be, and in such way? This poor mother, all unknowing, and all for the best as she think, does such thing as lose her daughter body and soul.... Oh how we are beset!’” (124), is the Professor’s despairing cry of confusion. In England the Count attempts to form sacrilegious syzygies with women from a speciﬁc milieu; as Ruthven had only been interested by Aubrey’s sister, the Count is exclusively interested in possessing a pair of women connected to Jonathan, inserting himself into Jonathan’s place, donning his clothes so to speak. In proclaiming “the man belongs to me,” the Count lays claim to his wife and her bosom companion as well. All phenomenological evidence presented through the text indicates that the Un-Dead otherwise only crave the blood of the innocent. A regular parade of suckling babes is represented along with the sufferance and incidental sacriﬁce of grieving mothers. The Count hunts for infants to provide for the Weird Sisters, but abandons consort Lucy to fend for herself. In her short career the false Lucy snared numerous tots, piercing their ﬂesh with her transformed dentition; the children described are pre-verbal infants clinging at her breast. Seward recalled the graveyard scene in a record- ing on a wax cylinder, as the Professor “pointed, and far down the avenue of yews we saw a white ﬁgure advance—a dim white ﬁgure, which held some- thing dark at its breast” (187). “With a careless motion, she ﬂung to the ground, callous as a devil, the child that up to now she had clutched strenu- ously to her breast, growling over it as a dog growls over a bone” (188). The Westminster Gazette of 25 September reports on a series of child abductions, observing, that when recovered, examination reveals “the children ... have been slightly torn or wounded in the throat” (160). “In all these cases the chil- dren were too young to give any properly intelligible account of themselves, but the consensus of their excuses is that they had been with a ‘bloofer lady’” (159), belle dame sans merci. One child explained that the “‘bloofer lady’ had asked him to come for a walk, the others had picked up the phrase and used it as occasion served” (160). The latter part of the 19th and beginning of the Kingdom Come 175

20th centuries record several occurrences of children claiming to have seen a beautiful lady who appears with various instructions. The Virgin Mary was reported to have appeared at LaSalette (1846), at Lourdes (1858), at Knock (1879) and at Fatima as Our Lady of the Rosary (1917), and millions of people, including members of the press, believed in and communally witnessed certain of these apparitions. A perversion of the Holy Mother, stealing infants on the public ways, Lucy is debased through her unholy alliance with the Count. Lucy as false mother, throwing the infant down on the ground, contrasts to the true mother at Castle Dracula’s courtyard, selﬂessly sacriﬁcing her own life in the name of her child. The status of true and false mothers in Dracula seems attributable to marriage rites. Even in a text where all things and people ﬂow into one another, the most important acts of union were those contrasting events occur- ring in the Convent of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary, and in the Harker’s bedroom of the Purﬂeet asylum, where, it seems, Stoker’s portrayal of the Count’s sac- rilegious rite is an attempt at presenting a “black” reversal of the Valentinian sacrament of the bridal chamber. Unknown for over a millennium, this Gnostic rite has for recent gener- ations been an object of inquiry and speculation; doubtless little more about this rite is known today than at Stoker’s time, a half-century before the Nag Hammadi’s unearthing. Likely intended to help a sacred couple achieve mys- tical union—that is, spiritual and physical union as a single body and soul, and dissolution into the godhead—its logic was trinitarian. The presence of two individuals is brought into relation with a Third, ordinarily imperceptible being, made palpable due through ritual investment and preparation. The principle is comparable to the bipolar ebb and ﬂow of the oceans and periods of day and night that are due to the interaction of three heavenly bodies, yet whose triangular commerce is only made evident to mankind during lunar or solar eclipses. If the third presence in the bridal chamber should be the Holy Spirit, the probable intent is nonetheless the hierogamous generation of a Christ-like progeny. In the case of the Count’s moonlit violation of volition, with the groom in a stupor and the bride bound by the wrists, the third pres- ence, literally diabolic, was ungodly and dry of seed; the intent is to doom the spouses to stealing new life in order to stiﬂe it. Across the parable of the Vampire that is Dracula, the central role of binary phenomena, earlier attrib- uted to trinitarian tensions between Sun, Moon and Earth, in generating the story is an abstraction of the relationship existing between solar Jonathan, lunar Mina, and the chthonic Count. The Count is understandably interpreted as antichristic, the Cross of Jesus being posited as his countervailing force. Accordingly, the Count’s death should mark the novel’s ﬁnality. The entire last segment of the novel reinforces 176 The Theology of Dracula

that proposition, melodramatic suspense prolonging the hunt from Piccadilly to Transylvania. At last, in the shadow of Castle Dracula, the end seems near at hand. “Look! Look! Look! See, two horsemen follow fast, coming up from the south. It must be Quincey and John” (322). “At the same time I knew that Jonathan was not far off; looking around I saw on the north side of the coming party two other men, riding at break-neck speed. One of them I knew was Jonathan” (322). In their pincer movement, the horsemen trace the transversal arms of the cross whose principal axis runs along the West-East direction that their journey towards the Orient had drawn beneath the heavens. The travelers, pilgrims of a sort, have constructed in the moving world an open cathedral beneath the vaulting heavens. Like with a Celtic cross, at its center a double ring has been traced: a “Holy circle” (326), demarcated by the Professor, and a defensive “ring of Szgany” (323) surrounding the Count that “Mr Morris had had to use force to pass through” (323). At the very intersection, an over- turned wooden case containing earth forms an altar where the sacriﬁce of man, the transformation of mankind and an unorthodox exercise in transub- stantiation will be performed. As Quincey breaks through the circle, he is pierced through his side, blood spurting from his wound. He nonetheless aids Jonathan in cutting down the Count, stabbing him through the heart as Jonathan severs his head. With the Vampire turned to dust, “the dying man” (326) is left centered on the cross. In this passion, the mythologies of the North, East, South, and West meld in enduring faith in the symbol of the cross. For my own part, I see no difﬁculty in believing that it formed a portion of the primeval religion, traces of which exist over the whole world, among every people; that trust in the Cross was a part of the ancient faith which taught men to believe in a Trinity, in a War in Heaven, a Paradise from which man fell, a Flood, and a Babel; a faith which was deeply impressed with a conviction that a Virgin should conceive and bear a son, that the Dragon’s head should be bruised and that through Shedding of blood should come Remission. The use of the cross, as a symbol of life and regen- eration through water, is as widely spread over the world as the belief in the ark of Noah. May be, the shadow of the Cross was cast further back into the night of ages, and fell on a wider range of country than we are aware of. It is more than a coincidence that Osiris by the cross should give life eter- nal to the Spirits of the Just; that with the cross Thorr should smite the head of the Great Serpent, and bring to life those who were slain; that beneath the cross the Muysca mothers should lay their babes, trusting by that sign to secure them from the power of evil spirits; that with that sym- bol to protect them, the ancient people of Northern Italy should lay them down in the dust [Baring-Gould 384–85]. Kingdom Come 177

The Professor’s principal representational attribute is a black bag con- taining “the ghastly paraphernalia of our beneﬁcial trade” (112), extended to include sacred implements and The Sacral. On the day of Lucy’s initiation into the order of the True dead, he is seen carrying a second, larger satchel, which contains a wooden stake and a mighty hammer. To compensate for his suffering, the Professor allows Art to wield Helsing’s mighty hammer. As Helsing read the prayer for the dead, Godalming struck the stake with the hammer. “He looked like a ﬁgure of Thor as his untrembling arm rose and fell, driving deeper and deeper the mercy-bearing stake” (192). The stake, element of a sacred tree, perhaps related to the cross, may bear mercy to its receiver, but its force resides in the hammer and the arm that wields it. As Stoker makes clear, it is Thor’s hammer, the godly instrument Baring-Gould confounds with the cross, that communicates merciful death and separates the soul from its prison. It is this hammer that reappears at the conclusion: The Professor, having made the castle holy remarks: “The blacksmith hammer which I took in the carriage from Veresti was useful” (319). At the ends of the world, as the season of light yields to antithesis, the Count and the sun disappear. At that instant Quincey, pointing at Mina, cries out, “Look! Look!” (326) In drawing attention towards Mina, away from the dust that had been the Count, the dying man marks the novel’s indexical moment. Living, but having arrived at the threshold of death’s asylum, Adamic Quincey rejoices, having, at life’s liminal moment, attained gnosis. Mina, standing in the East, is ﬁgured against a deepening sky, celestial objects sparkling around her head. A rosy light reveals her to be immaculate. “The Syzygy” concludes that Mina was ﬁnally represented in the guise of a feminine divine: “Feet planted on the Earth, silhouetted against a darkening night sky that glitters with its brilliant inhabitants, crushed serpent, Little Dragon, at her feet, Mina presents an Isian or Marian ﬁgure and returns the narrative to its beginning and the rosary” that Jonathan accepted for the sake of his mother as the novel began. In Stoker’s next breath, he tells of Mina, who had worn a sky blue ribbon around her neck as she prepared to wed, becoming a true mother. Initially portrayed as a giddy young woman, playfully mischievous at times, she has changed and in so doing she has transformed others. At ﬁrst her vision was parochial and somewhat selﬁsh: “I suppose one ought to pity anything so hunted as is the Count,” she, unable to do so, would concede. “That is just it: this Thing is not human—not even beast. To read Dr Seward’s account of poor Lucy’s death, and what followed, is enough to dry up the springs of pity in one’s heart” (202). Indeed, the Count with his “cruel mouth” and sharp nose is depicted as incapable of love, and, since “the heart of him is not” (209), he is doomed to fail in his weighing of the heart. Through her 178 The Theology of Dracula

newly gained knowledge of good and evil, Mina, however, extends her own heart to him and becomes this Thing’s great champion, intervening to beg mercy for him, pleading that the world and the divine pity him. “The poor soul who has wrought all this misery is the saddest case of all. Just think what will be his joy when he too is destroyed in his worser part that his better part may have spiritual immortality. You must be pitiful to him too, though it may not hold your hands from his destruction” (269). As there was a false Lucy, fallen like Lucifer, and a true Lucy, the true Count Dracula, though long-cloaked in darkness, is now possessed of a solar sacred nature. Whether or not Stoker was a Golden Dawn adept, Dracula, reaching its conclusion in the rosy dusk, unquestionably casts a critical eye on secret soci- eties and brotherhoods to conﬁrm the New Woman’s position as a privileged agent of the Holy Spirit. The rosy light speaks not as much to the rosy cross as to the roses cradled in Our Lady’s arm, Mina being shown as her special ﬂower, “branch of wild rose” (212). Whether Dracula is or is not both evil and an aspect of God, or God’s double, working to awaken us from our spir- itual forgetfulness, or the antichrist that the engagement of Christian symbol and sacrament to bafﬂe the Count would seem to indicate, would seem to make little difference; these possible signiﬁcations tend to dissolve and crumble into dust along with the Vampire’s body. Through the complex ritual that is plot, Mina is transformed, in appearance and function, to become transfor- mative herself. While Mina is evocative of the Blessed Virgin, she is identiﬁed as “but mortal” (273), able to recollect the taste of “the original apple” (164), fruit of the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil. On her way through the bountiful ﬁelds of Mittel Land, Mina has been more than sated on the fruits of the Yggdrasil that she was made to taste. Mina, represented as an habitué of places evoking Ste. Mary, Mina who consulted the Oracle at Ste. Mary’s churchyard and married at the Convent of St. Joseph and Ste. Mary, is shown somehow elevated beyond the sphere of normal human beings, ‘“one of God’s women, fashioned by His own hand to show us men and other women that there is a heaven where we can enter, and that its light can be here on this earth” (168), one of those “whose lives and whose truths may make good lesson for the children that are to be” (166). The Holy Mother is humbly represented as her servant; it is she who shows the Professor into Mina’s life: “Mary opened the door, and announced “Dr Van Helsing” (163). In introducing himself the Professor makes a startling claim: “Madam Mina, it is on account of the dead I come” (163). Through Mina’s intervention, the dead are served and the living pro- tected. When we have become puriﬁed, undergone catharsis, and attained Sophia, becoming one with the great emanation, darkness will no longer obscure and cover truth. Kingdom Come 179

The Professor had prepared his Anglican friends to traverse the sacred threshold in commending their spirits into God’s care in the tongue of the Romans: “In manus tuas, Domine!” (220). If the Count had previously stum- bled at the threshold of this world and the next, Jonathan and Quincey had now helped him transcend it. Upon the Count’s dissolution, the season of darkness envelops the earth; like man, divided into carnal and spiritual, earthly time and space separate into day and night, summer and winter. Although the no-longer-visible Count may perhaps rematerialize in a whirlwind of dust, that now seems curiously unimportant. Stoker nonetheless troubles this placid resolution by interjecting the issue of the transmigration of the soul. On the anniversary of Quincey’s death the following year, a baby is born to Mina and Jonathan. The blessed child, Son of the New Man and New Woman, is habitually called “Quincey.” He seems as likely to be the reincarnation of the Count as the Texan, indeed more likely, since Dracula, little dragon, embodies the skin-shedding capacity of reincarnation. If it takes but nine days to be initiated into the unholy soul-stealing union of the vampire, it takes nine months to be initiated into the divine soul accorded man. The new generation that is young Quincey, revealed as he reaches the age of reason, was conceived at the antipodes of the anniversary of The Demeter’s grounding. Perhaps this contains Stoker’s last symmetric touch. While material mater, The Mother, Demeter, brought forth the chthonic lord, the God-chosen mother brings forth a spiritual New Man, answering the Professor’s prayer: “Oh! If such an one was to come from God, and not the Devil, what a force for good might he not be in this old world of ours” (279). Through the Phaedrus Plato has Socrates ask: Would a husbandman, who is a man of sense, take the seeds, which he val- ues and which he wishes to bear fruit, and in sober seriousness plant them during the heat of summer, in some garden of Adonis, that he may rejoice when he sees them in eight days appearing in beauty? at least he would do so, if at all, only for the sake of amusement and pastime. But when he is in earnest he sows in ﬁtting soil, and practises husbandry, and is satisﬁed if in eight months the seeds which he has sown arrive at perfection? Stoker has answered. 180 The Theology of Dracula

The Overturned Lamp “‘That poor creature that we all love has had put into her veins ... the blood of four strong men.... Then, coming close ... he spoke in a ﬁerce half-whisper: ‘What took it out?’ (138) I shook my head. ‘That,’ I said, ‘is the crux’”(138). If, indeed, “the blood is the life!” (130) then Dracula is but a pale and moribund entity—“bloodless” (105) is the term Dr. Seward employs in diag- nosing the condition. Prior to the mortal injury suffered by Quincey Morris in the very last of Dracula’s hundreds of pages, very little blood at all had been shed—only a small shaving accident, a superﬁcial wound caused by a dinner knife, slight trickles of coagulated blood visible at the corners of unwashed mouths, and a precious few “gouts of fresh blood” (53) spilling over to punctuate the text here and there. Rather than indulging bloodlust, the entire novel meditates upon blood’s apparent lack, its inexplicable absence, and the ill-phrased question: “And how the blood lost or waste?” (170), mean- ing: “Where did the blood go?” Not only are there great quantities of missing blood that have vanished from Lucy’s body without a trace, but prior to Quincey’s self-sacriﬁce, death only touched the reader through Lucy’s seemingly long, frantically pathetic struggle. All other deaths occur distantly, outside of plot, with the exception of the attack that claims Lucy’s mother. Mrs. Westenra, however, had “got her death warrant” previous to the Count’s arrival—“her doctor” having already “told her that within a few months, at most, she must die, for her heart [was] weakening” (91). By the end of August, still weeks before her ulti- mate demise, Art was preparing the way, warning, “Her doom is spoken— disease of the heart” (104), with all concurring that “any shock could prove fatal” (112). Hers was a bloodless and mercifully quick death, she expired “as if struck by lightning” (131). This is typical of Dracula as an anaemic vessel; the few vampiric assaults 181

that the novel does depict, rarely violent, merely involve a surrender of will, as disoriented victims yield themselves à contrecoeur to the clever and seductive wishes of Morpheus. Indeed it is the ideas of the crimes committed in Dracula that shocked generations, not their portrayal. Renﬁeld’s motto, “The Blood is the Life!” is in fact a logician’s well- formed phrase, uttered to establish identity between “blood” and “life,” the oddly-applied deﬁnite article “The” expansively assuring universality. The question of “Where did the blood go?” thus becomes identical to the question of “Where did the life go?” More to the point the question “Where did the Life go?” is, in the logic of Dracula, simply another way of asking “From where did the Life come?” for it has been determined that it comes from and goes to the same state of pre-mythic unbegottenness. The vehicle Stoker employs to pose and incarnate this transformational question is Lucy Westenra. While much of the novel concerns itself with the daily rotation of the Earth, its annual revolution around the sun, and the movements across its surface of wooden cases intended to accommodate the Count’s body, the thor- oughly parochial comings and goings of the Un-Dead body of Lucy lend unique substance to the mysteries at hand. When the Professor blocked the Westenra crypt’s thresholds or “joinings” (227) with the Body and Blood of Christ he established that “there was no exodus” (186). This was hardly an innocent turn of phrase on the Professor’s part. Exodus is the story of human deliverance from a state of captivity and enslavement to a promised land through God’s direct intervention. It is also the story of people becoming lost, losing faith, worshipping idols before dis- covering their error and regaining and retaining true faith—trusting to the true God to enable them to reach that which is His goal for them, as ratiﬁed through a sacred covenant. In a more abstract sense—and explicitly through Jesus’ 40 days of fasting in the desert and implicitly through a host of scriptural links—Exodus is the Christian story, a story of individual pilgrimage, retrac- ing a journey from the moving world to the moment that ﬁlls the empty- because-inexistent space/time–time/space of pre-creation that fully continues after time’s exhaustion. It speaks about being held captive by the moment’s temporal ruler, about crossing the desert of Sin, worshipping the golden calf, knowing thirst without the possibility of quenching it, knowing hunger and despairing of it, and then, through faith, of being nourished with unleavened bread through the hand of God, the Eucharistic Host’s unleavened bread mak- ing speciﬁc reference to the manna of the desert and the Passover bread. This journey towards knowledge of God, Gnosis, is necessarily contributory to the sacred discourse of Dracula. The grave normally represents the body’s Promised Land rather than its place of bondage, yet, in the case of Lucy, the sacred has imprisoned the 182 The Theology of Dracula

profaning body, the false Lucy—she who in life had been light, with hair like “sunny ripples” (146), has become a “dark-haired” (187) “foul [thing] of the night” (209). The organic shell that Socrates deﬁned as the soul’s prison is now itself imprisoned within the more durably material construct of the tomb by the Divine Presence made material. This illuminates Stoker’s insistence on the necessity of consecrating to God what is already sacred to man, and pro- vides a key to his complex construct of true and false entities that share a nominal identity. His job as a novelist is to move us from one towards another, East to West, in order to return again, East-West-East, with new knowledge and understanding—hence the importance of Lucy. While it is Lucy who ﬁrst connects us to Exodus through the Professor’s reference, the novel’s pages abound with many others. One particularly strik- ing and clear example comes through Mina thinking herself led by divine signs in her oneiric ordeals: “It got thicker and thicker, till it seemed as if it became concentrated into a sort of pillar or cloud in the room, through the top of which I could see the light of the gas shining like a red eye. Things began to whirl through my brain just as the cloudy column was now whirling in the room, and through it all came the scriptural words ‘a pillar of cloud by day and of ﬁre by night.’ Was it indeed some such spiritual guidance that was coming to me in my sleep?” (227). Plot eventually shows the wisdom of Mina’s question and justiﬁes her investment of faith. Internalizing the lessons of Exodus, Stoker often works to remind us that the reﬂected gleam of the golden calf blasphemously generates a travesty of God’s luminous brilliance. Gold, at a pagan, poetic level, exposes the hidden Apollonian nature of the Count, but at another, purely human and Christian, it is shown as a blinding hence corrupting agent. Posited as emerging from within the earth on a night when all evil has its way, it is consistently advertised as a substance falsely idolized by men: “His arguments were pointed with specie—we doing the punctuation—and with a little bargaining he told us what he knew” (302). From early on, Stoker issues frequent reminders of money’s function as a corrosive agent: “Backsheesh again” (81), they begin. “Thank God! This is the country where bribery can do anything, and we are well supplied with money.... Judge Moneybag will settle this case, I think!” (290). Those who power and animate the moving world, the shippers and haulers, constantly owe their devotion only to the golden calf: “So off we go to Doolittle’s Wharf, and there we ﬁnd a man in an ofﬁce of wood so small that the man looked bigger than the ofﬁce ... when Quincey give him some- thing from his pocket which crackle as he roll it up, and put it in a so small bag which he have hid deep in his clothing, he still better fellow and humble servant to us” (275). ‘“Well, guv’nor, you’ve treated me very ‘an’som’—I had The Overturned Lamp 183

given him half a sovereign—‘an’ I’ll tell yer all I know’” (229). “I told him that if he could get me the address it would be worth another half-sovereign to him” (229). “A half-crown tip put the deputy’s knowledge at my disposal” (231). The imperial yet temporal nature of metonymic half-crowns and half- sovereigns is insistent, even leading to a “half-consent” (290), as if trying to call attention to the divide separating that which is Caesar’s from that which is God’s. The half-sovereign also comments on the absence of the divine in men’s calculation of worth, wealth, and value. Only once is the sovereign por- trayed whole, entire, uniﬁed: “Through the sound of the shivering glass I could hear the ‘ting’ of the gold, as some of the sovereigns fell on the ﬂagging” (267). The Count, stooping to scoop them off the ground where they had fallen, will raise the sovereign from the earth to the heavens as he leads his hunters to the heights of “God’s seat” on the day of judgment, temporal antipode to the evening when gold manifests itself through the appearance of bluish ﬂames and all evil things hold sway. For the lower classes—“movers with thirst and needing bribe” (143)— drink is established as equivalent to money in its powers of corruption, in its ability to loosen tongues, and in its capacity to inspire a particularly legalese mode of euphemistic expression: “The boxes were ‘main and mortal heavy,’ and that shifting them was dry work. One of them added that it was hard lines that there wasn’t any gentleman ‘such-like as yourself squire,’ to show some sort of appreciation of their efforts in a liquid form; another put in a rider that the thirst then generated was such that even the time which had elapsed had not completely allayed it. Needless to add, I took care before leaving to lift, for ever and adequately, this source of reproach” (201). “The opportunities of acquiring an abnormal thirst had been here limited; a noble use of them had, however, been made, and again I was compelled to deal with the result in an ex post facto manner” (201). “Here again I found the tally agreeing exactly; the carriers’ men were able to supplement the paucity of the written words with a few details. These were, I shortly found connected almost solely with the dusty nature of the job, and of the consequent thirst engendered in the operators. On my affording an opportunity, through the medium of the currency of the realm, of the allaying, at a later period, this beneﬁcent evil” (201), information was forthcoming. For these workmen of mercantile forthrightness, Stoker’s metaphor join- ing money, thirst, dust, and labor, is deliberately very mixed. Their toils in the dust of mortality recall the fate of the Count’s victims, Lucy and Mina— who “had both a ﬁght for it with the dusty miller” (86), and the ﬁnal dispo- sition of all men, the Count included. The chronic thirst of these laborers emphasizes how our efforts in this mortally dusty place do bring about an enduring thirst that brute men little know how to satisfy. And while it is Lucy 184 The Theology of Dracula

who recalls “something very sweet and very bitter all around me at once” (94), it is the Professor who attempts to console us and to give us strength to per- severe by returning three times to the desert thirst of Exodus 15: “We ... will have to pass through the bitter water before we reach the sweet” (154); “a hundred thousand times more do I know that he must pass through the bitter waters to reach the sweet” (180); “You are now in the bitter waters, my child. By this time tomorrow you will, please God, have passed them, and have drunk of the sweet waters” (189). In his frequent trinitarian mode, the three- fold repetition always points out one of Stoker’s more ardently dispatched messages “Oh, about number three—I needn’t tell you of number three, need I?” (61) he teases. Indeed, every occasion of triple-telling always proves to be signiﬁcant, though on one occasion somewhat puzzling. Stoker thrice draws attention to the Professor’s curious habit of making the passive element active and the active passive in his rendering of common dictums: “You must not let your sight pass from her” (116); “The dilemma had me between his horns” (319); “The milk that is spilt cries not out afterwards” (208). It seems that the only explanation for these deliberately odd transformed ﬁgures of speech is that Stoker wishes to call his reader’s attention to the aspects of his work that are not seen turning as the rumbling coach careens on by, but that remain intent and steady, the axle rather than the wheel—the immutable. We are called to more fully consider the function of apparently passive elements, most espe- cially, it would seem, Lucy. Stoker’s most obvious embodiments of three-ness are given form in a lamia triune and in the three suitors of light that become part of the Broth- erhood. He introduces the human trio as they are caught up in the most cor- poral and lively aspects of life, providing them with a spiritual subtext as they present themselves, one after the other, to Lucy Westenra at Hillingham, all asking for her hand on the same day. The occasion is rendered brighter through contrast: Lucy’s light and joyous courtship occurs nearly concurrent to Jonathan’s somber encounter with Castle Dracula’s Lamiae. Considering Stoker’s typical word games, the Westenra’s estate, Hillingham, likely intends to situate its residents in a place of high sexual attractiveness to the male, Hi(gh) lingham, or Lingham Hill, where all the suitors, lost in love and given to forgetfulness, come, blood risen to high noon, to propose a union through marriage to the young beauty. Lucy describes each suitor’s charm—curly-haired Art, penetrating Seward, and good-natured Quincey—to Mina in a letter. She paints Quincey, a man who depicts her anticipated kiss recollected as a ﬂame to “keep off the darkness” (60), as amusing her with American slang. She says he reserves it for intimates, but when he feels he has licence to indulge his love of colloquial The Overturned Lamp 185

color, rather than just reciting a collection of pat lines, he invents curious phrases that seem tailor-made for each given occasion, and seems to hold in reserve an endless store of sayings for any and every situation imaginable. This apparently explains the down-home folksiness of his proposal of marriage: “Miss Lucy, I know I ain’t good enough to regulate the ﬁxin’s of your little shoes, but I guess if you wait till you ﬁnd a man that is you will go join them seven young women with the lamps when you quit. Won’t you just hitch up alongside of me and let us go down the long road together, driving in double harness?” (59).* The image of life as a journey is one he returns to upon her refusal of his marriage proposal, resigning himself to that “pretty lonely walk between this and Kingdom Come” (60). Quincey’s metaphor is Stoker’s, with the mov- ing world manifest in London ﬂies, and transcontinental trains, and steam- boats, and cargo ships, and charging coaches orbited by lunar predators—“We sped onwards through the gloom, with the howling of the wolves around us, as though they were following in a moving circle” (19)—that make clear the cosmic scope of his vision. Yet the rest of Quincey’s declaration of love is quite original in its mixing of referents. Quincey’s “slang” associates Lucy with the Vestals, keepers of the sacred ﬂame, protectresses of pagan Rome, and maidens whose blood could not be spilt. In the same phrase he references John the Baptist’s proclamation that he was unworthy to loose the sandals of Jesus. Matthew 3:11 has the Baptist join the image of ﬂame to the concept of baptism. “I indeed baptize you with water, for repentance. But he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to bear. He will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and with ﬁre.” John 1:26–27 has the Baptist simply say: “I baptize with water; but in the midst of you there has stood one whom you do not know. He it is who is to come after me, who has been set above me, the strap of whose sandal I am not worthy to loose.” Mark 1:7–8 quotes the Baptist as saying, “One mightier than I is coming after me, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to stoop down and loose. I have baptized you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Sprit.” Matthew seems to attach his imagery to the Mysteries of Eleusis as well, for he immediately adds: “His winnowing fan is his hand, and he will thoroughly clean out his threshing ﬂoor and will gather his wheat into the barn; but the 186 The Theology of Dracula *Lucy concludes her thoughts on Quincey’s verbal stream by noting that she sympathises “with poor Desdemona when she had such a dangerous stream poured in her ear, even by a black man” (59). chaff he will burn up with unquenchable ﬁre” (3:12). This image of the win- nowing of souls, common to post–Neolithic cults, is consonant with the weighing ﬂoor image of Hunefer’s book of the dead, “The Weighing of the Heart.” Dracula’s divine winnowing hand has been shown personiﬁed in the Brotherhood, composed largely of Lucy’s beaux. In harvesting evil and exer- cising forgiveness, it ﬁlls the storehouse with felicitous goodness. The suitors, even those rejected by Lucy, return to Hillingham three months later, their blood, despite Lucy’s metaphysical infection, still at high tide. Stoker assures that their donations to Lucy’s blood-starved heart will still—ﬁrst, foremost, and forthrightly—be eroticized. To begin, Arthur con- tributes his “so bright” (114) blood, “blood so pure” (114); the next day Lucy, ﬁguring Love as a stallion, claims that he “feels very, very close.... I seem to feel his presence warm about me. I suppose it is that sickness and weakness are selﬁsh things and turn our inner eyes and sympathy on ourselves, whilst health and strength give Love rein and in thought and feeling he can wander where he wills. I know where my thoughts are. If Arthur only knew!” (117). Next, it is Seward’s turn to contribute ﬂuids. His investment prompts the comment: “‘You are looking pale yourself. You want a wife to nurse and look after you a bit; that you do!’ As she spoke, Lucy turned crimson, though it was only momentarily, for her poor wasted veins could not stand for long such an unwonted drain to the head” (120). When the Professor transfuses his blood, Lucy again feels the beauty of the new day, but recalls her ordeal: “I have a dim half-remembrance of long, anxious times of waiting and fearing; darkness in which there was not even the pain of hope to make present distress more poignant; and then long spells of oblivion, and the rising back to life as a diver coming up through a great press of water” (124), the latter phrase recalling and completing her description of her baptism in vampirism at Whitby. Finally, it is Quincey who transfers his haematological quintessence to Lucy. “His very heart was bleeding, and it took all the manhood of him—and there was a royal lot of it, too—to keep him from breaking down” (138). Lucy’s passion was nearly at an end. Quincey, who, like Lucy, described himself as a “tough nut to crack” (66, 68), is destined to be her eternal soulmate as they mystically move in double-harness to preserve Mina, for, in this case, the Vestal’s blood, though not spilt, shall indeed cry out afterwards. Stoker’s interest in introducing and mixing classical pagan and biblical references appears to be, as usual, multiple. Should luminous Lucy be a guardian of a sacred ﬂame (for she never does marry) it is in keeping with her celestial identity. Her association with John the Baptist serves to justify a term the Professor applies to Mina’s Bridal Chamber anti-sacrament: “the Vampire’s baptism of blood” (280). Lucy serves as a true Baptist to Mina, as Renﬁeld serves as a false baptist to the Count. Mina was not baptized with water but, The Overturned Lamp 187

as Matthew quotes the Baptist as saying, “with the Holy Spirit and with ﬁre” (3:11): with the Holy Spirit during her eventual passage across “the ‘Mittel Land’” (14) in “the straggling ends of pine woods, which here and there ran down the hillsides like tongues of ﬂame” (13); and with ﬁre in being branded with the Eucharist, Jonathan even asserting that they “all went through the ﬂames” (326). As John the Baptist not only baptized Jesus but foreran him by being in essence accused of and martyred for the crime of the Word for which Jesus would later be cruciﬁed, Lucy will precurse Mina to reveal the nature of the Vampire’s unholy rites. The imagery of sandals and of going before, of preceeding Mina, is inti- mated from the moment of the Count’s arrival on English shores. On the occa- sion of Lucy’s initiation, an alarmed Mina hastened to bring Lucy back from her graveyard tryst. Reaching the suicide bench, Mina wraps Lucy, clothed only in her nightdress, in a shawl and puts her own shoes on Lucy’s feet before awak- ening her. Reaching a gravel path, now polluted Lucy offers Mina the shoes that she might walk in them. Mina ostensibly refuses, but then covers her bare feet in mud, as if standing in the chthonic and unclean place of Lucy, “so that as we went home no one, in case we should meet any one, should notice my bare feet” (89), and she remarks, “We got home without meeting a soul” (89). The blood brotherhood formed to save Lucy’s body will become a sacred broth- erhood in a struggle to safeguard Mina’s soul. Again, Lucy is largely responsible for alerting her one-time suitors to the spiritual dangers abroad. Driving the point home, they must kill her dead body to save her living soul. False Lucy is killed to bring forth true Lucy. False Count Dracula— “man-that-was” (212) become “the semblance of man” (39)—is killed to give rise to the true Count. By all rights, the novel should represent the killing of a false god in order to release the true God, since it is this ritual scenario, for millennia enacted annually through dying-god rites in post-Neolithic cultures, that was appropriated to give the Vampire tale form. Adamic Quincey’s self-sac- riﬁce on the virtual cross, undertaken to accomplish the birth of the half-sov- ereign, partially-divine New Man, hardly qualiﬁes as the death of a false god. Another violent death approaching plot is Renﬁeld’s, who returns the story to earlier renditions of the Vampire Tale in which the old chthonic god is killed in order to resurrect as the new chthonic god. But Renﬁeld’s mission, to serve as one who makes ready the way before the Count, was unrealized. Once he begins to weigh the heart as soul, his own and others, and to consider that it is the soul inviolate and not the blood that engenders life eternal, Renﬁeld abandons the Count and saves Mina. Renﬁeld’s death therefore tells a human story of personal redemption and selﬂessness, but nothing more. Beyond these martyrs, Dracula’s dead are vampires, seamen, infants, and mothers. Matthew’s report on the Baptist saying he is not worthy to loose Jesus’ 188 The Theology of Dracula

shoe, and then, attaching foot to hand, speaking of the winnowing hand of Jesus, clearly intends to engage the Mysteries, notably Demeter’s sacred implement, the winnowing fan. The Professor’s “ear of corn” Mysteries speech and other references in the work establish a ﬁrm connection between Dracula and earlier Platonic recountings of the Dionysian Vampire. Lucy, rather than retaining a ghostly form and being doomed, Ianthe-like, to eternally haunting Athenian neighborhoods in search of the simple violet, will be dispatched to an eternal and Christian slumber; she accomplishes good through awakening others, through alerting her friends and ﬁancé to their sacred mission: to facil- itate the exodus of the soul. Hearing her plea through the determined efforts of the Professor, the Brotherhood sees to it that she is laid to eternal rest, True Dead, and deposited alongside her True Dead mother. Through these and other actions, Stoker assigns the role of the false god to be sacriﬁced to Artemis-Diana in her avatar as Persephone. It is she whose death is to bring forth the True Divine, that is, the Sacred Mother and The Maiden united: the Blessed Virgin. Persephone’s elimination will be assured through the dissolution of her lover-son, the Dionysian Vampire, and the extinguishment of the sacral ﬂame of torch-bearing Demeter. Preceded by mares’ tails, The Demeter delivered her underworldly progeny in a snug harbor beneath the graves of Romanesque Whitby Abbey, a structure left a ruin by the near descendants of the self-same Goths that under Alaric had pulled Byron’s Temple of Ceres down to dust and rubble. The derelict vessel, her crew disappeared, is left beached, an abandoned wreck under a dead man’s hand. Her apostate helmsman espouses from beyond life a belief in Jesus Christ and in the mercy of His divine Mother. As the moment of the annual Mysteries celebration approaches in late September, Lucy’s mother is stricken as if by a ﬂash of lightning. Her death appears to signal Mystery Night’s arrival. The Daughter will soon follow The Mother across the Acheron to forever remain amongst the True Dead. The pagan winnowing fan has been replaced by the hand of Jesus; the rosy cross and golden dawn have been forsaken for a truer brotherhood maintaining Christian principles, gentlemanly comportment, and a willingness to enter the season of darkness unafraid, its members believing the light is now within them. The Vestals’ ﬂame, like that of graveyard Sleep, has been overturned and extin- guished so that, even at the price of Rome’s fall, a truer light might shine.* Although The Demeter births the Ploutonian ﬁgure that initiates Lucy’s ordeal, it will be Jesus Christ that resolves her wayward vagabonding. He, too, will bring peace to the Dionysian hunter through the intercession of the The Overturned Lamp 189 *Curiously, in the 1931 Universal ﬁlm entitled Dracula, the name of the ship conducting the Count to England became The Vestal.

Holy Mother and her instrument, the “quite heroic” (86) Mina. In her moment of liberation from evil, at the instance of her becoming immaculate, Mina is revealed bathing in the rosy light of the western light, Lucy Westenra, which lingers to illuminate her visage in its remarkable radiance. Like the Moses of Exodus, whose face after 40 days of divine discourse reﬂected the divine presence in light, the brilliance of goodness is given expression through the light of Lucy Westenra that lunar Mina reﬂects. While Mina is the wild rose branch, Lucy, repeatedly described as rosy, is the Blessed Virgin’s bouquet. Mina herself reminds the reader of “the roses in [Lucy’s] cheeks” (93) that were either “fading from her cheeks” (92) or “coming back already” (93). While Jonathan’s Transylvanian adventure—that circuitous coach ride to the castle, the dusty pile of gold and chains, and numerous other of its curious details—impinges on initiation rites of certain branches of Freema- sonry, these are but minor elements in a vast tapestry. Stoker joins the initia- tory procession along the Sacred Way to complete and redirect Byron and Polidori’s Neoplatonic vampire tale, calling most particularly on the “Phae- drus,” its Socratic proof of the soul, and related images, to make his case. Overturning the antique Mysteries, he argues—in a pilgrimage that, having completed the East-West itinerary of Polidori, again returns to the East—for a new Christian covenant. Until Stoker focused Dracula on trinitarian relationships, the Vampire Tale was enclosed within a bipolar universe. The feminine actors in the vam- pire drama were passive objects lacking original volition. In their annual Apol- lonian-Dionysian conﬂict, Polidori’s Aubrey would occasionally “bafﬂe” Ruthven, but Aubrey would ultimately be overwhelmed with grief from the loss of both his true love and his only sister to wily Ruthven. Nodier and Planché seemingly stripped Ruthven of his victories by having time run out on his attempts to wed the Apollonian ﬁgure’s maiden sister, condemning him to Gnostic annihilation, but in fortuitously dispatching evil, they risk dis- missing and belittling its compellingly seductive power. Dumas has Ruthven deprive Gilbert of two sisters, one spiritual, the other biological, at a six-month interval and climb out of the Black Sea on a 366th day to claim Gilbert’s ﬁancée in his stead. Ruthven’s betrayal by the Ghoul provides Gilbert with the means to defeat the unrepentant Vampire with a consecrated sword. Ruthven’s undoing unites Gilbert, his bride, and the spirits of the lost sisters at a felicitous sacred wedding, the Ghoul causing her own death through her act of love. Stoker maintains the vampire template through Apollonian Harker and Dionysian Dracula, but the Apollonian-Dionysian doppelganger is accom- modated by and subsumed within an eclipsing triadic solar-lunar-chthonic conﬁguration binding Jonathan to Mina to the Count—Jonathan even being present as one of a ménage-à-trois as the Count takes his wife in unholy 190 The Theology of Dracula

matrimony. Through the Lucy-Mina doppelganger, the triangular relationship is nearly squared, even tending towards, and ultimately reaching, the ogdoadic through the Brotherhood. By pairing solar Lucy and lunar Mina, Stoker greatly develops, clariﬁes, and empowers the feminine personality, assigning it a determinant role; women, no longer simple objects of contention, are resolving subjects and centers of power emanation. Although the spiritually devastating effects of the Count’s activities are reversed, he scores resounding temporal victories, irreversibly in Lucy’s case and nearly so in Mina’s. What is occulted in Dracula is always exposed, exoteric dominating the esoteric. The captain of The Demeter wrote out his tale of the Vampire on a scroll that he sealed in a water- and air-tight container conceived to weather a terrible storm so that his word and witness might eventually reach human eyes and understanding. Rather than an addendum to the canon of the ship’s log, his scroll was termed an apocryphal gospel. So many of Stoker’s positions, as they emerge from his own text, are consistent with the apparent stance of the apocrypha of ancient Gnostics as understood at the moment of modernity. It is mystifying to understand this correspondence, considering that though interest was high in the age of Theosophy, knowledge of Gnosticism was quite limited prior to the unearthing of the cache of documents known as The Nag Hammadi. The primary so-called Gnostic works that would have been avail- able to Stoker were limited to Irenaeus of Lyon’s polemical Against Heresies, published in English in 1885; The Book of Enoch, 1887; The Pistis Sophia, in Latin 1851 and English 1896; and Charles King’s The Gnostic and their Remains, 1864, revised 1887; with more fragmentary sources incidentally scattered throughout the writings of late classical writers, such as Hippolytus. Stoker’s “Gnostic” touches include the depiction of the body as a prison; the role of light as a divine marker; the temporal division of understanding, “six months turned to the left, six months turned to the right” (Pistis Sophia); the privileged place given to apostles John, Matthew and Thomas; the elevated posi- tion of women; the particularly stressed role of Mary; the suggestion of a com- posite feminine Sophia; and, more abstractly, the name Harker. Jonathan on one occasion actually scribes “Hark!” (54) to convey his listening “blindfold” (203, 305) to the exodus of the self-willed Count, abandoning his castle, as he heads for The Demeter and ﬂight to what he believes will be his promised land, England. Mina, too, accentuates hearing: “The sheep and the lambs are bleating in the ﬁelds away behind me” (68); before her, dueling orchestras, one playing the sensuously whirling, still-scandal-tainted triple-time of “a harsh waltz,” the other, the strident double-time of “the Salvation Army” (68). “Neither of the bands hears the other, but up here I hear and see” (69). In the Pistis Sophia, Jesus constantly stresses the word “Hark!” enjoining disciples, “Who hath ears to hear, let him hear!” It is the divine Word, not the image, that contains the Logos.
