The objective set out, to demonstrate that Dracula was written as a sacred text, has been attained. The Book of Stoker, commenting on an eastward pil- grimage whose record is ﬁlled with illuminations “such as we see in old missals” (11), is an epistolary text “‘focussing’ some account” (69) out of recordings, journal entries, memoranda, logs, and missives whose spiritual nature even the Count can appreciate, as he concedes to Jonathan, “Your letters are sacred to me” (46) (although the Count abhors shorthand as blasphemous). Decrying clerics “printin’ lies on paper an’ preachin’ them out of pulpits” (65), Stoker attempts to offer a contemporary clerk’s truer gospel for a newer time. To distil a theology from its many pages would be problematic; like other sacred texts, Dracula is not a catechism. Certain of its features are nonetheless remarkable. The triumph of Ste. Mary and the repeated disparaging of St. Peter seem to signal an acceptance of Catholic rites but a rejection of the Catholic insti- tution, the Vatican, and especially—recalling the gate keeper with his hand out—practices that might be seen as relating to simony. The elevated place accorded woman remains steadfastly within a traditionalist view of the sacred couple as formed by a man and a woman, the syzygy, and idealized in the sacred family of “St. Joseph and Ste. Mary” (96) and the Divine Child. The body, starkly established as a soul-enslaving prison, explains why, along with the dusty gold discovered in the Count’s chamber, “there were also chains and ornaments, some jewelled, but all of them old and stained” (50); no matter its ornamental splendor, a chain binds. The presence of pagan evil is seen as a poten- tial pillar of light and goodness, as the Irmunsul of Hildesheim’s Dom Santa Maria suggests. Forgiveness becomes a universal possibility for all those having slain or having had slain the unclean spirits residing within themselves, sacra- mental confession having no role in the dynamics of forgiveness. The Professor urges his Christian fellows of the Brotherhood to act on behalf of the Vampire as if for themselves. For should we become afflicted, he warns “us for ever are the gates of heaven shut; for who shall open them to us again?” (209). Mina, conceding the Professor’s case, argues more generally and with greater purity for the good of forgiveness as an exercise in the divine, especially rallying the “menfolk” to pity the Count. This marks the opening of a new era in which, Jonathan seems to suggest, the ﬂames of hell may be greatly contained. Life, the life of the blood, is the bitter water; the truly sweet water is the pure eternal soul life which connects to that which comes before and after everything. Stoker says as much: “Sweet it was ... but with a bitter [quality] underlying the sweet, a bitter offensiveness, as one smells in blood” (42). In hungering and plunging with Lucy “like a cormorant” (101) into the depth of these estuarial waters bitter and sweet we have come to encounter Matthew and John the Evangelists, Hesiod, Socrates, and Moses, all intent on resolving the question of what is, was and will be before and after being. But, most 192 The Theology of Dracula

particularly, we ﬁnd Jesus, the unblinking ﬁsh, multiplying bounty, who looked at Lucy as she delivered her body to the Count for his profaning baptism. How was Stoker to produce a sacred text if not through reference to ear- lier sacred texts, as the Prophets and Evangelists had done before him? The question of what was before the beginning and what endures after the end is the mystery that is sealed in the tomb we set out to resolve. The key is locked within but as it is immaterial Jonathan, despite his desperate intensity, could not at ﬁrst ﬁnd it. Mina’s attitude is more joyous: “Now I shall learn something pleasant, I am sure; for it will tell me the other side of a true love episode of which I know one side already” (196). Approaching the same question from a different angle, Jonathan consid- ered the comfort brought to him through the rosary difﬁcult to comprehend, but determined to “examine this matter and try to make up my mind about it. In the meantime I must ﬁnd out all I can about Count Dracula, as it may help me to understand” (33). Why he joins the two, rosary and vampire, is obscure, but he seems to think that darkness explains light the way death explains life. What he ﬁnds out about the Count is quite similar to what he ﬁnds out about himself. When he looked in the mirror while shaving, he mis- took seeing his own face for not seeing the Count’s, yet the Count, in his ways of Morpheus, has been shown sharing identities with most everyone, but particularly with Jonathan—even to the extent that he marries Jonathan’s wife. The Count, described as a guide and conductor in the same manner as the Professor, has also been qualiﬁed as hierophantic. Neither the Count nor the Professor constitutes, however, a psychopomp, their mission being not to lead the soul from the body, but to reconcile the living individual to the supremacy of the soul over the body even in the busiest of seasons in the mov- ing world. In this regard, both Dracula and Helsing function as special types of exorcists, one casting the soul out of the body, the other, remedially, the body from itself in order to recover the soul, again plying on the idea of making what is sacred to man sanctiﬁed to God. To seize the nature of the Count’s role in Dracula is no doubt to return to the 13 persons at the dinner table and Stoker’s Notes, and perhaps to gain some insight into Stoker’s struggle with his Transylvanian boyar and to clarify something of the Gnostic overtones of his work. Present at the Passover feast, foundation of the new Eucharistic age, and Last Supper of Jesus, was the apos- tle Judas. John claims that Judas was motivated by “Satan” to betray Jesus. Clearly Judas was required to effect the new era of man; his deliverance of Jesus had a tragic quality but gave rise to a joyous moment. Most importantly, this action, the sacriﬁce of the Paschal lamb, was determined by Jesus himself. Luke relates that there were contentious relations between the apostles that day of the Last Supper, and that Satan would also move Simon Peter to deny The Overturned Lamp 193

knowing Jesus as his master, as indeed came to pass. Mark tells the same story, that before Jesus declares “This is my blood of the new covenant, which is being shed for many” (4:17), he maintained that one amongst the 12 would betray him, and another deny him. Matthew has again a somewhat different version of the event to relate. Jesus foretells his betrayal by one at the table, and “Judas who betrayed him answered and said, ‘Is it I, Rabbi?’ He said to him ‘Thou hast said it’” (26:25). A conspiratorial shadow envelops this exchange. Judas hails Jesus as “Rabbi,” spiritual master, but Jesus turns the acknowledgment around through his reply, provisionally assigning Judas the masterly voice. Without Judas, the realization of Jesus’ mission could not have been attained: Judas effects His release from His corporeal form and the revelation of His True Self. Judas may be the stake, but Jesus is the hammer. The equation of the count and Judas is explicitly suggested by Jonathan: “The last I saw of Count Dracula was his kissing his hand to me, with a red light of triumph in his eyes, and with a smile that Judas in hell might be proud of” (52). The betrayal of the Count concerns his own spiritual nature; in denying it, in giving himself purely to the material, the Count is inescapably evil in a way that Judas is not, but he serves to remind us of the missing half- crown, the half of everything that goes unseen. Dumas assigned the Ghoul a very Judas-like role, in that she betrayed the Vampire at the cost of her own existence. Stoker conﬁdes this part to Renﬁeld. Unlike Dumas’ Ruthven, Count Dracula is never given the opportunity for repentance, but it seems unlikely he would ask for forgiveness, making Mina’s argument for forgiveness all the more stunning and profoundly Christian. There is, nonetheless, another aspect of the Count that is intermittently given expression: his role as Rex mundi. He is called “the King-Vampire” (320); Jonathan Harker hears him “like a king speaking” (33); Dracula enters London through King’s Cross, even if travelling as purely material freight; his victim Lucy is deposited in the “churchyard at Kingstead” (183); he is a king in a two- dimensional bivalent universe where the Professor, matching wits with the Count, can gleefully call, “Check to the King” (135). Like Jonathan at Castle Dracula, Jesus, on the occasion of His passing 40 days and nights in the desert, has only one companion: Satan. Satan would present Jesus with the material, asking Him, for example, to transform rock into bread. Upon His refusal, Satan led Jesus on high, above the temple, where he displayed the material splendor of the earth, promising all to Jesus in exchange for a declaration of subservience. Renﬁeld describes a similar scene in which he was tempted by the Count with millions of lives, in the form of masses of glowing-eyed rodents. Renﬁeld at ﬁrst succumbs to the Count’s temptation, but later redeems his crime by sacriﬁcing himself to save Mina. As he had with Judas, Jesus eventually 194 The Theology of Dracula

commands Satan, establishing His mastery: “Begone, Satan! for it is written, ‘The Lord thy God shalt thou worship and him only shalt thou serve’” (Matthew 4:10). Perhaps most importantly, the satanic aspect of the Count derives, in Cathar fashion, from his dusty nature: He is purely material. By going through the ﬁre of the material, puriﬁcation becomes possible. Stoker told Prime Minister Gladstone that he intended to purify his reader, that his work was conceived as cathartic. Perhaps his plan was to attach a forth- right and questing chivalrous romance to the Albigensian Cathari and their the- ologies, largely consistent with the ideas Stoker presents, and explaining the material Count’s portrayal as the worldly king. If so, could Stoker perhaps be relating his text to the Bogomili, a medieval sect native to the Count’s historic realm and the probable theological source of the Cathari heresy? Massimo Introvigne of the Centre for Study of New Religions kindly read certain sections of this text as it was being drafted. His encouraging comments were tempered by a cautionary note concerning Dracula’s author: “I would say, based on his non–Dracula writings and bio[graphy], that Stoker was more con- ventionally Christian than it appears in the text.” This is no doubt true. Yet in choosing not to represent the dark season, in joining at its threshold the light of Lucy and Mina’s radiant smile, in ending his novel by having his now wholly- sovereign heroine experience true catharsis and bask in the rosy light of the divine, Stoker nonetheless shows himself to be a true and dedicated torch- bearing illuminato. Stoker’s sacred text, The Book of Stoker, was designed not only to illuminate, but to spark the inner light within each reader. This is what he told William Gladstone he intended to do, and this is what he did. Only his sacred project can explain and unify the novel’s many motifs—from the gold to the dust, from the solar to the lunar, from the beads to the cross, from the spotless forehead to the repeated references to the superstition of the “evil eye” (14, 16, 302, 312), from the corpse to the key—to form a coherent and mighty artistic statement that continues to shine on brightly across time. The presence of the triumphant, evil-vanquishing Christian cross in Dracula does not preclude this ancient symbol from intersecting and inter- acting with other orders of signiﬁcation. Considering Stoker’s familiarity with Baring-Gould’s essays on the cruciform, the circle, Melusina, the shipping of the dead, and the Sangreal, it is telling that Stoker’s Christian symbols peace- fully coexist with heretical rites, ancient myths, and pagan gods; meaningful that, in interacting in ambiguous comfort with these remnants of the old beliefs, the icons of Christianity dissolve the fatal polarity Goethe established through “The Bride of Corinth.” Indeed Dracula’s compulsive, geometri- cally-balanced treatment of temporality, iconography, plot events, protagonist characterization, and geographic location tends—through cross, host, rosary, and other emblems—to index further authorial investment in a web of delib- erately layered meanings. Barbara Belford’s suggestion that Stoker considered using tarot imagery gains added sense once the discerned Cathari and Bogomili inﬂuences on the particular Christian theology that Stoker advances are taken into account. the imagery “found in missals” that Stoker cites as he begins his novel with a journey through the Mittel Land. As seems to be indicated by the name Van Helsing—so resonant with that of the author of Oriatrike, or Physick reﬁned, Dr. Van Helmont—Stoker is particularly eager to trade in distinctive appeals to alchemistic imagery and thought. He is also prepared to embody the Holy Spirit in a feminine form, transforming the trinitarian godhead into a quaternity, the Blessed Virgin Mary being assumed not only into heaven, but also into the divine amalgam of the godhead. The polysemous quality of Dracula’s symbolic system both in its indi- vidual and collective aspects (micro-and-macrocosmically) its proximity to Rosicrucian texts, alchemistic motifs, and its correspondence, through the triangular relationship linking Jonathan, Mina, and the Count to the allegoric transformative marriage of Sol and Luna unavoidably bring the Book of Stoker into direct contact with, to employ the term Christian Rosenkreutz celebrated in his allegory of the magically Christian Easter-time renaissance, the “Chymi- cal wedding.” This spring-rites royal union is motivated by the same dynamic as the antique agricultural Mysteries of Eleusis: Death giving rise to Life. In that regard, and going well beyond issues of temporal structuring, Stoker’s magnum opus is more ﬁrmly bound to Dumas’ “fantastical drama” than has previously been discussed, as is made clear by Renﬁeld’s notably improbable declaration that Seward “might as well ask a man to eat molecules with a pair of chop-sticks” (238) as to ask him not to want blood. The fre- quently cited interplay of polarities, trinities, and quaternities expressed though Dracula’s characters, actions, and elemental, ideational and geograph- ical paradox, strongly suggests that Dumas’s Mélusine interlude may inform a sub rosa armature that, in supporting the plastic, earthy clay of plot and character, structures the material body of Stoker’s Gnostic-ﬂavored novel. In Stoker’s quadrille the couples are more difﬁcult to discern than with Dumas, for they are never introduced as simple pairs: Lucy is ﬁrst shown with her many beaux, Jonathan with the three lamiae and his ﬁancée Mina, Mina with her several husbands, and the Count with his multiple wives. Yet a close look at the dance of Stoker’s cast reveals its own quadrille within a cosmic drama in which the Gnostic bridal chamber sacrament becomes an alchemistic exercise. The union of Sun and Moon is indeed conducted before the assembled mem- bers of the Purﬂeet Brotherhood as if a sacred rite in the Telesterion of Eleusis, bringing to light a son with many names, none of which are ever revealed. To understand this linkage, certain details of the French play must be recalled and juxtaposed with corresponding elements of the Anglo-Irish novel. His being offered three glasses, a ploy to loosen his tongue on the part of the travelers, is prefatory to his recounting a series of ghost stories about Tormenar. According to Lazarus, the Tormenar family was cursed and subject to a phenomenon of triple deaths. Dumas will offer, in triple triads, an ennead of victims, comprised of Lazarus’s tales of two generations of ill-fated brothers of Tormenar, three in each generation (Luis transgenerationally expiating the sins of the instigator of the family curse in his stead), and the mise-en-scène of the deaths of three sisters of Tiffauges— vessels ﬁlled with blood as anima—who are sacriﬁced to Ruthven. Alluding to an exchange he had with Charles Nodier that is recounted in Mes Mémoires (553), Dumas has Gilbert contest the materialist’s thesis through an invocation of the material’s microcosm as he discovered it revealed in the eyepiece of a microscope. The innovation of the compound lens made the mid–19th century microscope a powerful and revelatory scientiﬁc tool that provided proof of the existence of beings invisible to the naked eye. Dumas has the empirical and invisible lead directly to the spiritual and imma- terial, however, for the travelers enthusiastically question Gilbert on his pro- fessed belief in supernatural beings. Gilbert brightly explains how every Britton peasant has an elﬁn assistant to help with the chores, particularly with shoeing horses. He further notes that as an infant he had had a noble water- nixie as a nurse and counselor, even describing her dance and listing the co- residents of the tapestry she inhabited. Hardly gratuitous dialogue, Dumas is beginning to prepare his climax. A few scenes later, Lazarus recounts how, en route to Tiffauges from Nantes, Gilbert’s horse threw four shoes at once. Clearly this unlikely occurrence has been orchestrated with the complicity of the prescient elves of Clisson as a meaningful coincidence intended to lead us to Mélusine, the Tapestry Room, and an exercise in alchemy. In alchemy, which—seeing each existent thing as both itself and a sign of itself within a coextensive unity that permeates a signifying cosmos—func- tions as much through metaphor, metonymy and symbol as through substan- tive elemental interaction, the animal body exempliﬁes the world in microcosm. The complex of the living being, Gilbert’s horse, is understood as composed of Empedocles’s four elements (air, earth, ﬁre, and water) plus the ethereal life-force. The horse’s living-and-signifying four limbs (like the four limbs of the human being) represent the four codependent essential mate- rial elements. The ﬁfth, the quinta essentia, ethereal quintessence or anima, resides symbolically in what’s left—head, trunk, genitalia—but most partic- ularly in the retort of the heart, where the immaterial solar essence, said to burn with greater intensity than the hottest burning coal, is circulated throughout the body via the blood. The horse losing its shoes metaphorically separates out the four elements and isolates the quintessence. Coniunctio Oppositorium 199

Gilbert’s horse also functions as a powerful symbol of the ﬁnite limita- tions of humanity’s animal nature. The beast forces Gilbert to stop before reaching Tiffauges, his intended destination. With the loss of the horseshoes, he has been implicated in an alchemistic revelation concerning Ruthven, Hélène, and himself that is already in the midst of execution. As Lazarus recounts to Hélène at Tiffauges the ordeal he underwent in the deﬁle between two hills, Gilbert is being put through his own, similar trial. Upon his unshod steed, he encounters the masked Ruthven and a disguised love interest in the desolate, sylvan gorge between two eminences. The scene is triply reminiscent of Aubrey’s misadventures in Polidori’s Vampyre: ﬁrst, in the horse whose ani- mal nature forces the solar spiritual hero to stop; second, in the “ambuscade” occurring in the narrow “deﬁle” that must necessarily be traversed; and third, in the unexpected encounter with a woman. In Polidori’s mise-en-scène, Aubrey encountered his conductress Ianthe at the humble Telesterion where her material life was being sacriﬁced. With Dumas, the feminine ﬁgure is dis- covered to be the Ghoul, who, functioning more like a guardian angel than a stalking predator, is present to preserve the solar hero from saturnine Ruthven’s assassination attempt. Ziska not only urges Gilbert to ﬂee Ruthven, but later ﬁnds a way to instruct him to sleep in the Tapestry Room, where the transformation engaged with the ill-shod horse will continue towards its conclusion through the concourse of the tapestry’s fairy forms. She will further her role as conductress by preparing Hélène to receive a revelation. In the Tapestry Room, Mélusine is presented as being the familiar spirit of Gilles, le maréchal de Rais; the inhabitants of the Gothic tapestry provide the elements of his alchemistic undertakings. In the two knights who assist the ancient baron, Dumas undoubtedly seeks to personify the alchemist Anto- nio Francisco Prelati, and Rais’ right-hand man and betrayer, Étienne Cor- riault. Mélusine states her intention to rekindle yesterday’s ﬁres through her quadrille. “This ﬁre, [Paracelsus] says, contains nothing more of the ‘Sala- mandrine Essence or Melusinian Ares,’ but is rather a ‘retorta distillatio from the midst of the centre, beyond all coal ﬁre’” (Jung 13: 138), a divine ﬁre imbued with the golden solar nature of the anima. The tapestry chamber itself forms the alchemist’s crucible, the “philosophical egg” that is divided and subdivided in all its dimensions by the sign of the cross, in order to be rejoined as Unus mundus. This scene seems designed to establish the proof of the success of Gilles de Rais’ magnum opus. Orphan siblings Gilbert and Hélène represent the fruit of Rais’ chemical wedding of four centuries previ- ous. Through them, Ruthven shall renew himself. In Dumas’ alchemy subtext, Lazarus, recruited from the Bible for his knowledge of death and life, suffering and glory, constitutes and occupies the ﬁction’s middle ground, present to facilitate and enable the protagonists’ 200 The Theology of Dracula

movements from higher position to lower, lower position to higher, as they transform in their turn. A celebrated dictum of The Emerald Tablet of Hermes Trismegistus teaches that which is above is like that which is below; though it fails to explain that what is below is what is above but is inverted and reversed, even should that be the case. Heraclitus, propounding a corollary axiom, insists that the path up and the path down is one and the same. For Dumas, that path is Lazarus. Lazarus takes Ruthven’s place at the supper at Tormenar; informs Hélène of her spouse’s inhuman nature; opens the door to Gilbert when he rises from the mysterious place in Tiffauges’s depths in which Ruthven had conﬁned him; pulls Ruthven as Rex marinus out of the Black Sea’s depths; takes Gilbert’s sword to the cleric for its sanctiﬁcation leading to the black king’s death, surely a prerequisite to his rebirth in a puriﬁed state. In serving Gilbert, Lazarus serves Ruthven, and vice versa. Alchemist Michael Maier views Ruthven’s Rex marinus as the king fallen from on high “into the darkest depths of matter where he awaits deliverance. But no one will plunge into these depths in order, by his own transformation in the darkness and by the torments of ﬁre, to rescue his king” (Jung 13: 146). Paracelsus’s disciple Gerhard Dorn is recalled for theorizing that God requires saving by man, who ﬁnds his own salvation through the undertaking. In a near approximation of a Buddhist way of discovery, alchemy’s esoteric view is that the king—that is, the divine—can be redeemed through transformation and puriﬁcation and that puriﬁcation presumes as its prerequisite condition corruption. This understanding contrasts with the orthodox Christian view and particularly the Cathari view of the satanic black king, Rex mundi, as one given over to the material and mired in the evil of his own stony heart. Neither alchemistic nor Cathari, Lazarus’s intent in saving Ruthven falls fully within the limits of Christian orthodoxy. Indeed, Lazarus pursues a faithfully Catholic doctrine: He was seeking to overcome his cowardly nature, to perform a good and heroic deed, and to gain favor with heaven, thinking his action will enable him to redeem some of his sins—“Racheter quelques pêchés” (521) are his precise words. It was noted that while Montague Summers approved of Mélusine because of the position Paracelsus attributed to her, he could not envisage Dumas’ reason for inserting the Ghoul into plot. As mentioned earlier, Mélu- sine and the Ghoul appear to be at the very least closely allied beings, if not avatars, of the same force. Yet an additional need for Ziska seems likely in play: She was necessary to balance the masculine and feminine aspects of the supernatural to accommodate the Dumas explicit alchemy subplot. In Le Jour- nal des Débats of 7–8 July 1819, Nodier, in one of his earlier critical texts on the Vampire antihero, predicts that the Vampire’s deadly love would haunt the fantasies of womankind. Nodier, an expert on Galland’s Mille et Une Coniunctio Oppositorium 201

Nuits, also insists that the Vampire is a transformation of the Mesopotamian Ghoul, a notion that Dumas asserts as fact in Gilbert’s “last supper” dialogue. Therefore, to call on the feminine Ghoul to complement and counterbalance masculine Ruthven seems not merely natural but obligatory; to amalgamate her with Mélusine makes even more sense. Dumas ends his drama with the prospective wedding of Gilles and Anto- nia assured and blessed by celestial sister spirits. By the time the curtain falls on Circassia, Ruthven, seemingly true-dead at last, has made his ﬁnal appear- ance of the 19th century. Yet even as Nodier’s Lord Rutwen inspired Planché’s Bride of the Isle, Dumas’ Vampire, traveling incognito as The Phantom, quickly made its way across the channel. Dionysius Boucicault, proponent-in-chief of the “sensation” melodrama that enthralled the English-speaking world of the mid–Victorian period, Dublin-born-and-bred son of a Frenchman, spent several years of economic exile from his London theatrical base at Paris’s Porte Saint-Martin Theatre, out of the reach of his creditors. There he met his composer-collaborator, Robert Stoepel. In the early 1850s these two adapted the works of Sardou, Delavigne, and other French playwrights into English, their output including adaptations of Dumas’ Pauline, The Corsican Brothers and The Vampire. The French dramas were sufﬁciently lucrative to afford Boucicault return fare to England. As Planché had once served Samuel Arnold and the English Opera House, Boucicault would serve Charles Kean and his Princess Theatre, becom- ing house playwright and plying his trade by liberally borrowing from the French melodramatic stage. Of the numerous plots Boucicault imported into a lively English vernacular, nearly all brought Kean success, but when, in 1853, Boucicault handed him The Phantom, Kean thought the part of the Vampire beneath his talents or too sharply at odds with his image as an actor. Nonetheless The Princess put on the play—Boucicault taking on the role himself in what is generally, if erroneously, credited as his acting début. The play, which fared poorly, is better remembered for terminating Boucicault’s association with Kean and inaugurating Boucicault’s inﬂuential American career: Boucicault ran off and eloped to New York with Kean’s ward, 19-year- old Agnes Robertson, who had played opposite him as the V-Vampire’s vic- tim. Kean, a world-touring actor-theater manager celebrated for lavish, metic- ulously-detailed productions of Shakespearean tragedy thoroughly anticipated the theatrical enterprise of Henry Irving. Kean’s death from exhaustion coin- cided magically with Irving’s rise to celebrity in his breakthrough role in The Bells. Shortly thereafter, Kean protégée Ellen Terry launched a Kean-like the- atrical endeavor, leasing the Lyceum Theatre, formerly the English Opera House, and taking Henry Irving as her creative partner. Irving enticed solicitor 202 The Theology of Dracula

Abraham Stoker to quit his secure government job at Dublin Castle and to join him in London as the Lyceum business manager. Stoker stepped into Kean’s organizational shoes as Irving donned his Thespian mantle; Terry, Irv- ing, and Stoker, forming the Lyceum’s “unholy trinity,” dominated the London theatrical world of the late-19th century. Stoker knew the plays Boucicault adapted for Kean, as Townsend Walsh’s biography of Boucicault makes clear: “In after years, Henry Irving, at the instigation of Boucicault, took the role of Louis XI and played it, in Boucicault’s opinion, with much more force than Kean; while in The Corsican Brothers Kean excelled Irving in the depth of his intensity. But it was all inspired by the French” (Walsh 43). Irving and Kean shared in their contempt for the Vampire. In adapting Dumas’ Le Vampire Boucicault consciously sought to emulate Planché, whose adaptation of Nodier’s melodrama was still playing to appre- ciative audiences in the provinces, and, as Planché noted, continuously gen- erating revenue. Boucicault energetically set to work to condense Dumas and Maquet’s ﬁve-act monument by combining the scenes from Tormenar, Tiffauges, and Circassia and transferring them to Raby Castle, Wales. He dis- carded Ruthven, putting in his place Sir Alan Raby, a fratricidal Cromwellian Puritan; replaced Juana with a sunny English ﬁancée named Lucy; and, excis- ing Mélusine, introduced Dr. Rees, a medical doctor whose hobby is research into alchemy. Boucicault’s two-act play marries Dumas’s Spanish scenes to Planché’s last act with the Ruthven-Hélène dialogue of Hélène’s ﬁnal scene incorporated. The play emphasizes Dumas’ alchemistic core by making a John Dee tome instead of a sanctiﬁed sword the instrument of denouement and the Vampire’s destruction. Two lines reveal something of Boucicault’s percep- tion of Dumas’ alchemy subtext: Davy, a cowardly synthesis of Lazarus and Botaro, exclaims “Oh, mysterious matrimony—as the dying philosopher said, ‘Now for the great secret!’” (Act 2, 2) whereas “Yonder is the bridal chamber” (Act 2, 4) is reserved for alchemist Dr. Rees to announce, as he prepares to enter it to interrupt the great dark secret’s unveiling. The fruit of alchemy, which enjoyed a leaden golden age in post–Renais- sance Europe, survives primarily as a collection of allegorical texts and icono- logical woodcuts that purportedly form a repository of great, powerful, and ancient secrets. It is current to say these mysteries are of a spiritual and philo- sophical nature, but for centuries alchemists were equally focused on the sub- stantial, elemental, and medical—the material and the spiritual being so confounded and interrelated in the alchemists’ vision as to be initially indis- tinguishable. This is, in fact, the transformative heart of the alchemist’s proj- ect: division and conjunction. The unitary becomes a duality that requires a third to bind them; the trinity yields to the quaternity, and so on, reaching to the ogdoadic through division by the three-dimensional cross before Coniunctio Oppositorium 203

subdividing elements reunify in order to become one renewed, indivisibly whole entity, Unus mundus. As things unfold and reunite in inviolable pro- portions, accordance with Pythagorean principles, and eternal geometric rules—whose quantiﬁable ratios are made manifest at every level of our heuris- tic cosmos—alchemy perfectly anticipates the genius of baroque thought and aesthetics. Its grandeur is in its detail; its detail is the mirror of its grandiosity, all with a concentration on ratio as rationality. Even when anonymous or pseudonymous, these hermetic texts’ authors unfailingly represent themselves as devout students of nature humbly seeking to serve God by completing or perfecting His work. The ﬂowering of alchemy concurrent to the Reformation undoubtedly required the indication of theo- logical orthodoxy in Catholic countries; while a conspicuously pious stance may have been adopted to inoculate against the charges of witchcraft and heresy that were leveled against a certain number of alchemists, most writ- ers—not a few of whom were ordained priests—are convincingly devout, a religious faith underlying the enterprise. Although the Platonic component of the alchemists’ theoretical teachings and their search to transmute the sacred self retain the interest of contemporary New Age seekers, the elemental recipes the alchemists prescribe seem derisively at odds with current scientiﬁc knowl- edge. Paradoxically, it was precisely as scientiﬁc methods of inquiry and pro- duction became fundamental to society’s economic base that these tracts became more widely known, due, in no small part, to the late-Victorian theo- sophical spirit. Alchemy’s re-evaluation began, however, in France. The brilliant French chemist Marcellin Berthelot brought the more mys- tical origins of his discipline to light in the mid–1880s, publishing Les Origines de l’alchimie (1885), Introduction à l’étude de la chimie des anciens et du moyen âge (1889), as well as translating ancient Greek, Syriac and Arabic treatises on alchemy and chemistry (Collection des anciens alchimistes grecs, 1887–1888, and La Chimie au moyen âge, 1893). Arthur Edward Waite, using Berthelot’s mate- rial and translating treatises lodged in British libraries, made a wide variety of alchemistic works available in English across the 1890s. Nearly simultaneous to the Book of Enoch’s appearance, Waite brought out two anthologies, the Collectanea Chemica (1893), the Hermetic Museum (1893); the Turba Philosophorum (1896) followed; he also translated Paracelsus from German, beginning with The Hermetic and Alchemical Writings of Paracelsus (1894). An early member of the Hermetical Order of the Golden Dawn, eventual factional leader and founder of other mystical orders, Waite worked closely with his contemporaries, translating into English Eliphas Lévi’s Dogme et rituel de la Haute Magie and other works which were directly inﬂuential upon the Golden Dawn and its successors. Popularly recalled for the pursuit of transmuting lead into gold and for 204 The Theology of Dracula

counting among their number colorful charlatans, frauds, and scoundrels, European alchemists of the early modern period are seen as a driven and trou- bled lot, compulsively and frantically searching out an inexistent grail. The Faustian alchemist survives as modernity’s mad scientist, a cultural trope while still very much alive in the contemporary imagination, though as a rather clownish, degraded ﬁgure. In the 19th century the alchemist was a more trou- bling and riven character, a mortal trespasser into the divine reservation— Gilbert emerging haggard and wild-eyed from the Tapestry Room is as one affected by alchemy. Yet the studious alchemists were also placid Platonic heirs to Pico della Mirandola, Marsilio Ficino, and the Florentine Academy, and, as Berthelot realized, the substantive and practical forerunners to modern inorganic chemistry, physics, and industrial manufacturing processes. Paradoxically perhaps, brilliant minds pursuing alchemical thought brought about the rise of scientiﬁc materialism. Alchemists, peering into the inner-workings of the universe, leveraging observation with the fulcrum of rationality, exposing truths parabolically by means of analogy, intuited notions of the atomic, the molecular, and of the recombinant properties of the ele- ments, and conceived of a reﬂexive and fractal universe operating at macro- cosmic and microcosmic levels. Their philosopher’s stone is, as its name indicates, necessarily an abstraction, yet, in a world deﬁned by Cartesian dual- ism, alchemistic reasoning maintained that operations that can be performed on the substantive can be carried out on the spiritual and vice versa. The stone, elixir, panacea, arcanum, and solvent are all expressions of a quest for the universal principle of being, begottenness, some more sacred uniﬁed ﬁeld theory that offers insight into the divine through the material. Commenting on its multiple appellations Petrus Bonus Lombardus of Ferrara remarks, “The consequence of this great multiplicity of names is that our stone has no proper name of its own” (150); this is true not only of their stone but of all aspects of their entire enterprise. Despite inherently ﬂuid notions, deliberate efforts to occult meaning, and constant conceptual and lexical differences that separate alchemists one from another, certain general principles do emerge that are consistently founded on ideas of transformational separation and reunion. Alchemy’s great notion weds material synthesis and spiritual transportation, the puriﬁcation and subsequent enrichment of matter and soul, bringing both closer to a luminous essence and astral light: gold, God, and the good. Bringing binary alchemy in line with the Christian trinity, the matter-soul duality has been bound together by a third, mediating mind-force, thought (spirit), since Paracelsus. The separation of the material into its four constituent elements, two dyadic pairs binding male to female, prepares their recombination, through the “art,” into the magical prime matter. Four shared qualities— Coniunctio Oppositorium 205

moistness, dryness, heat and coldness—characterize these elements to different extents. Four colors—black (nigredo or putrefactio), white (albedo), yellow (citrinitas), and red (rubedo)—shape or reveal the state of inorganic transfor- mation; which also relate to organic Hippocratic humors. Yielding to the trinitarian ideal, in many post–Paracelsus accounts the processes of yellowing and reddening are combined into a syzygy, thereby reducing a quaternity to a trinity. The “great work,” or magnum opus, entails the successful transmutation of base earthly matter into the spiritual structural element from which all things can be built, commonly referred to as “the stone”; analogically this is equivalent to the attainment of a transporting self-knowledge that places the alchemist within the sphere of the divine. Step-by-step processes—seven, ten or 12 depending on the accounting—were enumerated in various grimoires, the number of steps undoubtedly reﬂecting mystical and numerological con- siderations. Seven steps illuminate the fact that the seven heavenly bodies of the classical sky—Mercury, Saturn, Jupiter, Luna, Venus, Mars, and Sol— intervene in a process that seeks to join heaven and earth. As the whole snake- enwrapped spherical or ovoid Orphic “egg” is divided into quadrants by the serpent-killing sign of the cross, the steps were grouped into the four-phased, color-coded process that met with general agreement. The ﬁrst phase consists of corruption and degradation through ﬁre, decay, and the agencies of Mercury and Saturn. The second, said to be a lunar process of puriﬁcation, engages Jupiter, Luna, and Venus, and results in a baptismal action. During the operations of burning, charring, extracting, humidiﬁca- tion, and distillation, etc., various substances are produced and believed to contain the sacrae particulae, the microcosmic essence of prima materia. The third phase, solar and masculine in its conjunctive force, centers on hieros gamos and requires the intervention of Mars and Sol. This transportation of the spiritual self entails the destruction of older identities; the former man and former woman, orphaned and sibling or related through blood, must be sacriﬁced individually and reborn collectively to give life to the new syzygy. The third phase’s sacred union of masculine and feminine in coniunctio oppos- itorium yields, through the spilling of blood, the fourth, ﬁnal phase’s produc- tive result: Mercurius philosophorum, the prime matter that marks the great work’s accomplishment. But Mercurius philosophorum is not merely a sub- stance, it is also an expression of an enigmatic being, a dual, living-and-dead force that is killed to be reborn and also goes by the name of Mercurius. Morpheus-like Mercurius accommodates serpentine, shape-shifting beings such as Mélusine, but stands as a distinct though double personality. Although Mercurius represents the universal Solvent, Arcana, life-force and soul, he is seen as dark and ﬁlthy without, associated with excrement and 206 The Theology of Dracula

everything repulsive to human senses, yet bearing within an unseen shining radiance. Masculine without, feminine within, requiring puriﬁcation and res- olution, Mercurius exists as alchemy’s object, the magnum opus being conceived to transform saturnine, soul-killing, material, grandfatherly -though -savage Mercurius senex, into the hermetic, glorious, spiritual infant Mercurius ﬁlius macrocosmi; that is, to transmute lead into gold. This transmutation is more profoundly an act of releasing Mercurius’s luminous nature, of liberating the divine from the most basely material. This is achieved through the above- outlined operations whose full sequence is termed the Chemical Wedding, and during which coniunctio oppositorium, the joining of opposites, is the principal operation, allowing the syzygy to ﬁnd its uniﬁed expression in ﬁlius. The infant born through the syzygy and old Mercurius’s death is Mercurius inverted and turned inside out. Christian Rosenkreutz’s allegorical account of a regal “Chymical Wed- ding,” celebrated over a seven-day period of revelation and transformation, makes clear the linkage between the wedding, the Mosaic account of creation, the Christian account of sacramental Transubstantiation and Resurrection, and alchemistic transmutation. As Genesis represents God creatively separating one existential element from another, deconstructive-reconstructive alchemy seeks to tease the material apart, isolating component elements in order to fuse them anew into the magical original matter: the primordial chaos, that formless plasmatic absence of stuff Nodier terms le néant, conceptualized as “the Stone,” lapis philosophorum. While the alchemists’ cryptic texts portray pious Christians striving to perfect the work of God, they simultaneously perpetuate, through the planets of the classical sky, the ancient gods as they reside in myth and matter, their proclivities and properties, ancient relationships and powers, bringing antique arcane knowledge to bear to inform a Christian-inﬂuenced view of resurrec- tion. Petrus Bonus declares in The New Pearl of Great Price, our Stone is cast out into the streets, raised aloft to the clouds, dwells in the air, is nourished in the river, sleeps upon the summits of mountains; its mother is a virgin, its father knows no woman. These ancient Sages also knew that God must become man, because on the last day of our Magistery that which generates, and that which is generated, become absolutely one; then the old man and the child, the father and the son, are indistinguish- ably united. Hence they concluded that the Creator must also become one with the creature; moreover, they knew that man was, alone of all created beings, made in the image of God [126]. This is what comes to pass at God’s seat on Judgment Day. Dracula’s unmistakeable and relentless use of Christian symbols cannot and does not account for the every detail of Stoker’s celestial drama, so ﬁlled Coniunctio Oppositorium 207

with heavenly personae whose desperate and daring deeds reverberate at diverse discursive levels. Stoker’s portrait of Jonathan, “so full of volcanic energy” (202) as Apollonian Sol, and Mina, “pearl among women” (194) as Luna, have been amply commented, but Lucy, though previously characterized as luminous or a western light, is, in her own way, very much presented as an independent heavenly body as well, and, as the Professor’s hammer forcefully attests, she is not alone in this. Lucy rules over Hillingham as Venus in all her complexities, being at once Venus Celeste and Venus vulgare. Lucy, hair shining like copper, embodies Venus’s paradox: virginal and pure, yet sensuous and earthy. Under the Count’s inﬂuence, her “sweetness was turned to adamantine, heartless cruelty, and the purity to voluptuous wantonness” (187), her sought-after embrace became mors osculi—the kiss of death—and her “whole carnal and unspiritual appearance, seeming like a devilish mockery of Lucy’s sweet purity” (190) confounded those who loved her. Ironic Quincey, the adamant Texan, “his hand ... as ﬁrm as a piece of steel” (285), with his Winchesters and fearsome Bowie knife, is ﬁgured as Mars, innately ready to lead the battle. “Quincey Morris had always been the one to arrange the plan of action.... With a swift glance round the room, he at once laid out a plan of attack, and, without speaking a word, with a gesture, placed us each in position” (266). Stoker originally considered the name Brutus Marix (Rosenbach #1 Notes 7) for Quincey, “Marix” undoubtedly couching a divine and planetary reference. Further supporting the template of an alchemical quadrille, the infant whom they will call “Quincey,” the Mercurius ﬁlius of the story, is born not only on the anniversary of Quincey Morris’s death but, ambiguously, that of the Count’s as well. The Count’s “malignant and saturnine” (29) nature trou- bles the world of the novel and spreads ambiguity with his mists and fogs. That Stoker indeed attributes the adjective saturnine to the Count as one of his primary qualities colors the Vampire’s identity and, indirectly, helps to explicate the hammer-wielding Professor, seen as Thor-like in his Nordic ways, as he confronts and counters the Count. If the latter is the grim-reaper and castrating god Saturn, then the former is his thundering offspring and nemesis Jupiter (Zeus), the two being sufﬁciently alike to make the Profes- sor-as-Jupiter the usurping, uncorrupted son of Saturn. As Saturn and Jupiter maintain their opposing roles, the constantly shifting equilibrium between them must be meticulously maintained. The Count, though saturnine, is not purely saturnian; while he leads to a golden age, he only does so indirectly and through a transformative process. As the Un-dead Dead personiﬁcation of paradox, the Count is necessarily the most difﬁcult personality to fathom, for he is what he seems and its opp- posite. He has been accorded a dual and contradictory nature, the engaging, 208 The Theology of Dracula

kingly entity waiting at the threshold with an antique lamp, and the cruel, lifeless “Thing—not even beast” (202)—living and thriving in absolute ﬁlth and decay. Like Jonathan’s coachman, the grizzled, lamp-carrying old man dwelling atop the mountain’s peak who disappears with the coming of the dawn is quickly discovered to be, if not what he seems, something more if less. He is both saturnine—gloomy, dark, fearsome, and static—and mercu- rial—shrewd, eloquent, swift, thievish, changeable. As Jonathan recognizes, “For a man who ... did not evidently do much in the way of business, his knowledge and acumen were wonderful” (37). Saturn, Kronos in his Greek form—a sort of parricide and paragon of agricultural gods, is associated with the soft metal lead and with giving birth to Time, traits Stoker acknowledges through the phrase “The minutes seemed to pass with leaden feet” (261). Given the scythe as his attribute, Saturn ﬁrst uses it to castrate his father. He is, in turn, usurped by his own thundering son, Zeus, child born to himself and his mother, the Earth. Mercury, Hermes to the Greek, is an intermediary and psychopomp, whose wings, some say, facilitate the communication of Morpheus’s dreams to those who sleep. Son of Zeus, Rome’s Jupiter, he main- tains frontiers and boundaries; master of ruse, associated with wealth, com- merce, synonymous with quicksilver (liquid metal), he mediates the eternal. Like Persephone and Lazarus, Hermes frequents both the world living people inhabit and the Hadean underworld. Taken as an ensemble these personalities—Sol, Luna, Venus, Mars, Mer- cury, Saturn and Jupiter—render an accounting of the classical heavens. They can be seen as individual entities that function as a uniﬁed whole, each inﬂuencing as they are inﬂuenced, reciprocally engaging themselves, the world of men, and the divine in their constant joining of hands. Theirs is a grandiose cosmic drama that—while concluding in Christian triumph and an engage- ment with a divinity beyond our mortal realm—plays upon a great store of mythologies, rites, and practices. Bram Stoker’s Notes for “Dracula” ﬁx Dracula’s genesis in the simple idea of placing a young man and an old man (Rosenbach #35, 17) in a triangular relationship with girls, the youth—tentatively named William Young— becoming Jonathan Harker, and the old man, the Count. Yet when ﬁrst con- fronted by the feminine, the Count, transforming Nodier’s “She is mine,” possessively claims Jonathan as his own, not the girls. “The man belongs to me” (43), he insists with such reverberating ferocity that it seems as if he were indeed defending some portion of himself, indeed his very virility. Jonathan forces the Count to bring to recollection that, once, he too could love. The simplicity of the scenario’s triangular concept, the chronologically organized plot, the emphasis on the geometric and the mystical serve to support the embroidery of an allegoric interpretation modeled after Hermetic texts like Coniunctio Oppositorium 209

Rosenkreutz’s “Chymical Wedding.” In such a scheme, Young Man, Sol, and Old Man, Sol niger, become, in part, linked, not only through girls, but, like Aubrey and Ruthven, as quasi-identical-since-oppositional ﬁgures whose dis- crepancies ﬂow from the fact that they exist at different phases of a transfor- mational process. Sol niger, great dark orb of the sky that opposes the sun, is indeed saturnine and embodied in the planet Saturn, yet, as will be seen, in a unique and complicated way, he conceals another identity. As plot introduces more characters, the geometry of the initial dynamic, while becoming more complex, is reinforced. Saturn and Mercury join as alchemy’s Mercurius, an amalgamating, par- adox-binding, enigmatic ﬁgure understandably referred to as “Duplex.” Mer- curius is at once Saturn and, potentially, Saturn’s grandson, Mercury. Jupiter, as son and usurper of the ﬁrst, father of the second, mediates their relationship. For Mercurius senex to become Mercurius ﬁlius requires various ritual acts of fertilization and the participation of surrogates to bind the paradoxical ele- ments: coniunctio oppositorium. Alone, Mercurius is sterile. Dracula dramatizes the ritual sequence of chemical wedding and its coni- unctio oppositorium through plot. The orphans King Sol and Queen Luna, Jonathan and Mina respectively, are joined as a syzygy through the aggressive conduit of saturnine Mercurius, the Count. This ménage-à-trois projects added dimension onto Stoker’s phrase “I needn’t tell you of number three, need I?” (61). Freshly orphaned, wandering Venus, the brightest light among the stars of the night, and war-like Mars, with his metallic armaments, die to facilitate the ecliptic royal union of Sun and Moon—Sol being transformed and puriﬁed through Venus’s blood-soul as Luna is through Mars. Sol and Luna, Venus and Mars: two dyads binding male to female that permit the chemical wedding. The royal mating produces Mercurius ﬁlius, the cosmic son, who, despite his “his great multiplicity of names,” is called by the name of a dead man. This synopsis of the Chymical Wedding distils Stoker’s plot to its quintessence. Like the Mysteries of Eleusis, the chemical wedding, unfolding over time, is organised into “lesser” and “greater” works—works feminine and masculine, white and red, circular and square. The lesser includes the phases nigredo, corruption and mortiﬁcation, and albedo, the cleansing, baptismal whitening that follows. The greater is comprised of citrinitas—entailing the separation of the Sol/Luna syzygy, the sacriﬁce of the subsidiary spiritual syzygy of Venus and Mars, whose blood permits illuminatio, and the Sol/Luna syzygy’s reuniﬁ- cation, ecliptic merging, and the fertilization of the seed—and rubedo, com- prising the death of Mercurius senex at the hand of Sol and the production of the sacred offspring Mercurius ﬁlius macrocosmi. It is unclear what corre- spondence if any these operations may have with Stoker’s initial four-book compositional structure, but they mirror plot to a remarkable degree. Coniunctio Oppositorium 211

Nigredo This phase begins with the polluting, chthonic dragon, embodied in the Count. The Little Dragon, Dracula, will exert its inﬂuence over all actors yet to be introduced. After a lengthy separation, a degrading initiatory ordeal on Jonathan’s part, and a trial of faith on Mina’s, word of Jonathan’s existence ﬁnally reaches Mina at Whitby. Fate has intervened through the appropriately named Sister Agatha, who summons Mina to her intended’s side. Mr. Hawkins, who had initially dispatched Jonathan to Transylvania, speeds Mina towards Budapest, urging her to marry Jonathan immediately upon reaching him. Sol, still suf- fering and diminished, requires Luna to exhibit greater strength in compen- sation for his weakened condition. Sol is married while reclining as an invalid, “propped up with pillows” (100), Luna taking “his poor weak hands” (101) as her own. Thus a long-intended marriage occurs as an impromptu rite in an alien environment. Hawkins, Jonathan’s “second father” (49), assumes the role of the active agent in this phase. When the newlyweds return to Exeter, he tells them: “I know you both from children, and have, with love and pride, seen you grow up. Now I want you to make your home here with me” (140). This suggests that orphans Sol and Luna were brought up under some form of Hawkins’ tutelage, spending their youths together in a brother-sister relationship, and it brings the Harkers into conformity with the classic situation of the sacred wedding, previously encountered with Aubrey and sister, Gilbert and Hélène. Curiously, Hawkins, who claims to have “neither chick nor child” (140), lives in a rookery, its “chattering and gossiping” (140) ﬂedglings reminding Mina of humans. When Hawkins dies, Mina has to admit that for her as for Jonathan it “really seems as though we had lost a father” (143). The dark bird, raven, eagle, hawk, is instrumental in nigredo. Saturnine Sol niger, the Count, arrives in England long weeks before Jonathan, already having encountered Mina on the Crescent through Venus- like Lucy. Mina “daubed [her] feet in mud” (89), covering her skin with the black ﬁlth of the earth as she returned from seeing him. As Saturn, “the Aud Man” (74) or “old scytheman” (216), begins his harvest immediately upon his mid-summer’s landfall. Venus, wandering light of the night, corrupted by contact with Mercurius senex, dies shortly after the return of the royal couple to Exeter. Venus’s blood illness, at ﬁrst suspected to be caused by a safety-pin, instigates the taking of extraordinary medical and metaphysical measures. It is the unusual corruption of Venus that requires the Professor, Jupiter, to be present on the Western Isle, where he ﬁrst resides in the Great Eastern Hotel (106). “A philosopher 212 The Theology of Dracula

and a metaphysician” (106) “with a strongly humorous side” (113), and “so abnormally clever” (182), the metaphysical nature of his patient’s condition informs his use of the sacred white Eucharist and the Cross as a shield, and sends him “off to the British Museum looking up some authorities on ancient medicine” (240). The death of Venus leads to the formation of a brotherhood of purity, and her body being placed in a “casing of lead” (176), the purely saturnine material. Death and burial of Lucy and those claimed by equinox terminate this phase. Albedo In the case of Hawkins, death transforms the dark bird of prey into a ghostly dove, an absent presence seen in “empty chairs” (155) and felt in the Exeter nest by his heirs returning from his interment. Before they can reach home, however, Jonathan believes he sees his nemesis in London. The mere sight of Mercurius causes him to turn ever more pale, distracted, and uncer- tain. This sighting marks the beginning of the successful process of puriﬁca- tion—while earlier attempts had been made to purify and protect Lucy, they were thwarted and to no avail as, in Byron’s phrase, it was not yet time. Indeed, the intermittent process of whitening continues until the snows fall on Judgment Day. To release Venus from her complete corruption, to save Venus Celeste from Venus vulgare, the Professor, Jupiter, penetrates the saturnine casing— the veil of lead—that is her shroud with “a swift downward stab” (176). Arthur “did not know that there was a leaden cofﬁn, or at any rate, had not thought of it. When he saw the rent in the lead, the blood rushed to his face for an instant, but as quickly fell away again, so that he remained of a ghastly white- ness” (185). The pure white Host, itself taking the form of the full moon, is frequently fragmented and atomized in order to serve as a magically potent sacrae moleculae, a kind of philosopher’s stone, the most minute particle con- taining the whole of the sacred principle. Whiteness and the image of baptism complete the section. The lesser works are recapitulated through a vision-fraught dream that Mina dreamt. “All was dark and silent, the black shadows thrown by the moonlight seeming full of mystery of their own” (226). She felt herself seized by “leaden lethargy” as her chamber was penetrated by a mist that became thick “like smoke” (227) and charged with “white energy” (227) that ﬁnally “concentrated into a sort of pillar of cloud” (227). “Things began to whirl” until “through it all came the scriptural words ‘a pillar of cloud by day and of ﬁre by night’” (227). “But the pillar was composed of both the day and Coniunctio Oppositorium 213

night” (227). The perceived pillars, beyond Exodus, instruct on the nature of day and night. They are the feminine and masculine principles, Venus and Mars, and between them passes the harrowing narrow deﬁle. The pillar of cloud also personiﬁes Mina herself; the pillar of ﬁre, Jonathan, Sol. In her dream, she watched with horriﬁed fascination as “the ﬁre divided, and seemed to shine on me through the fog like two red eyes, such as Lucy told me of in her momentary mental wandering when, on the cliff, the dying sunlight struck the windows of St Mary’s Church the ﬁre divided” in two, as if forming glow- ing eyes or, indeed, heavenly bodies; then “all became black darkness” (228). Like the pair Dumas formed from the eyes of Petra and Ziska, the two eyes of Mina’s vision belong one each to Sol and Sol niger. Nigredo yields to albedo, however, for she soon remarks “A livid white face bending over me out of the mist” (228). Joining above and below, Jonathan notes that when he woke Mina, “for a few seconds she did not recognize me, but looked at me with a sort of blank terror, as one looks who has been waked out of a bad dream” (224); she momentarily found it impossible to distinguish between the whitened black of Sol niger and the golden light of Sol. The division of the masculine will be more fully articulated on a succeeding day’s night with coin- cidencia, for after having requested Dr. Seward to make up some of the modern Morpheus, and having delivered herself to it, Mina comes to realize her error: “As sleep begins to ﬂirt with me, a new fear comes: that I may have been foolish in thus depriving myself of the power of waking” (228). Having com- pleted the lesser works, she has prepared the way for the greater, the hierog- amous coniunctio oppositorium. Citrinitas In clever wordplay, Stoker asserts the blind permitted sight: “The moon- light was so bright that through the thick yellow blind the room was light enough to see” (246). What the saffron ﬁlter allows to be seen is a mystical, trinitarian union dominated by saturnine Mercurius as the self-devouring Ouroboros. His self-consumption is facilitated by looping through the crescent of lunar Madam Mina. Luna, bitten by the serpent, drinks her own blood passed through the ﬁlter of the circular, ring-forming serpent. Jonathan, once again supine on his bed during the marriage ceremony, now “ﬂush-faced” (246) rather than pale, is a witless witness to his own coniunctio oppositorium; he has nonetheless been joined to the Count through his bride. Mina, whose “white nightdress was smeared with blood” while “a thin stream trickled down from the man’s bare breast” (247), is aware but drained of volition by Mor- pheus. The blood begins moving the prime material towards Rubedo. This 214 The Theology of Dracula
Coniunctio Oppositorium 215 Opposing hierophants contained in the Ouraboros- enveloping Above- Below Emblem—”Le Grand Symbole de Salomon”—of Eliphas Lévi’s Ritual Magic. 1841.

inverted bridal chamber ceremony is central to Stoker’s chemical wedding, for the chamber, crucible of the alchemistic operation, is the philosopher’s egg that must be divided into eight, the cross dividing each of its three dimensions. The rite initiated by one hierophant, the Count, changes signiﬁcance and theologies at its midpoint by the intervention of another; the Professor enters brandishing the Holy Eucharist, proclaiming that “all chambers are the same to the doctor; and even were they not they are all as one to me tonight” (246). Indeed, all are as one—Unus mundus—that night. The triadic tumbles into the quaternate with the Professor’s forming of the Sign of the Cross, and the subsequent division of the egg into four quadrants and four elements even as the quadrille of Mélusine had divided the moving world to reconstitute it transformed. But a second triangular relationship is also constituted. Each of the twin hierophants links the royal couple into a trinity. One from above, one from below. Their union forms the alchemical symbol that is identical to the interlinking Star of David, the Kabbalistic Magen David. Like Lazarus in Le Vampire, Renﬁeld enables those from above and below to move from one realm to another. Despite his birdlike spirit, provisionally unable to attain “Himmel” (118), he is conﬁned to earth, meaning very much Earth herself. As one so conﬁned, encaged, he is central, occupying the middle ground in which we all are held captive. Through his ofﬁces Dracula’s bridal chamber ceremony is conducted, Renﬁeld not only admitting the Count, but also dispatching the Professor. Deprived of the aerial view Seward imagines, Renﬁeld’s perspective deﬁnes the Earth’s central position of the pre–Coper- nican sky. The place where opposites, high and low, celestial and chthonic, masculine and feminine, active and passive, gold and silver, come together: Mittel Land. Beyond the symbolism of the Ragnarök, Mittel Land constitutes a space where things previously set apart come together once again. When the Professor gains ritual primacy in the bridal chamber sacrament, he renews Jonathan for a second time: Jonathan “seemed dazed for a few sec- onds and then full consciousness seemed to burst upon him all at once” (248). Full consciousness is not only brought to Jonathan but, shortly thereafter, to Mina as well; they attain gnosis and can now actively seek resolution through the completion of the alchemistic process. Although their volition is essential, the act of communion that Mina was engaged in brings about transforma- tions—immediate and eventual—of its own that progressively work to chal- lenge the syzygy as they complete the rites of coniunctio oppositorium. Astrology and alchemy associate the Moon with the brain and intellectual force; Mina becomes more man-like in her thinking after coniunctio, according to the Professor. Jonathan, on the other hand, becomes more rash, emotional, hysterical, his rational faculties being affected by his part in the ordeal of coni- unctio; he is dismissively told to “hush.” Through the Count, a 19th-century 216 The Theology of Dracula

feminine soul becomes apparent in Jonathan as a 19th-century masculine soul is reﬂected within Mina; this is as it is dictated by the philosophers. The result, however, separates the couple anew—Mina is isolated from Jonathan due to her changed state, and is joined through mind and spirit, to the Count’s dead body as he passes over the surface of the waters, even as God hovers above. It is now that volition is required to negotiate the ﬁnal and most delicate phase of the wedding ceremonies. Rubedo Reddening begins concurrent to yellowing with the discovery of Renﬁeld in “a glittering pool of blood” (241) and ends only on a Judgment Day marked by redness, from when “the red of the dawn began to fall through the snow- gloom” (318) to the moment of the miracle at which the “castle of Dracula now stood out against the red sky” (325). As the month-long ordeal unfolded, Mina, despite “the red blotch on [her] forehead” (280), “grew snowy white at times ... and red at others” (268). The ruddy dragon, entwining mercurial serpent, having long dwelt in the ﬁlth of the world, now gorged with blood, must be slain to permit the birth of the renewed, spiritually pure Mercurius. His cosmic counterweight, the Professor, cut by a gangrenous knife, was saved by Seward’s sucking the venom out of the blood before it could reach the heart; in Mina’s case the venom, absolutely immaterial, exists not in her blood, but in the absence of her blood—darkness, le néant, the soul-damning nigredo of the serpent replacing the world-creating soul-force, anima mundi, that was drawn from her. The exchange can only be reversed through the destruction of Mercurius senex. In a kind of Sign of the Cross, the Count is doubly killed: “But, on the instant, came the sweep and ﬂash of Jonathan’s great knife. I shrieked as I saw it shear through the throat; whilst at the same moment Mr Morris’s bowie knife plunged into the heart” (325). In his beheading, one hierophantic ﬁgure is reduced to dust, his corrupted body reduced to its prime matter. In Mars’ delivering the fatal blow to the heart—that retort that circulates the precious anima—Luna’s soul is restored as pure as 24 carat gold. Mina watched the ambuscade from “a wonderful spot ... with an entrance like a doorway between two boulders,” a deﬁle so narrow that the professor remarks, ‘“if the wolves do come I can meet them one by one”’ (321). As Mina looked on, she saw that even as Quincey’s right hand brought about the weighing of hearts in heaven, the Count’s and her own, “with his left hand he was clutching at his side, and that the blood was spurting through his ﬁngers” (324) on to the earth. In the piercing of the Adamic ﬁgure, celestial Mars, Morris’s blood Coniunctio Oppositorium 217

ﬂows and spills from the altar onto the Earth, now one with the Count, ren- dering the Mittel land fertile through sacriﬁce as the prelude to rebirth in the new Adam, founder of a new race in Christ. As Venus saved Luna from fully going through the ordeal of material feminine corruption, Mars, who must be lanced as if “in the side of Him who died for man” (209), spares Sol from the sacriﬁce coniunctio requires of the material masculine ﬁgure in dying. Correspondingly, since alchemy believes the male has a feminine soul, and the female a masculine, and that both Man and Woman are supported by the twin pillars of ﬁre and cloud, the sacriﬁce of Venus makes Sol’s soul ready for coniunctio as the sacriﬁce of Mars prepares Luna’s. Like Mrs. Westenra, Lucy and Quincey were destined to die. The lengthy attention to Quincey’s proposal of marriage to Lucy now becomes justiﬁed, explicated, for through their deaths the two are eternally joined in double-harness in the manner of Juana and Luis. As with Melusine’s quadrille, the changing of partners allows the joining of opposites and the binding of paradox. While both Sol Jonathan and Luna Mina lose some quantity of blood to Mercurius, the Vampire, Venus-Lucy and Mars-Quincey’s sacriﬁce and the resulting alloy of copper and iron brings about the fertilization and transformation of Mercurius. Much has been made of the symmetries that Dracula displays, of the importance attached to midnight and “the stroke of noon” (108), and of the fact that the narrative’s chronological midpoint is marked by the Count’s arrival in England. Although what happens on the tale’s dark side, from November to May, remains obscure, it can be presumed to reﬂect the occurrences of the half-year of light in negative image. It seems safe to conclude that the mercurial infant called Quincey was conceived 183 days after the wreck of The Demeter, opposing the spiritual infant to the material entity birthed by The Mother, Demeter—Stoker thus illustrating The Emerald Tablet’s great maxim: That which is below corresponds to that which is above, and that which is above corresponds to that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the One Entity. In the cycle of time, a cross has been formed, one axis running from St. George’s Day to the antipodal moment of the death of Quincey and the Count, the perpendicular joining the date of The Demeter’s dereliction to that of Luna’s insemination. The events transpiring across the luminous half of the annual solar rev- olution have been seen as being arrayed like a peacock’s tail spread in a fan- like semicircular form. Through the device of bilateral symmetry, the work issues an invitation to imagine its form further folded in two, one quadrant mirroring the other and revealing the four-fold’s essence through coniunctio. In this way, putting the ﬁrst last and the last ﬁrst, the plot reﬁgures so that, in reading it, the beginning sections inform the ending and the ending sections 218 The Theology of Dracula

the beginning. This is a particularly appropriate operation, since Dracula’s cyclic theme is treated in a ﬂat, linear manner; in spatial terms, the plot runs from East to West back to East without ever speciﬁcally marking a correspon- ding passage northward or southward. In the beginning that is wedded to the ending, Jonathan and Mina would simultaneously be driven towards God’s seat by their individual drivers; one would stop to be circled by wolves, the other by ﬁre. The Count would be seen opening his door with an antique lamp in his hand immediately after he dies and turns into dust. Jonathan would escape from the castle as the Count both sets sail from London to return to the castle and departs the castle to go to London. Mina would go to Whitby to see Lucy as she is introduced to the Brotherhood formed in the aftermath of Lucy’s death. Tides would be seen washing out even as they came ﬂooding in again. This reﬂection of ends in beginnings based on the symmetric cross, this coniunctio oppositorium, for- mulation of paradoxes and rendering of “possible impossibilities” (Stoker 172) clariﬁes the story’s essence. The mirror image provides no bauble of vanity but provokes more intently pious humility—it awakens. As Jung remarks: Coniunctio Oppositorium 219 Phases of opposing personalities as a uniﬁed celestial body. © Rarignac

“One ﬁnds in Christian symbolism the same ‘circular’ Gnostic thinking as in alchemy. In both the sacriﬁcer is the sacriﬁced, and the sword that kills is the same as that which is killed” (13, 84). The role of simple gold in Dracula, weighed in the scale of Themis, was found to be corrupting; it is dust that matters. The gold that is so important to Stoker is the luminous quality of being that unites the human and the divine: the good. Coniunctio oppositorium is designed to bind paradox in an act of puriﬁcation of cathartic essence. The purpose of this alchemy is purely sacred, the awakening to full consciousness. Stoker concludes the novel with the appearance of an undated “Note” in which Jonathan initiates a perspectival shift as he distances himself and the reader from the present tense of the events previously related through the insertion of a remove of seven years. He describes the protagonists as puriﬁed, saying, “We all went through the ﬂames; and the happiness of some of us since then is, we think, well worth the pain we endured” (326). That all have passed through the ﬂames appears to indicate that they all have been trans- formed, all been tested or tempered as if steel or some other forged or puriﬁed metal. Jonathan then refers to Mina’s “secret belief” “that some of our brave friend’s spirit” (326), implicitly meaning Quincey, has passed into her son, conﬁding that the son has been given a “bundle of names” (326) linking “all our little band of men together; but we call him Quincey” (326). This curious phrase reads as if “Quincey” were not the boy’s true name at all. Jonathan then accounts for the principal actors and their lives over the intervening years. As Seward and Holmwood have both been incorporated into a syzygy, it is safe to assume that Lucy was never either one’s true intended. The Pro- fessor has assumed a grandfatherly role in the upbringing of the child. All is right in the heavens. In The Book of Stoker, transmutation of matter is identical to the tran- substantiation of Christ’s body and blood, the Host becoming “the sacred emblem” (189). Even as the dead hand at the wheel was termed “emblemship,” it is the guiding element and emblem of the sacred discourse that the book promulgates. Its sacrae particulae mixed with “some whitish stuff, like dough” (186) allows the Professor to seal bodies hermetically within tombs as if prayers enclosed within bottles. It is the hermetically-sealed grave that becomes the ﬁnal philosopher’s egg. Through the transformational process brought about by King Sol’s slaying of Mercurius senex, Luna, Madam Mina, is healed, the metaphysical poison drawn out of her by the decimation of Saturn’s corrupt material, leaden being; Jung claims, “It is the task of alchemy to root out the original sin, and this is accomplished with the aid of the balsamum vitae” (14: 34). No ordinary gold is created in the magnum opus of Stoker—quite the opposite. 220 The Theology of Dracula

Jung concedes that it must be admitted that the fairytale and alchemy both show Mercurius in a predominantly unfavourable light, which is all the more striking because his positive aspect relates him not only to the Holy Spirit, but, in the form of the lapis, also to Christ and, as a triad, even to the Trinity. It looks as if it were precisely these relationships which led the alchemists to put particu- lar stress on the dark and dubious quality of Mercurius, and this militates strongly against the assumption that by their lapis they really meant Christ [13: 241]. The interest of Mercurius is his potential for enabling transformation, the radiant new Mercurius brings joy and hope after the dark, saturnine dragon has been slain. Mercurius teaches humanity that it is possible to perfect our- selves, to change, to overcome the blacker than black that is within our nature and to ﬁnd the gold that is surely hidden within as if a deep, bright secret, indeed a bright promise. Stoker’s fairytale rejects alchemy as anything more than the armature for supporting the Vampire, refusing any Faustian bargain. When Jonathan declares, “I would sell my soul to do it!” (265), meaning to kill the Count, he is recalled to the service of Christ. Like Mina, he must maintain his soul at all costs. As he sets off, Jonathan muses, “We saw little towns or castles on the top of steep hills such as we see in old missals” (11); as the Professor arrives at the end of the world he notes, “We were near the top of a steep-rising hill, on summit of which was such a castle as Jonathan tell of in his diary” (316). In the last of Stoker’s missal’s illustrations, (which so resembles an alchemist’s picture book), Mina stands a Marian ﬁgure by Mercurius’s perched castle, expired serpent at her feet, heavenly objects beginning to appear in the night sky, Mina’s face illuminated by a divine light. In the illuminated manuscript of Stoker, suddenly all becomes clear. More than a single Dionysian creature of the night invaded the day when from the “black mass of Kettleness” (75) The Demeter washed ashore and ran aground with her dark cargo at Whitby; it was sky of Night herself that appeared at mid–summer to wrest dominion from Day. Stoker has represented a coniunctio oppositorium and great work like no other, and in so doing he has puriﬁed earlier renditions of the Tale of the Vam- pire. Because of him, it is now clear that Nodier’s Lovette, the character whose pursuit across the proscenium into the audience’s side of the theater so shocked the Parisian critic of two centuries ago, was the goddess Venus herself, due to wed Edgar, the servant from Marsden whose name references Ares’ principal attribute, the lance. They underwent their ordeal to permit the orphaned Aubrey brother and sister to renew Mercurius, who dissolves into prime matter no doubt to emerge again. The growls of thunder that sounded in the plays of Coniunctio Oppositorium 221

Nodier and Dumas were the voice of Jupiter. The out-of-plot death of Ruthven’s brother, the Baron of Marsden—that is, Mars himself—was forever essential to enabling the saturnine, Diosyian Vampire to access Aubray’s lunar sister, whose “soul concious of a brighter realm” was “never brightened by the smile of joy; but when her brother breathed to her his affection”(278). The cycle has been completed; the ring that Byron’s Darvell had Aubrey toss into the Blessed Bay has been recovered. Petrus Bonus observes that “gold being worked up into different shapes is called by different names, such as ring, bracelet, crown, etc., though in substance all these are nothing but gold” (150). Ring, bracelet, and crown may all be of one substance but they are also of one shape, the ovoid of the Ouboros. This is what has been clariﬁed. One shape, one matter, Unus mundus. The philosophy that has endured since ancient times and informs the parables of Jesus reads as a missal to instruct the modern era. The marriage and birth viewed in the Telesterion of Eleusis is related to the wedding chamber ceremony of the Gnostics and the Chymical Wedding of the alchemists and certain rites of Hermetic orders of our current period, but they also inform and interact with the sacred history of Jesus Christ. Nearly two decades prior to Marcel Duchamp’s introduction of the notion of “readymade” art, Stoker created a masterful example. The Chymical 222 The Theology of Dracula Coniunctio oppositorium. © Rarignac

Wedding contains the essence of Dracula’s plot, and perhaps represents the very genesis of Stoker’s magnum opus. Alchemy reveals that the project was born whole, alive, hermaphroditic, and sacred, albeit with crowning Christian foliage, a Gnostic trunk, and ancient, pre–Christian roots. The baroque tale of Chymical Wedding, hieros gamos, and coniunctio oppositorium, already present in the Vampire Tale, provided the ﬁrm basis for further development beyond the few mornings that Polidori had to dedicate to his summer love. What becomes apparent through Stoker’s retelling of the Tale is that the ancient Mysteries, the Gnostic texts, fragments of Cathari creed, and hermetic alchem- ical allegories, concern the same aspects of humanistic beliefs that embrace with the basic tenets of the teachings of Christ in a pre-schismatic, indeed pre-institutional, form. Michael Maier, reminding one and all to be true Harkers, might have been speaking of Stoker’s Dracula when in “A Subtle Allegory Concerning the Secrets of Alchemy” he states, “Now, this whole tale ... is addressed to the mind rather than to the ear; it is a mystical narrative, and like the hieroglyphics of the Egyptians, should be mystically (not histor- ically) understood” (Hermetic Museum II 219). May the soul of Vlad Tepes ﬁnd repose! Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord; and let perpetual light shine upon him. May he rest in peace. Amen. Coniunctio Oppositorium 223
